Lecture 4.1: The Theory of Directory Traversal (The "x" Bit)
Before we move to the next chapter, we must understand why the setfacl command fixed our "Permission Denied" issue even though the destination folder had correct permissions.

In the Linux Virtual File System (VFS), a path like /app/gitea/data is not a single entity; it is a chain. To reach the end of the chain, a process must have the Execute (x) permission—often called the "search bit" or "traverse bit"—on every single parent directory in that chain.

The Logic: If a user has rwx on /app/gitea but --- on /app, they are essentially standing in front of a locked building that contains an unlocked room. They can't get to the room because they can't get through the front door.

The Linux Administration Lesson: Standard POSIX permissions (rwx) are often too "blunt." If you change /app to 755, everyone can see what’s inside. By using FACLs (File Access Control Lists), we create a "surgical" exception. We give only the git user the "hallway pass" (x) to walk through /app without letting them see (r) what else is stored there.

Chapter 5: The Post-Installation Hardening & Initial Configuration
The Goal: Now that the service is running, we must transition from "Installation Mode" (where things are loose and writable) to "Production Mode" (where things are restricted and secure).

Step 1: The App.ini Generation
Since the service is active, Gitea is waiting for you to visit the web interface to generate its core configuration file: /etc/gitea/app.ini.

The Pre-Flight Check
We need to verify that the git user has the necessary "Write" access to the configuration directory so it can actually save your settings.

Run these commands to verify the current state:

Bash
# 1. Check the owner and permissions of the config directory
ls -ld /etc/gitea

# 2. Check if a partial or empty app.ini already exists
ls -l /etc/gitea/app.ini
The Dense "Why"
ls -ld /etc/gitea: We need to ensure the directory has the w (write) bit for the git user or group. If it doesn't, the Web Installer will hang or crash when you click "Install" because it cannot save the app.ini file.

ls -l /etc/gitea/app.ini: If a file already exists but is owned by root, the Gitea process (running as git) won't be able to overwrite it with your new settings.

Welcome back. That is exactly the state we want to be in. The absence of app.ini confirms that Gitea is currently in its "Bootstrap Phase"—running purely in memory using hardcoded default values, waiting for your commands.

Let's apply the Architect's Protocol.

Lecture 5.1: The Bootstrap Phase and The EACCES Trap
When an application starts for the first time without a configuration file, it usually exposes a setup interface (the web GUI on port 3000). When you fill out that GUI and click "Install", the Gitea application will attempt to translate your web inputs into a permanent file on the disk.

Here is the Linux Administration reality:

The Gitea process is currently running as the restricted user: git.

The destination for the configuration file is inside /etc/.

By standard POSIX design, everything in /etc is strictly owned by root:root to prevent malicious software from altering system configurations.

If you were to go to the web GUI right now and click "Install," the git user would ask the Linux Kernel to execute an open() system call with the O_CREAT (create file) flag for /etc/gitea/app.ini. The Kernel would check the permissions, see that git has no write privileges in that folder, and immediately kill the request with an EACCES (Permission denied) error. The web GUI would crash.

To prevent this, we must temporarily hand the "keys" to the /etc/gitea directory to the git user, let it write the file, and then immediately revoke those keys.

The Pre-Flight Check
Before we change any permissions, we must verify the current ownership of that directory. I will not assume it was created a certain way.

Run this command to check the directory state:

Bash
ls -ld /etc/gitea
(You will likely see it is owned by root root with drwxr-xr-x permissions).

The Execution: Granting the Temporary Write Pass
Assuming the directory is currently locked down by root, we need to open it up just enough for the installation to succeed.

Run these commands:

Bash
# 1. Change the group ownership of the directory to 'git'
sudo chown root:git /etc/gitea

# 2. Grant Write (w) access to the group
sudo chmod 770 /etc/gitea
The Dense "Why"
chown root:git: We are leaving the primary owner as root (maintaining standard /etc hierarchy best practices), but we are assigning the directory's group to git.

chmod 770: We are setting the permissions to rwx for the Owner (root), rwx for the Group (git), and --- for Others. This gives the Gitea process the exact permissions it needs to create the app.ini file without opening the directory to every other user on the server.

The Next Step: The GUI Handshake
Once those permissions are set, the "Invisible Wall" is removed. We are ready to generate the configuration file.

Open your web browser.

You should see the Initial Configuration page.

Because we are using custom paths (/app/gitea) instead of the defaults, you must pay close attention to the paths requested in the web form. Do not blindly click next.

isn't that custom path already soft linked to the default path ?? so what would be the Problem here

This is an outstanding observation. You just caught a moment where I was being overly cautious and almost undermined our own architecture.

You are absolutely correct. Ten points to the Platform Engineer.

Let's break down why your logic is flawless, and then I will clarify what we actually need to be careful about in the GUI.

Lecture 5.2: Symlink Transparency and Abstraction
In Linux, a symbolic link (symlink) operates at the Virtual File System (VFS) layer. When an application like Gitea asks the kernel to open a file at /var/lib/gitea/data, the kernel intercepts the request, sees the symlink, and silently redirects the read/write operation to /app/gitea/data.

The application is completely unaware of this redirection. This is called Symlink Transparency.

The Architectural Benefit:
Leaving the path in the GUI as /var/lib/gitea is actually the correct and most professional move.

It creates an Abstraction Layer. Gitea thinks it lives in the standard system directory (/var/lib).

If you ever need to migrate your storage from /app to a new NAS drive mounted at /mnt/new_storage, you simply update the symlink. You will never have to touch Gitea's app.ini configuration file.

So, your intuition is spot on: the symlink handles the heavy lifting. You do not need to change the repository paths to /app/gitea/ in the GUI.

The Real GUI "Gotchas" (What we do need to watch out for)
My previous warning was poorly targeted. The paths are fine. The real danger in the Web Installer lies in the Environment and Network settings. If we leave these as defaults, the server will break or act unpredictably.

Here are the three critical sections you must configure manually:

1. Database Settings
The Default: Gitea defaults to SQLite3 (a file-based database).

The Problem: We built a systemd file that explicitly waits for mysqld.service. If you let Gitea use SQLite, your MySQL database sits empty, and our service dependencies are out of sync.

The Action: You must select MySQL and input the database credentials you set up previously.

2. General Settings: Run As Username
The Default: It often defaults to the user executing the web process, but sometimes tries to default to gitea or root depending on the environment.

The Problem: If this field does not perfectly match the user in our systemd file (User=git), Gitea's internal health checks will panic and shut down the service.

The Action: Ensure this is explicitly set to git.

3. Server and Third-Party Service Settings (The Clone URLs)
The Default: "Server Domain" and "Gitea Base URL" usually default to localhost.

The Problem: If you leave it as localhost, when you create a repository, the UI will tell you to run: git clone http://localhost:3000/admin/repo.git. If you run that on your laptop, your laptop will try to connect to itself, not the RHEL VM.

The Action: You must change localhost to the actual IP address of your RHEL VM (e.g., 192.168.x.x).

Execution: The Configuration Handshake

If yes, please open http://<YOUR_VM_IP>:3000 in your browser.

should I setup the Database with a table for gitea ?

The short, definitive answer is: No. Do not create any tables.

Here is the Database Administration (DBA) breakdown of exactly why, following our Architect's Protocol.

Lecture 5.3: Application-Driven Schema Generation (The ORM)
In modern web architecture, applications like Gitea (written in Go) use a software layer called an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper).

When you configure the database connection in the web GUI and click "Install," Gitea will log into the database and run a built-in script called a Migration. This script contains hundreds of CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, and CREATE INDEX commands. It will dynamically build the entire database schema (users, repositories, pull requests, issues) from scratch.

The DBA Trap:
If you try to "help" Gitea by manually creating a table (e.g., creating a table named user), the Gitea installation will violently crash. The ORM will attempt to create the user table, see that one already exists, assume the database is corrupted or already in use by another app, and abort the installation with a Table already exists fatal error.

The Rule: The application must be the absolute master of its own database schema. You only provide the empty "bucket" (the database) and the "keys" (the user permissions).

The Pre-Flight Check: The Empty Bucket
Before you click "Install" on the GUI, we must ensure your MySQL/MariaDB server has that perfectly empty bucket ready.

Log into your database as the root user:

Bash
sudo mysql -u root -p
Run this command to check your current databases:

SQL
SHOW DATABASES;
Look at the output.

Do you see a database named gitea?

Execution: Creating the "Bucket" (If it doesn't exist)
If you have not created the database yet, or if you want to be 100% sure it is configured correctly for a Git server, run these exact SQL commands inside the MySQL prompt.

The Dense "Why" (Character Sets)
We are not just creating a database; we are enforcing utf8mb4. If you just type CREATE DATABASE gitea;, the database engine might default to an older character set like latin1. If a developer later pushes a Git commit message containing an emoji (🚀) or non-English characters, the database will throw an exception and the push will fail. utf8mb4 guarantees full Unicode support.

Execute these commands inside MySQL:

SQL
-- 1. Create the empty database with strict UTF-8 encoding
CREATE DATABASE gitea CHARACTER SET 'utf8mb4' COLLATE 'utf8mb4_unicode_ci';

-- 2. Create the Gitea user and set a password (replace 'StrongPassword123!' with your choice)
CREATE USER 'gitea'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'StrongPassword123!';

-- 3. Grant the Gitea user absolute control OVER ONLY the 'gitea' database bucket
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON gitea.* TO 'gitea'@'localhost';

-- 4. Tell the MySQL engine to reload its security rules immediately
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;

-- 5. Exit the database prompt
EXIT;
Your Next Step
Ensure the empty gitea database exists using the steps above.

Go to your Web GUI (http://<YOUR_VM_IP>:3000).

Under Database Settings, enter:

Database Type: MySQL

Host: 127.0.0.1:3306

Username: gitea

Password: (Whatever you set in step 2)

Database Name: gitea

Once you hit "Install", Gitea will take that empty bucket and generate dozens of tables inside it in a matter of seconds.

Lecture 6.0: The Bootstrap Administrator Privilege (RBAC Initialization)
In modern web applications, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) dictates who can do what. But when an application is born, its user database is completely empty. There is no "root" user out of the box.  
IBM

To solve this, applications like Gitea use a "Bootstrap Admin" logic. The application is programmed with a hardcoded rule: The very first user account ever created in the database is automatically granted Site Administrator privileges. Once that first account (UID 1) is created, the "Bootstrap Mode" disables itself. Every user who registers after that will be created as a standard, unprivileged user.

The Pre-Flight Check
Right now, your server is in a vulnerable state. Because the admin slot is empty, if anyone else on your network navigates to your VM's IP address on port 3000 and clicks "Register," they will hijack the Site Administrator role.

Look at your sign-in page: Do you see the "Register" or "Sign Up" link near the login form?

The Dense "Why"
You must be the one to claim UID 1. This account will give you access to the hidden "Site Administration" control panel. From there, you will manage webhooks, configure the CI/CD runners (like Jenkins or Gitea Actions), set up branch protections, and disable public registration so random people cannot make accounts on your Vodafone internal tool.

should the email address be valid can it be changed later

The short answers are: 1. No, it does not need to be a real, working email address right now.

Here is the Architect’s breakdown of how email systems work in isolated, on-premise environments like the one you are building for Vodafone.

Lecture 6.1: Syntax Validation vs. SMTP Verification
When a web application asks for an email address, it performs two distinct types of checks:

Syntax Validation (The Regex Check): The application’s frontend uses a Regular Expression (Regex) to ensure the string you typed looks like an email. It just checks that there is text, followed by an @ symbol, followed by a domain and a dot (e.g., user@domain.com).

SMTP Verification (The Loop Check): The application's backend attempts to connect to a Mail Server (SMTP relayer) to send a unique token to that inbox, proving you own it.

The Dense "Why"
Right now, your Gitea server only possesses Syntax Validation.

Because this is a brand-new, offline installation, we have not yet configured an SMTP Relayer (like Postfix, Sendmail, or Vodafone's internal Exchange server) inside your app.ini file. Furthermore, the "Require Email Confirmation" setting is disabled by default in Gitea.

Therefore, Gitea has no physical way to check if the email actually exists. It will simply take the string you provide and inject it into the user table in your MySQL database.

Later on, as the Site Administrator, you have absolute CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) authority over the database. You can go into your Profile Settings -> Email tab and change it to your real Vodafone email whenever you want, especially if you decide to hook up an internal SMTP server later to get notification emails for Pull Requests.

The Execution: Proceed with Registration

Lecture 6.2: Database Persistence vs. Filesystem Persistence
Earlier, we performed a "Scorched Earth" reset on your Linux filesystem (/app/gitea and /etc/gitea). We wiped the directories completely clean.

However, we did not wipe the MySQL database.

If you had attempted the web installation during any of our earlier troubleshooting steps, Gitea might have already written a hidden "Admin" user into the MySQL tables. When you registered just now, Gitea saw that the database was not truly "empty" of users, so it assigned your new account standard user privileges instead of the Site Administrator role.

This is the beauty and the danger of an external database: it retains state independently of the application files.

The Pre-Flight Check: Interrogating the ORM via CLI
We are going to bypass the web interface completely. Gitea has a powerful built-in Command Line Interface (CLI) that allows the Linux root user to manipulate the database directly.

We will ask Gitea to print a list of every user currently in the database, along with their admin status.

Run this exact command in your terminal:

Bash
# -u git: Run as the git user
# /usr/local/bin/gitea admin user list: Call the built-in admin tool
# --config /etc/gitea/app.ini: Tell it where the database credentials are stored
sudo -u git /usr/local/bin/gitea admin user list --config /etc/gitea/app.ini
The Dense "Why"
When you run this command, the Gitea binary reads the app.ini file, finds the MySQL username and password, connects to 127.0.0.1:3306, queries the user table, and formats it for your terminal. This proves whether or not the database and the application are communicating properly, and it exposes exactly who holds the UID 1 admin token.

Look closely at the output. You only have one user in the entire database (ID 1), and its IsAdmin flag is set to true.

Chapter 7: The Security Lockdown (Crucial Step)
Now that the application is installed, the database is populated, and your admin account exists, we must immediately close the security hole we opened yesterday.

Lecture 7.0: The Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP)
Yesterday, we ran sudo chmod 770 /etc/gitea to give the git user temporary Write (w) access so the web wizard could generate the app.ini file.

In Linux Administration, leaving a configuration directory writable by the application user is a Critical Vulnerability. If a hacker finds a zero-day exploit in Gitea's web interface, they will be running commands as the git user. If the git user has write access to /etc/gitea/app.ini, the attacker can rewrite your configuration—pointing the database to their own server, or injecting malicious paths to gain root access to your Vodafone VM.

We must lock the git user into a Read-Only state for the configuration.

The Execution: Revoking the "Write" Pass
We will change the permissions so root retains full control, but the git group can only Read (r) and Enter (x) the directory.

Run these exact commands in your terminal:

Bash
# 1. Lock the directory (750 = root:rwx | git:r-x | others:---)
# The 'git' user can no longer create or delete files in /etc/gitea
sudo chmod 750 /etc/gitea

# 2. Lock the configuration file itself (640 = root:rw- | git:r-- | others:---)
# The 'git' user can read the settings, but cannot modify the file
sudo chmod 640 /etc/gitea/app.ini

# 3. Verify the lockdown (The Pre-Flight style check for confirmation)
ls -ld /etc/gitea
ls -l /etc/gitea/app.ini
Your Next Steps
Log into the GUI as Automation_Admins and locate the Site Administration panel.

Run the two chmod commands to lock down the server.

Once you confirm the GUI is working and the file is locked, we have officially finished the Infrastructure & Installation phase. We can then begin planning the Platform Engineering Workflow (Branch Protections, Webhooks, and preparing for your CI/CD pipeline). Let me know when you are ready!

This is a fantastic request. You are looking past the GUI and asking how the kernel, the binary, and the filesystem actually interact during a network operation. This is exactly how an architect should think.

To answer your question immediately: Yes, you are 100% correct. Every repository stored on a Git server (whether it is Gitea, GitLab, or GitHub) is a bare repository.

Let's break down exactly what happens when you type git push, using the Architect's Protocol.

Lecture 7.1: The Anatomy of a Git Push over SSH
When you create a repository on your local laptop, it has a "working tree" (the actual files you can open in an editor) and a hidden .git folder containing the history.

A bare repository has no working tree. It is only the contents of the .git folder. It exists purely to receive and serve data. If you were to look inside your Gitea server at /app/gitea/data/gitea-repositories/Automation_Admins/test-repo.git, you would just see directories like objects, refs, and hooks. There are no source code files to edit directly.

The Mechanics of the Push (How git-receive-pack works):
You mentioned git packet-recieve—the exact command name in the Git suite is git-receive-pack. Here is the step-by-step lifecycle of a push:

The Client (You): You type git push origin main. Your local Git client initiates an SSH connection to your VM: ssh git@<YOUR_VM_IP>.

The SSH Daemon (sshd): The Linux server receives the connection. It checks the /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file to verify your SSH key.

The Gitea Interception: Normally, SSH gives you a bash shell. But Gitea modifies the authorized_keys file to include a forced command. Instead of giving you a shell, SSH is forced to pass your connection directly to the Gitea binary.

The Security Check: Gitea looks at the SSH key you used, queries the MySQL database to see which user owns that key, and checks if that user has Write permissions to the requested repository.

The Execution: If approved, the Gitea binary acts as a wrapper. It tells the Linux kernel to execute git-receive-pack /app/gitea/data/gitea-repositories/Automation_Admins/test-repo.git.

The Transfer: Your local laptop and the server's git-receive-pack process open a pipeline and stream the compressed commit objects to the bare repository.

(Note: When you git pull, the exact same process happens, but the server runs git-upload-pack instead).

The Pre-Flight Check: The Target Repository
Before we can test this, we need a target. We cannot push to a server that has no repositories.

Go to your Gitea Web GUI.

Log in as Automation_Admins.

Click the + icon in the top right and select New Repository.

Name it linux-test.

Check the box to "Initialize Repository (Adds .gitignore, License and README)".

Click Create Repository.

By initializing it, Gitea creates the bare repository on the filesystem (/app/gitea/...) and adds a starting commit so we have something to pull.

The Execution: Testing the SSH Pipeline
To see this mechanism in action, we must set up your SSH keys. We do not use passwords for the git user.

Step 1: Get your Local SSH Public Key
On your local machine (your laptop, not the RHEL VM), retrieve your public SSH key.

If you develop on Linux/Mac: Run cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub or cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub.

(If you don't have one, generate it with ssh-keygen -t ed25519).

Copy the output string (it starts with ssh-rsa or ssh-ed25519).

Step 2: Add the Key to Gitea
In the Gitea GUI, click your profile picture (top right) -> Settings.

Go to the SSH / GPG Keys tab.

Click Add Key.

Name it "My Laptop" and paste the public key into the content box. Click Add Key.

Step 3: The Pull and Push Test
Open a terminal on your local laptop (not the server).

Run the Clone Command:

Bash
# Replace with your actual VM IP and username
git clone git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Automation_Admins/linux-test.git
(Type 'yes' to accept the SSH fingerprint if prompted).

Make a Change and Push:

Bash
cd linux-test
echo "Testing the git-receive-pack pipeline" > test-file.txt
git add test-file.txt
git commit -m "feat: infrastructure network test"
git push origin main
The Dense "Why" for SSH over HTTP
While you can clone using HTTP (http://<YOUR_VM_IP>:3000/...), HTTP requires typing your username and password every time unless you configure credential helpers. SSH uses cryptographic keys, which is not only more secure against brute-force attacks, but it is strictly required for CI/CD pipelines (like Jenkins) to authenticate automatically without human interaction.

Your Task:
Create the repo, add your key, and run the git clone and git push commands from your local machine.

Did the push succeed, or did the SSH daemon reject your connection?

This is the exact pivot point where you transition from a "Server Admin" to a "Platform Engineer." You are no longer just keeping a service alive; you are designing the developer experience (DevEx) and the security topology for multiple teams.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to design the optimal setup for your Windows 11 developers and prepare the ground for CI/CD.

Lecture 8.0: Enterprise Git Authentication Topology (SSH vs. HTTPS)
When multiple teams need to interact with a centralized Git server, you have two protocol choices: HTTPS or SSH.

The HTTPS Approach (The Novice Way): Developers clone using http://<VM_IP>:3000/.... Every time they push or pull, they must authenticate. On Windows 11, the Git Credential Manager can cache their username and password, but this relies on passwords. Passwords get compromised, expire, or get locked out.

The SSH Protocol (The Enterprise Standard):
Developers clone using git@<VM_IP>:<Organization>/<Repo>.git. They use Asymmetric Cryptography (Public/Private Key pairs).

The Private Key stays locked on the developer's Windows 11 machine.

The Public Key is uploaded to their Gitea profile.

The Multiplexing Magic:
Notice that every developer connects as the exact same Linux user: git. You do not create a Linux account for "John" and "Sarah". Instead, the Linux SSH Daemon (sshd) reads the incoming Public Key, passes it to the Gitea binary, and Gitea says, "Ah, this key belongs to Sarah's Gitea account. Allow her access to the Frontend repo, but block her from the Backend repo." The CI/CD Connection:
We must use SSH. Why? Because when we install the Gitea Runner (your CI/CD worker) later, that runner is essentially a "robot developer." It will need to clone code autonomously. We cannot give a robot a password; we give it an SSH Deploy Key. Setting up SSH now makes the runner integration seamless.

The Pre-Flight Check: The Gitea Hierarchy
Before a single Windows developer generates an SSH key, we must fix your Gitea data structure. Currently, you have personal repositories under your Automation_Admins namespace.

In an enterprise, developers should almost never push to a personal namespace. We need a "Bucket" for the teams.

Go to your Gitea Web GUI:

Click the + icon in the top right.

Select New Organization.

Name it Vodafone-Engineering (or similar).

Inside that Organization, go to the Teams tab.

Create a team (e.g., DevOps, Backend-Team).

This Organization will be the "owner" of the repositories, and the "owner" of the future CI/CD Runners.

The Execution: The Windows 11 Developer Setup
Here is the exact instruction set you will provide to your developers. You should test this yourself on your own Windows machine first.

The Dense "Why" (Ed25519 vs RSA)
We will instruct developers to generate Ed25519 keys. Older tutorials suggest RSA keys. Ed25519 is an elliptic curve cryptography algorithm that is significantly faster, generates much shorter keys, and is cryptographically stronger against brute-force attacks than RSA.  
Callgoose

Step 1: Key Generation (On the Windows 11 Client)
Have the developer open PowerShell and run:

PowerShell
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "developer.name@vodafone.local"
Press Enter to save it in the default location (C:\Users\<Name>\.ssh\id_ed25519).

They can press Enter to skip the passphrase for automated ease, or add one for max security.

Step 2: Retrieving the Public Key
In the same PowerShell window, run:

PowerShell
Get-Content ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub | Set-Clipboard
(This safely copies the public key directly to their Windows clipboard).

Step 3: Registering the Key with Gitea

The developer logs into the Gitea Web GUI.

Clicks their Profile Picture -> Settings -> SSH / GPG Keys.

Clicks Add Key.

Names it "Windows 11 Workstation" and pastes the clipboard contents.

Step 4: The Developer Workflow (Clone, Push, Pull)
Now, the developer goes to the Gitea GUI, finds a repository under the Vodafone-Engineering organization, and clicks the SSH clone button.

In PowerShell or Git Bash, they run:

Bash
git clone git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Vodafone-Engineering/my-app.git
From that moment on, their git push and git pull commands will authenticate invisibly, securely, and instantly.

Your Next Step as the Architect
Before we move on to installing the Gitea Runner for CI/CD, we must prove this foundation is solid.

Generate an Ed25519 SSH key on your local Windows machine.

Upload it to your Admin account.

Clone an Organization repository using the git@... SSH link.

Did the clone succeed without asking you for a password? Once you verify this, we will begin the CI/CD Runner architecture.

This is the exact moment we transition from basic hosting to Enterprise Git Governance. You are now designing the Access Control and Workflow topology for your engineering teams.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to build this structure, migrate your existing code, and enforce the "Admins-only Merge" rule.

Lecture 8.1: RBAC vs. Branch Protection (The Governance Model)
To achieve your goal (everyone can push/pull, but only Admins can merge), we must understand how Gitea layers its security. It uses a two-tier system:

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): This dictates what a user can do to the repository as a whole.

Read: Can git pull.

Write: Can git push to any unprotected branch.

Admin: Can delete the repository or change its settings.

Branch Protection (The Pre-Receive Hook): This dictates what a user can do to a specific branch (like main or master).

Even if a developer has "Write" access (RBAC), Branch Protection uses a server-side Git hook (pre-receive) to intercept their push. If they try to push directly to main, the server rejects the packet. It forces them to push to a feature branch and open a Pull Request (PR).

Your requirement perfectly matches this model: We will give the TxProject and TxCapacity teams Write access, but we will apply Branch Protection to main so that only the Admins team has the cryptographic authority to execute the merge.

I have some questions about git remote add origin git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Vodafone-Tx/tx-core.git



What is this tx-core.git . and Iam a bit affraid on relying on that bare repo ?

This is a very natural reaction. When you are used to seeing your source code as physical files in a folder (like main.py or index.html), handing all of your Vodafone team's work over to an "invisible" bare repository feels like throwing your code into a black hole.

As a Platform Engineer, your primary job is safeguarding data. Your hesitation is the exact right instinct.

Let's apply the Architect’s Protocol to completely demystify this so you can trust the architecture you are building.

Lecture 9.1: Decoding the SSH URI (What is tx-core.git?)
Let’s break down the command git remote add origin git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Vodafone-Tx/tx-core.git piece by piece.

This string is not magic; it is simply an SSH routing path that tells your local computer exactly how to find the database on the server.

git@: The Linux user we are logging in as (via SSH).

<YOUR_VM_IP>: The server we are connecting to.

:: The SSH delimiter. It tells the server, "Look relative to the Gitea application root."

Vodafone-Tx/: The Organization (Tenant) namespace.

tx-core.git: This is the actual directory name on the Linux filesystem where the data is stored.

The Dense "Why" on the .git suffix:
In Linux, extensions don't mean much, but in Git administration, adding .git to the end of a folder name is a strict naming convention. It tells any developer or system administrator looking at the filesystem: "Warning: This is a bare repository. Do not expect to find readable source code files in here." If you were to log into your RHEL server right now and run ls /app/gitea/data/gitea-repositories/Vodafone-Tx/tx-core.git, you would see exactly what is on your local laptop inside your hidden .git folder: objects, refs, config, HEAD.

Lecture 9.2: The Mechanics and Safety of the Bare Repository
You asked: "I am a bit afraid on relying on that bare repo?"

Here is the technical reality: A bare repository is mathematically the safest place for your code to live.

To understand why, we must understand why a normal repository (like the one on your laptop) is actually highly dangerous for a server to use.

The Non-Bare Danger (The "Desync" Crash)
Imagine your Gitea server used a normal repository. It has the .git database, but it also has the "Working Tree" (the actual readable files spread out in a folder).

The server currently has the main branch checked out. The file app.py says version=1.0.

A developer from the TxProject team runs git push from their laptop, updating app.py to version=2.0.

The Crash: The Git database updates to 2.0, but the physical app.py file sitting on the server's hard drive still says 1.0. The database and the working tree are now violently out of sync. Git panics, corrupts the index, and blocks all future pushes.

The Bare Repository Solution
A bare repository solves this by completely deleting the "Working Tree." It strips away the readable files and keeps only the database (the cryptographically hashed commits).
Because there are no readable files checked out on the server, it is impossible for the server to get "out of sync" when someone pushes new code. It just quietly accepts the new database objects and updates its pointers.

The Architect's Reassurance: The Distributed Backup
If your fear is about losing the code, remember what "Git" actually stands for: a Distributed Version Control System.

Unlike old systems (like SVN or Team Foundation Server) where the server held the only true copy of the code, Git gives everyone everything.

When you run git push origin main into that bare repository, the server gets a copy.
When developer Ahmed runs git clone, his laptop downloads the entire history of the project.
When developer Sarah runs git pull, her laptop downloads the entire history of the project.

If your RHEL VM catches fire tomorrow and the bare repository is completely destroyed:
You have lost nothing. You simply stand up a new Gitea server, go to Sarah or Ahmed's Windows 11 machine, and run git push origin main. Their local laptops contain the exact, mathematically perfect replica of the bare repository. They just push it back up, and the server is restored in seconds.

The Pre-Flight Check: Proving the Concept
Before you push your actual Vodafone code, let's prove to your own eyes that the bare repository is safe and functioning. Let's do a harmless test.

On your local Windows machine, create a totally fake project:

Bash
mkdir test-project
cd test-project
git init
echo "This is a test file" > test.txt
git add test.txt
git commit -m "Initial test commit"
Go to the Gitea GUI, create a new empty repository in the Vodafone-Tx organization called test-repo.

Add the remote and push:

Bash
git remote add origin git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Vodafone-Tx/test-repo.git
git push -u origin master
Did the push succeed? If it did, you can go look at the Gitea Web GUI, refresh the test-repo page, and you will beautifully see your test.txt file displayed in the browser!

Gitea reads the bare repository database and renders the files visually for you on the web, even though they don't exist as raw text files on the Linux hard drive. Let me know if you want to try this test!

okay answer this question when clonning a bare repo will I have the working tree history ?

This is an excellent question. It is one of the most common points of confusion when moving from local development to an enterprise server model.

The Short Answer: Yes, absolutely. When you clone a bare repository, your local machine will have the complete working tree (all your files) and the entire history of every commit ever made.  
Stegosaurus Dormant

Let's apply the Architect's Protocol to understand exactly how this translation happens.

Lecture 9.3: The Magic of git clone (From Bare to Working Tree)
To understand this, we have to separate the Server state from the Client (Developer) state.

The Server State (The Bare Repo): On your Gitea server, the repository is just the database. It contains no working tree and no readable files. It only holds the compressed history of the project.

The Command (git clone): When a developer on your TxProject team runs git clone git@... on their Windows 11 machine, their local Git client performs two distinct actions in the background:

Action A (Download): It copies the entire compressed .git database from the server to their local machine.

Action B (Checkout): It automatically executes a git checkout of the default branch (usually main).

The Client State (The Non-Bare Repo): That automatic git checkout is the magic step. It looks at the database it just downloaded, finds the latest commit, and unpacks those compressed objects into real, readable, editable files on the developer's hard drive. This unpacked snapshot is the Working Tree.

The Dense "Why"
A working tree is essentially just a temporary, physical manifestation of one specific moment in your project's history. The bare repository holds the master blueprints for every moment in history. Because the git clone command downloads all those blueprints, your local Git client has everything it needs to instantly reconstruct the files exactly as they were.

When you clone it, you aren't just getting the current files; you are downloading the entire, mathematically complete database, allowing you to view the entire history.

what is this git remote add origin git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Vodafone-Tx/tx-core.git

This is the exact right question to ask. A Platform Engineer never runs a command without understanding how it modifies the underlying system.

When you type git remote add origin git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Vodafone-Tx/tx-core.git, you are not actually moving any code, nor are you communicating with the server yet. You are simply creating a "Network Bookmark" on your local machine.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol and tear this command apart piece by piece to see exactly how it manipulates your local Git database.

Lecture 9.4: The Anatomy of a Git Remote (The Pointer System)
In Git, a "remote" is just a named pointer to another repository that lives somewhere else (like on your Gitea server). Because typing out git@192.168.1.50:Vodafone-Tx/tx-core.git every time you want to push code is exhausting and error-prone, Git uses an alias system.

Here is the exact breakdown of the command:

git remote add: You are telling the local Git executable, "I want to add a new network bookmark to my database."

origin: This is the Name (alias) of the bookmark.

The Dense "Why": There is absolutely nothing mathematically special about the word "origin". You could type git remote add vodafone-server git@..., and then you would push code by typing git push vodafone-server main. However, origin is the undisputed industry standard name for a repository's primary central server. If you use a different name, other tools and IDEs might get confused.

git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Vodafone-Tx/tx-core.git: This is the Target Value of the bookmark. It is the exact SSH routing string we decoded in the last lecture.

The Under-the-Hood Reality (Where does it go?)
As a Linux Administrator, you know that commands don't just do "magic"—they write to files.

When you run this command on your Windows 11 machine or Linux laptop, Git does not reach out to the network. It simply opens a hidden text file inside your local project folder and writes a few lines into it.

The Post-Flight Check (Proving the theory):
If you run that git remote add command, you can prove exactly what it did by looking at the raw configuration file.

If you are inside your project folder, run this command to read the hidden config file:

Bash
cat .git/config
You will see that Git simply appended a block of text that looks exactly like this:

Ini, TOML
[remote "origin"]
    url = git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Vodafone-Tx/tx-core.git
    fetch = +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*
The Architect's Conclusion:
The command is just a safe, CLI-friendly way of editing that .git/config text file.

Once that block is saved, whenever you type git push origin main, the Git client says:

"The human said 'origin'."

"Let me check my .git/config file to see what 'origin' means."

"Ah, it means git@<YOUR_VM_IP>:Vodafone-Tx/tx-core.git."

"I will now open an SSH pipeline to that IP address and send the code."

Does this demystify what that command is actually doing to your local environment? If so, we can proceed with your MVP overview!

This is exactly why we do this step-by-step. The environment changed: you are trying to push code from the same machine that is hosting the server, rather than from a remote developer's laptop.

This introduces a classic networking scenario. Let's apply the Architect's Protocol to solve it.

Lecture 10.1: The Loopback Paradox (Client and Server on the Same Metal)
When you try to use the SSH command (git@<YOUR_VM_IP>...) from the RHEL VM to the same RHEL VM, the Linux networking stack gets confused.

Here is the exact problem: To use that SSH string, the Linux user you are currently logged in as (likely root or your personal admin user) needs to have an SSH key generated and uploaded to your Automation_Admins Gitea profile. If you haven't done that, the SSH daemon will instantly reject your connection with a Permission denied (publickey) error.

The Solution: Because your code and your server are sharing the exact same hard drive and kernel, we do not need to deal with external IPs or SSH keys for this one-time migration. We can use the Local Loopback Adapter (127.0.0.1) and the HTTP protocol. This allows you to simply type in your username and password to instantly securely transfer the code into the database.

The Pre-Flight Check: Clearing the Bad Bookmark
Because the previous command didn't work, your local Git database currently has a broken "bookmark" saved. We must delete it before we create the correct one.

Run this command inside your project folder:

Bash
# This asks Git to list all current network bookmarks
git remote -v
(You will likely see the broken origin pointing to the old IP string).

The Execution: The Loopback Migration
We will delete the broken pointer, create a new one pointing specifically to the internal Gitea web service, and push the code.

Make sure you are inside your existing project folder (the one that has the .git directory inside it).

The Dense "Why"
remote remove: This deletes the [remote "origin"] block from your hidden .git/config file, wiping the slate clean.

http://127.0.0.1:3000: This tells the kernel, "Do not send this traffic to the network switch. Route it internally straight to port 3000 where Gitea is listening." It completely bypasses the SSH daemon and firewall.

Run these exact commands:

Bash
# 1. Delete the broken bookmark
git remote remove origin

# 2. Add the correct internal loopback bookmark
# (Notice we are using HTTP and the exact Org/Repo names you provided)
git remote add origin http://127.0.0.1:3000/TAT/TAT_Test_Env.git

# 3. Push the code and history into the Gitea database
git push -u origin main
(Note: If your local branch is named master instead of main, use git push -u origin master)

What to Expect
When you run the git push command, because it is using HTTP, the terminal will pause and ask you for a Username and Password.

Type: Automation_Admins

Type your Gitea admin password (the characters will be invisible as you type).

Lecture 11.0: The Enterprise Feature Matrix (Repository Level)
When you click Settings inside your TAT_Test_env repository, you are opening the control plane for how code, users, and external systems interact with this specific database.

Here is the Architect’s breakdown of the most critical tabs and features, and the Dense "Why" behind how they are used in a production environment.

1. Basic Settings (The Feature Toggles)
The Features: Enable/Disable Issue Tracker, Pull Requests, Wiki, Projects (Kanban boards), and Packages.

The Dense "Why": Cognitive load management. If your team uses Jira for tracking tasks, having Gitea's built-in "Issues" tab enabled just creates confusion about where a developer should report a bug. A clean platform is a secure platform. Turn off every feature your MVP does not explicitly need.

2. Collaborators / Teams (Granular RBAC)
The Features: Adding specific users or organization teams to the repository.

The Dense "Why": While the TAT Organization defines default permissions, this tab allows for "Surgical Overrides". For example, if you have an external auditor or a temporary contractor who needs to see TAT_Test_env but shouldn't see anything else in the organization, you add them here as a Read-Only Collaborator.

3. Branches (The Pre-Receive Shield)
The Features: Default Branch selection, Branch Protection Rules (Require Pull Requests, Require Approvals, Whitelist Pushes).

The Dense "Why": This is your primary defense mechanism against human error. We discussed this briefly before, but the most powerful feature here is "Enable Status Check". Later, when your Runner is active, you can tell Gitea: "Do not let anyone merge code unless the CI/CD pipeline reports a green 'Success' status." This mathematically guarantees broken code never enters the main branch.

4. Webhooks (The Event-Driven Engine)
The Features: Send HTTP POST requests to other servers when things happen in Gitea (e.g., a push, a new PR, a release).

The Dense "Why": This is the backbone of integrations. If you are ever building an internal enterprise notification system, you don't need the external tool to constantly poll Gitea asking "Are there updates?". Instead, you configure a Webhook. The second a developer pushes code, Gitea fires a JSON payload containing the commit details straight to your custom Flask application or a Microsoft Teams channel. It is instant and resource-efficient.

5. Actions / Runners (The Automation Bridge)
The Features: Enable Gitea Actions for this repo, and register repository-specific Runners.

The Dense "Why": Gitea Actions is an exact clone of GitHub Actions. This tab is where you tell the repository which physical servers (Runners) are allowed to execute its pipeline scripts. You can have a heavy, dedicated Runner just for TAT_Test_env, isolating its workload from the rest of the organization.

6. Secrets & Variables (The Vault)
The Features: Store encrypted key-value pairs.

The Dense "Why": Hardcoding passwords in your source code is a catastrophic security violation. When your pipeline needs to log into an AWS environment or a remote server, you store the password here. Gitea injects it into the Runner's memory at runtime and masks it in the logs so developers can't read it.

7. Packages (The Artifact Registry)
The Features: Gitea acts as a native package manager (npm, PyPI, Maven, Container Registry).

The Dense "Why": When you are building modern infrastructure, your final product is rarely just raw code. You package it. If your team writes a Python tool, they can publish it directly to Gitea's PyPI registry. If you are containerizing applications, Gitea acts as a private Docker Registry. Your CI/CD pipeline builds the Docker image and pushes it straight back into Gitea, completely ready for a Kubernetes cluster to pull and deploy.

Lecture 12.1: The Production Sync Dilemma (To Runner or Not to Runner?)
You asked a very perceptive question: "I want the master VM used in production to be in sync with the test VM... I don't know whether that is even possible without a runner."

The Architect's Answer: Yes, it is absolutely possible without a Runner, but it dictates how the deployment behaves. You have two architectural choices:

Option A: The Legacy Way (No Runner - Git Server Hooks / Webhooks)

How it works: When a Spoke merges a PR, Gitea fires a Webhook (an HTTP POST request) over the network to a lightweight listening script on your Production VM. That script simply runs git pull origin master and restarts the services.

Pros: Zero extra infrastructure. Instant.

Cons: "Blind" deployment. Gitea just throws the code over the wall. If the git pull fails, or the Production VM crashes during restart, Gitea has no idea. The UI will just show a merged PR, leaving you unaware that Production is broken.

Option B: The Enterprise Way (Using a Gitea Runner)

How it works: When a Spoke merges a PR, Gitea wakes up a Runner. The Runner executes a strict YAML pipeline: it securely SSHs into the Production VM, pulls the code, restarts the service, and runs a health check curl command.

Pros: Total visibility. If the Production VM fails to restart, the Runner catches the error, marks the deployment as Failed (Red X) directly inside the Gitea UI, and can even automatically roll back the code.

Cons: Requires installing the Gitea Runner binary.

The Next Step
I highly recommend we use Option B (The Runner) because it is the industry standard for DevOps and sets you up perfectly for your future Kubernetes/Docker workflows.

However, we must test the IAM foundation first.

Sprint 1: The Infrastructure Stabilization
Looking at your screenshots, you have two distinct issues happening simultaneously. Let's break them down.

Issue A: The ROOT_URL Mismatch (Image 3)
The Theory: Gitea needs to know its own "public face." It uses the ROOT_URL setting inside /etc/gitea/app.ini to generate absolute links for everything: the clone URLs it shows to developers (git clone http://...), the webhook payloads it sends to your pipelines, and OAuth2 redirects.
If Gitea thinks it is running at http://localhost:3000/, but you are accessing it via http://10.30.121.51:444/, its internal security checks panic because of a potential "Host Header Injection" attack, and it throws that yellow warning box.

Lecture 13.0: The Reverse Proxy Architecture (Apache & Gitea)
When you place Apache in front of Gitea, you are creating a Reverse Proxy.  
GitHub

The Frontend (Apache): Listens on the public network at 10.30.121.51:444.

The Backend (Gitea): Listens on the internal loopback at 127.0.0.1:3000.

The yellow warning box you saw in the Gitea UI happens because of Header Stripping.
When your browser asks for http://10.30.121.51:444/, Apache receives the request, strips away your original URL, and essentially says to Gitea, "Hey, give me the page for localhost:3000." Gitea looks at its configuration file, sees that its official ROOT_URL is localhost:3000, but notices the traffic is magically appearing from an IP and a weird port (444). It throws a security warning because it suspects a man-in-the-middle attack.

The Dense "Why" (The Fix)
To fix this, we have to do two things:

Tell Gitea in its app.ini that its true public face is 10.30.121.51:444.

Tell Apache to pass the Host headers transparently so Gitea knows the traffic is legitimate.

Lecture 13.1: Identity Management Without Active Directory
You mentioned the "TAT Users DB". Because we don't have AD, we cannot use Gitea's native LDAP plugin. However, Gitea has a brilliant feature designed specifically for this scenario: Reverse Proxy Authentication.

Here is how we will automate user creation using what you have:

The Apache Gatekeeper: We will configure Apache to connect directly to your TAT Users DB (using an Apache module like mod_auth_dbd or mod_auth_mysql).

The Authentication: When a developer hits port 444, Apache prompts them for credentials and checks the TAT DB.

The Header Injection: If the credentials match, Apache forwards the traffic to Gitea on port 3000 and injects a special HTTP header (e.g., X-WEBAUTH-USER: dev_ahmed).

The Gitea Auto-Provisioning: Gitea reads that header. It says, "I trust Apache. If Apache says this is dev_ahmed, I believe it." Gitea will automatically generate a profile for dev_ahmed on the fly and log them in. Zero manual user creation required.

Alternatively, if configuring Apache's database modules becomes too rigid or complex, a lightweight Flask microservice could easily be spun up to act as an OAuth2 bridge between Gitea and the TAT SQL database. Gitea would simply redirect login requests to the Flask app, which verifies the database and passes the token back.

Lecture 13.0 The Reverse Proxy Architecture (Apache & Gitea)

Walkthrough in detailed steps

This is where we bridge the gap between internal services and the external network. Setting up a reverse proxy correctly is the hallmark of a mature enterprise platform.

Let's apply the Architect's Protocol. We will tear down exactly how Apache and Gitea communicate, fix the "Identity Crisis" (the yellow warning box), and build the configuration files step-by-step.

Lecture 13.0: The Reverse Proxy Architecture and Header Propagation
When a developer types http://10.30.121.51:444/ into their browser, the TCP packet hits your RHEL VM.

The Interception: Apache (listening on port 444) intercepts the packet.

The Translation: Apache acts as a middleman. It opens a second, completely separate connection to Gitea at 127.0.0.1:3000. It downloads the web page from Gitea, and then hands it back to the developer.

The Disconnect (The cause of your error): By default, when Apache opens that second connection to Gitea, it changes the HTTP Host header to localhost. Gitea looks at the request, sees localhost, but knows its own configuration says something else. Gitea panics, assuming a malicious actor is spoofing the URL, and throws the yellow warning box.

The Solution: We must configure Gitea to know its true "Public Face," and we must instruct Apache to explicitly pass the original HTTP headers through the proxy tunnel untouched.

The Pre-Flight Check: Apache Modules
Before we write the configuration, we must ensure Apache actually has the "Reverse Proxy Engine" loaded into its memory.

Run this command to interrogate Apache:

Bash
sudo httpd -M | grep proxy
What we are looking for: You need to see proxy_module (shared) and proxy_http_module (shared) in the output. If you see them, your Apache server is ready to route traffic.

Execution Step 1: Curing Gitea's "Identity Crisis"
We need to edit Gitea's brain (app.ini) so it stops generating links for localhost and starts generating them for your production IP on port 444.

1. Open the configuration file:

Bash
sudo nano /etc/gitea/app.ini
# (or use vi/vim)
2. Locate the [server] section and modify these exact lines:

The Dense "Why"
DOMAIN: Used for SSH cloning (e.g., git@10.30.121.51:TAT/TAT_Test_Env.git).

HTTP_PORT: The port the Gitea Go binary actually binds to internally on the VM. We leave this at 3000.

ROOT_URL: This is the most critical variable. This is the absolute URL that Gitea uses to generate Webhook payloads, OAuth redirects, and Web UI links. It must match exactly what the user types in their browser.

Ini, TOML
[server]
APP_DATA_PATH    = /var/lib/gitea/data
DOMAIN           = 10.30.121.51
SSH_DOMAIN       = 10.30.121.51
HTTP_PORT        = 3000
ROOT_URL         = http://10.30.121.51:444/
DISABLE_SSH      = false
SSH_PORT         = 22
LFS_START_SERVER = true
Save the file and exit.

Execution Step 2: Building the Apache Tunnel
Now we tell Apache to listen on port 444 and tunnel the traffic seamlessly.

1. Create a new VirtualHost file for Gitea:

Bash
sudo nano /etc/httpd/conf.d/gitea.conf
2. Paste this exact configuration block:

The Dense "Why"
Listen 444: Forces Apache to open port 444 on the server (ensure your firewall allows this).

ProxyPreserveHost On: This is the magic command. It stops Apache from rewriting the Host header to localhost. It passes 10.30.121.51:444 straight to Gitea, completely eliminating the yellow warning box.

ProxyPass / ...: Maps the root directory (/) of port 444 to the internal port 3000.

Apache
Listen 444

<VirtualHost *:444>
    ServerName 10.30.121.51
    
    ProxyPreserveHost On
    ProxyRequests Off

    # Proxy all traffic to the internal Gitea service
    ProxyPass / http://127.0.0.1:3000/
    ProxyPassReverse / http://127.0.0.1:3000/

    # Optional but highly recommended logging
    ErrorLog /var/log/httpd/gitea-error.log
    CustomLog /var/log/httpd/gitea-access.log combined
</VirtualHost>
Save the file and exit.

Execution Step 3: The RHEL "Invisible Shield" (SELinux)
If you are running RHEL, Rocky, or AlmaLinux, there is a 99% chance SELinux is enabled in Enforcing mode.

By default, SELinux considers it a massive security risk for the httpd (Apache) process to initiate outbound network connections—even to another port on the exact same machine (localhost:3000). If you skip this step, Apache will start, but when you visit the page, you will get a 502 Bad Gateway or 503 Service Unavailable error because SELinux silently assassinated the proxy connection.

Run this command to give Apache the "Network Connect" permission:

Bash
# -P makes the rule Permanent across reboots
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1
Execution Step 4: The Restart Protocol
Everything is configured. We must now restart the services to load the new settings into memory.

Bash
# 1. Restart Gitea to load the new ROOT_URL
sudo systemctl restart gitea

# 2. Restart Apache to load the Reverse Proxy VirtualHost
sudo systemctl restart httpd

# 3. Verify both are running without errors
sudo systemctl status gitea
sudo systemctl status httpd
Your Next Step
Once the services are restarted, open your browser and navigate to http://10.30.121.51:444/.

Lecture 13.2: The Frontend vs. Backend Mismatch
You asked: "If Apache changes the request to localhost, why did it generate the yellow box?"

Here is the exact logic of the trap:

The Browser (Frontend): When you open Chrome and type http://10.30.121.51:444, your browser's JavaScript engine knows exactly where it is.

The Backend: Apache catches that traffic, strips the 10.30.121.51 part, and whispers to the Gitea backend: "Hey, someone is asking for localhost:3000."

The Clash: Gitea's backend sends the webpage back to your browser. Embedded in that webpage is a security script that basically says: "My backend told me I am localhost, but my browser URL bar says 10.30.121.51:444. We are being lied to by a proxy. Throw the yellow warning box!"

To permanently kill the yellow box, two things must be perfectly aligned:

Gitea's ROOT_URL in app.ini must match the browser. (You mentioned changing DOMAIN and SSH_DOMAIN, but did you change ROOT_URL?)

Apache must inject specific X-Forwarded headers to tell Gitea, "I am a proxy, do not panic, the user is actually at 10.30.121.51."

The Pre-Flight Check: Verifying the Variables
Let's check exactly what your system says right now. Run this command to see your [server] block:

Bash
sudo grep -E "^(DOMAIN|SSH_DOMAIN|ROOT_URL|HTTP_PORT)" /etc/gitea/app.ini
What you MUST see for port 444 to work:

DOMAIN = 10.30.121.51

SSH_DOMAIN = 10.30.121.51

HTTP_PORT = 3000

ROOT_URL = http://10.30.121.51:444/ (If this still says localhost:3000, that is why the box is still there).

Execution: The Apache Header Injection
If your app.ini is correct and the box is still there, Apache is failing to send the proxy headers. We need to add the X-Forwarded headers that Gitea explicitly asked for in your screenshot.

1. Open your Apache config:

Bash
sudo nano /etc/httpd/conf.d/gitea.conf
2. Update the VirtualHost to look exactly like this:

The Dense "Why"
ProxyPreserveHost On: Forces Apache to send 10.30.121.51:444 to Gitea instead of localhost.

RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "http": Explicitly tells Gitea's security mechanisms that the original connection from the user was unencrypted HTTP, satisfying Gitea's internal checks.

nocanon: Tells Apache not to mess with the URL encoding (crucial for Git operations over HTTP).

Apache
Listen 444

<VirtualHost *:444>
    ServerName 10.30.121.51
    
    ProxyPreserveHost On
    ProxyRequests Off

    # Inject the headers Gitea expects
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "http"
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "10.30.121.51:444"

    # Pass the traffic without altering the URL encoding
    AllowEncodedSlashes NoDecode
    ProxyPass / http://127.0.0.1:3000/ nocanon
    ProxyPassReverse / http://127.0.0.1:3000/

    ErrorLog /var/log/httpd/gitea-error.log
    CustomLog /var/log/httpd/gitea-access.log combined
</VirtualHost>
3. Restart the services:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart gitea
sudo systemctl restart httpd
Check your app.ini output, apply the new Apache headers, and refresh the browser. That yellow box should vanish. Let me know the result!

This is a massive win. You just successfully configured a production-grade Reverse Proxy and resolved a Layer 7 networking mismatch. This is exactly what separates a junior admin from a Platform Engineer.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to break down exactly what you just did to the HTTP packets, and why Gitea needed those specific headers to calm down.

Lecture 13.3: The "Middleman" Problem and X-Forwarded Headers
When you put Apache in front of Gitea, Apache acts like an Executive Assistant.

The Client (Developer): Calls the Assistant (Apache) at 10.30.121.51:444.

The Assistant (Apache): Turns around, picks up a completely different phone, calls the Boss (Gitea) at 127.0.0.1:3000, and says, "Hey, give me the dashboard page."

The Boss (Gitea): Looks at the Caller ID. The Caller ID says 127.0.0.1 (localhost).

Before we added those headers, Gitea thought Apache was the end-user. It was generating internal links, webhook payloads, and security tokens meant for localhost. Then it saw the browser's URL didn't match, and it threw the yellow warning box.

The X-Forwarded Standard:
Because proxies inherently mask the original user, the web engineering community created the X-Forwarded family of HTTP headers. They are basically "sticky notes" that Apache attaches to the packet before handing it to Gitea, telling Gitea the true origin of the request.

The Dense "Why": Proto vs. Host
Here is the exact difference between the two headers you added:

1. X-Forwarded-Host (The "Where")
What it means: "Host" refers to the exact Domain/IP and Port the developer typed into their browser's address bar.

Your Value: 10.30.121.51:444

Why Gitea needs it: When a developer clicks a repository, Gitea has to render a little text box that says "Copy this link to clone: http://...". If it doesn't have the X-Forwarded-Host header, it will tell the developer to run git clone http://localhost:3000/TAT/TAT_Test_Env.git (which would fail on their Windows machine). By passing this header, Gitea knows to dynamically render http://10.30.121.51:444/... on the web page.

2. X-Forwarded-Proto (The "How")
What it means: "Proto" is short for Protocol. It tells the backend whether the original user connected securely (HTTPS) or insecurely (HTTP).

Your Value: http

Why Gitea needs it: Right now, you are using http. But in a real enterprise, you will eventually install an SSL Certificate on Apache so developers can use https://. When you do that, Apache will handle the heavy encryption (SSL Termination), decrypt the traffic, and pass it to Gitea as plain http.
If Gitea doesn't know the original connection was secure, it will generate insecure http:// links in its UI, breaking the site. X-Forwarded-Proto tells Gitea: "I am talking to you via HTTP, but the developer outside the firewall is using HTTPS. Generate all your links with HTTPS."

(Since you are using HTTP everywhere right now, this header was just Gitea being strict and demanding to know the full context of the connection before it removed the warning).

Lecture 14.0: The Cryptographic Collision and The Identity Bridge
Your database is storing passwords hashed in SHA-256. This is a standard and secure practice for internal tools.

However, we face a "Cryptographic Collision."
Modern applications like Gitea natively use Bcrypt or Argon2 for password hashing because they are intentionally slower (to prevent brute-force attacks). If we tried to forcefully point Gitea’s internal database engine at your users_hashed table, it would crash because it doesn't know how to natively compare its Bcrypt logic against your SHA-256 strings.

Furthermore, Apache's native database authentication module (mod_authn_dbd) also expects passwords to be formatted in specific Apache-friendly hashes (like crypt or $apr1$), so it will also reject raw SHA-256 hashes.

The Solution: We must build a Translator—a small piece of logic that sits between Gitea and your MySQL database, takes the user's password, hashes it into SHA-256, and checks the database on Gitea's behalf.

Here are the two professional Platform Engineering ways to build this translator. Both are excellent; it just depends on the architecture you prefer.

Architecture Path A: The OS-Level Hook (Linux PAM Integration)
Linux has a built-in authentication framework called PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules). Gitea natively supports asking Linux PAM to verify a user.

How it works: 1. A developer goes to the standard Gitea login screen and types their credentials.
2. Gitea hands the username and password to the Linux Kernel (PAM).
3. We configure PAM to execute a tiny, custom Python script (auth_bridge.py).
4. The script takes the password, runs a sha256 hash, and runs a SELECT query against your MySQL users_hashed table.
5. If the hash matches, the script tells PAM "Success," and Gitea logs the user in and auto-creates their profile.

The Pros: The developers use the native, beautiful Gitea login screen. It feels like a built-in feature.

The Cons: Debugging Linux PAM permissions can sometimes be strict, as the script must be executed securely by the system.

Architecture Path B: The Identity-Aware Proxy (Microservice)
This is the "Cloud-Native" approach. We completely bypass Gitea's login screen and build an SSO (Single Sign-On) gateway, just like an enterprise uses Keycloak or Okta.

How it works:

We spin up a tiny internal web service running a lightweight framework (like Python with Flask).

We configure Apache to say: "If the user isn't logged in, redirect them to the Python Microservice."

The Microservice presents a custom Vodafone TAT login screen, checks the MySQL database using the SHA-256 logic, and authenticates the user.

Upon success, the Microservice passes the traffic back to Apache, injecting the X-WEBAUTH-USER header we discussed earlier. Gitea blindly trusts the header and logs them in.

The Pros: Ultimate flexibility. You can completely customize the login UI, add Vodafone branding, and easily reuse this exact same microservice later to protect other internal tools, not just Gitea.

The Cons: Requires running and managing one extra small service on the VM.

The Architect's Choice
Both paths eliminate the need for you to ever manually create a user again. If someone is added to the TAT database, they instantly get access to Gitea.

Which architecture fits your vision for the platform better?

Path A: Stay native, use the OS (PAM), and keep the Gitea UI.

Path B: Go microservice, use Apache headers, and build a custom SSO gateway.

A little modification we use sha1 in hashing

SHA-1 requires a slight adjustment, but it makes no difference to the overall architecture. We simply swap the cryptographic library call. While SHA-1 is considered legacy for modern public-facing applications, in Platform Engineering, we integrate with the reality of the existing internal enterprise systems.

Here is the Architect's view of how this specific cryptographic translation will work.

Lecture 14.1: The SHA-1 Translation Logic
Regardless of whether we use the OS-level PAM hook (Path A) or the Identity-Aware Proxy (Path B), the core validation engine will do exactly the same thing:

Capture the plain-text password the developer typed.

Run it through a SHA-1 hashing function.

Compare the resulting hexadecimal string against the password column in your users_hashed table.

Because developing internal tools and web applications using Python and the Flask framework is already a core part of your engineering workflow, building this translation layer will be incredibly lightweight.

The core validation engine for your architecture looks exactly like this:

Python
import hashlib
import mysql.connector

def verify_tat_user(username, plain_text_password):
    # 1. Hash the incoming password with SHA-1
    hashed_input = hashlib.sha1(plain_text_password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
    
    # 2. Query the TAT database
    # (Connecting to the local MySQL instance, checking the users_credentials DB)
    cursor.execute("SELECT password FROM users_hashed WHERE username = %s", (username,))
    result = cursor.fetchone()
    
    # 3. Compare the hashes
    if result and result[0] == hashed_input:
        return True # Authentication Success!
    return False    # Authentication Failed
The Decision Point: Finalizing Sprint 2
This SHA-1 validation logic will serve as the brain for your Identity Access Management layer.

If we execute Path A (Linux PAM), we wrap this Python script in a command-line interface. The Linux OS will execute it in the background every time someone clicks "Sign In" on the native Gitea UI.

Lecture 14.2: Self-Registration vs. Automated Provisioning
The Approach You Proposed (Self-Registration)
How it works: You enable public registration. Developers go to http://10.30.121.51:444/, click "Register", and create their own username and password (which will be completely separate from the TAT DB). They log in, but see an empty screen. You (the Admin) get pinged, log in, find their new account, and manually add them to the TAT Organization and their specific team.

Is it valid? Yes, it is 100% valid. It requires zero custom scripting and works out of the box.

The Architectural Flaw (The Offboarding Risk): When a developer leaves the company or changes teams, someone deletes them from the main TAT Users DB. But because Gitea is disconnected, their Gitea account remains fully active with all source code access until you explicitly remember to go in and delete it. Furthermore, you are back to the manual "hassle" you wanted to avoid: manually clicking through menus to assign 7 teams worth of developers to their proper groups.

The Enterprise Approach (Path B: Identity Proxy + API Automation)
In modern infrastructure, we aim for Zero-Touch Provisioning.

If we use Path B (the lightweight Python/Flask microservice), we don't just automate the login; we can automate the team assignment as well.
Since building and maintaining internal enterprise web tools using Python and Flask is a highly effective way to manage network and user data, this path gives you absolute programmatic control over the workflow.

How it works:

The developer goes to Gitea. Apache intercepts and asks for their TAT credentials.

Your microservice checks the SHA-1 password against the users_hashed table.

(The Magic Step): If the password is correct, your script checks if this user is a "Spoke" or a "Developer".

Your script fires a silent REST API call to Gitea in the background: "Put this user in the TAT_Spokes team."

The script logs them in.

The Result: The developer logs in with their existing company password and instantly sees their repositories, fully authorized to merge or push, without you ever lifting a finger. If their password is revoked in the TAT DB, they instantly lose access to Gitea.

The Architect's Recommendation
If your priority right now is speed to delivery to just get the MVP running for the teams today, your proposed approach (Self-Registration + Manual Assignment) is the fastest way forward. You can literally turn it on in 5 seconds.

However, if your priority is building a scalable enterprise platform, you should stick with the Identity Proxy (Path B). It completely eliminates human error, solves the security offboarding problem, and automates the exact RBAC privilege assignments you asked about.

(If you make changes, remember to run sudo systemctl restart gitea).

Looking at the screenshot of your "New Team" page, Gitea is asking you to define the Baseline Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) for the team.

Here is the Architect's breakdown of what these options mean, followed by the exact configuration you need to satisfy your MVP.

Lecture 15.0: The Granular Permission Matrix
In older systems, you just made someone a "Reader" or a "Writer". Modern platforms like Gitea split a repository into distinct "Units" (Code, Issues, Actions, etc.) so you can give granular access.

Let's decode the options in your screenshot:

1. Repository Access

Specific repositories: (Recommended) The team can only see repositories you explicitly link to them. This is the safest enterprise default.

All repositories: The team can see every single repo in the TAT Organization.

Create repositories: Gives the team the right to create brand new buckets. (We usually reserve this for Admins).

2. Permission (The Big Switch)

General Access: Unlocks the table below so you can fine-tune exactly what they can do.

Administrator Access: Gives the team absolute power over the repo (deleting it, changing settings, renaming it). Never give this to standard developer teams.

3. The Unit Table (Allow Access to Repository Sections)

Code (Read vs. Write): Read allows git clone and git pull. Write allows git push.

Pull Requests (Read vs. Write): Read lets them view existing PRs. Write lets them open new PRs and comment on them.

The Rest (Wiki, Projects, Packages, Actions): These are the extra features we discussed earlier. If your MVP doesn't need them, turn them off to keep the UI clean for your developers.

The Execution: Configuring Your MVP Teams
Here is the secret to your specific MVP requirements: Both the TAT_Developers and TAT_SPOCS teams will have the exact same settings on this page.

Why? Because both teams need the ability to push code (feature branches) and open Pull Requests. The rule that "only SPOCS can merge to master" is not handled on this page. It is handled by Branch Protection later. This page just gives them the baseline ability to interact with the repository.

Step 1: Create the TAT_Developers Team
Fill out the form exactly like this:

Team Name: TAT_Developers

Repository access: Select Specific repositories.

Permission: Select General Access.

Unit Table Configuration:

Code: Select Write (So they can push feature branches).

Issues: Select Read (Or No Access, if you don't use Gitea for issue tracking).

Pull Requests: Select Write (So they can open a PR to ask for a merge).

Releases, Wiki, Projects, Packages, Actions: Select No Access (Keep the MVP clean).

Click Create Team.

Step 2: Create the TAT_SPOCS Team
Go back to the Teams tab, click New Team, and fill out the form exactly the same way:

Team Name: TAT_SPOCS

Repository access: Select Specific repositories.

Permission: Select General Access.

Unit Table Configuration: Code (Write), Pull Requests (Write), Everything else (No Access / Read).

Click Create Team.

Step 3: Link the Repository to the Teams
Now that the empty teams exist, we must drop the repository into their bucket.

Click on the TAT_Developers team.

Go to the Repositories tab.

Click Add Repository and select TAT_Test_Env.

Repeat this for the TAT_SPOCS team.

Lecture 16.0: Branch Protection (The Cryptographic Lock)
Right now, because both TAT_Developers and TAT_SPOCS have "Write" access, any member of those 7 teams can push code directly to your master branch.

We are going to configure a rule that tells the Gitea backend: "If anyone tries to alter the master branch, intercept the request. If they are trying to push directly, reject it. If they are trying to merge a Pull Request, check if they are in the TAT_SPOCS team. If they aren't, grey out the button."

The Execution: Configuring the master Lock

Disable push: Check this box.

A Platform Engineer never assumes a security policy works until they test it from the user's perspective.

This is a very sharp question. You are looking at the advanced pattern-matching engine of the Branch Protection system.

To answer your specific question first: No, this does not prevent developers from pushing badly named branches. It will not stop a developer from typing git checkout -b test-123 and pushing it.

Instead, these configurations control which branches and files receive the "Security Lock" we just talked about (disabling pushes and restricting merges to SPOCS).

Let's apply the Architect's Protocol and break down exactly what each of these three text boxes does so you can decide if you need them for your MVP.

Lecture 16.1: Glob Patterns and Micro-Permissions
Instead of creating a single rule for exactly one branch (like master), Gitea allows you to use wildcards (called "Glob syntax") to apply security rules dynamically to hundreds of branches or specific files at once.

1. Protected Branch Name Pattern
What it does: Applies your security rules to any branch that matches this text pattern.

The Enterprise Use Case: Let's say your 7 teams maintain multiple versions of the Vodafone platform simultaneously. You have branches named release/v1.0, release/v1.1, and release/v2.0. Instead of creating three separate protection rules, you type release/* in this box. Gitea will automatically lock down any branch that starts with release/, past, present, or future.

(For your current MVP, you can just type master here).

2. Protected file patterns
What it does: Locks down specific files inside the repository, even against people who normally have Write access to the branch.

The Enterprise Use Case: Imagine you have an infrastructure configuration file called database-config.yml. You want the SPOCS to be able to merge normal code to master, but you never want anyone to accidentally alter the database IP. You would put database-config.yml in this box. Even if a SPOC tries to merge a PR that edits this file, Gitea will reject it.

3. Unprotected file patterns
What it does: The exact opposite of the above. It creates a "loophole" in your protected branch.

The Enterprise Use Case: You locked down the master branch completely. But what if a developer just needs to fix a spelling mistake in the README.md file? It seems like a waste of time to force the SPOC to review a typo. If you type README.md in this box, Gitea will allow standard developers to push changes directly to the master branch, but only if the commit exclusively contains changes to the README.

How to Enforce Branch Naming Conventions
If your true goal is to control the branch names that are pushed (e.g., forcing developers to name their branches feat/ticket-123 and blocking them if they use ahmed-test), that cannot be done on this screen.

To achieve that, you would need to use a Git Pre-Receive Hook. This is a custom shell script that sits on the Linux VM. When a developer pushes, the script reads the branch name, checks it against a Regular Expression (Regex), and rejects the entire push if the name is non-compliant.

Your Next Step

Type exactly master into the Protected Branch Name Pattern box.

Leave the File Pattern boxes completely empty.

Scroll down, configure the "Disable push" and "Enable merge whitelist" (selecting TAT_SPOCS) as we discussed previously.
