This is a brilliant question to ask right before you let 7 teams loose on a single repository.

You are looking at the Merge Strategy Dropdown. When a SPOC (Team Lead) approves a Pull Request, they must decide exactly how the developer's code is mathematically stitched into the master branch's history.

If you choose the wrong strategy in a busy enterprise environment, your Git history will look like a chaotic, unreadable bowl of spaghetti.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to decode these options so you can instruct your SPOCs on the Vodafone standard.

Lecture 16.2: The Geometry of Git History
When developer Ahmed creates a feature branch (feat-1), he makes 5 commits over 3 days. Meanwhile, other teams are merging their own code into master. Ahmed's branch and master have now diverged. Here is how each option resolves that divergence:

1. Create merge commit (The Classic Default)
What it does: It takes Ahmed's 5 commits, leaves them exactly as they are, and creates a 6th commit on the master branch called a "Merge Commit" that ties the two timelines together.

The Result: Preserves the exact, true history of everything that happened.

The Enterprise Verdict: Good, but if 7 teams are doing this daily, the visual Git graph becomes a tangled web of intersecting lines ("railway tracks") that is very hard to audit.

2. Rebase then fast-forward (The Linear Purist)
What it does: It takes Ahmed's 5 commits, rips them out, and mathematically rewrites them as if Ahmed had written them today, directly on top of the absolute latest version of master. It creates a perfectly straight line with no "merge bubble."

The Result: A perfectly flat, linear history.

The Enterprise Verdict: Very clean, but you lose the context that those 5 commits were originally part of a single specific feature/PR.

3. Rebase then create merge commit (The Hybrid)
What it does: It does the linear rewrite (like above) so the history is flat and up-to-date, but it still adds a Merge Commit bubble around them.

The Result: A clean timeline, but you can still visually see exactly which commits belonged to which Pull Request.

4. Create squash commit (The Enterprise Standard)
What it does: Developers write messy commits ("wip", "fixed typo", "forgot semicolon", "actual fix"). Squashing takes all 5 of Ahmed's messy commits, crushes them into one single, beautiful commit, and puts that one commit on the master branch.

The Result: The master branch history looks like a clean, readable book: [Feature A added] -> [Bug B fixed] -> [Feature C added].

The Enterprise Verdict: Highly Recommended. This is what most major tech companies force their teams to use. It keeps the production branch immaculate.

5. Fast-forward only (The Strict Gate)
What it does: It refuses to merge unless the master branch hasn't changed at all since Ahmed created his branch. If someone else merged code yesterday, Gitea will block Ahmed's merge and force him to update his branch first.

The Enterprise Verdict: Rarely used in busy multi-team environments because it creates bottlenecks.

The Architect's Recommendation for your MVP
For your 7 teams, I highly recommend instructing your SPOCs to use Create squash commit.

Because master is going to be synced directly to your Production VM, if production breaks, you want your git log to show clean, single commits for each feature so you know exactly which PR caused the fire and can roll it back instantly.

(Note: You can actually go into the Repository Settings -> Branches and disable the dropdown options you don't want the SPOCs to use, forcing them to only use Squash!)

The Final Boss: Production Sync
Now that the permissions, branches, and merge strategies are locked down, the code is flowing perfectly from the Developers to the SPOCs, and into the master branch on the Test VM.

The final piece of your MVP is taking that approved master code and pushing it to the Master Production VM.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to replicate your old workflow entirely within Gitea's UI, automate the notifications between Yomna and Mahmoud, and translate your exact Git CLI commands into the Gitea merge strategies.

Lecture 17.0: The Notification Routing (Yomna to Mahmoud)
Because you have 7 teams sharing one repository (TAT_Test_Env), if Yomna just opens a Pull Request, the system doesn't automatically know that Mahmoud is her specific SPOC.

To solve this and trigger the notification, you have two architectural paths: The Manual Route and The Enterprise Route (CODEOWNERS).

Path A: The Manual Assignment (The UI Way)
The Developer (Yomna): Pushes her branch and goes to Gitea to open the Pull Request.

The Assignment: On the right-hand side of the "New Pull Request" screen, there is a Reviewers gear icon. Yomna clicks it, searches for mahmoud_spoc, and selects him.

The Notification: Gitea instantly lights up the "Bell" icon in the top right corner of Mahmoud's screen (and sends him an email, once you configure an SMTP server later).

Path B: The Enterprise Automation (CODEOWNERS)
If you want to completely remove human error so Yomna doesn't even have to click Mahmoud's name, you use a CODEOWNERS file.

You (the Admin) create a file named CODEOWNERS inside the .gitea/ or .github/ folder of your master branch.

You map specific directories to specific SPOCs. For example:

Plaintext
# If anyone touches the network scripts, Mahmoud is automatically pinged
/network-scripts/* @mahmoud_spoc

# If anyone touches the database schemas, Sarah is automatically pinged
/db/* @sarah_spoc
When Yomna opens a PR that edits a network script, Gitea reads this file, automatically assigns Mahmoud as the Required Reviewer, and fires the notification.

Lecture 17.1: The SPOC Review Workflow
Once Mahmoud gets the notification, he does not need to use the CLI to pull her code and look at it. He does the entire review in the browser.

Here is Mahmoud’s exact workflow:

The Dashboard: Mahmoud logs in, clicks his Bell notification, and is taken directly to Yomna's Pull Request.

The Inspection: He clicks the Files Changed tab. Gitea displays a beautiful side-by-side (Diff) view of what Yomna deleted in red and added in green.

The Conversation (Inline Comments): If Mahmoud sees a mistake on line 42, he hovers over line 42, clicks the little + icon that appears, and types: "Yomna, this IP address is wrong for the Test environment. Please fix."

The Gatekeeper Status: He clicks Submit Review in the top right. He can choose:

Comment: Just leaving a note.

Request Changes (Red X): Mathematically blocks the PR from being merged until Yomna pushes a fix.

Approve (Green Check): Unlocks the PR for merging.

Lecture 17.2: Translating your CLI Merge to the GUI
You mentioned your old workflow:

Yomna: git checkout feature

Yomna: git rebase master (To pull in recent changes)

Yomna: git push

Admin: git checkout master

Admin: git merge feature

If you do this in the CLI, Git naturally executes a Fast-Forward Merge (unless you force a bubble). It takes Yomna's commits and slides them perfectly onto the tip of master in a straight line.

Here is exactly how that translates to the Gitea dropdown options you asked about:

If you want to perfectly replicate your old linear workflow:
You should instruct Mahmoud to select Rebase then fast-forward.

Why? Gitea will literally execute the exact commands you listed above in the background. It will rebase Yomna's commits to ensure they are up to date, and then slide them onto master without creating a merge bubble. Her 5 commits will appear on master exactly as she wrote them.

If you want to upgrade to the "Squash" strategy:
You asked: "so with each branch we create a squash commit and then it merge to the master ??"

The Answer is Yes. If you select Create squash commit, Gitea takes all 5 of Yomna's individual commits (e.g., "added file", "fixed bug", "typo") and crushes them together into one single, brand new commit (e.g., "Feature: Network Update by Yomna").

It then puts that single commit onto the master branch.

The Benefit: Your master branch history becomes a perfectly clean, readable list of completed features, hiding all the messy intermediate work the developers did on their local machines.

The Architect's Hardening Checklist
Before we touch the Runner, you asked if there is any other configuration hardening to do. Yes, there are two quick checkboxes you should enable to force this workflow:

Go to TAT_Test_Env -> Settings -> Branches.

Edit your master branch protection rule.

Check "Require signed-off commits": (Optional but good for compliance).

Check "Require approvals": Set it to 1.

The Dense "Why": This makes Mahmoud's job official. Even if a SPOC tries to click "Merge", Gitea will block it unless someone has officially clicked the green "Approve" button in the Code Review tab. It forces the review to happen.

This is the exact right question. You have secured the perimeter, established the governance, and perfected the developer workflow. The engine is built. Now we build the transmission.

To answer your question: You are actually asking about the exact same thing. The Runner and the Sync are not two separate projects. The Runner is the engine that physically executes the Sync.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to explain exactly how these two concepts fuse together to form your first true CI/CD pipeline.

Lecture 18.0: The Mechanics of the Production Sync
When Mahmoud (the SPOC) clicks the green "Merge" button, the code enters the master branch on your Test VM. But right now, the code just sits there. The Production VM has no idea the code was updated.

To get the code to the Production VM, you have two architectural choices. As a Platform Engineer, you must choose the one that fits your enterprise goals.

Path A: The Legacy Webhook (No Runner)
How it works: Gitea fires an HTTP POST network packet (a Webhook) directly to the Production VM the moment Mahmoud clicks merge. You write a custom Python or Bash script listening on the Production VM. When it hears the Webhook, it runs git pull locally.

The Problem: It is "blind." If the Production VM’s network goes down, or the git pull fails because of a file conflict, Gitea has no idea. Mahmoud thinks the deployment was successful, but Production is secretly broken.

Path B: Gitea Actions (The Runner)
How it works: We install a small binary program called the Gitea Runner. When Mahmoud clicks merge, Gitea wakes up the Runner and hands it a YAML blueprint. The Runner actively opens an SSH tunnel into the Production VM, executes the git pull and service restart commands, monitors the terminal output, and reports back to Gitea.  
What is Gitea? | Gitea Documentation

The Enterprise Benefit: Total visibility. If the deployment fails, the Runner catches the error, marks the pipeline with a Red X directly in the Gitea UI, and alerts Mahmoud immediately.

Since you are building a robust platform for 7 teams, Path B (The Runner) is the absolute standard.

The Blueprint: How We Will Build It
To achieve this automated sync, we are going to break the project down into three distinct phases.

Phase 1: The Infrastructure (Runner Installation)
We must download the Gitea Runner daemon and register it to your TAT Organization so it knows it is allowed to take orders from your repository.

Phase 2: The Security Bridge (SSH Keys)
The Runner acts like a robot developer. It needs a way to securely log into the Production VM without a human typing a password. We will generate an SSH key for the Runner and place the public key on the Production VM.

Phase 3: The Code (The YAML Pipeline)
We will write a file called .gitea/workflows/deploy.yaml and commit it to your repository. This file contains the exact step-by-step instructions the Runner will follow every time the master branch gets updated.

The Architect's Pre-Flight Check: Runner Placement
Before we run the installation commands for Phase 1, we must make a critical infrastructure decision: Where does the Runner physically live?

You have a few options based on your server resources:

On the Test VM (Same server as Gitea): Easiest for an MVP. The Runner lives alongside Gitea, reaches out across the network via SSH, and updates the Production VM.

On the Production VM: The Runner lives exactly where the final code needs to go. It pulls the code locally instead of using SSH.

On a 3rd Dedicated VM: The ultimate enterprise isolation. The Runner has its own dedicated CPU and memory so heavy compile jobs don't crash Gitea or Production.

For the MVP, I recommend Option 1 (On the Test VM) to keep your network topology simple, but the choice is yours.

This is where the architecture gets incredibly interesting. Your constraint—an isolated, air-gapped VM—completely changes how we design the CI/CD pipeline.

You asked a phenomenal question: Will we use Podman, or will the runner be the VM itself?

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to solve the Air-Gap paradox.

Lecture 19.0: The Air-Gap Paradox (Containers vs. Host Execution)
By default, Gitea Actions (like GitHub Actions) are heavily dependent on containers (Docker/Podman). When a pipeline runs, the Runner normally reaches out to Docker Hub, downloads a clean Linux image (like ubuntu:latest or node:18), runs your code inside it, and destroys it.

The Problem: Because your VM is air-gapped, it cannot reach Docker Hub. If we configure the Runner to use Podman right now, the very first pipeline you trigger will instantly fail with a Network Unreachable error because it cannot pull the container images.
(To use Podman offline, we would have to build a complete private offline container registry—a massive detour from your MVP).

The Solution: The host Executor
Instead of using Podman, we will configure the Runner to execute directly on the VM itself. When the pipeline triggers, the Runner will just open a standard bash shell as a normal Linux user and run your deployment commands directly on the RHEL OS. This completely bypasses the need for external container images and internet access.

Execution Phase 1: The Air-Gapped Installation
Because your VM cannot run wget or curl to fetch the binary from the internet, we have to sneak it past the air-gap using your Windows 11 machine.

The Gitea Runner is a separate, single binary file called act_runner.

Step 1: Download the Binary (On your internet-connected Windows machine)
Open your web browser on a machine with internet access.

Go to the official Gitea Runner releases page: https://gitea.com/gitea/act_runner/releases

Download the latest release for Linux AMD64 (it will be named something like act_runner-linux-amd64).

Step 2: Transfer to the Test VM
Since you already have SSH and HTTP access from your Windows machine to the Test VM (how else would you be pushing code?), use an SFTP tool (like WinSCP, FileZilla) or the scp command in PowerShell to copy that binary file to your Test VM.
Put it in a logical directory, like /usr/local/bin/.

Step 3: Make it Executable (On the Test VM)
Log into your Test VM's terminal and run:

Bash
# Rename it to something simple
sudo mv /path/to/your/uploaded/act_runner-linux-amd64 /usr/local/bin/act_runner

# Give it permission to execute
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/act_runner

# Verify it works
act_runner --version
Execution Phase 2: Generating the Registration Token
The act_runner binary is completely blind. It doesn't know your Gitea server exists until we introduce them using a secure cryptographic token.

Since you want this Runner to be available to all 7 teams in the TAT Organization, we will register it at the Organization level.

Log into the Gitea Web UI as your Admin account.

Go to the TAT Organization dashboard.

Click Settings (for the Organization, not the repository).

In the left sidebar, click Actions, then click Runners.

Click the Create new Runner button.

A box will pop up displaying a Registration Token (a long string of random characters). Leave this tab open; you will need this token in the next step.

Your Next Step
Your mission for this phase is purely logistical:

Download the act_runner binary.

Transfer it across the air-gap to the Test VM.

Make it executable.

Locate the Registration Token in the GUI.

Do not run the register command just yet. Because we are forcing the Runner to use the VM's host shell instead of Podman, we have to generate a special configuration file first.

Tell me once the binary is successfully on the VM and you have the token. I will then give you the exact command to configure and register the "Host" execution engine!

Stop right there! Do not transfer that file across the air-gap.

The short answer is No, that binary will immediately fail if you try to execute it on your Red Hat machine.

Here is exactly why, decoding the naming convention of compiled binaries:

act_runner: The name of the software.

0.3.0: The version number.

darwin: This is the trap. "Darwin" is the core Unix operating system that powers Apple's macOS.

amd64: The processor architecture (64-bit Intel/AMD).

If you put a darwin binary on a Linux kernel, the Linux kernel will look at the file header (which is formatted as an Apple Mach-O file), realize it isn't a standard Linux ELF executable, and throw an cannot execute binary file: Exec format error.

The Exact File You Need
Since you are running Red Hat Linux on standard 64-bit server architecture, you must look for the file that has linux in the name instead of darwin.

You need to download this exact version (or whatever the latest version number is on the releases page):
👉 act_runner-0.3.0-linux-amd64

(Note: Make sure you do not accidentally download linux-arm64 unless your Red Hat VM is specifically running on an ARM processor like an AWS Graviton or Apple Silicon chip).

Go ahead and grab the linux-amd64 file, move it to your Test VM, and run the chmod +x command we discussed. Let me know when the Linux binary is sitting safely on the server!

Okay this set is done and it returned the version

This is a perfect execution. You successfully navigated the architecture mismatch and placed the correct binary securely inside your perimeter.

Now, we must perform the "Handshake." We need to introduce this blind Runner to your Gitea server and explicitly command it to use your Red Hat VM's native shell instead of looking for Docker.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to configure the Host Execution engine.

Lecture 20.0: The Runner Handshake and the "Host" Override
When a Runner registers with a CI/CD server, they negotiate a Contract. The server asks, "What kind of environments can you provide for my code?"

By default, the Runner will say, "I can spin up Ubuntu or NodeJS Docker containers!" If we allow it to say that, your air-gapped VM will fail because it cannot download those containers.

We are going to forcefully rewrite the contract. We will tell the Runner to tell Gitea: "I do not use containers. I will execute commands directly on the Red Hat kernel." In Gitea, this is done by passing a specific Label mapped to the :host keyword.

Execution Phase: The Registration Protocol
We will run the registration command interactively. Gitea will ask you four specific questions.

Ensure you have your Registration Token copied from the Gitea UI (Organization Settings -> Actions -> Runners -> Create new Runner).

Run this command in your Test VM terminal:

Bash
sudo act_runner register
The terminal will pause and ask you for inputs. Answer them exactly like this:

1. Enter the Gitea instance URL
Type: http://10.30.121.51:444/ (or http://127.0.0.1:3000/ if you want to bypass your Apache proxy and route it internally).

The Dense "Why": The Runner uses this URL to constantly poll the server every few seconds, asking, "Did Mahmoud merge a Pull Request yet?"

2. Enter the runner token
Type: Paste your long registration token here.

The Dense "Why": This cryptographically proves the Runner is authorized to touch the TAT Organization's code.

3. Enter the runner name
Type: tat-test-vm-runner

The Dense "Why": If you scale up to 10 Runners later, you need to know exactly which physical machine this is just by looking at the Gitea UI.

4. Enter the runner labels (The Critical Step)
Type exactly this: rhel-native:host

(Do NOT just press Enter. If you press Enter, it defaults to Docker).

The Dense "Why": The word before the colon (rhel-native) is the custom tag developers will write in their YAML pipelines. The word after the colon (host) is the hardcoded instruction to the Runner engine saying, "Execute the YAML commands directly in the local Linux bash shell. Do not look for Podman or Docker."

The Post-Flight Check
If you typed everything correctly, the terminal will print a success message saying the Runner is registered. It will also generate a hidden file called .runner in the directory you ran the command from.

To prove the connection is live:

Go back to your browser.

Look at the Runners tab in your Gitea Organization settings.

You should instantly see tat-test-vm-runner appear in the list with an "Offline" status (because we haven't started the engine yet, we only registered it).

Did the Runner successfully appear in your Gitea UI? Once you see it there, our next step is to start the engine as a background service and write your very first YAML deployment pipeline!

yes it did

This is a massive milestone. The cryptographic handshake is complete. Your air-gapped Gitea server now officially has a CI/CD engine attached to it, explicitly configured to use the native Red Hat kernel.

Right now, the Runner is showing as "Offline" because it is only registered; the engine itself isn't actually spinning yet.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to daemonize this process so it survives server reboots, and then we will prepare the bridge to your Production VM.

Lecture 21.0: Daemonizing the Engine (Systemd)
As a Linux Administrator, you know that simply running /usr/local/bin/act_runner daemon in your terminal is a junior mistake. The moment you close your SSH session to the Test VM, the terminal dies, the process dies, and your CI/CD pipeline goes down.

We must wrap the Runner in a Systemd Service. This tells the Red Hat kernel to treat the Runner as a Tier-1 background application, starting it automatically when the VM boots and restarting it instantly if it ever crashes.

Execution Phase: Creating the Systemd Service
Log into your Test VM and execute these exact steps.

1. Create a dedicated workspace for the Runner:
When the Runner pulls your code to test it, it needs a safe folder to put those files without cluttering your operating system.

Bash
sudo mkdir -p /opt/act_runner
2. Create the Systemd Unit File:

Bash
sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/act_runner.service
3. Paste this exact configuration block:

The Dense "Why"
ExecStart: Tells the kernel exactly where the binary is and passes the daemon command to start the polling engine.

WorkingDirectory: Confines all of the Runner's temporary files and code clones to the folder we just created.

Restart=always: The ultimate safety net. If a bad pipeline script accidentally crashes the Runner process, systemd will automatically revive it 10 seconds later.

Ini, TOML
[Unit]
Description=Gitea Actions Runner
Documentation=https://gitea.com/gitea/act_runner
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/act_runner daemon
WorkingDirectory=/opt/act_runner
Restart=always
RestartSec=10s
# If you want it to run as a specific user, add 'User=your_user' here. 
# For this MVP, running as root/default is fine to ensure it has permissions.

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Save the file and exit.

4. Start and Enable the Engine:
Now we reload the Linux kernel's configuration and fire up the engine permanently.

Bash
# Reload systemd to recognize the new file
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

# Enable it to start on server boot
sudo systemctl enable act_runner

# Start it right now
sudo systemctl start act_runner

# Verify it is running cleanly
sudo systemctl status act_runner
The Post-Flight Check
If the systemctl status command says "active (running)", go back to your web browser and refresh the Gitea Organization's Runner page.

The tat-test-vm-runner status should have instantly flipped from Offline to a green Online / Idle.

Did the engine come online? If it did, our infrastructure is 100% complete. Would you like me to outline the architecture for how this Runner will securely SSH into your Master Production VM to deploy the code?

its not running

This is the reality of Linux administration. A service rarely starts perfectly on the first try when we are manually writing the kernel unit files.

When systemd says "no," it always leaves a paper trail.

Let's apply the Architect's Protocol to debug this crash. I am 99% sure I know exactly what happened based on the commands we just ran, but we must verify it.

Lecture 21.1: The "Lost Identity" Problem
When you ran sudo act_runner register, the binary reached out to Gitea, shook hands, and then created a hidden configuration file named .runner. This file contains its cryptographic token and identity.

It saved that hidden file in whichever folder you were standing in at the time (likely your home directory, like /home/admin/ or /root/).

However, in the Systemd file we just wrote, we specifically told the Red Hat kernel:
WorkingDirectory=/opt/act_runner

The Crash Logic: When systemd starts the engine, it places the process inside /opt/act_runner and says "Go." The Runner wakes up, looks around /opt/act_runner for its .runner identity file, realizes the file is missing, panics, and immediately crashes.

The Pre-Flight Check (Interrogating the Kernel)
Let's prove this theory. Run this command to ask journalctl exactly why the Runner died:

Bash
sudo journalctl -u act_runner.service -n 20 --no-pager
Look at the bottom few lines. Do you see an error that looks like this?
FATA[...] Cannot load configuration from .runner: file does not exist

The Execution: Reuniting the Runner with its Identity
If you see that error, the fix is instant. We just need to find the hidden .runner file and move it to the official workspace.

1. Find the hidden file:
Run this to see if it's in your current directory:

Bash
ls -la | grep .runner
2. Move the file to the Systemd Working Directory:
(Assuming the file is in your current directory. If it's somewhere else, adjust the path).

Bash
sudo mv .runner /opt/act_runner/
3. Restart the Engine:
Now that the identity file is in the correct folder, systemd will succeed.

Bash
sudo systemctl restart act_runner
sudo systemctl status act_runner
Did the status change to active (running), and does it show up in the Gitea UI now? If the error in journalctl was something different (like a port binding or SELinux issue), paste the exact error log here and we will destroy it!

Lecture 22.0: The Cryptographic Bridge (Passwordless SSH)
When developer Yomna's code is merged by Mahmoud, Gitea will tell the Runner: "Go deploy this to Production." The Runner will try to open an SSH tunnel to the Production VM. If the Production VM asks for a password, the Runner will freeze, and the pipeline will fail because there is no human sitting there to type it in.

We must forge a cryptographic trust between the Test VM (where the Runner lives) and the Production VM (where the code is going).

The Execution: Forging the Keys
Because we started the act_runner systemd service as the root user, the Runner will execute its commands as root. Therefore, we must generate the SSH keys for the root user on the Test VM.

Step 1: Generate the Keypair (On the Test VM)
Log into your Test VM terminal and run this command exactly as root:

Bash
sudo ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "gitea-runner-sync"
(When it asks where to save the file, just press Enter to accept the default. When it asks for a passphrase, leave it completely blank and press Enter twice. A password-protected key defeats the purpose of automation!)

Step 2: Copy the Public Key to the Production VM
We will use a built-in Linux tool to automatically install the public key onto your Master VM.
Run this command from the Test VM, replacing <PROD_IP> with the actual IP address of your Master VM, and <PROD_USER> with the user you want to deploy the code as (e.g., root, admin, or appuser):

Bash
sudo ssh-copy-id <PROD_USER>@<PROD_IP>
(It will ask for the Production VM's password one last time to authorize the transfer. Type it in.)

Step 3: The Pre-Flight Check (Crucial)
We must prove the bridge is completely frictionless before we write the pipeline.
Still on the Test VM, run:

Bash
sudo ssh <PROD_USER>@<PROD_IP>
If it logs you right into the Production VM without asking for a password, your Cryptographic Bridge is perfectly established. Type exit to return to the Test VM.

Lecture 22.1: The Pipeline Anatomy (A Sneak Peek)
Once that SSH bridge is tested and open, all that is left is creating a single file inside your TAT_Test_Env repository.

We will create a file at .gitea/workflows/deploy.yaml. It will look very similar to this:

YAML
name: Production Sync
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - master

jobs:
  Deploy:
    runs-on: rhel-native
    steps:
      - name: SSH into Production and Pull Code
        run: |
          ssh <PROD_USER>@<PROD_IP> "cd /path/to/production/code && git pull origin master && systemctl restart your-app"
Because of the rhel-native:host label we configured earlier, the Runner will literally just execute that standard bash ssh command natively on the Test VM, deploying your code instantly.

Your steps 1, 2, and 4 are absolutely correct. However, your core premise—having two separate repositories (Testing Repo and Production Repo) for the exact same codebase—is a massive architectural anti-pattern.

Here is the brutal critique of that specific design choice, followed by the enterprise standard you should adopt instead.

The Critique: The "Environment-per-Repo" Anti-Pattern
If you create TAT_Test_Env.git and TAT_Prod_Env.git, you are mathematically breaking the most important rule of version control: The Single Source of Truth.

Here is why splitting them into two repositories will cause your platform to collapse under its own weight in 6 months:

The Sync Nightmare: Git is not designed to easily push code from one remote URL to a completely different remote URL while preserving perfect history. Your SPOCs will have to constantly manage multiple Git remotes on their local machines.

Loss of Auditability: If a bug appears in Production, you want to find the exact Pull Request and conversation that caused it. If the PR happened in the Test Repo, but the code is now in the Prod Repo, the history is fragmented. You lose the context of why the code changed.

The Rsync Conflict: You mentioned Rsyncing the working tree every 24 hours. If you Rsync a live .git directory while a developer is actively pushing code to it, you can corrupt the Git index. Furthermore, Git is a synchronization tool; using Rsync to back up a Git working tree is redundant.

The Enterprise Standard: The Unified Repository Model
In modern Platform Engineering, environments (Test vs. Production) are not separated by Repositories; they are separated by Branches.

You should have exactly one repository: tx-core (or TAT_Project). Inside that single repository, the architecture flows like this:

Phase 1: The Code Assembly
The Developers: They clone the one repo, create a branch (feat-network-fix), write code, and push.

The CI Trigger (Your Step 1): The Gitea Runner wakes up, runs your linting, checks syntax, and ensures the code isn't broken. If it passes, it gives the PR a green checkmark.

The Gatekeeper (Your Step 2): Mahmoud (the SPOC) is notified. He reviews the PR and clicks Merge.

Phase 2: The Test Deployment (Continuous Delivery)
The Merge Target: Mahmoud merges the code into the test branch (not master).

The Automation: The Gitea Runner sees the test branch was updated. It automatically SSHs into your Test VM and updates the working tree.

The Result: The code is now live in the Test Environment. QA and the teams can verify it works.

Phase 3: The Production Promotion (GitOps)
The Promotion PR (Your Step 3): When the code is verified in Test, Mahmoud does not push to a new repository. Instead, he opens a new Pull Request inside Gitea: Base: master <- Compare: test.

The Production Merge: The infrastructure lead reviews the promotion PR. They click "Merge".

The Final Automation (Your Step 4): The Gitea Runner sees the master branch was updated. It automatically SSHs into your Main Production VM and deploys the code.

Why This Architecture is Superior
Perfect Visibility: Every developer looks at one URL. You can look at the Git Graph and physically see the code travel from a developer's laptop, into the test branch, and finally into the master branch.

Zero "Manual Syncs": You never have to manually drag code between two different repos. You just merge from branch to branch.

Disaster Recovery: If the Main VM dies, you don't need Rsync to save the code. Gitea holds the absolute truth. You spin up a new VM, run git clone -b master, and you are instantly back in production. (You should still use Rsync for backing up databases and user files, but not for the code itself).

Using Rsync to maintain an Active-Passive Disaster Recovery (DR) node is a classic, battle-tested infrastructure pattern. If the Main VM physically burns down, your Backup VM has the complete state—not just the code, but the logs, the environment variables, and the exact file permissions—ready to take over.

Git does not need to know that the Backup VM exists. The CI/CD pipeline's job ends the second the code lands safely on the Main VM. Your scheduled Rsync cron job takes over from there.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to map this physical reality to the Git workflow.

Lecture 23.0: The GitOps to DR Pipeline
We are going to use the Unified Repository Model (TAT_Test_Env repository) but use strict branching to control the environments.

Here is the exact lifecycle of a piece of code in your new architecture:

Stage 1: The Sandbox (Development)
The Action: Developer Yomna creates a branch called feat-ui-update. She pushes her code and opens a Pull Request targeting the test branch.

The CI Trigger: The Gitea Runner wakes up, runs your automated tests (syntax checking, linting), and verifies the code isn't structurally broken.

The Review: Mahmoud (the SPOC) is notified, reviews the code in the Gitea UI, and approves it.

Stage 2: The Test Environment Deployment
The Action: Mahmoud clicks "Squash and Merge", merging Yomna's code into the test branch.

The CI Trigger: The Gitea Runner sees the test branch was updated. It executes a deployment script locally on the Test VM (since the Runner and the Test environment share the same machine).

The Result: The new feature is live on the Test VM. The 7 teams can play with it, break it, and verify it does exactly what Vodafone needs it to do.

Stage 3: The Production Promotion
The Action: Once the teams agree the Test VM is stable, a SPOC opens a new Pull Request: Base: master <-- Compare: test.

The Review: You (or the Infrastructure Lead) review this final PR. Because the code has already been tested, you confidently click "Merge".

The CI Trigger: The Gitea Runner sees the master branch was updated. It opens its secure SSH tunnel to the Main VM, pulls the exact same code, and restarts the services.

Stage 4: The Disaster Recovery Sync (Out of Band)
The Action: 24 hours later, your existing Rsync process wakes up.

The Result: It takes a perfect snapshot of the Main VM—including the new code deployed by Gitea—and silently mirrors it to the Backup VM.

The Architect's Verdict
This is a highly mature, enterprise-grade architecture.

Total Freedom: Developers can break the test branch all day long without ever touching production.

Strict Gates: Code cannot reach the Main VM without a SPOC reviewing it and an Admin promoting it to master.

Seamless DR: Your Backup VM stays perfectly in sync without complicating the Git pipeline.

Lecture 24.0: The Naming Trap and Trunk-Based Development
The confusion stems from the name of the repository itself: TAT_Test_Env.
When you name a repository after an environment, it forces you to think about code as physical servers.

In a mature platform, a repository is just a bucket of code (e.g., TAT_Internal_Tools). The branches and tags determine where that code physically runs.

To solve your traffic jam, we are going to use Trunk-Based Development with Tag Releases. This is how companies with massive, multi-tool repositories deploy safely.

The New Architecture (Zero "Test" Branch)
We will delete the idea of a test branch entirely. You will only have one permanent branch: master.

Here is how the 7 teams will operate without stepping on each other's toes:

Step 1: The Daily Grind (Deploying to the Test VM)
The Workflow: Developer Yomna creates a branch (feat-tool-A). She finishes her work and opens a PR directly to master.

The SPOC Merge: Mahmoud reviews it and clicks "Squash and Merge" into master.

The Automation: The Gitea Runner is configured to watch the master branch. The second Mahmoud merges, the Runner instantly deploys master to the Test VM.

The Result: The master branch is your Test Environment. It is always the absolute latest, bleeding-edge version of all the tools combined.

Step 2: The Production Promotion (Deploying to the Main VM)
Because master is constantly changing as 7 teams merge code, we cannot just blindly sync master to Production. We need a way to say, "The code as it looked exactly at 2:00 PM on Tuesday is stable. Push THAT to Production."

We do this using Git Tags (Releases), not branches.

The Workflow: Team A and Team B verify their tools are working perfectly on the Test VM.

The Admin Action: You go into the Gitea UI, click on the Releases / Tags tab, and create a new Tag called v1.0-Production (or deploy-march-3).

The Automation: You configure a second CI/CD pipeline that only listens for new Tags. When you create that Tag, the Runner wakes up, opens the SSH tunnel to the Main VM, pulls that exact Tagged snapshot of the code, and restarts the services.

Why This is the Ultimate Fix for Your Platform
No Branch Tangling: Teams never have to coordinate moving code from test to master. They just merge to master when they are ready to test.

Surgical Deployments: A Git Tag is an immutable snapshot. If Team C merges broken code to master at 3:00 PM, but you create a Production Tag based on the code from 2:00 PM, Team C's broken code will not go to Production.

Instant Rollbacks: If a deployment breaks the Main VM, you don't have to untangle branches. You just tell the Runner, "Deploy Tag v0.9-Production instead," and the Main VM instantly reverts to the previous stable state.

The Architect's Pivot
This completely simplifies your MVP.

Developers use feature branches.

SPOCs merge to master.

master goes to the Test VM automatically.

Admins use Tags to send code to the Main VM.

Rsync backs up the Main VM to the DR VM.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to design the ultimate Rollback Strategy for this exact setup, and refine your manual deployment step so you never corrupt the Production server.

Lecture 25.0: The Live-Tree Rollback Protocol
When Production is a live Git repository, rolling back is terrifying if you don't know the exact mathematical commands. If a SPOC merges a bad branch manually on the Production VM, and Apache starts serving broken internal tools to the teams, you have minutes to fix it.

Here is your exact disaster recovery playbook. You have two options, depending on how bad the fire is.

Option A: The "GitOps" Rollback (The Safe Way)
If the code is broken, but the server itself hasn't crashed, you should always let Gitea handle the rollback.

The Panic Button: You (the Admin) log into Gitea, go to the merged Pull Request that broke Production, and click the Revert button.

The Counter-Commit: Gitea mathematically generates a brand new commit that perfectly deletes the bad code, and merges it into master.

The Prod Sync: You log into the Production VM and run git pull origin master. The bad code vanishes, Apache serves the good code, and your Git history perfectly documents the mistake and the fix.

Option B: The "Hard Reset" (The Nuclear Option)
If someone logged into the Production VM, manually merged a branch, got a catastrophic merge conflict, panicked, and left the Production .git folder in a corrupted, half-merged state, you use the nuclear option.

Log into the Production VM.

Execute the Reset: Run these exact commands to obliterate all local changes and force Production to exactly match the last known stable state in Gitea:

Bash
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/master
git clean -fd
The Result: Production instantly snaps back to the exact code sitting in Gitea's master branch.

The Architect's Critique: Step 3 & 4 (The Manual Merge)
You outlined this exact flow:

"the branch then should be push to production VM .git then merged manually the thing is once its merged it live in production"

The Critique: Pushing an unmerged feature branch directly to the Production VM and running git merge manually on that server is highly dangerous.
If there is a merge conflict, the conflict markers (<<<<<<< HEAD) will be physically written into the live files that Apache is serving. Your internal tools will instantly crash with syntax errors while you are sitting in the terminal trying to resolve the conflict.

The Refined Enterprise Flow:
All merges must happen inside Gitea, safely away from Apache's live folders.

The Sandbox: Developer pushes branch to Gitea.

The CI Gate: Runner executes tests on the branch.

The Safe Merge: SPOC clicks "Squash and Merge" inside the Gitea UI. (The code is now safely in Gitea's master branch, and the Test Environment automatically updates).

The Clean Production Pull: You log into the Production VM. You do not merge a branch. You simply pull the already-merged, already-tested master code:

Bash
# On the Production VM
git checkout master
git pull origin master
Because the merge already happened securely inside Gitea, git pull simply downloads the finished product. There is a 0% chance of a live merge conflict taking down Apache.

Here is the Architect's breakdown of your rules, categorized exactly into how we will enforce them across your Gitea platform.

Bucket 1: The "Native Locks" (Gitea Settings & CODEOWNERS)

Gitea's UI does not have a simple checkbox to force branch names before they are created. To stop developers from pushing a branch named ahmed-test-123, we must use a Server-Side Git Hook.

Rule: Branch Name must start with newtool/, bugfix/, or update/.

Bucket 3: The CI/CD Gates (The Gitea Runner)
Since your internal enterprise tools rely heavily on Python, Flask, and HTML templates, we can program the Gitea Runner we just installed to act as a ruthless, automated code reviewer. It will fail the pipeline before the SPOC even looks at it.

BE Rule 6: No Prints.

The Execution: The CI runner checks the file paths of all new .html files in the commit. If an HTML file is placed outside the designated Flask template directories, the pipeline fails.

FE Rule 6: JS Scripts at the end of the <body> tag.

The Execution: We can run a lightweight HTML linter in the CI pipeline that scans for <script> tags placed in the <head> and fails the build, forcing the developer to move them to the bottom.

Bucket 4: The "Headaches" (The SPOC's Domain)

We will start with the absolute first line of defense: The Branch Naming Gatekeeper.

If a developer cannot even push a badly named branch to the server, it saves your SPOCs the headache of cleaning up a messy Git tree later.

Here is the Architect's guide to building your first Server-Side Git Hook.

Step 1: The Pre-Receive Hook (Branch Naming Enforcement)
Gitea has a hidden superpower: it allows you to write custom Bash scripts that intercept a developer's git push command before the code is written to the Test VM's disk. If the script exits with an error, the push is mathematically rejected, and the developer sees your custom error message directly in their terminal.

We are going to write a script that enforces your rule: Branches must start with newtool/, bugfix/, or update/.

The Execution (Applying the Hook)
You do not need to SSH into the VM to do this; you can do it right from the Gitea UI as an Admin.

Log into Gitea with your Automation_Admins account.

Navigate to your TAT_Test_Env repository.

Click Settings -> Git Hooks (in the left-hand menu).

You will see a list of hooks. Look for pre-receive and click the pencil icon (Edit) next to it.

Paste the following Bash script exactly as it is written below:

Bash
#!/bin/bash

# Loop through all the branches being pushed
while read oldrev newrev refname; do
    
    # We only care about branches, ignore tags
    if [[ $refname != refs/heads/* ]]; then
        continue
    fi
    
    # Extract just the branch name (e.g., from refs/heads/bugfix/LLD_Tool)
    branch_name=$(basename $refname)
    
    # We must allow pushes to the 'master' branch (by SPOCs) to bypass this rule
    if [[ "$branch_name" == "master" ]]; then
        continue
    fi
    
    # THE REGEX GATE: Check if it starts with the 3 allowed prefixes
    if [[ ! "$branch_name" =~ ^(newtool/|bugfix/|update/) ]]; then
        echo " "
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo "🚫 FATAL VODAFONE TAT ERROR: Invalid Branch Name! 🚫"
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo "You tried to push a branch named: '$branch_name'"
        echo " "
        echo "RULE: Your branch must start with one of the following:"
        echo "  - newtool/"
        echo "  - bugfix/"
        echo "  - update/"
        echo " "
        echo "EXAMPLE: git checkout -b bugfix/LLD_Tool"
        echo "Please rename your branch locally and try pushing again."
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo " "
        exit 1 # This immediately rejects the push
    fi

done

# If all checks pass, allow the push
exit 0
Click Update Hook at the bottom.

The Validation: Scenario 1

She types: git checkout -b ahmed-5G-test (A bad branch name).

She commits her Python code.

The Network Action:
Her laptop reaches out to the Test VM. Gitea catches the incoming packet, pauses, and hands the branch name (ahmed-5G-test) to your Bash script.

The Result:
Your script evaluates it. It doesn't start with newtool/. The script triggers exit 1.
Instantly, Yomna's terminal spits out the giant red error message we wrote in the script. Her push fails. The server remains perfectly clean.

The Correction:
Yomna reads the terminal output, realizes her mistake, and fixes it locally:

She types: git branch -m ahmed-5G-test newtool/5G_Batches (Renaming the branch).

She types: git push origin newtool/5G_Batches.

The script evaluates it, sees newtool/, triggers exit 0, and the branch successfully appears in Gitea!

I can't find the the git hooks tab

This is a classic Gitea security feature doing exactly what it was designed to do. You cannot see the tab because the platform is protecting the underlying Linux server.

By default, Gitea completely hides the "Git Hooks" tab from everyone—even Administrators.

The Dense "Why": A Git Hook is literally a raw Bash script that executes directly on the Red Hat kernel. If a malicious user gained Admin access to Gitea, they could write a Git Hook containing rm -rf / or open a reverse shell, completely destroying your Test VM. To prevent this, Gitea disables the UI for it globally.

Since you own the infrastructure, we need to explicitly tell the Gitea configuration file: "I am the Platform Engineer, and I authorize the execution of custom server-side hooks."

Here is how to unlock the tab.

Execution Phase: Unlocking Git Hooks
You will need to jump into the terminal of your Test VM (the server hosting Gitea) to flip this switch.

1. Open the Gitea Configuration File:
Open the app.ini file using your preferred text editor. (If your installation path is different, adjust accordingly, but this is the standard location).

Bash
sudo nano /etc/gitea/app.ini
2. Modify the Security Section:
Scroll through the file until you find the [security] block.
Add this exact line under it:

Ini, TOML
[security]
DISABLE_GIT_HOOKS = false
(If the [security] block doesn't exist, just type it in at the bottom of the file).

3. Restart the Engine:
Save the file and exit the editor. Then, tell systemd to reload Gitea so it reads the new configuration:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart gitea
The Post-Flight Check
Go back to your web browser.

Hard refresh the Gitea page (Ctrl+F5).

Navigate back to TAT_Test_Env -> Settings.

Look at the left-hand menu. Did the "Git Hooks" tab just appear? Once you see it, you can click it, find the pre-receive hook, and paste in the Bash script we wrote in the previous step to lock down your branch names! Let me know when you are ready to test the script.

Let's apply the Architect's Protocol to break down exactly what that script is doing line-by-line, and explicitly answer your question about why we must "allow pushes to master."

Lecture 26.0: The "Master Bypass" Trap
You asked: "What do you mean by allow pushes to the master?"

Think about the workflow we just designed for your 7 teams:

Yomna pushes a branch named newtool/5G_Batches. (The script checks it, sees it is valid, and allows it).

Mahmoud (the SPOC) goes into the Gitea UI, reviews the code, and clicks the green "Squash and Merge" button.

Here is the secret of how Gitea works under the hood: When Mahmoud clicks that Merge button, Gitea is technically executing a git push directly to the master branch on the server.

If we did not put that "Master Bypass" rule in the script, here is what would happen:

Mahmoud clicks Merge.

Gitea tries to push the merged code to the master branch.

Your Bash script intercepts it and asks, "Does the word 'master' start with newtool/, bugfix/, or update/?"

The script realizes it does not.

The script immediately crashes the merge. Mahmoud would get a giant red error on his screen, and no code would ever make it to production.

By adding if [[ "$branch_name" == "master" ]]; then continue; fi, we are telling the script: "If the system is trying to update the master branch, ignore the naming rules and let the code through." (Note: Standard developers still cannot push to master directly from their laptops because we locked that down earlier using Gitea's Branch Protection UI settings. The UI lock and this script work together perfectly).

Lecture 26.1: Line-by-Line Script Breakdown
Here is exactly how the rest of the script mathematically processes an incoming push.

1. The Interception Loop

Bash
while read oldrev newrev refname; do
When a developer runs git push, Git sends three pieces of data to the server: the old commit ID, the new commit ID, and the raw reference name (e.g., refs/heads/newtool/LLD_Tool). This line catches that data.

2. The Tag Filter

Bash
    if [[ $refname != refs/heads/* ]]; then
        continue
    fi
A developer might push a Git Tag (like v1.0-Prod). Tags look like refs/tags/v1.0. We don't want to block tags, so this line says, "If this isn't a branch (refs/heads/), skip the checks."

3. The Name Extractor

Bash
    branch_name=$(basename $refname)
This strips away the refs/heads/ part, leaving us with exactly what the developer typed: newtool/LLD_Tool.

4. The Master Bypass (Discussed Above)

Bash
    if [[ "$branch_name" == "master" ]]; then
        continue
    fi
Allows SPOCs to merge code into master without the script rejecting the word "master".

5. The Regex Gate (Your Vodafone Rules)

Bash
    if [[ ! "$branch_name" =~ ^(newtool/|bugfix/|update/) ]]; then
This is the core logic engine. It uses Regular Expressions (Regex).

! means NOT.

=~ means MATCHES.

^ means STARTS WITH.

| means OR.
If the branch name does not start with newtool/, bugfix/, or update/, it triggers the error block, prints the custom red text to the developer's terminal, and runs exit 1 to instantly kill the push.

It is excellent that you caught that. You should never let a script bypass a security gate on your server unless you know exactly what type of traffic is flowing through it.

Let’s apply the Architect's Protocol to look at exactly what a Git Tag is, why it looks different to the server than a branch, and why bypassing it is the secret to your Production deployment.

Lecture 28.0: Branches vs. Tags (The Production Snapshot)
In Git, Branches and Tags are mathematically different entities, even though they both point to code.

1. A Branch (refs/heads/...) is a Living Workspace.
Think of a branch like a Google Doc. It is constantly changing. Developer Yomna creates newtool/5G_Batches, adds a commit, changes her mind, removes a commit, and pushes again. The branch moves forward with her.

2. A Tag (refs/tags/...) is a Frozen Snapshot.
Think of a Tag like exporting that Google Doc as a PDF. It is an immutable, permanent milestone. You cannot add new commits to a Tag. It is a mathematical guarantee that "this exact state of the code will never change."

Why We Bypassed Tags in the Script
Remember the architecture we mapped out for your Main Production VM:

Test VM Deployments: Triggered automatically when code is merged to the master branch.

Production VM Deployments: Triggered manually when you create a Tag (like v1.0-Prod or Release-March-4).

When you create that tag in Gitea, Git sends it to the server as refs/tags/v1.0-Prod.

If our Bash script did not have that bypass line, the script would catch the Tag, run the regex, and scream: "FATAL ERROR: v1.0-Prod does not start with newtool/, bugfix/, or update/!" You would be permanently blocked from ever creating a Production Release Tag because your own script would reject it. By adding if [[ $refname != refs/heads/* ]]; then continue; fi, we are telling the script: "Only enforce the naming rules on living branches. Let Production Tags pass through freely."

The Execution: Locking it In

Production VM Deployments: Triggered manually when you create a Tag (like v1.0-Prod or Release-March-4).

You are 100% technically correct. At its core, a Git Tag is literally just a human-readable sticker slapped onto a long, ugly commit hash (like a1b2c3d4).

But in Platform Engineering, that simple "sticker" is the difference between a stable High-Availability cluster and a catastrophic production outage.

Let’s apply the Architect’s Protocol to look at why we use Tags instead of just deploying the master branch or using raw commit hashes for your Main VM.

Lecture 29.0: The Superpower of the Tag
Remember your exact environment: You have 7 different teams constantly building internal tools and merging them into the TAT_Test_Env repository.

Here is why relying on branches or hashes for Production will fail, and why Tags solve it:

1. Branches are Moving Targets; Tags Freeze Time
The Branch Problem: The master branch is constantly moving forward. If you tell your CI/CD Runner to "deploy master to Production," what happens if a SPOC from Team B merges a buggy feature exactly three seconds before your pipeline runs? You just accidentally deployed Team B's broken code to Production without knowing it.

The Tag Solution: A Tag is immutable. It freezes time. When you create a tag called v1.0-Release on a specific commit, that tag can never accept new code. Even if 50 developers merge new code into master five seconds later, v1.0-Release remains perfectly frozen. You are deploying a guaranteed, unchanging snapshot to the Main VM.

2. The CI/CD Trigger Separation
You want the Test VM to update automatically so people can test, but you want Production to update only when you are absolutely ready.

If you use branches, how does the Runner know the difference between a "Test Merge" and a "Production Merge"? It doesn't.

By using Tags, we create a strict mathematical rule for the Runner:

"If a Developer pushes a branch -> Do nothing."

"If a SPOC merges to master -> Deploy to Test VM."

"If an Admin creates a Tag -> Deploy to Production VM."

3. The "Human Readable" Rollback
You asked earlier about rollbacks. If your Main VM crashes at 3:00 AM, you need to revert it instantly.

Without Tags: You have to scroll through a Git log of 500 commits from 7 teams, trying to guess which hash (f83j2p or b29x1z?) was the last stable version.

With Tags: You just tell the server: git checkout v1.4-Stable. It takes two seconds, zero guesswork, and Production is back online.

The Summary
You use commit hashes for computers. You use branches for developers to write code. You use Tags for infrastructure to safely deploy to Production.

Ah! I see exactly what happened, and this is a classic Linux bash scripting trap. I owe you an apology for this bug, but it is a perfect learning moment.

Look closely at the error message the server sent back:
You tried to push a branch named: 'ElkarimBranch'

Even though you pushed newtool/ElkarimBranch, the server thought the name was just ElkarimBranch.

The Dense "Why": In the script, I used the command basename $refname to extract the branch name from refs/heads/newtool/ElkarimBranch.
The basename command is designed to strip away file paths. It looks for the very last slash / and deletes everything before it. Because your branch name actually contains a slash (newtool/), basename aggressively deleted refs/heads/newtool/, leaving only ElkarimBranch.

Because ElkarimBranch doesn't start with newtool/, the script rejected it!

The Execution: The Fix
We need to tell Bash to only strip away exactly refs/heads/ and leave the rest of the string completely alone.

Go back to your TAT_Sandbox -> Settings -> Git Hooks -> pre-receive.

Replace the entire script with this updated version. Notice the change on line 10.

Bash
#!/bin/bash

# Loop through all the branches being pushed
while read oldrev newrev refname; do
    
    # We only care about branches, ignore tags
    if [[ $refname != refs/heads/* ]]; then
        continue
    fi
    
    # THE FIX: Strip exactly "refs/heads/" from the start of the string.
    # Do not use 'basename' because it destroys branch names that contain slashes!
    branch_name=${refname#refs/heads/}
    
    # Allow pushes to the 'master' branch (by SPOCs) to bypass this rule
    if [[ "$branch_name" == "master" ]]; then
        continue
    fi
    
    # THE REGEX GATE: Check if it starts with the 3 allowed prefixes
    if [[ ! "$branch_name" =~ ^(newtool/|bugfix/|update/) ]]; then
        echo " "
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo "🚫 FATAL VODAFONE TAT ERROR: Invalid Branch Name! 🚫"
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo "You tried to push a branch named: '$branch_name'"
        echo " "
        echo "RULE: Your branch must start with one of the following:"
        echo "  - newtool/"
        echo "  - bugfix/"
        echo "  - update/"
        echo " "
        echo "EXAMPLE: git checkout -b bugfix/LLD_Tool"
        echo "Please rename your branch locally and try pushing again."
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo " "
        exit 1 # This immediately rejects the push
    fi

done

# If all checks pass, allow the push
exit 0

Because Gitea updates its interface frequently, the wording is a bit more granular. Let’s map this exactly to what you are seeing on your screen.

In Gitea, you don't "Enable" pull request approvals with a single checkbox; you enforce them by requiring a specific number of approvals and disabling direct pushes.

Here is the exact layout of the Gitea Branch Protection screen for your master branch.

The Exact Gitea UI Steps
Go back to Settings -> Branches and edit your master rule. Scroll down and set these exact fields:

1. The Fundamental Lock:

Find Enable Branch Protection: Check this box. (This turns the shield on).

Find Disable push: Check this box. (This physically stops developers from typing git push origin master. It forces them to open a Pull Request).

2. The Approval Engine:

Find Required approvals: This is a number field. Change it from 0 to 1. (This tells Gitea that no Pull Request can be merged without at least one SPOC clicking "Approve").

Find Require review from Code Owners: Check this box. (It usually sits right below the Required Approvals number. This tells Gitea: "If main.py is touched, the required approval MUST come from the people listed in the CODEOWNERS file, not just any random user").

3. Optional but Highly Recommended:

Find Dismiss stale approvals: Check this box. (If Mahmoud approves a PR, but then Yomna pushes more code to that same PR, Mahmoud's approval is instantly revoked. He must review the new code).

Scroll to the bottom and click Save.

The Validation Check
Once you set "Required approvals" to 1 and check the "Code Owners" box, the lock is fully engaged.

This is the exact reason we test everything in the TAT_Sandbox first. When UI elements don't appear in Gitea, it is almost always the system protecting itself because a prerequisite is missing.

Let's apply the Architect's Protocol to force that checkbox to appear, and then walk through the exact "Bait and Switch" scenario that makes the stale approvals option so critical.

Part 1: Why the "Code Owners" Box is Missing
Gitea is very strict: It completely hides the "Require review from Code Owners" checkbox if it cannot physically see a perfectly valid CODEOWNERS file on the branch you are trying to protect.

If you don't see the box, one of these three things happened when you created the file:

The Hidden Extension Trap: You might have accidentally saved it as CODEOWNERS.txt. Gitea strictly requires the file to have no file extension.

The Wrong Branch: You might have committed the file to a new branch instead of committing it directly to the master branch. The file must live on master for the branch protection settings to see it.

The Invalid User: If Gitea cannot find the user or team you mentioned (e.g., @TAT/spocs), it will ignore the file.

The Fix:
Go to the code tab of your TAT_Sandbox repository. Make sure you are on the master branch.

Do you see the CODEOWNERS file sitting right there in the main folder?

Click on it. Ensure it has no .txt extension.

Edit it and change the assignee to your exact Gitea username for this test (e.g., @karim or whatever you log in with).

Commit it directly to the master branch.

Once Gitea detects that valid file on master, go back to the Branch Protection settings. That checkbox will magically appear under the "Required approvals" number.

Part 2: The "Stale Approvals" Scenario (The Bait and Switch)
You asked for a practical scenario of why we check the "Dismiss stale approvals" box.

In Platform Engineering, we call the lack of this setting the "Bait and Switch" vulnerability. Here is exactly how a developer could accidentally (or maliciously) bypass your SPOCs and take down the Production VM if you leave this unchecked.

Scenario: Without "Dismiss Stale Approvals" Checked
The Good Code: Developer Yomna creates a branch (update/dashboard-fix). She fixes a simple HTML bug and opens a Pull Request.

The Approval: Mahmoud (the SPOC) looks at the code. It is perfectly safe. He clicks Approve. The PR turns green and is ready to merge.

The "Oops" Moment: Mahmoud goes to get a cup of coffee before clicking the final "Merge" button. While he is gone, Yomna realizes she forgot to add a database connection. She quickly adds the DB code to her local laptop and pushes it to the same branch (update/dashboard-fix).

The Disaster: Gitea automatically updates the Pull Request with Yomna's new database code. Because "Dismiss stale approvals" is unchecked, Mahmoud's original "Approve" green checkmark remains valid.

The Merge: Mahmoud returns from his coffee, sees his green checkmark is still there, and clicks Merge. He just deployed unreviewed database code to the Test VM, and eventually, the Main VM.

Scenario: With "Dismiss Stale Approvals" Checked
Yomna opens the PR.

Mahmoud clicks Approve.

Yomna pushes new database code to the same branch.

The Shield Activates: The exact millisecond Yomna's new code hits the server, Gitea completely deletes Mahmoud's approval. The PR turns yellow again. It flags the PR with a message: "Approval dismissed because new commits were pushed."

Mahmoud returns from his coffee, sees the approval is gone, and is forced to review Yomna's new database code before the green Merge button will activate again.

This setting mathematically guarantees that every single line of code merged to master was looked at by a SPOC.

First, I must be completely candid: I cannot see the screenshots you uploaded. My current interface does not process image attachments, so I am completely blind to what the Gitea UI is showing you right now.

But I do not need the screenshot, because your architectural critique is 100% correct.

I completely missed your intent. The CODEOWNERS file only activates when a developer opens a Pull Request to merge their code into master. As you rightly pointed out, it does absolutely nothing to stop them from modifying main.py on newtool/ElkarimBranch and pushing it to the server.

If you want to catch this at the source—blocking the developer's terminal the exact second they try to push a locked file—we must abandon the Gitea UI checkboxes and upgrade our Gatekeeper (the Bash script).

Since we already proved the pre-receive hook works flawlessly for branch names, we will simply teach it how to read the files inside the commit.

The Upgraded Architecture: The File Scanner Hook
We are going to replace your current Git Hook with this upgraded version.

Here is what the new logic does:

It checks the branch name (just like before).

It generates a list of every single file the developer modified in their push.

If it spots main.py or __init__.py anywhere in that list, it violently rejects the push and tells them to revert those files.

SPOCs are still completely unaffected because the master bypass lets them merge approved changes.

The Execution: Deploying the Upgraded Gatekeeper
Go to your TAT_Sandbox -> Settings -> Git Hooks -> pre-receive.

Delete everything in the box, and paste this exact script:

Bash
#!/bin/bash

while read oldrev newrev refname; do
    
    # Ignore tags, only look at branches
    if [[ $refname != refs/heads/* ]]; then
        continue
    fi
    
    branch_name=${refname#refs/heads/}
    
    # 1. THE SPOC BYPASS: Allow merges to master to pass through freely
    if [[ "$branch_name" == "master" ]]; then
        continue
    fi
    
    # 2. THE BRANCH NAMING GATE
    if [[ ! "$branch_name" =~ ^(newtool/|bugfix/|update/) ]]; then
        echo " "
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo "🚫 FATAL VODAFONE TAT ERROR: Invalid Branch Name! 🚫"
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo "You tried to push a branch named: '$branch_name'"
        echo "RULE: Must start with newtool/, bugfix/, or update/"
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo " "
        exit 1 
    fi

    # 3. THE PROTECTED FILES GATE (BE Rule 2 & 3)
    # Determine exactly which files the developer changed
    if [ "$oldrev" = "0000000000000000000000000000000000000000" ]; then
        # If it's a brand new branch, compare it against master
        changed_files=$(git diff --name-only master...$newrev 2>/dev/null)
    else
        # If it's an existing branch, compare the old commit to the new commit
        changed_files=$(git diff --name-only $oldrev $newrev 2>/dev/null)
    fi

    # Search the changed files for main.py or __init__.py
    if echo "$changed_files" | grep -qE '(^|/)main\.py$|__init__\.py$'; then
        echo " "
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo "🚫 FATAL VODAFONE TAT ERROR: Core File Modification! 🚫"
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo "You are trying to push changes to a protected file:"
        echo " - main.py  OR  __init__.py"
        echo " "
        echo "RULE: Developers cannot push changes to core files directly"
        echo "without prior alignment from the Digital Transformation Team."
        echo " "
        echo "Please revert your changes to these files to continue."
        echo "=========================================================="
        echo " "
        exit 1
    fi

done

exit 0
Click Update Hook.

You are reverse-engineering Gitea’s permission model perfectly. You just hit the exact limitation of the native UI checkboxes, and your logic is flawless.

Let's address the Jenkins question first, and then map out exactly how we achieve your two-tier approval requirement.

1. The Jenkins Question
Can the Gitea Runner do Jenkins-style manual approvals?
No. Gitea Actions (which is essentially a clone of GitHub Actions) does not have a native input("Waiting for Admin to click Proceed") pause block like Jenkins does.
Pipelines in Gitea run top-to-bottom. If we want a manual gate, we have to enforce it via Pull Request approvals, not by pausing the YAML runner.

2. The UI Limitation You Discovered
You correctly observed that the Gitea UI Branch Protection settings are Branch-Level, not File-Level.

If you set "Require approvals" to 1 and allowlist the TAT_SPOC team, Gitea says: "I don't care what files are in this PR. As long as one SPOC approves it, it can merge."

The "Protected file patterns" box simply triggers the branch's generic approval rule. It does not let you assign a different team to those specific files.

The Architecture: How to Build a Two-Tier Approval
You are asking for a Two-Tier system:

Tier 1 (Standard Code): Developer -> PR -> TAT_SPOC approves -> Merge.

Tier 2 (Core Files): Developer touches main.py -> PR -> Admin must approve -> Merge.

There is only one native way in Gitea to achieve file-level routing like this, and this is exactly why we were trying to set up the CODEOWNERS file earlier.

The CODEOWNERS file was designed specifically to override the UI checkboxes.

If you have a CODEOWNERS file that says:

Plaintext
* @TAT/TAT_SPOC
main.py @TAT/Admins
**/__init__.py @TAT/Admins
Here is what Gitea does when a developer opens a PR:

It looks at the files. If it's just HTML or regular Python, it assigns the PR to TAT_SPOC.

If it sees main.py, the Gitea engine overrides the normal rules, completely blocks the SPOC from merging it, and physically tags the Admin team, stating: "CODEOWNERS rule engaged. Admin approval required."

Our Options Forward
Since Gitea UI cannot do file-specific routing, and the Runner cannot pause like Jenkins, we have two choices for how to enforce this rule for your Digital Transformation Team:

Option A: We finally beat the CODEOWNERS file into submission.
If we can get the exact team syntax right, this will solve your problem elegantly and natively. (For example, we need to make sure the Admin team actually exists in Gitea and has write access to the repo).

Option B: The CI/CD "Scream and Fail" Method (The Workaround).
We write a YAML pipeline that runs on every Pull Request. The Runner executes git diff. If it detects that main.py was modified, the pipeline immediately turns RED and fails the build with a message: "WARNING: Core file modified. SPOCs, do not merge. Admin review required." * Pros: 100% reliable, no Gitea UI bugs to fight.

Cons: It doesn't technically lock the merge button if a SPOC decides to ignore the red warning and force-merge it anyway.

Which path do you want to take? Do you want to try getting CODEOWNERS working one more time to physically lock the button, or should we build the Runner pipeline to act as an automated alarm system?

Lets ask you this question can we hide the CODEOWNERS Folder ?

Here is the candid architectural truth about how Git works:

No, you cannot physically hide a file (or folder) in a Git repository from someone who has clone access. If a developer is allowed to run git clone to download your 4.5 GB Back-End repository, they are mathematically downloading every single file inside it. That is the fundamental nature of a distributed version control system.

However, depending on why you want to hide it, we have two excellent solutions:

1. If you want to hide it to "keep the folder clean"
If you just hate seeing a giant CODEOWNERS file sitting in your main directory next to main.py and app.py, Gitea has a built-in feature for this.

You can create a hidden directory called .gitea (with a dot at the beginning) and move the file inside there.

Path: .gitea/CODEOWNERS

Result: Gitea will still read it perfectly, but because the folder starts with a dot, it acts as a hidden folder on Linux and Mac. Developers won't see it cluttering their screens unless they explicitly run ls -a.

2. If you want to hide it for "Security" (Preventing Tampering)
If your concern is that Developer Elkarim will open the file, delete @TAT/Admins, and give himself permission to edit main.py, you do not need to hide the file at all.

Gitea automatically protects the CODEOWNERS file itself.
Because that file lives strictly on the master branch, and we have Disable push checked on the master branch, a developer is completely blocked from changing the rules. If Elkarim tries to modify the CODEOWNERS file, he has to open a Pull Request... which goes straight to you for approval.

We are at a crossroads for enforcing your Two-Tier rule (SPOCs for normal files, Admins for main.py).

Option A: We stay in the Gitea UI. You move the file to .gitea/CODEOWNERS to keep it clean, and we figure out exactly why Gitea is rejecting your owners team syntax.
Option B: We abandon the finicky UI file entirely. We write a CI/CD Runner pipeline that automatically screams and fails the PR if someone touches main.py, acting as a giant red alarm for the SPOCs not to merge it.

Which path feels better for your team?

I completely agree with this roadmap.

First, we build the "Scream and Fail" pipeline to absolutely lock down main.py and __init__.py using your Runner. Once you confirm the trap successfully catches a developer, we will immediately move to Part 2: architecting the High-Availability Test-to-Prod sync.

Here is exactly how we deploy the automated CI/CD alarm in Gitea.

Step 1: Write the Core File Guardian Pipeline
In Gitea, pipelines are just YAML files stored in a specific hidden folder. When a Pull Request is opened, the act_runner reads this file and executes the commands.

Go to your TAT_Sandbox repository in the Gitea UI. Make sure you are on the master branch.

Click Add File -> New File.

In the file name box, type this exact path to create the hidden workflow folder:

Plaintext
.gitea/workflows/core-guardian.yaml
Paste this exact YAML code into the file:

YAML
name: Core File Guardian

# This tells the Runner to trigger ONLY when a Pull Request targets 'master'
on:
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - master

jobs:
  check-core-files:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest # This matches your act_runner label
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0 # Downloads the history so we can compare branches

      - name: Scan PR for Locked Files
        run: |
          echo "Scanning files changed in this Pull Request..."
          
          # Compare the PR code against the master branch
          BASE_BRANCH="origin/${{ github.base_ref }}"
          CHANGED_FILES=$(git diff --name-only $BASE_BRANCH...HEAD)
          
          echo "Files modified by the developer:"
          echo "$CHANGED_FILES"
          
          # Search the list for the forbidden files
          if echo "$CHANGED_FILES" | grep -qE '(^|/)main\.py$|__init__\.py$'; then
              echo " "
              echo "=========================================================="
              echo "🚨 FATAL VODAFONE TAT ERROR: CORE FILE MODIFIED 🚨"
              echo "=========================================================="
              echo "This Pull Request touches main.py or __init__.py."
              echo " "
              echo "SPOCs: DO NOT MERGE THIS PULL REQUEST."
              echo "Only the Digital Transformation Admin team can approve this."
              echo "=========================================================="
              echo " "
              exit 1 # This explicitly CRASHES the pipeline (turns it Red)
          fi
          
          echo "✅ No core files modified. Standard SPOC review allowed."
          exit 0 # This PASSES the pipeline (turns it Green)
Click Commit Changes at the bottom.

Step 2: Connect the Lock to Branch Protection
Just having the pipeline isn't enough; we have to tell Gitea that a failing pipeline physically disables the Merge button.

Go to Settings -> Branches.

Edit your master branch protection rule.

Scroll down and check the box for Enable Status Check (or "Require Status Checks to Pass").

A text box will appear asking which checks are required. Type the exact name of our job:

Plaintext
check-core-files
(Optional but recommended): Keep Required approvals at 1 so SPOCs still have to manually approve normal code.

Scroll down and click Save.

The Validation (The Trap is Set)
The second you save that branch protection rule, your Two-Tier approval requirement is mathematically enforced.

If Developer Elkarim modifies main.py and opens a PR:

The act_runner wakes up and runs the YAML file.

It detects main.py, prints the giant red warning, and exits with a fatal error (exit 1).

Gitea sees the pipeline failed. Because "Enable Status Check" is checked, Gitea completely grays out the Merge button.

The SPOC cannot merge it, even if they click "Approve". Only you (the Admin) can bypass the branch protection to force it through.
