To make this 100% clear, we have to separate the two different times a merge happens in this architecture:

The PR Merge: When you click the green button in the Gitea UI.

The Deployment Pull: When the runner on the .51 server downloads the code using --ff-only.

Let's look at exactly how your examples (Rebase and Squash) tie into this.

1. Is a Fast-Forward like a Rebase + Merge?
Yes, exactly. If you have a feature branch that has diverged from master, and you run git rebase master, you are physically picking up your feature commits and placing them directly on the very tip of master. You just turned a messy, diverged history into a perfect, straight line.

Because it is now a straight line, when you go back to master and run git merge feature-branch, Git doesn't have to do any complex math. It just "fast-forwards" the master label to point to the newest commit.

2. Is it the same as a Squash Commit in the Gitea UI?
Fundamentally, yes. When you choose "Squash Merge" in the Gitea UI, Gitea takes all 50 of your messy feature branch commits, crushes them down into one single, clean commit, and appends it directly to the tip of master.

Just like a rebase, a Squash Merge guarantees that the master branch remains a perfect, straight, single-file line of history.

How this protects the .51 Test Server
This brings us back to why we use git pull --ff-only on the .51 Apache server.

When your runner logs into /app/www/TAT_Sandbox to deploy the new code, the server looks at its local files and looks at Gitea's new master branch.

If the history is a straight line: (Because nobody touched the .51 server, and Gitea just moved forward via your Squash Merge), the server says: "Great, I am just 1 step behind. I will fast-forward my files to match Gitea." (Deployment Success)

If the history is NOT a straight line: (Because a developer secretly logged into .51 and edited a Python file directly), the server says: "Wait, Gitea went one way, but my local files went a different way. We have diverged. A fast-forward is mathematically impossible." (Deployment Fails & Protects the Server)

The Verdict
Because you are using Gitea, you can use Squash Merges or Rebase Merges in the UI all day long. They keep your history perfectly clean. And because your history is perfectly clean, git pull --ff-only is the ultimate, fail-safe way to deploy that code to the Test server.

Let's tackle the SPOC (Reviewer) question first, because it dictates how your team will actually handle day-to-day operations, and then break down the exact mechanics of those 5 Gitea merge styles.

How the SPOC Handles Merge Conflicts in Gitea
Yes, Gitea is incredibly smart about this. The moment a developer opens a Pull Request, Gitea automatically does a dry-run merge in the background.

The Warning: If there is a merge conflict, the SPOC will see a clear warning on the PR page saying the branch has conflicting files. The big green "Merge" button will be physically disabled.

The UI Resolution: Gitea does have a built-in web editor for conflicts. The SPOC can click "Resolve Conflicts", and Gitea will show the files with the <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> markers. The SPOC can edit the text right there in the browser, mark it as resolved, and Gitea will automatically create a new commit to fix it.

The Enterprise Warning: While the SPOC can fix it in the web UI, doing this for Python/Flask code is highly risky. If the SPOC deletes the wrong line of code in the browser, they can't test if the Flask app still runs before hitting save. The safest, standard practice is for the SPOC to tell the developer: "You have conflicts. Pull the latest master to your local machine, resolve the conflicts locally, test the app, and push the fix back to this PR."

The 5 Gitea Merge Styles Explained
When the PR is clean and the SPOC is ready to merge, Gitea offers these 5 buttons. Here is exactly what happens to your Git database for each one:

1. Create merge commit (The Classic)

What it does: It takes all the commits from the feature branch, plugs them into master, and creates one brand-new, extra commit that says "Merge branch X into master."

Best for: Preserving the exact, untouched historical record of every single thing the developer did.

The Downside: Your Git history graph ends up looking like a messy, tangled spiderweb of diverging and converging lines.

2. Rebase then fast-forward (The Clean Line)

What it does: It picks up the feature branch commits, mathematically alters their timestamps/bases, and places them directly on the very tip of master. Then, it just slides the master pointer forward. No "merge commit" is created.

Best for: Keeping a perfectly straight, linear history without losing the individual commit messages the developer wrote.

3. Rebase then create merge commit (The Best of Both Worlds)

What it does: It does the exact same rebase as above to make the history a straight line, but it deliberately adds a "Merge branch X" commit at the end anyway.

Best for: A perfectly clean graph, while still giving you a visual "knot" in the history so you know exactly where a specific feature started and ended.

4. Create squash commit (The Clutter Killer)

What it does: It takes all 15 messy commits a developer made ("wip", "fix typo", "forgot a file", "final fix"), crushes them down into one single, clean commit, and puts that one commit onto master.

Best for: This is the gold standard for most DevOps pipelines. It keeps the master branch completely free of garbage commits. Every commit on master represents one complete, working feature.

5. Fast-forward only (The Strict Gatekeeper)

What it does: It refuses to do any rebasing, squashing, or merging for you. If the feature branch is not already a mathematically perfect continuation of master, it violently rejects the merge and throws an error.

Best for: Forcing developers to do all the rebasing and conflict resolution on their own laptops before Gitea will even allow the PR to be merged.

Which one should you use for your TAT_Sandbox pipeline?
If we are using git pull --ff-only on your .51 Test Server to keep deployments safe, you should configure your Gitea repository to default to Create squash commit.

Squashing guarantees that master moves forward in a perfectly straight line, one clean feature at a time, which guarantees your test server's fast-forward deployment will execute flawlessly every single time.

Here is the exact sequence to configure your repository and deploy the automation.

Step 1: Enforce the Merge Style in Gitea
We want to physically prevent anyone from using the messy "Create merge commit" option so your Test environment never crashes.

Go to your TAT_Sandbox repository in Gitea.

Click Settings (top right).

Scroll down to the Pull Requests section.

Under Merge Style, uncheck everything except Enable Squash Merge and/or Enable Rebase then Fast-Forward.

Click Save at the bottom.

Now, when your SPOC goes to merge a Pull Request, they will only have the safe options available.

Step 2: Write the Test Deployment Pipeline
Create a new file in your .gitea/workflows/ directory named deploy-test.yaml. Paste this exact code into it.

This uses the strict --ff-only safety valve we discussed.

YAML
name: Deploy Test Environment

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - master

jobs:
  deploy-local-test:
    runs-on: rhel-baremetal
    steps:
      - name: Update Test Working Tree
        run: |
          echo "Merged to Master! Updating the Test Git Working Tree..."
          
          # Navigate to your live Test Apache directory
          cd /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
          
          # Safely pull the latest code using fast-forward only
          echo "Pulling latest changes from Gitea..."
          git pull origin master --ff-only
          
          # Restart the Apache service to load the new Python code
          echo "Restarting Apache WSGI..."
          sudo systemctl restart httpd
          
          echo "✅ Test Environment Successfully Updated!"

Setting the ACLs was exactly the right move to solve the Linux permission side of the equation. You handled the OS layer perfectly.

The error fatal: not a git repository is purely a Git layer issue.

When the runner executes cd /app/www/TAT_Sandbox and then runs git pull, it looks for a hidden folder named .git. Because you manually created this dummy folder and just put folders with prints inside it, that hidden .git database doesn't exist. Git is essentially saying: "I am in a standard Linux folder, I have no idea what Gitea is, and I don't know how to pull."

We need to do a one-time "initialization" to wire this folder into the Gitea matrix.

Since you already have dummy files in there, a standard git clone will fail (Git refuses to clone into a non-empty directory). We have to build the connection manually.

The One-Time Setup
Log into your .51 terminal and run these exact commands. We are going to use sudo -u git to ensure the new .git database is created strictly with the runner's ownership, matching your ACLs perfectly.

Bash
# 1. Navigate to the directory
cd /app/www/TAT_Sandbox

# 2. Initialize the empty Git database as the git user
sudo -u git git init

# 3. Link this folder to your local Gitea server
sudo -u git git remote add origin http://127.0.0.1:444/TAT/TAT_Sandbox.git

# 4. Download the repository history from Gitea
sudo -u git git fetch origin

# 5. Force the folder to exactly match the master branch
sudo -u git git reset --hard origin/master
(Note: We are using reset --hard just this one single time to overwrite your dummy print folders and formally establish the Git baseline. From this second onward, your automated pipeline's safe --ff-only command will take over).

The Re-Test
Once you run those 5 commands, your folder is officially a live Git working tree.

Look very closely at the last few lines of the error log you pasted:

Cleaning up container for job deploy-local-test

Here is the massive plot twist: Your Gitea Action is not running on your .51 Linux server. It is running inside an invisible Docker container.

The Architecture Trap
When you SSH into the terminal as the git user and run the commands, you are standing on the actual, physical hard drive of the .51 server. You can see /app/www/TAT_Sandbox, you can see the .git folder, and you have the ACL permissions.

But by default, Gitea's act_runner traps every single CI/CD job inside an isolated Docker container.

Inside that container, /app/www/TAT_Sandbox either doesn't exist, or it is a completely empty void.

When the script ran cd /app/www/TAT_Sandbox, it likely failed silently.

Then, it ran git pull origin master, but because it was inside an empty container, Git threw the error: fatal: not a git repository.

Furthermore, if it had reached the sudo systemctl restart httpd command, it would have failed anyway, because Docker containers don't have systemctl!

The Fix: Unleash the Runner
Since you have already done the hard work of giving the OS git user ACL permissions and sudo rights, we do not want to use Docker. We want to tell the act_runner to run directly on the bare metal of your .51 server, just like you were typing in the terminal.

We need to switch your runner from docker mode to host mode.

Step 1: Find the Runner Configuration
Log into your .51 terminal and find the act_runner configuration file. It is usually located where you installed the runner, or in /etc/act_runner/config.yaml.

Open it with your editor:

Bash
nano config.yaml
Step 2: Change to Host Mode
Scroll down until you find the labels array. It probably looks something like this right now, mapping your rhel-baremetal label to a docker image:

YAML
labels:
  - "rhel-baremetal:docker://node:16-bullseye"
You need to change the docker://... part to exactly -host. It should look exactly like this:

YAML
labels:
  - "rhel-baremetal:-host"
(Save and exit).

Step 3: Restart the Runner
Now, restart the service so it picks up the new host configuration:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart act_runner
The Re-Test
By making this one configuration change, your CI/CD pipeline is no longer trapped in a container. When it runs, it will literally execute the bash commands natively as the git user on the .51 server, perfectly mirroring what you did in the terminal.

This is a classic Git security trap, and I know exactly why the command didn't work when you typed it.

In 2022, Git released a massive security patch. It physically prevents User A from running Git commands inside a folder owned by User B. This stops malicious code from executing during a git pull.

Git threw this error because your Gitea runner is operating as the Linux user git, but /app/www/TAT_Sandbox is likely owned by root, apache, or yourself.

Why the fix command failed
When you copied and pasted Git's suggested fix (git config --global...) into your terminal, you likely ran it as your own user (or as root).
That means you added the safety exception to your personal ~/.gitconfig file.

But the runner doesn't care about your config file. It only looks at the git user's config file.

Here are the two ways to fix this instantly. You only need to choose one.

Option 1: Add the exception for the Runner (Recommended)
You need to run that exact command, but explicitly force it to run as the git user so it saves to the correct configuration file.

Run this exact command in your .51 terminal:

Bash
sudo -u git git config --global --add safe.directory /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
Option 2: Fix the Folder Ownership
If you don't want to mess with Git config exceptions, the cleanest architectural fix is to simply make the git user the official owner of that directory and everything inside the .git database.

Run this in your .51 terminal:

Bash
sudo chown -R git:git /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
(Since you already set up ACLs for Apache to read the files, changing the base ownership to git won't break your web server).

The Re-Test
Execute either Option 1 or Option 2. Once you do, Git will finally trust the directory.

how is the updates available when I only used git fetch all folders are now local ?

This is one of the biggest "Aha!" moments when mastering advanced Git workflows. You are looking at the exact difference between Git's hidden database and your Linux filesystem.

To understand how the files actually appeared in /app/www/TAT_Sandbox, you have to split your repository into two completely separate zones: The Vault and The Storefront.

Zone 1: The Vault (The .git folder)
When you run git fetch, Git talks to your Gitea server over the network and says, "Give me all the new commits, branches, and code." * Gitea sends the data, but Git only saves it inside the hidden .git database (The Vault).

git fetch is specifically designed to be invisible. It will never touch or update the actual Python or HTML files you see on your Linux server. It just updates the local database in the background so it knows what the new code looks like.

Zone 2: The Storefront (The visible files)
The actual files you see when you run ls /app/www/TAT_Sandbox are your "Working Tree" (The Storefront). For those files to update, you have to explicitly tell Git to take the new data out of the Vault and overwrite the Storefront.

If your files are now fully updated locally, it happened because of one of two commands you ran:

1. The Pipeline (git pull --ff-only)
If your Gitea Action successfully ran, it executed a pull. git pull is actually just a lazy shortcut for two commands chained together:

Step A: git fetch (Download to the Vault)

Step B: git merge --ff-only (Take the code from the Vault and update the Storefront).

2. The Manual Setup (git reset --hard)
If you are looking at the files after doing the 5 manual terminal commands from earlier, the update happened because of step 5: git reset --hard origin/master.

You fetched the data into the Vault, and then reset --hard aggressively unpacked that data, forcefully overwriting your dummy print folders with the actual code from Gitea.

Why this architecture matters for DevOps
This separation is exactly why git fetch is so safe. You can run git fetch on a live production server a hundred times a day to check if new code exists, and it will never disrupt the running Apache application until you explicitly run a merge or a reset to apply it to the working tree.

This is the ultimate trap of background automation! You are 100% correct about what is happening.

When a pipeline is "running" forever without failing or succeeding, it means it is stuck at a hidden terminal prompt waiting for a human to type something and hit Enter.

Because we set up the /app/www/TAT_Sandbox folder to use the local HTTP address (http://127.0.0.1:444/...), Git is literally sitting in the background right now asking: Username for 'http://127.0.0.1:444': and waiting infinitely.

We need to give the pipeline the keys so it can walk right through that door without stopping.

The Fix: The Ephemeral Token
Remember in our guardian.yaml workflow how we used ${{ github.token }} to clone the code? We need to use that exact same trick for the git pull command. This token is a temporary password Gitea generates specifically for the runner, and it expires as soon as the job finishes.

We are going to update your deploy-test.yaml file so it doesn't rely on the folder's saved origin address, but instead passes the token directly into the pull command.

Update your deploy-test.yaml
Go into your Gitea UI, edit the deploy-test.yaml file on your master branch, and replace the run: block with this exact code:

YAML
      - name: Update Test Working Tree
        run: |
          echo "Merged to Master! Updating the Test Git Working Tree..."
          
          # Navigate to your live Test Apache directory
          cd /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
          
          # Safely pull the latest code using the automated Gitea token
          echo "Pulling latest changes from Gitea..."
          git pull http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@127.0.0.1:444/${{ github.repository }}.git master --ff-only
          
          # Restart the Apache service to load the new Python code
          echo "Restarting Apache WSGI..."
          sudo systemctl restart httpd
          
          echo "✅ Test Environment Successfully Updated!"
(Notice the git pull line: we injected http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@... instead of using the word origin).

Cancel the Hung Job and Retest
First, go to the Actions tab, click on the job that is currently spinning/halted, and hit the Cancel button so it stops eating up your server's memory.

Save the updated deploy-test.yaml file.

Open a quick dummy Pull Request to trigger the process again.

By explicitly handing Git the token in the command, it will completely bypass the username/password prompt and execute the fast-forward instantly.

(Note: The only other thing that could cause a hang is if your /etc/sudoers file is still prompting the git user for a password when running sudo systemctl. But if you already set that to NOPASSWD, the Git HTTP prompt is definitely the culprit here!) Let me know if injecting the token pushes it across the finish line!

it worked thats great now another question which is very important in the file guard workflow we used to clone the whole repo do you know that is a 4.5 GB repo the clone happens in the same VM btw will that make performance issues when we apply to the test environment ?

You just identified one of the most notorious performance killers in enterprise CI/CD. That is an incredibly sharp systems engineering catch.

If you run a standard git clone on a 4.5 GB repository every single time a developer opens or updates a Pull Request, you will absolutely destroy your .51 VM's disk I/O and CPU. Even though it is running locally, copying 4.5 GB of data over and over will cause the pipeline to take minutes to run instead of seconds, and it will eventually wear down the server's resources.

We need to completely change how the guardian.yaml workflow looks at the code.

The Fix: The "Blobless" Clone
Because our Guardian script only runs a git diff --name-only to look at the names of the files that changed, it does not actually need to download the 4.5 GB of file contents (images, binaries, heavy libraries).

We are going to add two magic flags to our clone command: --no-checkout and --filter=blob:none.

--no-checkout: Tells Git, "Download the database, but do not extract the files onto the hard drive."

--filter=blob:none: Tells Git, "Only download the commit history and file names. Do NOT download the actual contents (blobs) of the files unless I specifically ask for one."

Instead of downloading 4.5 GB, this command will download about 2 to 5 Megabytes and execute in milliseconds.

The Optimized guardian.yaml
Go to your guardian.yaml file, edit it, and replace the run: block with this high-performance version:

YAML
      - name: Air-Gapped PR Scan
        run: |
          AUTHORIZED_ADMINS="${{ vars.Automation_Admins }}"
          ACTOR="${{ github.actor }}"
          
          echo "Authorized Admins List: $AUTHORIZED_ADMINS"
          echo "Pull Request opened by: $ACTOR"
          
          # 1. High-Performance Clone (Downloads MBs instead of 4.5 GB)
          git clone --no-checkout --filter=blob:none http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@127.0.0.1:444/${{ github.repository }}.git pr-workspace
          cd pr-workspace
          
          # 2. Fetch the specific Pull Request
          git fetch origin pull/${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}/head:pr-branch
          
          # 3. Get the list of changed file names
          CHANGED_FILES=$(git diff --name-only origin/${{ github.base_ref }}...pr-branch)
          
          # 4. Run the VIP Trap
          if echo "$CHANGED_FILES" | grep -qE '(^|/)main\.py$|__init__\.py$'; then
              if echo "$AUTHORIZED_ADMINS" | grep -qw "$ACTOR"; then
                  echo "🛡️ ADMIN OVERRIDE ACCEPTED: $ACTOR"
                  exit 0
              else
                  echo "🚨 FATAL: Unauthorized edit to core files by $ACTOR. Blocked."
                  exit 1
              fi
          fi
          echo "✅ Clean PR. Standard review allowed."
          exit 0
By adding those two flags, your Guardian pipeline is now fully enterprise-grade. It will aggressively protect your core files without ever putting a dent in your server's RAM or CPU, no matter how massive the repository gets.

Good catch. There are two specific traps in this snippet that will cause it to fail, and they are both related to the environment you are running this in.

Here is exactly what needs to be fixed:

Trap 1: YAML Indentation (The Silent Killer)
In your snippet, the bash script directly under run: | is perfectly flush with the word run. YAML is incredibly strict about spacing. Because the bash script is not indented, the YAML parser will crash immediately, thinking the run block is empty. Every line of the bash script must be pushed in by at least two spaces.

Trap 2: The "Host Runner" Directory Collision
Remember earlier when we switched your runner from a Docker container to the rhel-baremetal Host mode?

In Docker, the container is deleted when the job finishes, so the pr-workspace folder disappears.

In Host mode, the runner operates directly on your .51 hard drive. That means the pr-workspace folder is permanently left behind. If this workflow runs a second time, git clone will hit a fatal error because the pr-workspace directory already exists and isn't empty.

The Fix: We must add rm -rf pr-workspace at the very beginning of the script to guarantee a clean slate for every run.

The Corrected Workflow
Here is the fully fixed, properly indented, and perfectly safe YAML. You can copy and paste this exactly as it is:

YAML
name: Core File Guardian

on:
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - master
      - production

jobs:
  check-core-files:
    runs-on: rhel-baremetal
    steps:
      - name: Phase 1 Core Files Guard
        run: |
          # 1. CLEANUP PREVIOUS RUNS (Crucial for baremetal/host runners)
          rm -rf pr-workspace
          
          AUTHORIZED_ADMINS="${{ vars.Automation_Admins }}"
          ACTOR="${{ github.actor }}"
          
          echo "Authorized Admins List: $AUTHORIZED_ADMINS"
          echo "Pull Request opened by: $ACTOR"
          
          # 2. High-Performance Clone (Downloads MBs instead of 4.5 GB)
          git clone --no-checkout --filter=blob:none http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@10.30.121.51:444/${{ github.repository }}.git pr-workspace
          cd pr-workspace
          
          # 3. Fetch the specific Pull Request
          git fetch origin pull/${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}/head:pr-branch
          
          # 4. Get the list of changed file names
          CHANGED_FILES=$(git diff --name-only origin/${{ github.base_ref }}...pr-branch)
          
          # 5. Run the VIP Trap
          if echo "$CHANGED_FILES" | grep -qE '(^|/)main\.py$|__init__\.py$'; then
              if echo "$AUTHORIZED_ADMINS" | grep -qw "$ACTOR"; then
                  echo "🛡️ ADMIN OVERRIDE ACCEPTED: $ACTOR"
                  exit 0
              else
                  echo "🚨 FATAL: Unauthorized edit to core files by $ACTOR. Blocked."
                  exit 1
              fi
          fi
          echo "✅ Clean PR. Standard review allowed."
          exit 0

This is the final piece of the puzzle. We are now building Pillar 3: The Production Delivery Bridge.

Because your architecture is a High-Availability setup (using Keepalived and Rsync between .50 and .51), we must treat the .50 Production server with extreme care. We do not want Gitea restarting Apache on .50 automatically in the middle of the day.

Instead, we will use a "Sleeping Branch" deployment pattern.

The Strategy
You merge code from master into production in the Gitea UI.

The Gitea runner on .51 wakes up.

It packages the new code and uses SSH to push it securely across the network to .50.

It places the code into a hidden branch called ready-for-prod on the .50 server and stops.

The result: The code is securely waiting on the .50 machine. Your live Apache site hasn't changed. Later, during your official maintenance window, you log into .50, run git merge ready-for-prod, and gracefully reload Apache.

The Missing Information
Before I give you the final YAML, we need to map the network bridge. The runner acts as the git user on the .51 machine. To push code to .50, it needs two things to exist:

The SSH Trust: Does the git user on .51 already have an SSH key pair generated, and is the public key inside the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file of the deployment user on .50? (If it prompts for a password, the pipeline will freeze just like it did earlier).

The Target Directory: What is the exact folder path on the .50 server where the live TAT_Sandbox application runs? (e.g., /app/www/TAT_Sandbox?).

The Draft deliver-prod.yaml
Here is exactly what the pipeline will look like. You can see how we configure it to push to that sleeping branch.

YAML
name: Deliver to Production Server

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - production

jobs:
  deliver-prod:
    runs-on: rhel-baremetal
    steps:
      - name: Push to Prod (Air-Gapped)
        run: |
          # 1. Cleanup previous runs
          rm -rf prod-workspace
          
          echo "Packaging Production Release..."
          
          # 2. Clone the production branch from local Gitea
          git clone -b production http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@10.30.121.51:444/${{ github.repository }}.git prod-workspace
          cd prod-workspace
          
          # 3. Add the .50 Production Server as an SSH remote destination
          # (We will update this URL once you confirm the path and user)
          git remote add prod-server ssh://<USER>@10.30.121.50/<EXACT_APP_PATH>
          
          # 4. Push the code silently to a sleeping branch called 'ready-for-prod'
          echo "Pushing code across the network to .50..."
          git push prod-server production:ready-for-prod --force
          
          echo "✅ Code successfully delivered to .50 sleeping branch."
          echo "⏳ Awaiting manual activation via 'git merge ready-for-prod' on .50."

Path B: The SSH Trigger (The Hybrid Method)

This is a very common point of confusion because the term "git user" is doing double duty here! You are thinking about the Gitea Web UI, but this specific action happens entirely in the Linux basement.

Let's separate the two layers:

Layer 1: The Gitea UI (Developer Keys)
When you put an SSH key into the Gitea website settings, you are telling Gitea: "Allow Karim's laptop to push code INTO the Gitea database." Layer 2: The Linux OS (Server Keys)
We don't need Gitea's UI for this step at all. We are telling the Linux operating system on .51: "Allow this machine to open a secure terminal connection to the .50 machine."

Because the Gitea Runner executes jobs as the local Linux OS user named git, we just need to generate a standard Linux SSH key for that user on the .51 terminal, and hand it to the .50 terminal.

Here is exactly how you build that bridge in 3 quick terminal commands.

Step 1: Generate the Key on .51
Log into your .51 machine's terminal and run these commands to create a password-less key specifically for automation:

Bash
# 1. Switch to the OS git user
sudo su - git

# 2. Generate an SSH key (Press Enter to accept all defaults, DO NOT type a passphrase)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
Step 2: Copy the Key to .50
Now we need to send that public key across the network to the .50 server.
(Note: Replace <USER> with whichever Linux OS user owns the /app/www/TAT_Sandbox folder on .50—often root, apache, or yourself).

Bash
# 3. Send the key to .50 (It will ask for the .50 user's password one final time to authorize the transfer)
ssh-copy-id <USER>@10.30.121.50
Step 3: The Verification Test
While still logged in as the git user on .51, try to SSH directly into .50:

Bash
ssh <USER>@10.30.121.50
If it drops you directly into the .50 terminal without asking for a password, you have successfully built the bridge!

will git is in a group called toolbox_admin and they are the group owners ?

That is an excellent architectural choice. Using a dedicated Linux group like toolbox_admin instead of granting full root access is exactly how enterprise environments handle secure deployments.

By making the group the owner of the folder, you allow the SSH deployment user to safely write files to the Apache directory without breaking the web server's ability to read them.

Here is exactly how this toolbox_admin group strategy fits into both servers.

The Architecture
On the .51 Server (The Sender):
The Gitea runner is operating as the local git user. This user just needs to generate the SSH key. It doesn't actually matter what groups the git user belongs to on .51, because it is just acting as the sender.

On the .50 Server (The Receiver):
This is where your toolbox_admin group strategy shines. You will SSH into .50 using a specific user account.

That user account must be a member of the toolbox_admin group.

The /app/www/TAT_Sandbox directory must be owned by the toolbox_admin group.

The group must have write permissions.

How to set up the .50 Server perfectly
Log into your .50 Production server and run these commands to lock in this group-based security:

1. Assign the folder to the group:

Bash
# Change the group ownership of the entire directory to toolbox_admin
sudo chown -R :toolbox_admin /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
2. Give the group write permissions:

Bash
# Ensure anyone in the toolbox_admin group can read, write, and execute in that folder
sudo chmod -R g+rwX /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
3. The "Sticky Group" Magic Trick (Crucial for Git):
When Git receives new files via SSH, it creates them using the default permissions of the user. To guarantee that every new file Git pushes is always owned by toolbox_admin (so Apache never gets locked out), we set the setgid bit on the folder:

Bash
sudo chmod g+s /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
Tying it into the SSH Bridge
Now that .50 is perfectly configured to accept files from anyone in the toolbox_admin group, you just need to complete the SSH bridge we talked about in the last step.

Go to .51 as the git user.

Run ssh-keygen -t ed25519.

Run ssh-copy-id <USERNAME>@10.30.121.50 (Replace <USERNAME> with the account on .50 that belongs to your toolbox_admin group).

Once you can type ssh <USERNAME>@10.30.121.50 from the .51 git user and get right in without a password, your cross-server deployment pipeline is officially ready to be written.

Because you only deploy once a week and want to push the exact specific branch name (like newtool/5g_extraction), we are going to use a Manual Dispatch workflow. The Final YAML (deliver-prod.yaml)
Create this file in your .gitea/workflows/ directory on your master branch.

Make sure to replace <USERNAME> on line 18 with the exact Linux user account you used to set up the SSH bridge.

YAML
name: Deliver to Production Server

# This creates the manual "Run Workflow" button in Gitea
on:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  deliver-prod:
    runs-on: rhel-baremetal
    steps:
      - name: Push Branch to .50 via SSH
        run: |
          # 1. Clean up previous runs
          rm -rf prod-workspace
          
          # 2. Get the exact branch name you selected in the UI dropdown
          BRANCH_NAME="${{ github.ref_name }}"
          echo "Preparing to deliver branch: $BRANCH_NAME to .50"
          
          # 3. High-Performance Clone of that specific branch
          git clone --no-checkout --filter=blob:none -b $BRANCH_NAME http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@10.30.121.51:444/${{ github.repository }}.git prod-workspace
          cd prod-workspace
          
          # 4. Push the exact branch securely over SSH to the .50 Apache directory
          echo "Pushing $BRANCH_NAME across the network to Production Server..."
          git push <USERNAME>@10.30.121.50:/app/www/TAT_Sandbox $BRANCH_NAME:$BRANCH_NAME --force
          
          echo "✅ Branch '$BRANCH_NAME' successfully delivered to .50."
          echo "⏳ Waiting for your weekly maintenance window to merge it locally."

This is the exact same 2022 Git security patch we hit on the .51 server, but this time it is happening across the network on your .50 Production server.

The Root Cause
Here is exactly what is happening under the hood:

Your .51 runner successfully connects to .50 over SSH using your designated user.

It reaches the /app/www/TAT_Sandbox folder and tries to inject the new branch.

Because we set up the toolbox_admin group, Linux says: "Yes, you have write permissions, go ahead."

But Git wakes up on the .50 server, looks at the .git database, and says: "Wait a minute. The SSH user trying to push this code is not the exact primary owner of this folder. This is dubious ownership. I am blocking the push."

Linux allowed the connection, but Git's internal security killed the transaction because of the group-ownership mismatch.

The Fix (Applied on the .50 Server)
Since this folder is designed to be managed collaboratively by the toolbox_admin group, the cleanest way to fix this is to tell Git on the .50 server to universally trust that specific directory, regardless of which user is executing the command.

Log into your .50 Production server's terminal and run this system-wide Git configuration command:

Bash

sudo git config --system --add safe.directory /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
(Note: Sometimes Git is exceptionally stubborn and wants the explicit path to the .git folder as well. To be 100% bulletproof, run it for the subfolder too):

Bash

The error you hit ([rejected] master -> master) is actually a hardcoded physical safety mechanism built directly into the core Git software itself.

The Root Cause: The "Checked-Out Branch" Rule
Your /app/www/TAT_Sandbox folder on the .50 Production server is a non-bare repository. That means it has a working tree (actual Python and HTML files that Apache is currently reading).

By default, Git strictly forbids you from pushing code over a network directly into a branch that a server currently has "checked out" and active.

If .50 is currently sitting on the master branch running your live site...

...and your runner tries to violently push new code directly into .50's master branch...

Git panics. It says: "If I accept this code, my active Apache files will suddenly be completely out of sync with my internal database!" and it blocks the push entirely.

The Architecture Fix: The "Incoming" Namespace
Since the whole point of our Weekly Maintenance Window strategy is to push the code to .50 so it sits safely in the background until you are ready to merge it, we should never push directly to the same name as the live branch.

We can fix this permanently by tweaking one single line in your deliver-prod.yaml. We will tell the runner to always push the branch into a safe "sleeping" namespace on the .50 server.

Change your git push line in the YAML to look exactly like this:

YAML
          # 4. Push the exact branch securely over SSH to an 'incoming' sleeping branch
          echo "Pushing $BRANCH_NAME across the network to Production Server..."
          git push <USERNAME>@10.30.121.50:/app/www/TAT_Sandbox $BRANCH_NAME:incoming/$BRANCH_NAME --force
Why this is the ultimate solution:
Notice the $BRANCH_NAME:incoming/$BRANCH_NAME part.

If you go to Gitea and trigger the workflow for the master branch.

The runner will push it to .50, but it will name it incoming/master.

Because .50 is actively running master, but receiving incoming/master, Git says "Ah, this is a different branch name. I will safely store it in the database without touching the live Apache files." The push succeeds instantly!

This is a classic CI/CD "Chicken and the Egg" Catch-22, and the screenshot shows exactly what is happening.

You have accidentally locked yourself out by telling Gitea to wait for an event that hasn't happened yet.

The Root Cause: The Catch-22
Look closely at the triggers in parentheses in your screenshot:

check-core-files is waiting for a (pull_request). Since this PR exists, it ran and passed.

deploy-local-test is waiting for a (push) to master.

In Gitea, a push to master only happens after you click the red merge button.

However, in your Gitea Branch Protection settings, you have marked deploy-local-test as a "Required" status check (you can see the grey "Required" badge next to it).

Gitea is saying: "I cannot let you click the Merge button until the deployment finishes... but the deployment will not start until you click the Merge button!" So it sits there spinning as a yellow dot forever.

The Fix: Adjust Branch Protection
You only want pre-merge checks (like the Guardian) to be required. Deployments are post-merge actions, so they should never block a PR.

Here is exactly how to untangle this:

Go to your TAT_Sandbox repository Settings -> Branches.

Click Edit on your Branch Protection rule for the master branch.

Scroll down to the "Require Status Checks to Pass" section.

Look at the list of checks. Uncheck Deploy Test Environment / deploy-local-test.

Keep Core File Guardian / check-core-files checked (that one must remain required so no one bypasses it).

Save the settings.

Go back to your Pull Request page and refresh it. The yellow pending dot will instantly stop blocking you, and the red Rebase then fast-forward button will unlock.

Explain to me the deliver to production workflow because the Run workflow only appears for admins I want the button to appear for the SPOCS also

This is a strict built-in security feature of Gitea (and GitHub Actions), but it is very easy to adjust once you know which permission lever controls it.

The Root Cause: The "Write" Permission Requirement
Gitea hides the Run Workflow button for the workflow_dispatch trigger based on two specific security rules:

Repository Access: To manually trigger a pipeline that runs code on your servers, a user must have at least Write access to the repository. If your SPOCs only have "Read" access, the button is physically hidden from them.

Branch Protection (The most likely culprit): Even if a SPOC has Write access to the repository, they can only run a manual workflow on a branch if they have permission to push to that specific branch. If your production branch is heavily protected and only Admins are allowed to push/merge to it, Gitea will hide the Run button for everyone else.

Since SPOCs are your designated reviewers who need to execute these deployments, we just need to explicitly grant them the keys to the production branch.

How to Unlock the Button for SPOCs
You need to verify two settings in your TAT_Sandbox repository.

Step 1: Verify Repository Write Access
If your SPOCs are already able to click the green "Merge" button on standard Pull Requests, they likely already have this. But let's verify:

Go to your TAT_Sandbox repository.

Click Settings -> Collaborators (or Teams if you use organizations).

Ensure your SPOCs are assigned the Write permission level, not just Read.

Step 2: Whitelist SPOCs in Branch Protection (The Key Fix)
This is almost certainly what is blocking them. We need to tell Gitea that SPOCs are legally allowed to interact with the production branch.

In the repository Settings, go to Branches.

You have hit the exact crossroads where security architecture meets daily convenience. Choosing between a manual button and an automated merge trigger is one of the most important decisions in pipeline design.

To make the right choice, you need to know exactly what keys you are handing to the SPOCs.

What "Write" Permission Actually Does in Gitea
In Gitea, permissions are generally tied to the repository level. If you bump a SPOC from "Read" to "Write" so they can use the Actions UI, you are granting them the following powers:

1. Actions & CI/CD Powers:

Run Manual Workflows: They can click the "Run Workflow" button for workflow_dispatch pipelines.

Cancel Jobs: They can physically abort a pipeline that is currently running.

Re-run Jobs: They can click "Re-run all jobs" on failed pipelines.

2. Repository Powers (The Catch):

Push Code: They can push code directly from their local terminal to any branch that is not strictly protected.

Manage PRs: They can approve, merge, and close Pull Requests.

Manage Issues: They can create, edit, and label repository issues.

The Verdict on Write Access: Giving SPOCs "Write" access is standard practice, provided your branch protection rules are solid. As long as master and production are locked down (requiring PRs and passing checks like your Guardian pipeline), it is perfectly safe. They can't break the main code, but they get the power to operate the pipelines.

Option A vs. Option B: The Branch Name Dilemma
Aside from permissions, there is a massive technical difference between these two options that directly impacts the requirement we discussed earlier: Keeping the exact branch name (e.g., newtool/5g_extraction) on the .50 server.

Option A: The Manual Button (Write Permission + workflow_dispatch)
How it works: The SPOC goes to the Actions tab, selects newtool/5g_extraction from a dropdown menu, and hits Run.

The Advantage: The runner instantly knows the name of the branch. It easily pushes incoming/newtool/5g_extraction to the .50 server.

The Cost: SPOCs must be granted "Write" permission to the repository to see the button.

Option B: The Automated Merge Trigger (Merge to production)
How it works: The SPOC reviews a Pull Request and clicks the green "Merge into production" button. The pipeline automatically wakes up and pushes the code to .50.

The Advantage: No extra "Write" permissions needed for the Actions tab. It is a seamless, one-click GitOps flow.

The Cost (The Dealbreaker?): When you merge a PR into production, the code technically becomes the production branch. When the pipeline wakes up, it only sees "production". It forgets that the code used to be called newtool/5g_extraction. It will push incoming/production to the .50 server instead of your specific feature name, unless we write a very complex bash script to dig through the Git commit history and extract the old branch name.

The Architect's Recommendation
If tracking the exact feature branch names on your .50 server is a hard requirement for your weekly maintenance window, Option A (Manual Dispatch) is significantly cleaner.

Just give the SPOCs "Write" access to the repository, ensure your master and production branches are protected by your Guardian rules, and let them use the "Run Workflow" dropdown.

Which path feels better for your team's workflow: managing the Write permissions (Option A), or losing the specific branch names on the .50 server (Option B)?

This is one of the most famous architectural quirks in all of version control. You have just discovered the massive difference between Git (the local software) and Gitea (the network bouncer).

To understand exactly whose permissions are being applied and why the UI looks wrong, you have to separate "The Letter" from "The Mailman."

The Disconnect: The Letter vs. The Mailman
1. The Letter (The Git Commit Author)
When you type git commit on your local CLI, Git stamps a name and email onto the code. It gets this strictly from your local terminal's configuration (git config). Git does not care if this is true or fake. It is just text written on the inside of the envelope. Right now, your local terminal is stamping the name of your local OS user (e.g., git or your computer login name).

2. The Mailman (The Gitea Network Authentication)
When you type git push, the envelope is handed to a mailman. The mailman walks up to your Gitea server. Gitea stops the mailman and asks for a password or token. You typed in your Gitea credentials.

Whose Permissions Are Applied?
Gitea ALWAYS applies the permissions of the Mailman (Your Credentials).

Even though the commit says it was written by the local "git" user, Gitea checked your Gitea account to see if you had the right to push to that repository. If your Gitea account did not have Write access, the push would have been violently rejected, regardless of what name was stamped on the commit.

However, because the email stamped on the commit didn't match the email attached to your Gitea profile, the Gitea UI couldn't link the commit to your avatar. It just displayed the raw text from the envelope.

The Fix: Syncing Your CLI to Your Identity
To make the UI match reality and ensure a clean audit trail, you must tell your local CLI to stamp your exact Gitea identity onto all future commits.

Open your local terminal (the one where you are writing the code) and run these two commands, replacing them with your exact Gitea username and the email associated with your Gitea account:

Bash
git config --global user.name "YourExactGiteaUsername"
git config --global user.email "your.email@example.com"
Note: Any commits you already made with the wrong name are permanently baked into the history with that old name, but all future commits will now be perfectly linked to your Gitea avatar.

The DevSecOps Hardening Step (Enforcing Identity)
Since you are building an enterprise pipeline, you should not allow developers to push code with mismatched identities. What if a developer maliciously changes their local user.name to make it look like you wrote a bad piece of code?

You can lock this down in Gitea so that the Mailman and the Letter are mathematically forced to match.

Go to your TAT_Sandbox repository Settings in the Gitea UI.

Click on Branches and edit your protected branch rules (for master and production).

Scroll down and look for the option: Block commits with email addresses that do not match the authenticated user. (Or similarly worded depending on your exact Gitea version, sometimes found under repository-level settings as "Enforce commit signing").

Check that box.

If you turn that on, Gitea will intercept the push, check the email stamped on the commit, compare it to the network token, and instantly reject the push if they are different.

Would you like to run those git config commands on your local machine and push a quick test commit to verify your avatar finally shows up correctly in the UI?

Tracing the raw backend execution and building a strict Linux permission matrix is exactly what separates a basic setup from a true, enterprise-grade DevSecOps architecture.

To make sure we are 100% aligned before we start tailing logs and changing Linux permissions, I want to map out the "Three Actors" in your current environment. Everything that happens in your backend is a conversation between these three entities.

The Three Actors
The Core Gitea Service (The Brain on .51): This is the main application running in the background. It listens for web traffic, handles the database, and catches incoming code pushes from developer laptops. It typically runs under a dedicated Linux user (usually git).

The act_runner Service (The Muscle on .51):
This is the completely separate background service we configured in "Host" mode. It waits for the Brain to give it a YAML file, and then it executes bash commands directly on the .51 hard drive.

The Target Server (The Receiver on .50):
This is your live Apache environment. It passively waits for the Muscle (.51) to open an SSH tunnel and forcefully inject a new branch.

Option A: The Front Door (Dev to Gitea)

Option B: The Pipeline (Runner to Production)
Do you want to trace the CI/CD automation? We would trigger the deliver-prod.yaml pipeline and watch the act_runner on .51 wake up, package the files, negotiate the SSH keys, and inject the branch into the .50 server.

Option C: The Local Test Deploy (Runner to Local Apache)
Do you want to trace the deploy-test.yaml pipeline? We would watch the runner on .51 execute the fast-forward pull directly into the /app/www/TAT_Sandbox dummy folder and restart the local HTTP service.

Let's start by clearing up your biggest question: The git user and the OpenSSH security config. ---

1. The "git" User & The OpenSSH Security Mystery
You are right to be cautious here. The Linux user named git is the central nervous system of your entire setup. Here is exactly what it does, and why the OpenSSH config does not break your runner.

Where is the git user used?

The Gitea Core Service: The main Gitea web application runs under this user. It owns the database and the hidden repository files in the background.

The act_runner Service: Because we configured the runner to operate natively on the host, it is executing its pipeline scripts as the git user.

The SSH Sender: We generated an SSH key specifically for the git user on .51 so the runner could securely push code across the network to .50.

The OpenSSH Security Config Explained:
When hardening Gitea, standard security practice dictates locking down the git user's SSH access. This usually means editing the .51 server's /etc/ssh/sshd_config or the ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file to prevent anyone from logging in interactively and opening a bash terminal as git.

Will this hinder the runner? No. * Why? SSH restrictions lock the incoming front door (preventing people from SSHing into the .51 server as git). Your runner is making an outgoing connection (SSHing out of .51 to reach .50). Outgoing connections are completely unaffected by incoming shell restrictions. Your runner will push code perfectly fine.

2. Infrastructure Locations (Binaries & Logs)
Here is where your critical components live on the .51 server:

Gitea Core:

Binary: Usually located at /usr/local/bin/gitea.

Logs: We traced this using the system journal: sudo journalctl -u gitea -f. (File-based logs are typically in /var/lib/gitea/log/ or /var/log/gitea/).

The Action Runner (act_runner):

Config: Located where you installed it, usually /etc/act_runner/config.yaml.

Logs: We traced this using sudo journalctl -u act_runner -f.

3. The Project Journey & Hurdles Overcome
We built three distinct pillars for your CI/CD architecture. Here is exactly what we built, the traps we hit, and how we solved them.

Pillar 1: The Local Test Environment (deploy-test.yaml)
The Goal: Automatically deploy code to the .51 Apache dummy folder (/app/www/TAT_Sandbox) whenever a PR is merged into master.

The Strategy: We configured Gitea to enforce "Squash" or "Rebase then fast-forward" merges to keep the Git history perfectly straight. Then, the pipeline runs git pull origin master --ff-only and restarts Apache.

The Hurdles:

The Docker Void: The pipeline failed silently because act_runner was running inside an isolated Docker container. Solution: We edited config.yaml and switched the runner to -host mode so it runs directly on the bare metal.

The Unlinked Folder: The runner hit fatal: not a git repository because the dummy folder didn't have a .git database. Solution: We manually ran git init, remote add, and reset --hard to link it.

Git Dubious Ownership: Git's 2022 security patch blocked the pull because of mismatched folder ownership. Solution: We ran git config --global --add safe.directory to authorize the folder.

The Infinite Hang: The pipeline froze waiting for a password. Solution: We swapped the standard HTTP URL for the ephemeral Gitea token: http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@...

Pillar 2: The Core File Guardian (guardian.yaml)
The Goal: Block unauthorized users from modifying main.py or __init__.py.

The Hurdles:

The 4.5 GB Performance Killer: A standard git clone would have choked your server's RAM and CPU. Solution: We implemented the "Blobless Clone" (--filter=blob:none) which only downloads file names, reducing the download to a few megabytes.

Host Workspace Collision: Because the runner is on bare metal, old files were left behind, crashing future runs. Solution: We added rm -rf pr-workspace at the start of the YAML.

The PR Catch-22: We accidentally set the Deployment pipeline as a "Required" check, which blocked the PR from merging entirely. Solution: We removed the deployment pipeline from the Branch Protection whitelist.

Pillar 3: The Production Bridge (deliver-prod.yaml)
The Goal: Manually push a specific feature branch (e.g., newtool/5g_extraction) across the network to the .50 Production server, waiting safely for your weekly Sunday maintenance window.

The Hurdles:

Cross-Server Permissions: We needed the .51 runner to write to the .50 Apache folder safely. Solution: We created the toolbox_admin group on .50, assigned the folder to it, and used a passwordless SSH key pair from the .51 git user.

The "Checked-Out Branch" Rejection: Git physically blocked us from pushing directly to master on the live server. Solution: We implemented the incoming/ namespace. The runner now pushes the code as incoming/master, leaving the live site totally unaffected until you manually merge it locally on .50.

The Hidden Run Button: Your SPOCs couldn't see the "Run Workflow" button. Solution: We explained that they need Repository "Write" permissions and to be whitelisted in the Branch Protection rules.

Final Fix: The Identity Sync
We noticed that commits in the UI were showing the local OS username instead of the developer's avatar. Solution: We updated the local CLI using git config user.name and user.email, and discussed enabling the "Block mismatched emails" security setting in Gitea.

Where We Are Right Now
Your infrastructure is fully operational. The code is protected, the Test server updates automatically, and the Production server receives air-gapped weekly branches.

The Mystery of the act_runner Logs
If your act_runner binary is sitting in /opt/act_runner, where are the logs?

By default, the act_runner application does not write to a log file. It is designed to vomit its logs directly onto the screen (Standard Output).

Because you are running it in the background as a Linux service using systemctl, the systemd daemon acts as a net. It catches all that screen output and stores it in the system journal.

That is why sudo journalctl -u act_runner -f is the correct command. The journal is the log file.

If you absolutely want it to write to a traditional file (e.g., /opt/act_runner/runner.log), we would have to edit your /etc/systemd/system/act_runner.service file and tell systemd to redirect the output. But using journalctl is actually the enterprise standard, so I recommend leaving it as is!

/app/gitea.log where is this configured I want to change it

This is controlled entirely by Gitea's master configuration file: app.ini.

Because your environment uses custom paths, we shouldn't just guess where app.ini is hidden. As a Linux admin, the most bulletproof way to find exactly which configuration file a service is using is to ask systemd.

Here is exactly how to find it, change the log path, and ensure the Linux permissions don't break when you move it.

Step 1: Locate your app.ini
Run this command on your .51 server:

Bash
sudo systemctl cat gitea
Look at the output for the ExecStart= line. It will look something like this:
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/gitea web -c /etc/gitea/app.ini

That -c flag tells you the exact, absolute path to your active app.ini file. (If there is no -c flag, Gitea usually defaults to /custom/conf/app.ini relative to where the binary lives).

Step 2: Edit the Log Path
Open that app.ini file with your text editor (e.g., sudo nano /etc/gitea/app.ini).

Scroll down until you find the [log] section. It will look something like this:

Ini, TOML
[log]
MODE = file
LEVEL = info
ROOT_PATH = /app
FILE_NAME = gitea.log
(Note: Gitea sometimes splits the path using ROOT_PATH for the directory and FILE_NAME for the file, or just puts the absolute path directly in FILE_NAME = /app/gitea.log depending on the version).

Change those values to wherever you want the new logs to live. For enterprise Red Hat environments, the standard best practice is:

Ini, TOML
[log]
MODE = file
LEVEL = info
ROOT_PATH = /var/log/gitea
FILE_NAME = gitea.log
Save and exit the file.

Step 3: The Permission Trap (Crucial)
Before you restart the service, you must put on your DevSecOps hat.

If you just told Gitea to write logs to /var/log/gitea/, the service will instantly crash when you restart it. Why? Because the background service runs as the git user, and the git user does not have permission to create folders inside /var/log/!

You must manually create the new log folder and hand ownership to the git user:

Bash
# 1. Create the new directory
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/gitea

# 2. Give ownership to the git user
sudo chown -R git:git /var/log/gitea
Step 4: Apply the Changes
Now that the directory exists and the permissions are tight, restart the Brain:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart gitea
To verify it worked perfectly, check the status:

Bash
sudo systemctl status gitea
If it is green and active, run ls -l /var/log/gitea/. You should see a brand new gitea.log file sitting there, happily owned by the git user.

This is a fantastic catch. You have just uncovered a classic Linux infrastructure trap: The Systemd Override.

Look closely at your app.ini file:
MODE = console

Because the mode is set to console, Gitea itself is not writing to any file at all. It is just shouting its logs directly into the void (Standard Output).

If Gitea isn't creating /app/gitea.log, who is? Systemd.

Whoever originally set up this .51 server configured the Linux background service to catch Gitea's "console" shouting and forcefully pipe it into /app/gitea.log. Systemd is acting as a middleman, completely ignoring the ROOT_PATH in your app.ini.

How to Find and Fix the Override
We need to edit the actual gitea.service file to stop Linux from forcing the logs into /app.

Step 1: Find the Systemd rule
Run this command to look at the raw service file:

Bash
sudo systemctl cat gitea
Look at the output. You are specifically looking for lines that look like this:

StandardOutput=append:/app/gitea.log

StandardError=append:/app/gitea.log

Or, an ExecStart line that has a bash redirect like: ExecStart=/bin/sh -c '/usr/local/bin/gitea web > /app/gitea.log 2>&1'

Step 2: Edit the Service File
To change this, you need to edit the service file directly. (The cat command above will tell you exactly where the file lives, usually /etc/systemd/system/gitea.service).

Open it with your editor:

Bash

Your instinct about Apache is incredibly sharp. If Apache is acting as a reverse proxy in front of Gitea, it might be configured to dump its access or error logs into that /app folder.

Instead of guessing, we are going to use the ultimate Linux truth-teller. We will ask the operating system kernel exactly which program currently has its hands on that file.

The Investigation: The lsof Command
The lsof (List Open Files) command bypasses all configuration files and looks directly at active memory.

Run this exact command on your .51 server:

Bash
sudo lsof /app/gitea.log
How to Read the Results
This command will immediately expose the culprit. Here is what the output will tell you:

If the COMMAND column says httpd or apache2:
You nailed it. Apache is the one writing to the file. We will need to check your Apache VirtualHost configuration (likely in /etc/httpd/conf.d/ or /etc/apache2/sites-available/) to change where it stores the proxy logs.

If the COMMAND column says gitea:
Gitea is actively ignoring the MODE = console setting. This usually means there is a hidden [log.file] or another [log] block further down at the very bottom of your app.ini file that is overriding the top settings.

If the command returns absolutely NOTHING:
It is a "Ghost File." Nothing is actively writing to it. It is an old log file leftover from a previous configuration before you set it to console. If you run ls -l /app/gitea.log, the timestamp will likely show it hasn't been modified in days or weeks.

This is where we lock the front door. We are going to harden the OpenSSH daemon (sshd) on your .51 server specifically for the git user.

The goal here is to enforce the Principle of Least Privilege. If a hacker somehow guesses the git user's password, or steals an incoming SSH key, we want to guarantee they cannot open a command-line terminal to snoop around your server.

At the same time, we must ensure the Gitea service can still accept code pushes, and your runner can still make outgoing connections to .50.

Here is the exact enterprise hardening procedure for Red Hat.

Step 1: Backup the SSH Configuration
Before touching the primary security daemon of a live server, always create a fallback copy.
Run this on the .51 terminal:

Bash
sudo cp /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak
Step 2: Inject the Security Rules
Open the SSH configuration file in your text editor:

Bash
sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
Scroll to the absolute bottom of the file. (This is critical. Match blocks must always go at the very end of sshd_config, or they will accidentally apply to other users).

Paste this exact block at the bottom:

Plaintext
# --- Gitea Service User Hardening ---
Match User git
    PasswordAuthentication no
    AllowTcpForwarding no
    X11Forwarding no
    PermitTTY no
The Matrix Breakdown (What this actually does):
PasswordAuthentication no: Kills brute-force attacks dead. The git user can now only be accessed via cryptographic SSH keys. Passwords are mathematically rejected.

AllowTcpForwarding no & X11Forwarding no: Closes network loopholes. Hackers often use compromised service accounts to build hidden SSH tunnels or forward malicious traffic through your server. This physically cuts the wires on those tunnels.

PermitTTY no (The Silver Bullet): This prevents the server from granting a Pseudo-Terminal (a shell prompt). Even if someone possesses a valid SSH key for the git user, if they try to log in, Linux will accept the key, realize they want a terminal, and instantly drop the connection. They can only execute background data transfers (which is exactly what Git needs to receive code).

Step 3: Validate and Restart
Whenever you edit SSH configurations, you must validate the syntax before restarting the service. If there is a typo, restarting SSH could lock you out of the server completely.

Run the validation check:

Bash
sudo sshd -t
(If it returns absolutely nothing, your syntax is perfect).

Now, reload the SSH daemon to enforce the new rules:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart sshd
The Outgoing Guarantee
Because we applied these rules specifically inside sshd_config (which controls the server listening for incoming connections), your act_runner on .51 is completely unaffected. When the runner wakes up to push code to .50, it acts as a client making an outgoing connection, bypassing these incoming defensive walls entirely.

With the OpenSSH configuration locked tight, the .51 server's Linux layer is officially hardened against interactive shell attacks on the git account.

No, actually the exact opposite! This is a fantastic question and a very common trap when setting up Linux permissions.

You must run all of those SSH hardening commands while logged in as your normal administrative user (the account you use that has sudo privileges), not as the git user.

Why? The Privilege Divide
The Target File: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file controls the security for the entire server. Linux strictly protects this file. Only an administrator (Root or a user with sudo) is allowed to open it, edit it, or restart the sshd service.

The git User's Limits: The git user is just a lowly service account. It does not (and should never) have sudo privileges. If you log in as git and try to type sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config, Linux will immediately throw a security alert saying "git is not in the sudoers file. This incident will be reported."

The Proper Stance
Think of yourself as the Server Warden.
You log into the .51 server as the Warden (your normal admin account). You open the master security log (sshd_config), and you write a new rule that says: "From now on, the prisoner named 'git' is no longer allowed to have a terminal."

Once you save that file and restart the SSH service (still acting as the Warden), the rule instantly applies to the git user.

Run those sudo nano, sudo sshd -t, and sudo systemctl restart sshd commands exactly as I wrote them.

I love the strategic thinking here. You are trying to perfectly mirror your physical infrastructure (Test -> Prod) inside Git's architecture.

However, since I have my DevSecOps Architect hat on, I am going to throw a massive, enterprise-sized red flag on the play regarding your Upstream/Fork proposal.

Let's break down exactly why that specific Git topology is a trap, how we fix it to industry standards, and then design your "Oh No" rollback button.

The Critique: Why Production Should NEVER Be "Upstream"
In your proposal, the .50 live Apache server holds the "Upstream" repository, and Gitea holds the "Fork".

Here is why this architecture will eventually burn you:

Reversing the Source of Truth: Gitea is your secure, backed-up, permission-controlled fortress. A live web server (.50) is a volatile combat zone. In GitOps, the fortress must be the Upstream (the ultimate source of truth). If .50's hard drive dies, or an application vulnerability wipes the directory, you lose your Upstream repository.

Bypassing the Brain: If developers (or pipelines) are pushing directly to the .50 upstream, you are completely bypassing Gitea's Pull Requests, your Guardian pipeline, your branch protection rules, and your audit logs.

The "Fork" Overhead: Managing a fork requires constantly syncing upstream remotes. It adds unnecessary manual steps to your developers' daily lives.

The Enterprise Pivot: The "Sun and Planets" Model
Instead of a Fork/Upstream relationship, we keep Gitea as the Sun (The one and only Upstream Source of Truth). Your servers are just planets that orbit it.

We actually already built the perfect mechanism for this in our previous steps using Branch-Based Environments:

The Sun (Gitea): Hosts the TAT_Sandbox repository.

Planet 1 (The .51 Test Env): It tracks the master branch. When a developer merges a PR into master, our deploy-test.yaml runner pulls it locally.

Planet 2 (The .50 Prod Env): It tracks the production branch. When you are ready, the SPOC hits the manual button, and the runner pushes the specific feature branch to .50's sleeping incoming/ namespace.

Why this is better: Your developers only ever deal with one single Gitea URL. Your permissions are centralized. And .50 remains a "dumb consumer" of code, rather than a master database.

The "Oh No" Button: Rollback Strategy for .50
Since you are running a High-Availability active/passive setup with Keepalived and Rsync, a bad deployment on .50 is actually a double-threat. If you merge bad code on Sunday night, Rsync will immediately wake up and happily copy that bad code to your .51 backup server!

Here is your official three-stage emergency rollback plan.

Stage 1: The "Abort Merge" (Mid-Deployment Failure)
If you are logged into .50 during the maintenance window, you run git merge incoming/newtool/5g_extraction, and you get a massive merge conflict or an immediate failure before Apache even restarts:

The Button: git merge --abort

What it does: Instantly wipes the attempted merge from the .50 working directory and returns the live files exactly to how they were 5 seconds ago.

Stage 2: The "Instant Rewind" (Post-Deployment Failure)
The merge was successful, you restarted Apache, but the web app is throwing 500 Internal Server Errors. You need to go back to last week's code immediately.

The Button: git reset --hard HEAD~1 (or git reset --hard <commit-hash-of-last-week>)

What it does: Git violently forces the Apache directory to perfectly match the previous commit. You then run sudo systemctl restart httpd, and the site is back online in under 10 seconds.

Stage 3: The Rsync Pause (The HA Safety Net)
To prevent Rsync from copying a broken deployment to your backup server while you are testing it on Sunday night, you should wrap your deployment in an Rsync freeze.

Pre-Deployment: sudo systemctl stop crond (or temporarily disable your Rsync cron job).

Deploy & Test: Merge the code, restart Apache, verify the site works.

Post-Deployment: sudo systemctl start crond. If it failed, you hit Stage 2 to rewind, then turn Rsync back on so the backup server never even knew a failure happened.

The Rsync vs. Git Collision (The Trap)
Before we run the Git commands, we have to look at how your physical folders are mapped:

Server .50 (Active Prod): Runs the live site. Git tracks the production branch here.

Server .51 (Standby Prod / Test?): You have the Gitea runner deploying master (the Test environment) here.

The HA Standby (Owned by Rsync): /app/www/TAT_Sandbox on .51 should not be a Git repository at all. It should just be a dumb mirror that Rsync updates from .50.

The Test Environment (Owned by Git): You should create a completely separate folder on .51 (e.g., /app/www/TAT_Test) specifically for testing the master branch.

The "Dubious Ownership" Git Trap: We just created a brand new folder on .51 and changed its ownership to apache:toolbox_admin. Hardcoded URLs: If any of your YAML files specifically referenced the old TAT_Sandbox.git URL instead of using dynamic variables like ${{ github.repository }}, they will be pointing to a ghost repository.

To fix this with surgical precision, I need to see exactly where the pipelines are bleeding.

Go to the Actions tab in your new Tat_sandbox_test repository in the Gitea UI. Click on the workflow that failed, and open the specific job step that has the red X.

Copy and paste the exact error output it gave you, and we will patch it up instantly! Which workflow crashed first?

/home/git/.cache/act/d800e24aa8190581/act/workflow/0.sh: line 5: cd: /app/www/TAT_Sandbox: No such file or directory

Job 'deploy-local-test' failed

This is the exact kind of error we expect after a physical server migration!

The error is beautifully clear: cd: /app/www/TAT_Sandbox: No such file or directory.

The act_runner woke up, read your YAML file, and blindly tried to walk into a room called TAT_Sandbox (all caps TAT, capital S). But when it opened the door, the room wasn't there.

This happens for one of two reasons:

1. The Linux Case-Sensitivity Trap
Linux is mathematically strict about capitalization. TAT_Sandbox is a completely different folder than Tat_sandbox or tat_sandbox.
In my previous step, I suggested the clone command: git clone ... Tat_sandbox (with a lowercase 'at' and lowercase 's'). If your YAML file is hardcoded to cd /app/www/TAT_Sandbox, Linux will reject it.

2. The Missing Clone Argument
If you ran git clone http://10.30.121.51:444/TAT/Tat_sandbox_test.git without explicitly telling it what to name the folder at the end of the command, Git would have automatically created a folder named Tat_sandbox_test.

The Fix: Aligning the Map with the Territory
We need to make the YAML file and the physical Linux folder perfectly match.

Step 1: See what actually exists
Log into your .51 server and run this command to see the exact spelling and capitalization of the folder you just cloned:

Bash
ls -ld /app/www/*
Step 2: Make your choice
Once you see the exact name of the folder, you have two options:

Option A (Change the folder): Rename the physical folder to exactly match the YAML file:
sudo mv /app/www/<Whatever_It_Is_Named> /app/www/TAT_Sandbox

Option B (Change the YAML): Open your deploy-test.yaml file in Gitea and change cd /app/www/TAT_Sandbox to perfectly match the folder name you see in the ls output.

The Impending Security Trap (Don't skip this!)
Once you fix this typo, the runner will successfully cd into the folder. But the very next command (git pull) is going to trigger Git's "Dubious Ownership" security alarm, because the folder is now owned by apache:toolbox_admin, but the runner is executing as the git user.

To preemptively defuse that bomb, run this command on .51 (making sure to use the exact, correct folder name!):

Bash
sudo -u git git config --global --add safe.directory /app/www/<EXACT_FOLDER_NAME>
Run that ls -ld /app/www/* command and let me know exactly what folder names are sitting in there, or go ahead and align them and re-run the pipeline!

Merged to Master! Updating the Test Git Working Tree...

Pulling latest changes from Gitea...

fatal: not a git repository (or any parent up to mount point /)

Stopping at filesystem boundary (GIT_DISCOVERY_ACROSS_FILESYSTEM not set).

We got past the front door! The runner successfully navigated into the folder. But now, Git is throwing its hands up.

fatal: not a git repository means exactly what it sounds like. The runner (act_runner) walked into the /app/www/TAT_Sandbox directory, looked around for the hidden .git database to figure out what to pull, and couldn't find it.

When this happens right after a fresh clone, it is almost always one of two DevSecOps traps.

Suspect 1: The "Inception" Clone (Nested Folders)
When you ran the clone command, if you were already inside an empty TAT_Sandbox folder, Git might have created a new folder inside it based on the repository name.
Instead of /app/www/TAT_Sandbox/.git, your database might accidentally be sitting at /app/www/TAT_Sandbox/Tat_sandbox_test/.git. If the runner stops at the first folder, it won't see the Git database.

Suspect 2: The Blindfold (Linux Permissions)
This is the most likely culprit based on our last step. We ran sudo chown -R apache:toolbox_admin.
The act_runner service runs as the Linux user named git. If the git user does not have strict Read/Execute permissions on that newly cloned folder, it acts like a blindfold. The runner walks into the folder, but Linux refuses to let it "see" the hidden .git directory. Because it can't see it, it assumes it doesn't exist.

The Investigation
Let's ask the Linux kernel exactly what is sitting in that folder and who owns it.

Run this exact command on your .51 server terminal:

Bash
ls -la /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
Look closely at the output and ask yourself:

Do you see the .git folder in the list? Or do you just see another folder called Tat_sandbox_test?

If .git is there, what are the permissions? (e.g., does it say drwxr-x--- apache toolbox_admin?)

Paste the output of that ls -la command right here. Once I see how the folder is structured and who owns it, we will apply the exact fix to take the blindfold off the runner!

ls -la Tat_sandbox_test/

total 28

drwxrwx---+ 4 apache toolbox_dev 4096 Mar  9 13:28 .

drwxrwx--x+ 6 rsync         1000   91 Mar  9 13:28 ..

drwxrwx---+ 8 apache toolbox_dev 4096 Mar  9 13:28 .git

drwxrwx---+ 3 apache toolbox_dev   23 Mar  9 13:28 .gitea

-rw-rw----+ 1 apache toolbox_dev  214 Mar  9 13:28 hello.py

-rw-rw----+ 1 apache toolbox_dev  295 Mar  9 13:28 home.py

-rw-rw----+ 1 apache toolbox_dev   14 Mar  9 13:28 __init__.py

-rw-rw----+ 1 apache toolbox_dev  115 Mar  9 13:28 main.py

This ls -la output is a beautiful DevSecOps crime scene. It tells us exactly why the runner crashed.

You have two massive Linux security walls completely blocking the git user from seeing that .git folder. Let's break down the forensics of what you just pasted:

The Clues in the Output:

The Target Folder: Your folder is exactly named Tat_sandbox_test.

The Group Shift: Look at the owner and group: apache toolbox_dev. In our previous setups, we were using toolbox_admin. You have shifted to toolbox_dev.

The Brick Wall (---): Look at the permissions on the .git folder: drwxrwx---+.

Owner (apache) has rwx (Read, Write, Execute).

Group (toolbox_dev) has rwx.

Others (Everyone else) has --- (Absolute zero access).

The Verdict: The act_runner executes as the Linux user named git. When the git user walks into Tat_sandbox_test and tries to look at the .git folder, Linux checks its ID badge. It isn't apache, and it isn't in the toolbox_dev group. So, it falls into the "Others" category, hits the --- brick wall, and gets completely blinded. Because it can't see the .git folder, it fails and screams: "fatal: not a git repository!"

The Three-Step Fix
We need to give the git user the correct ID badge, register the exact path in Git's security ledger, and make sure your YAML matches.

Run these exact commands on your .51 server:

Step 1: Give the Runner the Right ID Badge
We must add the git user to your new toolbox_dev group so it inherits those rwx permissions and bypasses the brick wall.

Bash
sudo usermod -a -G toolbox_dev git
(Note: Background services usually need to be restarted to pick up new group memberships. Restart the runner so it gets its new badge: sudo systemctl restart act_runner)

Step 2: Tell Git the Exact Directory is Safe
Now that the runner can physically see the folder, Git's 2022 security patch will still block the pull command because the folder is owned by apache, not git. We must whitelist this specific path.

Bash
sudo -u git git config --global --add safe.directory /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test
Step 3: Update the Pipeline YAML
In your Gitea UI, open your deploy-test.yaml pipeline file. You need to change the cd command to match the exact folder name we see in your output.

Change this:
cd /app/www/TAT_Sandbox
To this:
cd /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test

Commit the change to the YAML file. That commit will instantly trigger the workflow to run again.

Check the Actions tab—does the runner finally see the database and pull the code successfully?

Let's take the pipeline out of the equation completely and test the git user's access directly on the bare metal.

Run this exact command on your .51 server terminal. This forces the server to act exactly like the runner:

Bash

What happens when you run that?
