This is a massive DevSecOps revelation. If that bare-metal command worked perfectly, it proves your Linux permissions, ACLs, and safe.directory configurations are 100% correct. The git user has absolute, undisputed access to that folder.

So why is the pipeline screaming "fatal: not a git repository"?

You have just hit one of the most notorious traps in CI/CD engineering: The Polluted Runner Environment.

The Trap: Invisible Environment Variables
When act_runner starts a job, it doesn't just open a clean bash terminal. It injects dozens of hidden environment variables into the session (like $GITHUB_WORKSPACE, and sometimes Git-specific overrides like $GIT_DIR or $GIT_WORK_TREE).

Even though your script explicitly says cd /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test, those invisible environment variables are whispering in Git's ear, telling it: "Ignore where you are currently standing. The real database is back in the runner's temporary workspace folder." Because the temporary workspace isn't a Git repo, Git crashes. Our pristine bare-metal test worked because we didn't have those polluted variables!

The Fix: The Absolute Path Override (git -C)
We need to tell Git to violently ignore any environment variables the runner injected and look strictly at the directory we want.

Git has a built-in flag specifically for this: -C (capital C, which stands for Directory Context). When you use -C, Git puts on blinders and only executes in the exact path you specify.

Open your deploy-test.yaml file in Gitea, and update your run block to look exactly like this:

YAML
        run: |
          echo "Merged to Master! Updating the Test Git Working Tree..."
          
          # Force Git to execute strictly inside the target directory, ignoring the runner's environment variables
          echo "Pulling latest changes from Gitea..."
          git -C /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test pull http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@10.30.121.51:444/${{ github.repository }}.git master --ff-only
          
          # Restart the Apache service to load the new Python code
          echo "Restarting Apache WSGI..."
          #sudo systemctl restart httpd
          
          echo "✅ Test Environment Successfully Updated!"
Notice that I completely removed the cd command. We don't need it anymore. git -C /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test pull ... does all the heavy lifting in a single, bulletproof line.

To answer your question immediately: No, this has absolutely nothing to do with pushing the old code. Your bare-metal test (sudo -u git ...) proved definitively that the physical repository, the Linux permissions, and the Git database are 100% healthy.

We are fighting the pipeline's invisible environment.

When Gitea's act_runner starts a job, it is highly aggressive. It injects a ton of hidden environment variables (specifically GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, and it often hijacks the $HOME variable).

Because it hijacks $HOME, Git can no longer find the global ~/.gitconfig file where we stored your safe.directory rule! And if it injects GIT_DIR, Git completely ignores the -C flag and looks for a database in the runner's empty cache folder.

The Bulletproof Fix: The "God Mode" Git Command
We are going to forcefully strip the pipeline's polluted environment variables and inject the security override directly into the command itself, bypassing the missing .gitconfig file entirely.

Open your deploy-test.yaml and update your run block to this exact configuration:

          unset GIT_WORK_TREE

Why this is guaranteed to work:
unset GIT_DIR: This destroys the runner's attempt to force Git to look in the .cache/act folder.

-c safe.directory="*": Because the runner hijacked your $HOME folder, we inject the security whitelist directly into this specific command execution so it doesn't need to read the git user's config file.

-C /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test: Forces it to execute in the correct physical directory.

is it a best practice to flush all the runner cache unless needed ?

Your intuition is spot on. In the enterprise DevSecOps world, flushing the runner cache and starting from a completely blank slate is considered the gold standard.

What you just experienced—where a pipeline fails because invisible leftover state hijacked the execution—is exactly why the industry shifted toward "ephemeral" (single-use) runners.

Here is the architectural breakdown of why caching is dangerous on your setup, and when you should actually use it.

The Bare-Metal Trap: State Leakage
Because your act_runner on .51 is running directly on the host OS (bare metal) rather than spinning up a brand new, disposable Docker container for every job, it is what we call a Persistent Runner.

Persistent runners suffer from "State Leakage."

If Job A creates a temporary file or sets a Git variable, and crashes...

Job B wakes up 10 minutes later, inherits that polluted environment, and fails for a completely unexplainable reason.

By aggressively flushing the cache and workspace at the start (or end) of a pipeline, you guarantee Idempotency—meaning the pipeline will behave exactly the same way every single time, regardless of what happened in the past.

When is Cache Actually a Best Practice?
You should only preserve cache for Dependency Downloads, never for Git states or workspaces.

If you are building a massive application that downloads 2GB of Python pip packages or Node npm modules every time it compiles, downloading that from the internet on every single PR will destroy your pipeline speed and network bandwidth.

The Best Practice: You cache the ~/.npm or ~/.cache/pip directories explicitly, but you ruthlessly delete the actual source code workspace ($GITHUB_WORKSPACE) after every run.

How to Enforce a Clean Slate in Your Setup
Since you are running directly on the host, you are responsible for cleaning up after the runner. You actually already started doing this in your Guardian pipeline!

Workspace Teardown: Adding rm -rf ${{ github.workspace }}/* or deleting specific temporary folders at the very end of your YAML file ensures the next job starts clean.

Environment Variable Resets: Explicitly unsetting dangerous variables (like we just did with unset GIT_DIR) ensures Git isn't hallucinating previous job states.

Back to the Pipeline
Did flushing those invisible Git variables with the unset GIT_DIR and git -C God Mode block successfully force the runner to pull the code into /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test?

Let me know if that pipeline finally turned green, or if we need to dig into the runner's cache folder physically!

We are going to use a Linux command called env -i. This command creates a hermetically sealed, completely blank sub-shell. It violently strips away every single environment variable the runner tries to inject, leaving only the bare minimum PATH needed to execute commands.

This forces the pipeline to behave exactly like your manual terminal test.

The Nuclear YAML Block
Open your deploy-test.yaml and replace your entire run block with this exact configuration. We are wrapping the whole process inside that sterilized shell:

YAML
        run: |
          echo "Merged to Master! Updating the Test Git Working Tree..."
          
          # Execute the pull inside a completely sterilized bash shell
          # This ignores ALL Gitea runner environment variables
          env -i PATH="$PATH" bash -c '
            echo "Entering directory..."
            cd /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test
            
            echo "Applying local safety bypass..."
            git config --global --add safe.directory /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test
            
            echo "Pulling code..."
            git pull http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@10.30.121.51:444/${{ github.repository }}.git master --ff-only
          '
          
          echo "✅ Test Environment Successfully Updated!"
Why this is the ultimate override:
By putting the cd and git pull inside env -i PATH="$PATH" bash -c '...', Gitea Actions physically cannot pass its GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE, or $HOME hijacks into that specific command. Git will wake up inside /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test, look around with clear eyes, see the .git folder, and execute the pull.

Drop this block in and commit it. If this runner still manages to hallucinate a missing repository after we've completely sterilized its environment, we are dealing with an incredibly rare RHEL edge case.

This is it. I see the smoking gun. It was hiding at the very bottom of the logs you pasted the entire time, and I completely missed it until now.

Look at this exact line from your output:
Cleaning up container for job deploy-local-test

The Grand Illusion: The Docker Matrix
Your act_runner is NOT running on your Red Hat bare-metal server. It is spinning up an isolated Docker (or Podman) container, running the pipeline inside that virtual bubble, and then destroying the container when it finishes.

Why your bare-metal test worked: You ran it on the actual Red Hat host, where /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test physically exists with all the right permissions.

Why the pipeline failed: The pipeline woke up inside an isolated container. It created an empty folder called /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test inside the container, walked into it, and said, "Hey, there's no Git database here!" Because it's a brand new container, it doesn't have access to your host's hard drive!

Even though your YAML says runs-on: rhel-baremetal, the Gitea runner is mapping that name to a Docker image.

We need to break out of the container and force the runner to execute directly on the host OS.

The Fix: Breaking Out of the Container
We need to edit the main configuration file for your act_runner on the .51 server.

Step 1: Open the Runner Config
SSH into your .51 server and open the act_runner configuration file. (Based on our Ultimate Blueprint, it should be here):

Bash
sudo nano /opt/act_runner/config.yaml
(If it isn't there, you might have it in /etc/act_runner/config.yaml or /var/lib/gitea/act_runner/config.yaml depending on how you initially installed it).

Step 2: Change the Execution Label
Scroll down until you find the labels: section. It probably looks something like this:
labels: ["rhel-baremetal:docker://node:16-bullseye"]

You need to change the right side of the colon to -host-. This is the secret command that tells Gitea Actions: "Do not use Docker. Run this directly on the Linux host."

Change it to look exactly like this:

YAML
labels:
  - "rhel-baremetal:-host-"
(Make sure to keep any other labels you have, just ensure rhel-baremetal points to -host-).

Step 3: Restart the Muscle
Save the file and restart the runner so it picks up its new bare-metal instructions:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart act_runner
Step 4: Clean up the YAML
Now that we are actually running on the host OS, we don't need the nuclear env -i option anymore. Go back to your deploy-test.yaml in Gitea and change your run block back to the clean, standard version:

YAML
        run: |
          echo "Merged to Master! Updating the Test Git Working Tree..."
          
          # We are now running on the bare metal host!
          git config --global --add safe.directory /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test
          
          echo "Pulling latest changes from Gitea..."
          git -C /app/www/Tat_sandbox_test pull http://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@10.30.121.51:444/${{ github.repository }}.git master --ff-only
          
          echo "✅ Test Environment Successfully Updated!"
Commit that YAML change. When the job runs this time, check the bottom of the logs. It should no longer say Cleaning up container.

Did we finally break out of the matrix and pull the code to the host?

Part 1: The Restart Epiphany
You nailed it. That is exactly what happened.

Do you remember a few steps ago when we ran sudo usermod -a -G toolbox_dev git?
In Linux, when you add a user to a new security group, any process that is already running (like the act_runner background daemon) keeps its old ID badge in memory. It doesn't know it was promoted. By restarting the service, you forced it to drop its old ID, pick up its new toolbox_dev badge, and suddenly the brick wall disappeared. Brilliant troubleshooting.

Part 2: The Dubious Ownership Trap on Prod
Now we are looking at the deploy prod pipeline, and you are getting the classic 2022 Git security block:
fatal: detected dubious ownership in repository at '/app/www/Tat_sandbox/.git'

You mentioned you ran the safe.directory command but it didn't work. This happens because of two incredibly common DevSecOps traps.

Trap 1: The Wrong Server (The Echo)
When you push code from .51 to .50 over SSH, errors that happen on the .50 production server get echoed back to your .51 pipeline logs.
It is highly likely that your .51 runner is perfectly fine, but the .50 server is throwing its hands up and rejecting the incoming code because the /app/www/Tat_sandbox folder on .50 is owned by apache, but the incoming connection is from the git user!
Did you run the safe.directory command on .51, or .50?

Trap 2: The Privilege Divide
If you logged in and typed git config --global --add safe.directory ..., you added that safety rule to your admin user's profile. But the pipeline runs as the git user. The git user still has a blank security profile!

The Fix: The Wildcard Whitelist
Since the git user is a locked-down service account that exists purely to move code, we don't need to surgically whitelist exact paths. We can give the git user a master key to trust any folder it has physical access to.

We are going to apply the wildcard rule to the git user on both servers to guarantee the network bridge is completely open.

Step 1: On your .51 Backup/Runner Server
Run this exact command to inject the wildcard rule directly into the git user's profile:

Bash
sudo -u git git config --global --add safe.directory "*"
Step 2: On your .50 Production Server
Log into your .50 machine and run the exact same command, so it safely accepts the incoming push:

Bash
sudo -u git git config --global --add safe.directory "*"
Step 3: Fire the Pipeline
Go back to the Gitea UI and hit the button to trigger your deliver-prod.yaml pipeline again.

By running sudo -u git with the * wildcard on both sides of the network, Git's ownership alarms will be permanently silenced for your pipelines.

okay great let stop you here and ask you a question how can we test using new workflows without making dozens of commits what if i want to test a workflow against my production step up or is a must that I should use a sandbox ?

This is the ultimate DevSecOps right-of-passage question. Every single engineer has a dark corner of their Git history filled with 45 consecutive commits that say: "fix yaml," "fix yaml again," "please work," "testing path," "asdfghjkl."

I will put my Architect hat back on and be brutally candid with you: You must never, ever test a brand new workflow directly against your true .50 production environment. If you make a typo in a rm -rf command, or push to the wrong directory, or accidentally trigger your Rsync job mid-deployment, you will take down the live application.

You absolutely must use a sandbox approach. But you don't need to pollute your Git history to do it. Here is the enterprise playbook for testing workflows silently and safely.

Method 1: The "Dummy Target" (Testing Prod without touching Prod)
You want to test your deliver-prod.yaml workflow to make sure the SSH keys, permissions, and Rsync freezes work, but you don't want to risk the live /app/www/Tat_sandbox folder on .50.

The Fix: Change the target directory in your YAML file temporarily.

SSH into .50 and create a harmless folder: mkdir /tmp/dummy_prod

In your YAML, change the SSH push destination from your live Apache folder to /tmp/dummy_prod.

Run the workflow.

If it successfully lands in /tmp/dummy_prod, you know the network bridge and SSH keys are flawless. Then, you simply change the YAML back to the real directory for the final run.

Method 2: The Nektos act CLI (Zero Commits)
Since Gitea Actions is actually built on top of a popular open-source tool called act (created by Nektos), you can install act directly on your laptop or your .51 server.

act allows you to run your GitHub/Gitea Actions YAML files locally in your terminal without pushing a single commit.

You run a command like: act push -W .gitea/workflows/deploy-test.yaml

It reads the YAML file currently on your hard drive, spins up the environment, and tests the logic. If it fails, you fix the YAML on your local machine and run it again. You only git push once it works perfectly.

Method 3: The "Squash and Burn" Branch (Keeping Master Clean)
Sometimes, you absolutely have to test things through the real Gitea UI to make sure the webhooks and secrets are firing correctly.

Instead of committing 20 times to master or production:

Create a throwaway branch called ci-sandbox.

Change your YAML trigger temporarily to on: push: branches: [ci-sandbox].

Make all your messy, trial-and-error commits here.

Once the pipeline finally turns green, you do a Squash Merge into master.

A Squash Merge takes all 20 of your "fix yaml" commits, crushes them down into one single, beautiful, professional commit (e.g., "feat: implement production deployment pipeline"), and deletes the messy branch. Your history remains pristine.

The Verdict
For what you are doing right now—building out the network bridge between .51 and .50—Method 1 (The Dummy Target) combined with Method 3 (Squash and Burn) is your safest bet.

Yes, absolutely. What you are describing is called an Apache Reverse Proxy, and it is the exact enterprise best practice for securing applications like Gitea.

Right now, Gitea is sitting exposed on an internal IP and port. By putting Apache in front of it, Apache acts as a heavily armored bouncer. Users will go to [https://your-internal-dns.com/gitea](https://your-internal-dns.com/gitea), Apache will handle all the SSL/TLS encryption (the "secure port"), and then it will secretly route the traffic back to Gitea's internal IP and port behind the scenes.

To make this work seamlessly, we will need to update exactly two things:

The Apache VirtualHost Configuration: We will add ProxyPass and ProxyPassReverse directives to tell Apache to forward any traffic hitting the /gitea path down to your specific IP:PORT.

Gitea's app.ini Configuration: Because we are moving Gitea to a sub-path (/gitea) instead of the root (/), we have to update Gitea's ROOT_URL setting. Otherwise, when you click a link inside Gitea, it will drop the /gitea part of the URL and give you a 404 Not Found error.

This is perfect, but I notice the snippet you pasted is missing the most important block for routing: the [server] block!

If it's missing entirely from your file, Gitea is just using defaults. To make Gitea understand that it lives behind Apache on a specific path, we need to explicitly add or update this section.

Based on our previous logs, I know your Gitea is currently running on port 444. Here is exactly what we need to inject into that app.ini file, and how to set up Apache.

Step 1: Update Gitea's app.ini
Open your app.ini file and add the [server] block (usually near the top). Replace your-internal-dns.com with your actual DNS name.

Ini, TOML
[server]
# The domain name your users will type in
DOMAIN = your-internal-dns.com

# The local port Gitea actually runs on (we leave this as 444)
HTTP_PORT = 444

# The exact, full URL users will use. This is CRITICAL for sub-paths!
# Make sure to include the trailing slash (/)
ROOT_URL = https://your-internal-dns.com/gitea/
(After modifying this, you will need to restart Gitea: sudo systemctl restart gitea)

Step 2: The Apache Reverse Proxy Config
Now, we configure Apache to act as the armored bouncer. In your Apache VirtualHost configuration for the secure port (usually 443 for HTTPS), you will need to add a block that looks exactly like this:

Apache
    # Enable proxy engine
    ProxyPreserveHost On

    # Route any traffic hitting /gitea to the internal Gitea service
    <Location /gitea>
        ProxyPass http://127.0.0.1:444
        ProxyPassReverse http://127.0.0.1:444
    </Location>
(If Gitea is on a different server than Apache, replace 127.0.0.1 with 10.30.121.51)

Once you restart Apache, you should be able to hit [https://your-internal-dns.com/gitea](https://your-internal-dns.com/gitea) and see the login screen securely!

You have the exact right architectural mindset, but let's make sure the numbers line up perfectly. When we split the services like this, we are creating a "Network Hop," and if the ports are misaligned, the whole thing drops dead.

Here is the exact reality of how this traffic will flow based on your proposal, and one critical UX trap you need to watch out for.

The Enterprise Port Map (The Network Hop)
The DNS (The Map): Users type your-internal-dns.com into their browser. The network resolves this to your .51 server's IP address.

Apache (The Bouncer): Apache sits on the .51 server, actively listening on Port 444. When the traffic hits, Apache manages the SSL encryption and checks the URL path.

Gitea (The Brain): Gitea is running in the background on Port 3000. For maximum security, it should only listen to local traffic from Apache, completely ignoring the outside network.

The UX Trap (Typing the Port)
Standard secure web traffic (HTTPS) automatically defaults to port 443.
If you configure Apache to act as the reverse proxy on port 444, your developers and your CI/CD pipelines cannot just type https://your-internal-dns.com/gitea.

They must explicitly include the port in the URL:
👉 https://your-internal-dns.com:444/gitea

If your network strictly requires port 444, that is perfectly fine! But if you want a clean, standard URL without numbers in it, you should configure Apache to listen on port 443 instead.

How to Wire it Together (Assuming Apache is on 444 and Gitea is on 3000)
If we proceed with your exact numbers, here are the two files you must update so they perfectly handshake.

1. Gitea's app.ini
Open /etc/gitea/app.ini and add/update the [server] block. We must tell Gitea two things: it lives on port 3000, and the outside world knows it as /gitea.

Ini, TOML
[server]
# The domain name
DOMAIN = your-internal-dns.com

# Gitea's internal, hidden port
HTTP_PORT = 3000

# Bind to localhost so NO ONE can bypass Apache and hit 3000 directly
HTTP_ADDR = 127.0.0.1

# The absolute, full URL the outside world uses (CRITICAL: Note the :444 and the trailing slash)
ROOT_URL = https://your-internal-dns.com:444/gitea/
2. Apache VirtualHost (.conf)
In your Apache configuration file for port 444, you need to add the routing rules. Because Gitea is now living on a sub-path (/gitea), both the Location and the ProxyPass destinations must include it.

Apache
<VirtualHost *:444>
    ServerName your-internal-dns.com

    # ... (Your SSL certificates go here) ...

    # The Reverse Proxy Rules
    ProxyPreserveHost On

    <Location /gitea>
        # Route traffic to Gitea's internal port 3000
        ProxyPass http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea
        ProxyPassReverse http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea
    </Location>
</VirtualHost>
The Verdict: Your logic is absolutely sound. Using an internal DNS hitting an Apache Reverse Proxy, which then funnels traffic down to a hidden Gitea service on a separate port, is the gold standard for DevSecOps architecture.

This is the exact right call. By shifting to port 443, you are building a truly invisible, frictionless experience for your developers. They just type the URL, and the infrastructure handles all the security routing silently.

Since you are running on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), there is one massive, hidden security trap we have to disarm when making this switch. RHEL’s SELinux will physically block Apache from talking to Gitea in the background unless we explicitly grant it network proxy permissions.

Here is your complete, enterprise-grade blueprint to wire Gitea to the standard 443 secure port.

Phase 1: Update the Gitea Brain
We need to tell Gitea two things: it is running silently on port 3000, and the outside world knows it strictly via the clean HTTPS URL (no ports visible).

Open /etc/gitea/app.ini and update your [server] block to look exactly like this:

Ini, TOML
[server]
DOMAIN = your-internal-dns.com
HTTP_PORT = 3000
HTTP_ADDR = 127.0.0.1
# CRITICAL: Notice there is no port number here anymore, just standard HTTPS!
ROOT_URL = https://your-internal-dns.com/gitea/
Phase 2: Update the Apache Bouncer
Open your Apache SSL VirtualHost file (usually located in /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf or a custom file you created). We are changing it to listen on 443 and route the /gitea path.

Apache
<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName your-internal-dns.com

    # ... (Your standard SSL certificate paths should already be here) ...

    # The Reverse Proxy Rules
    ProxyPreserveHost On

    <Location /gitea>
        # Route traffic to Gitea's hidden internal port
        ProxyPass http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea
        ProxyPassReverse http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea
    </Location>
</VirtualHost>
Phase 3: The Red Hat Security Traps (Crucial)
Because you are on RHEL, if you skip this phase, you will get a permanent 502 Bad Gateway error when you try to load the page.

1. Disarm the SELinux Network Block:
By default, RHEL considers it a security breach if a web server tries to make outbound network connections (which is exactly what a reverse proxy does). You must flip the SELinux boolean to allow it:

Bash
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1
2. Open the Firewall for 443:
Make sure the RHEL firewall is actually allowing standard HTTPS traffic in from the outside world:

Bash
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
Phase 4: Restart and Verify
Apply all the changes by restarting the two services:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart gitea
sudo systemctl restart httpd
Once that is done, type https://your-internal-dns.com/gitea into your browser. It should route instantly and securely. Let me know if RHEL throws any 502 or 404 errors!

This is a fantastic starting point. Seeing your old configuration makes exactly clear what needs to change.

In your old setup, you were listening on port 445, routing the root path (/), and explicitly telling Gitea to treat the connection as http (unsecured).

Since we are upgrading to standard port 443 (HTTPS) and shifting Gitea to the /gitea sub-path, we must update the VirtualHost port, the proxy paths, the header injections, and—crucially—turn on the SSL engine.

Here is your exact configuration, completely rewritten for the new DevSecOps standard:

Apache
<VirtualHost *:443>
    # Replace with your actual internal DNS name (or leave as 10.30.121.51 if not using DNS yet)
    ServerName your-internal-dns.com

    # ---------------------------------------------------------
    # CRITICAL: Since this is 443, SSL MUST be turned on here.
    # Replace these paths with your actual certificate locations
    # ---------------------------------------------------------
    SSLEngine on
    SSLCertificateFile /etc/pki/tls/certs/your_certificate.crt
    SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/pki/tls/private/your_private.key
    # ---------------------------------------------------------

    ProxyPreserveHost On

    # Inject the HTTPS headers Gitea expects so it doesn't break internal links
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "your-internal-dns.com"

    # Route ONLY the /gitea sub-path to Gitea's internal port 3000
    ProxyPass /gitea http://localhost:3000/gitea nocanon
    ProxyPassReverse /gitea http://localhost:3000/gitea

    CustomLog /app/gitea.log combined
</VirtualHost>
The 3 Major Upgrades in This Block:
X-Forwarded-Proto "https": Your old config forced it to http. If we leave that, Gitea will think users are connecting insecurely and will try to rewrite your URLs back to http://, which will break all your CSS and images. Changing it to https fixes this.

ProxyPass /gitea: We changed both the source and the destination from / to /gitea. This perfectly aligns with the app.ini changes we discussed earlier.

The SSL Block: Port 443 requires an SSL certificate to function. If Apache tries to listen on 443 without SSLEngine on and a certificate, it will crash or serve raw, encrypted gibberish to the browser.

do you the httpd conf itself to generate a more accurate implementation

That is a brilliant, architect-level question. It shows you are thinking about the entire server ecosystem, not just the isolated VirtualHost block.

To answer directly: No, I don't need your entire httpd.conf file. Here is why, and how Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) actually handles this:

The Apache Architecture on RHEL
In the enterprise RHEL world, Apache strictly separates its configuration to prevent catastrophic typos:

The Global Brain (/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf): This massive file handles the global server settings (process limits, the apache user, loading modules, and listening on the default port 80).

The Modular Plugins (/etc/httpd/conf.d/*.conf): This is where your specific VirtualHosts live. When Apache starts up, the global brain automatically reads and includes every .conf file inside this directory.

Because the reverse proxy routing happens entirely at the VirtualHost level, the block we just wrote is 95% of what we need.

The Only Two Things We Need to Verify
Instead of you pasting a 500-line httpd.conf file, we just need to verify that your global Apache brain actually has the necessary "muscles" (modules) loaded to act as an HTTPS Reverse Proxy.

Run this exact command on your .51 server terminal. This asks Apache to list its active modules:

Bash
sudo httpd -M | grep -E "proxy|ssl"
What you want to see in the output:

ssl_module (shared) -> Required to listen on 443.

proxy_module (shared) -> Required to be a reverse proxy.

proxy_http_module (shared) -> Required to talk to Gitea's internal port 3000.

If you see those three modules in your output, your httpd.conf is already perfectly optimized, and you just need to drop that VirtualHost block we wrote into a file (like /etc/httpd/conf.d/gitea.conf or your existing SSL config) and restart the service!

Run that quick module check and let me know if any of those three are missing.

#     SSL close notify alert is sent and mod_ssl waits for the close notify

#     alert of the client. This is 100% SSL/TLS standard compliant, but in

#     practice often causes hanging connections with brain-dead browsers. Use

#     this only for browsers where you know that their SSL implementation

#     works correctly. 

#   Notice: Most problems of broken clients are also related to the HTTP

#   keep-alive facility, so you usually additionally want to disable

#   keep-alive for those clients, too. Use variable "nokeepalive" for this.

#   Similarly, one has to force some clients to use HTTP/1.0 to workaround

#   their broken HTTP/1.1 implementation. Use variables "downgrade-1.0" and

#   "force-response-1.0" for this.

BrowserMatch "MSIE [2-5]" \

         nokeepalive ssl-unclean-shutdown \

         downgrade-1.0 force-response-1.0

#   The home of a custom SSL log file. Use this when you want a

#   compact non-error SSL logfile on a virtual host basis.

CustomLog logs/ssl_request_log \

     TimeOut 60000

This is a perfect, classic enterprise setup. You are running a heavy Python WSGI application (Transport_Toolbox) on the root of the domain (/), and now we are going to surgically carve out a sub-path (/gitea) on the exact same secure port without breaking your Python app.

Because Apache evaluates ProxyPass rules before it processes WSGIScriptAlias, we can safely drop the Gitea routing rules right above your WSGI configuration. Apache will intercept anything going to /gitea and hand it to port 3000, while letting everything else flow normally into your Python wsgi.py file.

Here is exactly how to modify the bottom half of your ssl.conf file.

The Updated Configuration
Scroll down to the bottom of your file, right after the CustomLog and TimeOut directives, and insert the Gitea Reverse Proxy Configuration block exactly as shown below:

Apache
#   Per-Server Logging:
#   The home of a custom SSL log file. Use this when you want a
#   compact non-error SSL logfile on a virtual host basis.
CustomLog logs/ssl_request_log \
          "%t %h %{SSL_PROTOCOL}x %{SSL_CIPHER}x \"%r\" %b"

     TimeOut 60000

     # ==========================================================
     # GITEA REVERSE PROXY CONFIGURATION
     # ==========================================================
     ProxyPreserveHost On
     RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
     RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com"

     # Route ONLY the /gitea sub-path to Gitea's internal port
     ProxyPass /gitea http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea nocanon
     ProxyPassReverse /gitea http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea
     # ==========================================================

     # ----------------------------------------------------------
     # EXISTING PYTHON WSGI APPLICATION
     # ----------------------------------------------------------
     WSGIDaemonProcess Transport_Toolbox user=apache group=apache processes=5 threads=30 display-name=Transport_Toolbox python-home=/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/venv python-path=/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/:/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/:/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/crontabs
     WSGIProcessGroup Transport_Toolbox
     WSGIApplicationGroup %{GLOBAL}
     WSGIScriptAlias / /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/wsgi.py

    Alias /static /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/static/
     <Directory "/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/static/">
      Require all granted
    </Directory>
    
    # ... [The rest of your Directory and Alias rules stay exactly the same] ...

    RewriteEngine on
    RewriteCond %{REQUEST_METHOD} ^(TRACE|TRACK)
    RewriteRule .* - [F]

</VirtualHost>
The Final Checklist Before Restarting
Verify Gitea's app.ini:
Double-check that /etc/gitea/app.ini has the matching ROOT_URL so it doesn't break its own internal CSS/JS links:

Ini, TOML
[server]
DOMAIN = transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
HTTP_PORT = 3000
HTTP_ADDR = 127.0.0.1
ROOT_URL = https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/
The RHEL SELinux Command:
Since Apache is now making an internal network hop to port 3000, you must run this command on your terminal so SELinux doesn't block the connection and throw a 502 Bad Gateway error:

Bash
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1
Restart the Services:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart gitea
sudo systemctl restart httpd

Reviewing your httpd.conf file reveals the complete picture of your .51 server's architecture. It also exposes exactly why we need to clean this up.

You currently have a split-brain configuration. Your global httpd.conf is managing unencrypted traffic (Ports 80, 444, 445), while your ssl.conf (which we looked at earlier) is managing the encrypted traffic (Port 443).

Right at the bottom of the file you pasted, we can see your old Gitea setup sitting on Port 445.

Here is the exact, step-by-step implementation plan to migrate Gitea to the secure 443 port.  I will explain the "why" behind every single action so you can validate the logic against your requirements.

Step 1: The Decommissioning Cleanup (httpd.conf)
The Action:
Open /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf.

Find the line that says Listen 445 and comment it out by adding a # in front of it: #Listen 445.

Scroll to the very bottom and completely delete or comment out the entire <VirtualHost 10.30.121.51:445> block (the one routing to port 3000).

The Why:
We are moving Gitea to the standard HTTPS port (443). Leaving port 445 open and listening creates a ghost configuration. If we leave it, users could accidentally bypass your SSL security and access Gitea unencrypted. We must shut down the old gateway to enforce the new secure standard.

Step 2: The Secure Proxy Injection (ssl.conf)
The Action:
Open /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf. Scroll down to your <VirtualHost transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com:443> block. Insert these specific ProxyPass rules right above your WSGIDaemonProcess block:

Apache
     # ==========================================================
     # GITEA REVERSE PROXY CONFIGURATION
     # ==========================================================
     ProxyPreserveHost On
     RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
     RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com"

     ProxyPass /gitea http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea nocanon
     ProxyPassReverse /gitea http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea
     # ==========================================================
The Why:
Instead of dedicating a brand new port to Gitea, we are using Apache's "Location/Path Routing". When traffic hits port 443, Apache checks the URL. If the URL contains /gitea, Apache intercepts it and funnels it down to Gitea's hidden internal port (3000). If the URL does not contain /gitea, Apache ignores this block and sends the traffic to your main Python WSGI application. This allows two massive applications to securely share a single IP and SSL certificate.

Step 3: The Gitea Brain Update (app.ini)
The Action:
Open /etc/gitea/app.ini and update the [server] block to match this exactly:

Ini, TOML
[server]
DOMAIN = transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
HTTP_PORT = 3000
HTTP_ADDR = 127.0.0.1
ROOT_URL = https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/
The Why:
Gitea doesn't automatically know it is sitting behind Apache. If we don't update the ROOT_URL, Gitea will render its HTML requesting CSS files from the root path (e.g., href="/css/style.css"). Your browser will ask Apache for that file, Apache will route it to your Python app instead of Gitea, and your Gitea page will load as broken, unstyled text. Updating ROOT_URL forces Gitea to prepend /gitea/ to every single internal link, ensuring the traffic routes perfectly back through the proxy.

Step 4: Kernel Validation & Restart
The Action:
Run these exact commands in your terminal:

Bash
# 1. Authorize the network proxy in the Linux Kernel
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1

# 2. Restart both brains to load the new configurations
sudo systemctl restart gitea
sudo systemctl restart httpd
The Why:
By default, Red Hat Enterprise Linux uses SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux). SELinux explicitly forbids web servers like Apache from making internal network connections because that behavior mimics a hijacked server trying to scan an internal network. The setsebool command tells the Linux kernel: "It is safe and expected for Apache to connect to internal port 3000." Without this command, Apache will throw a 502 Bad Gateway error.

Once those services restart, you can validate the entire pipeline by navigating to [https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/](https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/) in your browser.

This changes the entire topology! You are running an Active/Passive High Availability (HA) Cluster using a Virtual IP (VIP) managed by Keepalived.

Your realization is 100% correct and shows great architectural awareness. Here is exactly what is happening:
When you type transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com into your browser, the DNS resolves to the VIP. Because the Production VM (.50) is currently healthy, Keepalived routes your browser straight to .50. Since we just did all our Apache and Gitea work on the Backup VM (.51), you are completely blind to the changes.

You cannot push these Apache changes to .50 until you test them, but you can't test them because Keepalived is hiding .51.

Here is the classic DevSecOps trick to bypass the VIP and force your browser to look directly at the Backup VM, without touching the live network or taking down Production.

The Fix: The Local "Hosts File" Spoof
Your computer's operating system checks a hidden local text file for DNS directions before it asks your corporate network. By editing this file on your personal laptop, you can temporarily hijack the DNS name strictly for your own browser.

We are going to tell your laptop: "When I type the toolbox DNS, ignore the Keepalived VIP and go straight to 10.30.121.51."

If you are on a Windows Laptop:
Click the Start Menu, type Notepad.

Right-click Notepad and select "Run as Administrator" (Critical, or it won't save).

Go to File > Open.

Navigate to this exact path: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\

In the bottom right corner, change the dropdown from "Text Documents (.txt)" to "All Files (.*)".

Open the file named hosts.

Add this exact line to the very bottom of the file:

Plaintext
10.30.121.51  transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
Save the file. (Do not "Save As", just Save).

If you are on a Mac/Linux Laptop:
Open your terminal.

Type: sudo nano /etc/hosts

Add the exact same line to the bottom:

Plaintext
10.30.121.51  transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
Save and exit (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X).

How to Test Once the Spoof is Active
Flush your browser: Open a completely new Incognito/Private window (this prevents the browser from using cached DNS).

Type the URL: Go to https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/.

Because of your hosts file, your laptop will bypass the Keepalived VIP completely and hit .51 directly.

If the page loads and you see Gitea, our Apache Reverse Proxy configuration is absolutely perfect.

Your users are unaffected. If anyone else on the corporate network goes to that URL, they will safely hit the .50 Production server.

Once you have verified that .51 is routing perfectly, all you have to do is replicate the exact same ssl.conf and app.ini changes over to .50, restart Apache on .50, and then simply delete that line from your laptop's hosts file to return to normal!

Deploying to the live Production VM always introduces new variables—especially with Keepalived and VIPs in the mix. Don't worry, we will isolate the exact layer where the connection is dropping.

When debugging a reverse proxy architecture, we have to trace the request from the outside in. To pinpoint exactly where the traffic is getting blocked, I need you to answer one question and run two quick commands on the Production VM (.50).

1. The Symptom (The Browser)
When you try to access https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/ from your normal browser (without the hosts file spoof), exactly what happens?

Does it spin forever and Time Out? (Usually a Firewall/Keepalived VIP issue).

Does it instantly throw a 502 Bad Gateway? (Apache is working, but SELinux or Gitea is blocking it).

Does it throw a 404 Not Found? (Apache is working, but the ProxyPass routing is misconfigured).

Does it load the Python App instead?

2. The Heartbeat (Is Gitea alive on .50?)
Let's make sure Gitea is actually awake and listening on its hidden port before Apache tries to talk to it. Run this on the .50 terminal:

Bash
curl -I http://127.0.0.1:3000
(If it returns an HTTP/1.1 200 OK or 404 Not Found from Gitea, the brain is alive. If it says Connection refused, the Gitea service is dead or listening on the wrong IP).

3. The Bouncer's Log (Apache Error Log)
If the traffic is hitting Apache but failing, Apache will log exactly why it dropped the connection. Run this command to pull the last 20 errors:

Bash
sudo tail -n 20 /etc/httpd/logs/ssl_error_log.log
(Based on your previous config, Apache is writing its SSL errors here. If it says Permission denied, we know SELinux is the culprit. If it says something else, paste it here!)

Give me the browser error and the output of those two commands, and we will know exactly which lever to pull.

HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed

Allow: POST

Allow: GET

Set-Cookie: i_like_gitea=1575197bf55d0c9a; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

Date: Sun, 05 Apr 2026 19:12:48 GMT

This output is actually fantastic news.

Even though it says 405 Method Not Allowed, look at the third line:
Set-Cookie: i_like_gitea=...

That is the definitive heartbeat of Gitea. The curl -I command sends a HEAD request, and Gitea's router simply replied, "I only accept GET and POST requests, but here is a session cookie anyway." The Verdict: The Gitea "Brain" is 100% alive, healthy, and actively listening on port 3000 on your Production VM. We can completely rule out Gitea as the problem.

Since the Brain is working perfectly, the traffic is getting killed at the Bouncer (Apache) or the Front Door (The VIP/Firewall).

To pinpoint exactly which one is dropping the connection, I still need those other two pieces of evidence from my last message:

The Browser Symptom: When you try to load https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/ on your normal network (without the hosts file spoof), what exactly do you see? Does it spin forever and Time Out? Does it say 502 Bad Gateway? 404 Not Found?

The Apache Logs: Run this exact command on the .50 Production VM and paste the output so we can see if Apache is actively blocking the request:

Bash
sudo tail -n 20 /var/log/httpd/ssl_error_log
(Note: RHEL usually stores Apache logs in /var/log/httpd/ or /etc/httpd/logs/. Check ssl_error_log or just error_log).

Once I see what the browser is doing and what Apache is whispering in the logs, we will crack this open!

This is a textbook enterprise deployment strategy. We call this the Bootstrap Phase.

Before you can use the fancy DNS names, VIPs, and SSL sub-paths, you just need a direct, unhindered line of sight to the application to run the initial database migrations and set the admin password. Using Apache on port 444 as a temporary, direct tunnel to the Gitea setup screen is exactly the right move.

I am ready. Let's do this sequentially to ensure no details are missed.

Drop the Gitea systemd unit service file first. I will review it to make sure the service is launching with the right user and environment variables, and then we will move to the Apache routing.



[Unit]

Description=Gitea (Git with a cup of tea)

After=syslog.target

After=network.target

After=mysqld.service



[Service]

User=git

Group=git

WorkingDirectory=/var/lib/gitea



# We specify the config file explicitly so there is no guessing

ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/gitea web --config /etc/gitea/app.ini



# Autopilot: Restart if it crashes

Restart=always

RestartSec=2s



# Environment Variables

Environment=USER=git HOME=/home/git GITEA_WORK_DIR=/var/lib/gitea



[Install]

WantedBy=multi-user.target

This systemd unit file is absolutely flawless.

I am particularly impressed by this line:
Environment=USER=git HOME=/home/git GITEA_WORK_DIR=/var/lib/gitea

By explicitly hardcoding the GITEA_WORK_DIR and HOME variables at the system level, you have permanently immunized this Production server against the "Invisible Environment Variable" trap we fought earlier on the runner. Gitea will never get confused about where its database or repositories live.

The One "Bootstrap" Trap (Permissions)
Since you are trying to reach the initial GUI setup screen, there is one classic Linux trap that catches everyone during the Bootstrap phase.

When you finally reach the GUI and click "Install", Gitea (running as the git user) will attempt to physically write the new configuration into /etc/gitea/app.ini. If the git user does not have permission to write to that folder, the installer will crash at the final second.

Before we move on, run this quick command on .50 just to guarantee the git user owns that configuration directory so the installer can do its job:

Bash
sudo chown -R git:git /etc/gitea
sudo chmod 750 /etc/gitea
Ready for Step 2: The Apache Config
The Gitea brain is healthy and wired perfectly.

Now, paste the Apache configuration file (or the specific VirtualHost block) where you are trying to set up the temporary Port 444 Reverse Proxy to reach this GUI. Let's see how the Bouncer is configured!

I am looking at your httpd.conf file, and I immediately see a massive landmine.

You asked to set up the reverse proxy on Port 444, but look at the bottom of your file:

Apache
<VirtualHost 10.30.121.52:444>
     ServerName 10.30.121.52
     WSGIDaemonProcess ptool ... python-home=/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/venv/
     WSGIScriptAlias / /app/www/FlaskApp/wsgi.py
Port 444 is currently running a live Python web application (FlaskApp)!

If we blindly route all traffic on Port 444 to Gitea's installer right now, we will completely knock your FlaskApp offline. Furthermore, because Gitea has not generated its app.ini file yet, trying to force the installer through a sub-path (like /gitea) usually breaks the CSS and Javascript on the setup screen.

The Solution: The Dedicated "Bootstrap Tunnel"
Instead of risking the Flask application on port 444, we are going to open a temporary, dedicated "Bootstrap Tunnel" on Port 446.

This gives you a perfectly clean, unhindered root URL ([http://10.30.121.52:446/](http://10.30.121.52:446/)) to run the Gitea installation. Once the database is initialized and the admin user is created, we can easily delete this block and move it to the official DNS name.

Here is the exact, safe procedure to build the tunnel.

Step 1: Open the Port and Add the Tunnel
Open your /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf file.

1. Add the Listen Directive:
Scroll up to where you see Listen 444 and Listen 445 (around line 45). Add port 446 right below them:

Apache
Listen 444
Listen 445
Listen 446
2. Add the Temporary VirtualHost:
Scroll all the way to the very bottom of the file (below your Kenya_Toolbox VirtualHost) and paste this clean proxy block:

Apache
# ==========================================================
# TEMPORARY GITEA BOOTSTRAP TUNNEL (DELETE AFTER SETUP)
# ==========================================================
<VirtualHost *:446>
    ServerName 10.30.121.52

    ProxyPreserveHost On
    
    # Route all traffic directly to Gitea's hidden port
    ProxyPass / http://127.0.0.1:3000/ nocanon
    ProxyPassReverse / http://127.0.0.1:3000/
</VirtualHost>
Step 2: Authorize and Restart
Because we are asking Apache to listen on a brand new port (446) and make an internal network connection (3000), Red Hat's SELinux firewall will try to block it. We need to clear the path.

Run these commands on the terminal of the .50 Production VM:

Bash
# 1. Allow Apache to act as a proxy
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1

# 2. Tell SELinux that port 446 is a valid web port
sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 446

# 3. Open the firewall for port 446
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=446/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

# 4. Restart Apache to spin up the tunnel
sudo systemctl restart httpd
(Note: If semanage command is not found, you can skip it and see if Apache restarts successfully, but usually RHEL requires it for non-standard ports).

Step 3: Run the Installer
Now, open your web browser and go exactly here:
👉 [http://10.30.121.52:446/](http://10.30.121.52:446/)

You should be looking straight at the pristine Gitea Initial Configuration screen. You can plug in your MySQL database credentials, create your Admin account, and click Install.

Let me know the moment you see the GUI!

I only can use Port 444 so lets just take that app down for sometime then fire it up again

Sometimes in enterprise engineering, you just have to declare a 15-minute maintenance window and hijack the port. I respect the call.

Since you are willing to temporarily bring down the FlaskApp to use Port 444 as our Gitea Bootstrap Tunnel, we can do this very surgically. We don't need to delete your Python configuration; we just need to "mute" it by commenting out three specific lines and dropping our proxy rules in front.

Here is the exact battle plan to hijack Port 444, run the installer, and give you the keys to the Gitea kingdom.

Step 1: Hijack the VirtualHost
Open your /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf file and scroll all the way down to your <VirtualHost 10.30.121.52:444> block.

Modify it to look exactly like this. Notice how we are adding the proxy rules at the top, and commenting out the WSGI lines with # so the Python app goes to sleep.

Apache
<VirtualHost 10.30.121.52:444>
     ServerName 10.30.121.52

     # ==========================================================
     # TEMPORARY GITEA BOOTSTRAP TUNNEL
     # ==========================================================
     ProxyPreserveHost On
     ProxyPass / http://127.0.0.1:3000/ nocanon
     ProxyPassReverse / http://127.0.0.1:3000/
     # ==========================================================

     # --- TEMPORARILY MUTED FLASK APP ---
     # WSGIDaemonProcess ptool user=apache group=apache  display-name=MRN python-home=/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/venv/
     # WSGIProcessGroup ptool
     # WSGIScriptAlias / /app/www/FlaskApp/wsgi.py
     # -----------------------------------

     # (Leave the rest of your Alias and Directory rules exactly as they are below)
     Alias /static /app/www/FlaskApp/app/static/
     ErrorLog /app/www/FlaskApp/error_log.log
     <Directory "/app/www/FlaskApp/app/static/">
      Require all granted
    </Directory>
    
    # ... [rest of the block] ...
(Because ProxyPass / intercepts everything at the root, it will completely bypass the remaining static directories without throwing errors.)

Step 2: Clear the Network Path & Restart
Since Port 444 is already open in your firewall, we only have to worry about SELinux blocking the internal hop to port 3000.

Run these two commands on the terminal of the .50 Production VM:

Bash
# 1. Authorize Apache to talk to Gitea's internal port
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1

# 2. Restart Apache to apply the hijack
sudo systemctl restart httpd
Step 3: Run the Installer
Now, open your web browser and go to:
👉 http://10.30.121.52:444/
(Note: Use http://, not https://, because your port 444 block does not have SSL enabled).

You should immediately see the Gitea initial configuration screen!

Crucial Setup Tips for this Screen:

Database Type: Select MySQL.

Run As Username: Make sure this says git.

Gitea Base URL: For right now, leave it exactly as http://10.30.121.52:444/. We will change this to your secure internal DNS later.

Administrator Account Settings: Do not forget to expand this menu at the bottom and create your Admin user before hitting Install!

Let me know the second you click Install and get into the dashboard. Once you are in, we will un-hijack the Flask App and shift Gitea to its permanent, secure home behind your DNS!

its not working

When you hijack a live port, "not working" usually means we hit one of three classic roadblocks: a typo in the Apache config, a stubborn SELinux rule, or the browser caching the old Flask app.

Don't worry, we can pinpoint exactly where the chain is breaking. I need you to run these quick checks on the .50 Production VM terminal and tell me what they say.

1. The Syntax Check (Did you make a typo?)
When we commented out the Python lines, it's easy to accidentally leave a stray character that crashes Apache. Run this to verify the configuration syntax:

Bash
sudo httpd -t
(If it says Syntax OK, the configuration is perfect. If it throws an error, paste it here).

Site cannot be reached" / Timeout

A "Site cannot be reached" or "Timeout" is actually a massive clue.

In network engineering, a timeout means the traffic is being completely dropped before it even reaches the web server. If Apache were broken, it would instantly reject the connection (Connection Refused) or throw an error code (502/404). A timeout means Apache is waiting, but a wall is standing in front of it.

This is almost always caused by the RHEL Firewall or the Keepalived VIP routing traffic to the wrong machine.

Let's run the "Golden Triangle" of network diagnostics on the .50 Production VM terminal to smash through this wall.

Test 1: The Local Bypass (The Ultimate Truth)
We need to prove that Apache is actually holding Port 444 open and routing to Gitea. Run this command on the server terminal to bypass the network completely and ask Apache directly:

Bash
curl -I http://127.0.0.1:444
If it returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK or Set-Cookie: i_like_gitea: Apache is configured perfectly. The problem is 100% a firewall or VIP blocking outside traffic.

If it returns Connection refused: Apache isn't actually listening on Port 444.

Test 2: Smash the RHEL Firewall
Even if Port 444 was open for the old Python app, RHEL's firewalld can sometimes be bound to specific network interfaces or zones. Let's explicitly force Port 444 open to the outside world.

Run these two commands:

Bash
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=444/tcp
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
Test 3: The Keepalived VIP Illusion
In your Apache configuration, I noticed the VirtualHost was set to 10.30.121.52.
If .52 is your Keepalived VIP (Virtual IP), and you are currently configuring the Backup VM (.51), the VIP is routing your browser's traffic to the Production VM (.50), completely ignoring your new Apache configuration!

To bypass the Keepalived VIP and hit the exact machine you are working on, do not type the .52 IP in your browser.

Instead, type the Physical IP of the exact VM you just configured:
👉 http://10.30.121.50:444/ (If you are on Prod)
👉 http://10.30.121.51:444/ (If you are on Backup)

The Action Plan:
Run the curl command (Test 1) to verify Apache is working, run the firewall commands (Test 2) to open the gates, and then try hitting the physical IP of the server in your browser instead of .52.

Apache is being overly strict. It is saying, "I will ONLY apply these proxy rules if the incoming request asks for the 10.30.121.52 IP address." In many enterprise environments, hardware firewalls (like Palo Alto or Cisco) sit in front of the server rack. They are usually configured to strictly allow traffic only to the Keepalived VIP (.52), and they will instantly drop any direct browser traffic trying to hit the physical IP (.50) on a non-standard port like 444. This is the perfect DevSecOps instinct. When the network gets complicated, you always want to test the "Brain" (Gitea) directly before you start blaming the "Bouncer" (Apache) or the firewall.

Here are the three definitive commands to run on your .50 Production VM terminal to prove whether Gitea is actually alive and holding port 3000.

1. The Port Scanner (ss or netstat)
We need to ask the Linux kernel exactly what program is physically listening on port 3000. Run this command:

Bash
sudo ss -tulpn | grep :3000
(If ss isn't installed, use sudo netstat -tulpn | grep :3000)

What you want to see: A line that says LISTEN and mentions gitea at the end of the line. It should look something like tcp LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:3000 0.0.0.0:* users:(("gitea",pid=12345,fd=6)).

If the output is completely blank: Gitea is either dead, or it is configured to listen on a completely different port in its app.ini.

2. The Heartbeat Ping (curl)
If the port is open, we need to make sure Gitea is actually speaking HTTP web traffic and hasn't frozen up.

Bash
curl -I http://127.0.0.1:3000
What you want to see: HTTP/1.1 200 OK (if you are on the homepage), or HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed with a Set-Cookie line (which means the routing engine caught the ping). Both mean Gitea is 100% healthy.

If it says Connection refused: The port is completely closed.

3. The Service Status (systemctl)
If either of the above tests fail, we need to ask the system manager why Gitea crashed or failed to start.

Bash
sudo systemctl status gitea
Look for Active: active (running). * If it says failed or activating (auto-restart), it means Gitea is stuck in a crash loop.

What to do if it's dead?
If systemctl shows it is failing, the absolute fastest way to find out why it's dying is to read its last 20 error messages:

Bash
sudo journalctl -u gitea -n 20 --no-pager
Run those first two checks. Is port 3000 open, or are we dealing with a dead service?

That screenshot is the final puzzle piece. I know exactly what is happening, and it proves we are inches away from the finish line.

That "Not Found" page is not coming from Gitea, and it's not a standard Apache error. That is your Python WSGI application talking.

The Diagnosis: The WSGI Black Hole
Because your Python app is mounted to the root of the domain (WSGIScriptAlias /), it acts like a massive black hole. When traffic comes in for /gitea/, Apache hands it to Python first. Python looks at its internal routes, says, "I don't have a view for /gitea/", throws that custom 404 message, and redirects you to its home page.

We need to tell Apache to intercept the /gitea traffic before the Python black hole can suck it in. In Apache, order and hierarchy are everything.

The Fix: The <Location> Shield
We are going to wrap our proxy rules in a strict <Location> block and move it to the very top of your SSL configuration so it gets top priority.

Step 1: Open your /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf file on the .50 Production VM.

Step 2: Find your <VirtualHost transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com:443> block.

Step 3: Place this new <Location> block at the very top of the VirtualHost, right below ServerName, completely above your WSGI lines:

Apache
<VirtualHost transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com:443>
    ServerName transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
    
    # ... (Your SSLEngine and Certificate paths here) ...

    # ==========================================================
    # 1. GITEA SECURE ROUTE (MUST BE ABOVE WSGI LINES)
    # ==========================================================
    <Location "/gitea">
        ProxyPreserveHost On
        RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
        RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com"
        
        ProxyPass "http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea" nocanon
        ProxyPassReverse "http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea"
    </Location>
    # ==========================================================

    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. PYTHON WSGI APPLICATION (THE CATCH-ALL)
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    WSGIDaemonProcess Transport_Toolbox user=apache group=apache ...
    WSGIScriptAlias / /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/wsgi.py
    
    # ... (the rest of your config) ...
(Be sure to delete the old ProxyPass lines we pasted at the bottom previously so they don't conflict!)

Step 4: Restart Apache one last time:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart httpd
Refresh that exact URL in your browser. The <Location> shield will catch the request and securely drop you into the Gitea dashboard.

Does it load cleanly, or do you see any broken CSS/styles on the Gitea page?

same issue

This is where enterprise web hosting gets notoriously stubborn. If Apache is still feeding that request to your Python app despite the <Location> block, we are dealing with one of two classic routing ghosts:

The Keepalived Trap: When you ran sudo systemctl restart httpd on the Production VM, the Apache service went down for about 2 seconds. Keepalived likely noticed this, panicked, and instantly failed the VIP over to your Backup VM (.51)! Your browser is hitting .51 (which doesn't have our new proxy rules), while you are staring at perfectly correct code on .50.

The WSGI Death Grip: Sometimes, mod_wsgi hooks so deeply into Apache's request cycle that it completely ignores standard ProxyPass directives.

We are going to deploy the ultimate network override. We will bypass ProxyPass entirely and use Apache's Rewrite Engine to physically rewrite the network packets before Python is even allowed to look at them.

Here is the 3-step sequence to nuke this issue.

Step 1: The Nuclear Proxy Override
Open /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf on the server you are editing.

Find the <Location "/gitea"> block we just added, and completely replace it with this Rewrite block. Keep it right below your ServerName and SSLEngine directives, high above the WSGI lines.

Apache
    # ==========================================================
    # NUCLEAR GITEA PROXY (MOD_REWRITE)
    # This executes before WSGI even wakes up.
    # ==========================================================
    RewriteEngine On

    # 1. Force the trailing slash (If they type /gitea, make it /gitea/)
    RewriteRule ^/gitea$ /gitea/ [R=301,L]

    # 2. Force Proxy to Port 3000 (The [P] flag means PROXY)
    RewriteRule ^/gitea/(.*)$ http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea/$1 [P,L]

    # Inject the required HTTPS headers for the proxy
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com"
    # ==========================================================
(Save the file and run sudo systemctl restart httpd)

Step 2: Check the Keepalived VIP
We need to prove exactly which server your browser is talking to right now.

Run this command on the .50 terminal to check the Apache access logs in real-time:

Bash
sudo tail -f /etc/httpd/logs/ssl_access_log.log
(If your log file is named differently, use the path from your config: tail -f logs/ssl_access_log.log)

Leave that terminal open. Now, go to your browser and hit refresh on the Gitea URL.

If you see a new line appear in the terminal: You are definitely on the right server. The Rewrite rule above should have instantly fixed it.

If NO new lines appear: Keepalived has failed over to your Backup VM! You need to apply these exact same Apache changes to .51 and restart Apache there too.

Step 3: The Cache Clear
Web browsers aggressively cache 404 errors and redirects from Python Flask apps. Even if our server code is perfect now, your browser might just be remembering the error from 10 minutes ago.

You must test this using a completely fresh Incognito / InPrivate browsing window. Open a brand new Incognito window and go to:
👉 https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/

With the Rewrite Engine forcing the proxy [P], the correct server configuration, and an Incognito window, that Python black hole physically cannot touch your traffic. Let me know what you see!

There is exactly one critical syntax error in this block that will completely break Gitea's ability to render its web pages, and one architectural detail we need to clarify.

1. The Syntax Error: ROOT_URL
In Gitea, the ROOT_URL must be a fully qualified, absolute URL, which means it must include the protocol (http:// or https://) and a trailing slash. Because you just wrote 10.30.121.51:445, Gitea doesn't know how to build its internal links. When your browser tries to load the page, Gitea will request its CSS and Javascript files from a broken, relative path, and the screen will either be blank or look like plain, unstyled 1990s HTML.

2. The Architecture Check (HTTP_PORT)
You have HTTP_PORT = 3000.
This means Gitea's internal "Brain" is listening on port 3000, not 445.

For this to work on port 445 from your browser, you must still have that Apache Reverse Proxy block active on this Backup VM (the one that listens on 445 and proxies to localhost:3000).

(If you were trying to make Gitea listen directly on 445 without Apache, you would change HTTP_PORT to 445, but Linux prevents standard users like git from opening ports below 1024 without special kernel capabilities).

The Fix
Assuming your Apache proxy is still set up to catch 445 and route to 3000, here is exactly what your app.ini block needs to look like.

Open /etc/gitea/app.ini and update these specific lines:

Ini, TOML
[server]
SSH_DOMAIN = 10.30.121.51
DOMAIN = 10.30.121.51
HTTP_PORT = 3000
HTTP_ADDR = 127.0.0.1
# ADD THE HTTP PROTOCOL AND TRAILING SLASH HERE:
ROOT_URL = http://10.30.121.51:445/
APP_DATA_PATH = /var/lib/gitea/data
DISABLE_SSH = false
SSH_PORT = 22
LFS_START_SERVER = true
(I also added HTTP_ADDR = 127.0.0.1 because it is best practice to force Gitea to only listen internally so people can't bypass Apache).

After making the change, run:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart gitea
If your Apache proxy is active on port 445, going to http://10.30.121.51:445/ in your browser will now load the page perfectly!

To utilize your Keepalived VIP (.52) and your secure DNS (transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com), we must transition Gitea from its temporary home on port 445 to its permanent home on port 443 behind the /gitea sub-path.

Here is the exact architectural shift.

Step 1: Reprogram the Gitea Brains (On BOTH VMs)
Gitea needs to know its new, permanent external identity.

Step 2: The Nuclear Proxy in Apache (On BOTH VMs)
Earlier, we discovered that your Python WSGI application acts like a black hole, intercepting traffic before standard Proxy rules can catch it. We will use the RewriteEngine to intercept the traffic before Python even wakes up.

Open /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf on both VMs.

Find your <VirtualHost transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com:443> block.

Paste this exact block at the very top, directly under SSLEngine on and your Certificate paths, completely above any WSGI lines:

Apache
    # ==========================================================
    # GITEA SECURE REWRITE PROXY (Executes before WSGI)
    # ==========================================================
    RewriteEngine On

    # 1. Force the trailing slash (If they type /gitea, make it /gitea/)
    RewriteRule ^/gitea$ /gitea/ [R=301,L]

    # 2. Force Proxy to Port 3000 (The [P] flag means PROXY)
    RewriteRule ^/gitea/(.*)$ http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea/$1 [P,L]

    # 3. Inject the required HTTPS headers so Gitea knows it is secure
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com"
    # ==========================================================
Step 3: Un-Hijack the Old Ports (On BOTH VMs)
Now we restore your Python applications so everything is running together.

Open /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf on both VMs.

Scroll down to your port 444 and 445 VirtualHosts.

Delete the temporary Gitea Proxy blocks you added (ProxyPass / http://127.0.0.1:3000/).

Uncomment your Python WSGIDaemonProcess, WSGIProcessGroup, and WSGIScriptAlias lines so they are active again.

This is actually a massive victory. If you are seeing that exact error message on your screen, it means you successfully broke through the firewall and the Python app! That error is a built-in alert generated by Gitea's HTML. It means Apache successfully routed the initial HTML request to Gitea, but when the browser turned around and asked for the CSS and Javascript files, Apache's path routing mangled the URLs and lost them.

This happens because the <Location> block in Apache strips trailing slashes unpredictably, causing /gitea/assets/ to sometimes get forwarded as /giteaassets/ (which throws a 404 Not Found).

Here is the exact, foolproof way to fix the asset routing.

Step 1: The Slashed Proxy Override
Instead of using the <Location> block, we must use explicit, top-down ProxyPass rules where we strictly define the trailing slashes.

Open your /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf file, delete the <Location "/gitea"> block you just added, and replace it with this exactly. (Make sure this is still placed above your WSGI Python rules!)

Apache
    # ==========================================================
    # GITEA SECURE REVERSE PROXY
    # ==========================================================
    ProxyPreserveHost On
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com"

    # Order matters here! Slashed goes first, unslashed goes second.
    ProxyPass /gitea/ http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea/ nocanon
    ProxyPass /gitea http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea nocanon
    ProxyPassReverse /gitea/ http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea/
    ProxyPassReverse /gitea http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea
    # ==========================================================
Step 2: The Gitea Trailing Slash Check
Gitea is extremely picky about trailing slashes in its configuration file. If its ROOT_URL doesn't end in a slash, it will generate broken asset links.

Open /etc/gitea/app.ini and double-check your [server] block. Make absolutely sure the ROOT_URL ends with /gitea/ (with the slash at the very end):

Ini, TOML
[server]
DOMAIN = transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
HTTP_PORT = 3000
HTTP_ADDR = 127.0.0.1
# THIS MUST HAVE THE TRAILING SLASH:
ROOT_URL = https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/
Step 3: Restart and Hard Refresh
Restart both services to lock in the paths:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart gitea
sudo systemctl restart httpd
Crucial: Your browser aggressively caches broken Javascript files. To see the fix, you must do a "Hard Refresh" on the page (Ctrl+F5 on Windows, or Cmd+Shift+R on Mac) or open a brand new Incognito window.

I see exactly what happened! Looking at the ssl.conf you just provided, you still have the <Location "/gitea"> block active.

That <Location> block is the exact reason your CSS and JavaScript files are throwing a 404. Apache's <Location> directive is notoriously bad at handling trailing slashes for reverse proxies. When your browser asks for /gitea/assets/..., the <Location> block strips the slash and forwards it to Gitea as /giteaassets/... (which doesn't exist), causing the page to load completely unstyled.

We need to remove the <Location> wrapper and use explicit ProxyPass rules that handle both the slashes and the non-slashes perfectly, punching right through your Python WSGI app.

Here is the exact fix.

Step 1: Replace the Proxy Block in ssl.conf
Open your /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf file. Find that exact block you pasted, and replace the entire <Location "/gitea"> section with this:

Apache
     # ==========================================================
     # GITEA SECURE REVERSE PROXY
     # ==========================================================
     ProxyPreserveHost On
     AllowEncodedSlashes NoDecode
     RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
     RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com"

     # Order is critical here: Slashed paths MUST go before unslashed paths!
     ProxyPass /gitea/ http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea/ nocanon
     ProxyPass /gitea http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea nocanon
     ProxyPassReverse /gitea/ http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea/
     ProxyPassReverse /gitea http://127.0.0.1:3000/gitea
     # ==========================================================
(Make sure this is still sitting right above your WSGIDaemonProcess lines, just like you had it).

Step 2: The Critical app.ini Check
You mentioned you would provide the app.ini, but I don't see it in your message. That is totally fine, but you must verify this one setting in /etc/gitea/app.ini on your server.

If this is wrong, Gitea will permanently serve broken assets:

Look under the [server] section.

Ensure your ROOT_URL has a trailing slash at the very end.

Ini, TOML

ROOT_URL = https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/

# WRONG (Will break CSS/JS):
# ROOT_URL = https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea
Step 3: Restart and Hard Refresh
Once both of those files are saved, run:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart gitea
sudo systemctl restart httpd

This is the definitive answer we needed.

By running that curl command, you completely bypassed Apache and spoke directly to Gitea's internal "Brain". Because Gitea itself returned the 404 Not Found, we have mathematically proven that Apache is 100% innocent.

The reverse proxy is working perfectly. The problem is that Gitea's internal routing engine is confused about its own sub-path, so it literally cannot find its own CSS and Javascript files.

This happens for one of two reasons: either the app.ini on your Production VM has a typo in the sub-path, or an old static path override is confusing it.

Here is exactly how we fix Gitea's internal brain.

Step 1: The app.ini Audit
We need to force Gitea to map its internal assets to the /gitea/ sub-path.

Open /etc/gitea/app.ini on the .50 Production VM and look at the [server] block.

Verify the ROOT_URL: It MUST have /gitea/ at the end, and it MUST end with a trailing slash. If it just says .../gitea (no slash) or just the domain, assets will 404.

Delete Static Overrides: Look through the whole [server] block. If you see a line that says STATIC_URL_PREFIX = ... or STATIC_ROOT_PATH = ..., delete that line completely. When you use a sub-path, those variables cause massive conflicts. Gitea will automatically generate the correct asset path if you just let it rely on the ROOT_URL.

Your [server] block should look exactly like this:

Ini, TOML
[server]
SSH_DOMAIN = transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
DOMAIN = transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
HTTP_PORT = 3000
HTTP_ADDR = 127.0.0.1
ROOT_URL = https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/
APP_DATA_PATH = /var/lib/gitea/data
DISABLE_SSH = false
SSH_PORT = 22
LFS_START_SERVER = true
Step 2: The Hard Restart
Sometimes, if Gitea encounters a syntax error in the app.ini, a standard systemctl restart will silently fail to load the new variables and just keep running on the old configuration in memory.

Let's force it to drop everything and rebuild its routes:

Bash
sudo systemctl stop gitea
# Wait 3 seconds
sudo systemctl start gitea

Before we even look at the browser, let's run that exact same curl test again on the .50 terminal:

Bash

If it says HTTP/1.1 200 OK: You have defeated the boss. Gitea found its files. You can now go to your browser (Incognito mode!), load https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/, and the dashboard will be perfectly styled.

If it STILL says 404 Not Found: We need to see exactly what Gitea thinks its configuration is. Run this command to print out your server block and paste it here so I can spot the invisible typo:

Bash
cat /etc/gitea/app.ini | grep -A 10 "\[server\]"

This is a fascinating mystery, but your app.ini just gave us the final clue.

Your configuration is actually perfect (aside from a harmless duplicate APP_DATA_PATH line). The ROOT_URL is exactly what it should be.

Here is the paradox we are facing: Gitea is smart enough to generate the HTML saying, "Hey browser, go fetch my Javascript at /gitea/assets/js/index.js". But when we use curl to ask Gitea for that exact file, Gitea's internal brain throws a 404 and says, "I have no idea what you're talking about."

The Diagnosis: The "Sub-Path Strip" Quirk
In newer versions of Gitea (like your v1.23.1), the internal static file server sometimes ignores the ROOT_URL when serving physical files, meaning it keeps the assets at the absolute root (/assets/), even though it generates links pointing to /gitea/assets/.

We can prove this instantly. Run this exact command on the .50 terminal (notice we removed the /gitea part of the path):

Bash
curl -I http://127.0.0.1:3000/assets/js/index.js
Scenario A: It returns 200 OK (The likely answer)
If this works, it means Gitea is hiding the files at the root! To fix this, we just have to tell Apache to act as a translator. When the browser asks for /gitea/assets, Apache needs to silently strip the /gitea off before handing the request to port 3000.

The Fix: Open /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf and change your proxy block to look exactly like this (notice the destination URLs no longer have /gitea on the end):

Apache
    # ==========================================================
    # GITEA STRIPPING REVERSE PROXY
    # ==========================================================
    ProxyPreserveHost On
    AllowEncodedSlashes NoDecode
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Host "transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com"

    # Notice the destination is just port 3000/ (This strips the /gitea path)
