I completely understand the frustration. When an application is hardcoded with absolute paths (/login, /main), trying to force it into a sub-folder using basic Apache proxy rules turns into a never-ending game of whack-a-mole. You fix the CSS, the routing breaks. You fix the routing, the headers break.

If you cannot change the Python code, cannot get a subdomain, and the custom port threw errors, we have to look deeper into enterprise-level reverse proxy patterns.

Here are the two "Platform-Level" solutions designed specifically for web applications with broken or stubborn routing. Both of these are configured entirely on your Production VM (.50) and require zero changes to your application code.

Platform Solution 1: "The Cookie Trap" Routing (Highly Recommended)
Instead of trying to catch every possible broken URL path, we ignore the URLs entirely and route the user based on a Session Cookie.

When a user visits /test/, Apache silently drops a temporary cookie in their browser. From that moment on, even if they click a completely broken link that tries to send them to the Production root (like /OLTConfigscript), Apache sees the cookie, intercepts the request, and invisibly routes them back to the Backup VM.

How to configure it on the Production VM (.50):
Open your ssl.conf, remove all the old /test proxy attempts, and add this inside your <VirtualHost *:443> block:

Apache
    RewriteEngine On

    # 1. THE EXCEPTION: Never trap Gitea, even if the user has the test cookie.
    RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} ^/gitea [NC]
    RewriteRule ^ - [L]

    # 2. THE ENTRY POINT: When they visit /test, set the cookie "AppEnv=test"
    # The [P] flag invisibly proxies to the Backup VM. 
    # The [CO] flag sets the cookie for the entire domain.
    RewriteRule ^/test/?(.*)$ http://10.30.121.51:444/$1 [P,CO=AppEnv:test:%{HTTP_HOST}:0:/]

    # 3. THE TRAP: If they click a broken absolute link (like /main)...
    # Apache checks: Do they have the AppEnv=test cookie?
    RewriteCond %{HTTP_COOKIE} AppEnv=test [NC]
    # If YES, ignore the Production Live App and proxy them to the Backup VM!
    RewriteRule ^/(.*)$ http://10.30.121.51:444/$1 [P]

    # 4. THE EXIT POINT: A hidden URL to clear the cookie if they want to go back to Prod
    # Sets cookie to "prod" and redirects to the live root
    RewriteRule ^/leave-test$ / [CO=AppEnv:prod:%{HTTP_HOST}:0:/,R=302,L]

    # 5. Standard Reverse Header Handlers
    ProxyPassReverse / http://10.30.121.51:444/
    ProxyPassReverseCookiePath / /test/
Why this works beautifully: The Python app can spit out as many absolute / paths as it wants. Because the routing decision happens at the HTTP Header level (the cookie), the browser stays locked onto the Backup VM seamlessly.

Platform Solution 2: DOM-Aware HTML Proxying (mod_proxy_html)
When we tried mod_substitute earlier, it used basic text string replacement, which is fragile. Apache actually has a dedicated, enterprise module specifically built for the problem you are facing: mod_proxy_html.

Unlike a text search-and-replace, this module parses the incoming web page as an actual HTML document and intelligently rewrites the href, src, and action tags before they reach the user's browser.

How to configure it on the Production VM (.50):

First, ensure the modules are loaded (usually found in /etc/httpd/conf.modules.d/00-proxy.conf):

Apache
LoadModule proxy_html_module modules/mod_proxy_html.so
LoadModule xml2enc_module modules/mod_xml2enc.so
Add this block to your ssl.conf inside your <VirtualHost>:

Apache
<Location /test/>
    ProxyPass http://10.30.121.51:444/
    ProxyPassReverse http://10.30.121.51:444/

    # Turn on the intelligent HTML parser
    ProxyHTMLEnable On
    ProxyHTMLInterp On

    # Define the exact HTML tags and attributes to rewrite
    ProxyHTMLExtended On
    ProxyHTMLURLMap / /test/

    # Fix the headers automatically
    RequestHeader unset Accept-Encoding
    Header edit Location "^/(.*)$" "/test/$1"
</Location>
Why this is the official "Apache Way": ProxyHTMLURLMap / /test/ tells Apache: "Any time you see a link pointing to the root (/) inside an HTML tag, dynamically change it to /test/ before giving it to the user."

Important Prep Work for Either Solution
If you choose either of these platform solutions, you must undo the WSGI changes on the Backup VM (.51). Because both of these solutions trick the browser and the server into acting normally, your Flask app needs to return to its default, unmodified state.

Remove the ReverseProxied middleware from your Backup VM's .wsgi file so it simply reads:

Python
import sys
# ... your paths ...
from app import create_app  
application = create_app()
My Recommendation: Try Solution 1 (The Cookie Trap). It is universally supported on all Apache versions, incredibly stable, and bypasses the HTML/CSS string rewriting problem entirely.

working with solution 1 wouldn't cause conflict with the production /

It is a brilliant question, and it shows you are thinking about this at the architecture level.

The short answer is: No, it will absolutely not conflict with your live Production users. But it will intentionally override Production for YOU (the tester).

Here is exactly how the "Cookie Trap" protects your live environment while fixing the broken links.

The "Per-Browser" Magic
The genius of this solution is that Cookies live in the user's web browser, not on the server. When you add those RewriteCond rules to the Production VM, Apache starts acting like a bouncer at a club checking VIP wristbands.

Scenario A: A Normal Production User
A normal employee goes to https://transport-toolbox.../LiveDashboard.

Apache checks their browser headers. No cookie is found.

Apache ignores the Proxy rules entirely.

The user is handed the Live Production Python app exactly as normal. Zero conflict.

Scenario B: You (The Tester)
You go to https://transport-toolbox.../test/.

Apache silently gives your browser the AppEnv=test cookie (the "VIP wristband").

The Python app sends you a broken link: <a href="/OLTConfigscript">.

You click it. Your browser tries to go to the Production root (/).

The Trap Springs: Apache checks your browser, sees the AppEnv=test cookie, and says: "Aha! You belong in the Test Environment!" 6. Instead of showing you the live app, Apache invisibly forwards your request to the Backup VM.

The Only "Conflict" (And How to Escape It)
The only side-effect of this solution is that while you have the cookie, you cannot see the Live Production app. Even if you manually type the production URL into your browser, Apache will keep shoving you into the Backup VM.

This is exactly why Step 4 of the configuration I gave you included the Escape Hatch:

Apache
# THE EXIT POINT
RewriteRule ^/leave-test$ / [CO=AppEnv:prod:%{HTTP_HOST}:0:/,R=302,L]
When you are done testing and want to see the real Production app again, you simply type https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/leave-test into your address bar. Apache deletes the cookie, redirects you to the live root, and you are back to being a normal user. (Alternatively, you can just test everything in an Incognito window—when you close the window, the cookie is destroyed).

The Verdict
Because it relies on a specific HTTP header that normal users will never receive, Solution 1 is completely safe to deploy alongside your Live Production application. It elegantly solves the "hardcoded absolute path" problem without requiring a single code change or DNS ticket.

It worked great I want in depth explanation of this solution the cookie trap with its implementation approach to return to it when I need to remember it

I am so glad to hear that it worked perfectly! The "Cookie Trap" is one of those incredibly satisfying, advanced server tricks that feels like magic once you understand the logic behind it.

Since you want to keep this as a master reference, I have broken down exactly how this architecture works, why it solves the "Absolute Path" problem, and a line-by-line breakdown of the code so you can easily deploy it on future projects.

The Core Problem: The "Absolute Path" Breakout
When developers build a web application, they often hardcode links to start with a root slash (e.g., <form action="/login">).

If you try to host that application inside a reverse proxy subfolder (like /test/), those hardcoded links act as a command to the user's web browser: "Erase /test/ from the URL and go straight back to the absolute root (/)." This causes the user to "break out" of the proxy tunnel and crash into your live production environment.

The Solution: The Cookie Trap Concept
Instead of trying to catch and rewrite hundreds of broken URLs as they leave the server, we change how the server reads the user.

We use Apache's RewriteEngine to silently drop a "VIP Wristband" (a Session Cookie) into the browser of anyone who visits the /test/ URL. Once the browser has that cookie, Apache stops looking at what URL the user is requesting, and instead looks at the cookie. If Apache sees the test cookie, it intercepts the request—even if it's pointing to the Production root—and invisibly shoves the traffic back down the /test/ tunnel.

The Implementation Master Code
Here is the exact block you place inside your <VirtualHost *:443> on the frontend proxy server.

Apache
    RewriteEngine On

    # 1. THE EXCEPTION
    RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} ^/gitea [NC]
    RewriteRule ^ - [L]

    # 2. THE ENTRY POINT (Set the Cookie)
    RewriteRule ^/test/?(.*)$ http://10.30.121.51:444/$1 [P,CO=AppEnv:test:%{HTTP_HOST}:0:/]

    # 3. THE EXIT POINT (Destroy the Cookie)
    RewriteRule ^/leave-test$ / [CO=AppEnv:prod:%{HTTP_HOST}:0:/,R=302,L]

    # 4. THE TRAP (Catch the escapees)
    RewriteCond %{HTTP_COOKIE} AppEnv=test [NC]
    RewriteRule ^/(.*)$ http://10.30.121.51:444/$1 [P]

    # 5. HEADER FIXES
    ProxyPassReverse / http://10.30.121.51:444/
    ProxyPassReverseCookiePath / /test/
Line-by-Line Explanation (How to read the rules)
Apache processes RewriteRules from top to bottom. Here is exactly what Apache is thinking at each step:

1. The Exception (Protecting other paths)
Apache
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} ^/gitea [NC]
RewriteRule ^ - [L]
What it does: If the user is trying to reach /gitea, stop processing all rules immediately ([L] means "Last rule").

Why it's needed: If we didn't have this, the Cookie Trap would intercept your Gitea traffic and accidentally send it to the Backup VM.

2. The Entry Point (Setting the Trap)
Apache
RewriteRule ^/test/?(.*)$ http://10.30.121.51:444/$1 [P,CO=AppEnv:test:%{HTTP_HOST}:0:/]
What it does: When a user explicitly goes to /test/, Apache acts as a Proxy ([P]) to the Backup VM. Simultaneously, it fires the [CO] (Cookie) flag.

The Cookie Syntax: CO=Name:Value:Domain:Lifetime:Path

It creates a cookie named AppEnv with the value test.

It binds it to your specific domain (%{HTTP_HOST}).

The 0 means it is a "Session Cookie" (it deletes itself when the browser closes).

The / means the cookie is valid for the entire website, not just the /test/ folder.

3. The Exit Point (The Escape Hatch)
Apache
RewriteRule ^/leave-test$ / [CO=AppEnv:prod:%{HTTP_HOST}:0:/,R=302,L]
What it does: Because the trap is so effective, you need a way to turn it off so you can view the normal Production site again.

How it works: If you type /leave-test, Apache overwrites the cookie (changing it from test to prod), issues a 302 Redirect ([R=302]) to the domain root (/), and stops processing rules ([L]).

4. The Trap (The Magic Trick)
Apache
RewriteCond %{HTTP_COOKIE} AppEnv=test [NC]
RewriteRule ^/(.*)$ http://10.30.121.51:444/$1 [P]
What it does: This is the core of the solution. RewriteCond checks a condition before running the rule. It checks the user's browser for the AppEnv=test cookie.

The Rescue: If the Python app spits out a broken absolute link (like <a href="/OLTConfigscript">), the browser tries to go to the Production root. Apache intercepts it, sees the wristband, and uses the [P] flag to invisibly proxy the traffic to the Backup VM instead of the Live App.

5. Header Fixes
Apache
ProxyPassReverse / http://10.30.121.51:444/
ProxyPassReverseCookiePath / /test/
What it does: If the Backup VM tries to send its own HTTP Redirects (like a 302 Location: / after a successful login), ProxyPassReverse intercepts that server header and translates it so the browser doesn't get confused.

When to use this in the future:
Keep this pattern in your back pocket anytime you are tasked with hosting a legacy, third-party, or un-editable web application inside a sub-folder on a reverse proxy. It completely separates the network routing logic from the application's internal code!

Okay now we will begin assesing how to setup the development workflow using gitea and the current setup

This is the perfect time to map this out. Now that your infrastructure is stable, isolated, and accessible—with Gitea securely routed and the Test environment safely behind the Cookie Trap—we can build a professional, predictable development lifecycle.

A solid development workflow bridges the gap between writing code and getting it onto those servers without breaking things or relying on manual file copying.

Here is a blueprint for a standard, enterprise-grade workflow using the exact architecture you have currently running.

The Proposed "TAT Tool" Workflow
Phase 1: Local Development & Version Control
The Workspace: Developers write and test code on their local machines (laptops/workstations), not directly on the servers.

The Repository: Code is pushed to your Gitea instance.

The Branching Strategy: You enforce a strict separation of code states:

main (or master): The sacred branch. This code is what currently runs on the Production VM (.50).

test (or develop): The staging branch. This code runs on the Backup VM (.51).

feature/*: Branches where developers build new tools or fix bugs (e.g., feature/olt-scripts).

Phase 2: Deployment to the Test Environment
When a developer finishes a feature, they merge it into the test branch in Gitea.

The Update: The code on the Backup VM (.51) needs to sync with this new test branch.

The Validation: You access https://transport-toolbox.../test/. Apache gives you the VIP cookie, trapping you in the Test environment. You test the new routing, the Python scripts, and the frontend logic exactly as it will behave in production, without actual production users seeing it.

Phase 3: Production Release
Once the new features are verified in the Test environment, a Pull Request (PR) is approved in Gitea to merge the test branch into the main branch.

The Deployment: The Production VM (.50) is updated to pull the latest main branch code.

The Go-Live: You navigate to https://transport-toolbox.../leave-test to drop your cookie and verify the live production site is running smoothly.

The Missing Link: How Code Actually Moves
The workflow above relies on getting the code out of Gitea and onto the actual server hard drives (/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/). There are two ways to do this:

Manual Git Pulls: You SSH into the Backup VM, navigate to the app folder, and type git pull origin test. Simple, but requires manual server access every time.

Automated Pipelines (CI/CD): Gitea has built-in features (Webhooks or Gitea Actions) that can automatically "push" or deploy the code to the correct VM the second a branch is updated. No SSH required.

To map out the exact pipeline setup for your team, how are you currently moving the Python code onto the servers when an update is ready—are you manually transferring files (like FTP/SCP), or are you already using git commands directly on the Linux command line?

There is an issue right now I can't sign in when I write my credentials it redirects me again to the landing page

This specific issue—getting immediately kicked back to the login page after entering the correct credentials—is the classic symptom of a "Lost Session Cookie" or a CSRF Token mismatch.

You are doing everything right; we just left one line of code from our old experiments in the configuration that is now sabotaging the Cookie Trap.

Why it is failing:
When we set up the Trap, I left this line in section #5:
ProxyPassReverseCookiePath / /test/

You log in successfully. Flask says, "Great! Here is your secure Session Cookie so I remember you."

Apache intercepts that cookie and says, "Only allow the browser to use this cookie if the URL says /test/."

The app redirects you to the dashboard: https://transport-toolbox.../main.

Because /main doesn't have /test/ in it, your browser refuses to send the Session Cookie.

The trap catches you and sends you to the Backup VM, but because your Session Cookie is missing, Flask thinks you are an anonymous intruder and kicks you straight back to the login page!

The Fix
We need to remove that restriction so your login session applies to the whole domain, and we need to add ProxyPreserveHost On so Flask's security tokens (CSRF) validate correctly.

Open your Production VM (.50) ssl.conf and update exactly Section 5 of the Cookie Trap to look like this:

Apache
    # 5. HEADER FIXES
    # Tell Flask the real domain name (Fixes CSRF token security)
    ProxyPreserveHost On
    RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
    
    # Handle the redirects
    ProxyPassReverse / http://10.30.121.51:444/
    
    # --> DELETE the ProxyPassReverseCookiePath line entirely! <--
Clear your Browser and Test
Because your browser is currently holding onto that broken session cookie, you must do this to test it:

Restart Apache: sudo systemctl restart httpd

Open a completely fresh Incognito/Private Window.

Go back to /test/ and log in.

By removing that single line, your session cookie will finally follow you through the trap. Let me know if you reach the dashboard successfully!

what is the effect of this line

That line—ProxyPassReverseCookiePath / /test/—acts like a strict security guard that restricts exactly which "rooms" of your website your browser is allowed to use its login badge in.

To understand why removing it fixed your login loop, we have to look at how web browsers handle security and cookies.

The Analogy: The Restricted VIP Badge
Imagine your website is a large office building.

Your Flask app issues VIP Badges (Session Cookies). When you log in, Flask intends for that badge to let you into every room in the building (Path = /).

When we added that line to Apache, we turned Apache into a security guard standing at the front door. Every time Flask handed out a VIP Badge, Apache intercepted it, scratched out "Everywhere", and wrote "VALID ONLY IN THE /TEST/ WING" on the front of it.

What was happening before we removed the line:
The Login: You type your password at /test/login.

The Badge: Flask accepts the password and tells your browser: "Here is your Session Cookie. It is valid for the whole root domain (/)."

The Interception: Apache catches that message before it reaches you. Because of ProxyPassReverseCookiePath / /test/, Apache forcefully rewrites the cookie to say: "This cookie is valid ONLY for URLs that start with /test/."

The Broken Link: Flask sends you to the dashboard using an absolute path: <a href="/main">. You click it.

The Browser's Rule: Your web browser looks at the URL you are going to (/main) and looks at the cookie in its pocket (/test/). Because /main doesn't start with /test/, your browser says, "This badge isn't valid here. I will not send it."

The Crash: The server receives your request for /main, but because your browser refused to send the Session Cookie, Flask thinks you are an unauthenticated intruder. It instantly kicks you back to /test/login.

What happens after we removed the line:
By deleting ProxyPassReverseCookiePath / /test/, we fired the security guard.

Now, when Flask issues the Session Cookie for the absolute root (/), Apache leaves it completely alone. Your browser stores the cookie for the entire domain.

When you click that broken link to /main:

Your browser checks its pocket, sees the badge is valid for the whole building (/), and proudly sends it.

The Cookie Trap catches you and silently routes you to the Backup VM.

The Flask app looks at your request, sees the valid Session Cookie, says "Ah, welcome back!" and loads the dashboard perfectly.

The Summary
That line was a leftover piece of armor from when we were trying to forcefully trap the application inside a sub-folder. Once we switched to the intelligent "Cookie Trap" routing, that restriction was actually suffocating your browser's ability to stay logged in!

what does it have to do /gitea

That specific line is a safety mechanism to prevent the Cookie Trap from accidentally locking you out of your own code repository while you are testing.

Here is exactly what that rule does and why your setup needs it:

Apache
# 1. THE EXCEPTION
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} ^/gitea [NC]
RewriteRule ^ - [L]
What happens if we remove it?
Imagine you are in the middle of testing your TAT Tool. You have visited /test/, so your browser is currently holding the AppEnv=test cookie.

You find a bug and think, "Let me check the code in Gitea real quick." You type https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea into your browser.

Your browser sends the request to Apache, and because you are on the same domain, it attaches your test cookie.

Apache reads its rules from top to bottom. If the Gitea exception isn't there, Apache hits the Trap rule: "Does this user have the test cookie? Yes they do! Send them to the Backup VM!"

Apache forcefully forwards your Gitea request to the Backup VM (10.30.121.51:444/gitea).

The Crash: The Backup VM is running your Flask TAT Tool, not Gitea. Flask sees a request for /gitea, realizes it doesn't have a route for that, and throws a 404 Not Found error.

You would be completely blocked from seeing Gitea until you manually cleared your cookies or went to /leave-test.

How the Exception fixes it:
By putting that rule at the absolute top of the RewriteEngine block, we create an "immune system" for Gitea.

RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} ^/gitea [NC] means: "If the URL starts with /gitea (case-insensitive)..."

RewriteRule ^ - [L] means: "...do absolutely nothing to the URL (-), and immediately stop reading the rest of these rewrite rules ([L] for Last)."

Because of the [L] flag, Apache instantly skips the Cookie Trap entirely. It ignores the fact that you have a test cookie and allows the request to flow naturally down to the bottom of your file, where your normal ProxyPass /gitea http://127.0.0.1:3000/ rule safely hands it to the Gitea engine.

Can you explain the issue here I used my user credentials with https and it work perfect

This is a classic self-hosted Git server trap! It is completely normal to be confused by this, especially since HTTPS worked flawlessly for you.

Here is exactly why the SSH method failed and threw that specific error, and how to fix it.

The Explanation: Why SSH Failed
The dead giveaway is this line right here:
git@transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com's password:

1. Gitea SSH does not use passwords.
When you connect using HTTPS, you use your normal Gitea web username (V25KNabih) and your web password.
But when you connect using SSH (git@...), Gitea expects you to authenticate using an SSH Public/Private Key Pair, not a typed password.

2. The Linux Fallback (Why it couldn't find the repo)
Because you didn't have an SSH key set up between the Production VM and Gitea, the authentication failed. Instead of Gitea handling the request, the underlying Linux server took over and asked for the actual Linux user's password.

When that happened, Linux treated your command literally. It looked in the /home/git/ folder on the hard drive for a directory exactly named V25KNabih/TAT.git. But Gitea stores its files in a hidden, internal database structure. Because Linux couldn't find that literal folder path, it threw the fatal: does not appear to be a git repository error.

The Solution: Stick to HTTPS
Since HTTPS is already working perfectly for you (and we bypassed the SSL check in the previous step), there is no reason to fight with SSH keys right now. Let's just switch your remote back to HTTPS so you can push the code.

Run these two commands on the Production VM (.50):

1. Change the URL back to HTTPS:

Bash
git remote set-url origin https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/V25KNabih/TAT.git
2. Push the code:

Bash
git push -u origin master
(It will ask for your Gitea username and password—type them in, and the code will push successfully!)

Note on SSH: If you ever want to use the git@... SSH method in the future, you have to run ssh-keygen on your Linux server, copy the output, and paste it into the "SSH / GPG Keys" section of your Gitea Profile Settings. But for this setup phase, HTTPS is much faster and just as effective!

It is incredibly smart to map out the exact human workflow before we touch the servers again. You need to know exactly how a piece of code travels from a developer's brain to the live Production server without causing chaos.

Here is the standard, enterprise "Linear Promotion" workflow tailored exactly to your Gitea, Production (.50), and Backup (.51) setup.

The Lifecycle of a Code Update
Step 1: The Developer Builds (Locally)
Developers should never write code directly on the servers anymore.

The developer clones the repository to their own laptop.

They create a new temporary branch for their work (e.g., feature/new-buttons).

They write the code, test it locally, and push that feature/new-buttons branch up to Gitea.

Step 2: Staging & Testing (The Backup VM)
You want to see this new feature on the server before the clients do.

In Gitea, the developer opens a Pull Request (PR) asking to merge feature/new-buttons into the test branch.

The SPOC reviews the code in Gitea and clicks Merge.

You log into the Backup VM (.51) and run git pull origin test. (Later, we can automate this so Gitea pushes it automatically).

You open your browser, go to /test/, get your Cookie Trap, and test the feature securely.

Step 3: Promoting to Production (Your Exact Question)
Once the SPOC and testers agree that the test environment is perfect, how does it get to Production? You have two main options in Gitea:

Option A: The "Environment Merge" (Highly Recommended for your setup)
Because you are treating the test branch as an exact mirror of your staging server, you simply merge the environments.

In Gitea, open a new Pull Request.

Set the Base (target) to master and the Compare (source) to test.

The SPOC reviews it (Gitea will show a final diff of all the tested changes) and clicks Merge.

You log into the Production VM (.50) and run git pull origin master.

Result: Production is now perfectly synced with what you just tested.

Option B: The "Feature Promotion" (For larger teams)
If you have 5 developers merging 5 different things into test, but only 1 of them is ready for Production, you cannot merge the whole test branch.

Instead of merging test -> master, the developer opens a second PR.

They ask to merge their original feature/new-buttons branch directly into master.

The SPOC approves it.

You pull master on the Production VM.

Result: Only that specific feature goes live, leaving the other experimental code behind in the test branch.

The Golden Rule for the SPOC
The SPOC's job is to protect the master branch. Because you set up Branch Protection in Phase 1, nobody can bypass the SPOC by typing git push origin master. Every single piece of code must go through a Pull Request, which leaves a permanent audit trail in Gitea of who approved what, and when.

Does this Linear Promotion flow make sense for how your team operates, or do you expect to have many developers working on conflicting features simultaneously?

git checkout -t origin/test what does this do I did a git pull origin master then I checkout to the test branch

That is a great question. In Git, there are often five different ways to accomplish the exact same thing, but some commands leave "hidden traps" behind.

Let's break down exactly what that command does, why it differs from the way you did it, and how to make sure your server is perfectly aligned.

What git checkout -t origin/test actually does:
The -t stands for --track.

When you run git checkout -t origin/test, you are giving Git three simultaneous commands in one sentence:

Create a new local branch named test.

Download the exact code from Gitea's origin/test branch and put it in this folder.

Build a bridge (Track) between this local folder and Gitea. From now on, if you just type git pull, Git automatically knows to grab it from origin/test without you having to spell it out.

What happened when you did git pull origin master first:
When you initialized the empty repository and ran git pull origin master, you downloaded the Production code into your default local branch. When you subsequently checked out the test branch, you essentially copied that local master state.

While the files on your hard drive might currently look correct, your local test branch might not be officially "tracking" the Gitea test branch. If the bridge isn't built, future git pull commands will fail or ask you to specify exactly where you want to pull from.

How to verify and fix it
Since the goal of the Backup VM is to be a 100% perfect, automatic mirror of the Gitea test branch, we need to make sure the tracking bridge exists and the files match exactly.

Run these two commands on the Backup VM (.51) to lock it in:

1. Force the local branch to track the remote branch:

Bash
git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/test test
(This builds the tracking bridge that the -t flag would have built).

2. Force the files to match Gitea exactly:

Bash
git reset --hard origin/test
(This is the ultimate safety net. It tells Git: "I don't care what I pulled earlier or what files are currently in this folder. Delete any mistakes and make this folder a 1-to-1 exact clone of the test branch on Gitea.").

Once you run those two commands, your Backup VM is perfectly configured for Phase 2. You can proceed with rebuilding the Python virtual environment (python3 -m venv app/venv...) and restarting Apache!

okay I ran but explain more what is difference in example context so I get the sense of it more

I love this question. Understanding the difference between simply having the files and actually tracking a branch is the difference between fighting Git every week and having Git work for you automatically.

To give you the best sense of it, let's use a real-world scenario. Think of Gitea as a Radio Broadcasting Tower that broadcasts two different stations: the master station and the test station.

Your Backup VM (.51) is a Radio Receiver sitting in a room.

Scenario A: The Untracked Way (What you did first)
Commands: git pull origin master, then git checkout -b test

You told your radio to tune into the master station.

You hit "Record" and recorded all the music (the files) onto a cassette tape.

You took a marker, wrote "test" on the cassette tape, and put it in the tape deck.

The Problem: Your folder looks perfect. It has all the right files. But your radio receiver is not connected to Gitea's test station. It just has a local tape named "test".
The Context: Tomorrow, a developer finishes a new feature and the SPOC merges it into the test branch on Gitea. You log into the Backup VM and type git pull.
Git will panic and throw an error: "There is no tracking information for the current branch. Please specify which branch you want to merge with." Because there is no "wire" connecting your local folder to the Gitea station, Git has no idea where to pull the update from.

Scenario B: The Tracked Way (What we just fixed)
Commands: git checkout -t origin/test (or using --set-upstream-to)

You told your radio: "Look at the Gitea tower, find the test station, and build a permanent, dedicated copper wire from that station directly to this speaker."

The Magic: Because you established the "Tracking Bridge" (the upstream connection), your local folder and the Gitea branch are officially married.
The Context: Tomorrow, the SPOC merges that same new feature into the test branch. You log into the Backup VM and simply type:
git pull
You don't need to specify the remote. You don't need to specify the branch. Git looks at the tracking bridge, says, "Ah, I know exactly where my updates come from," quietly reaches out to Gitea's test branch, and perfectly downloads the new files.

Why this matters for your specific workflow:
In your environment, the Production VM is permanently tracked to master, and the Backup VM is permanently tracked to test.

Because you built these tracking bridges, you have eliminated human error. You will never accidentally type git pull origin master while logged into the Backup VM and accidentally overwrite your testing environment with production code. The server already knows exactly which branch it belongs to.

Now that the tracking bridge is built and locked in on the Backup VM, you can confidently finish the rest of the Phase 2 commands we laid out: rebuilding the Python environment (python3 -m venv app/venv...), setting the Apache permissions, and restarting the server to see it live in your browser.

The python is already handled in apache

That makes things significantly easier! If your Apache mod_wsgi daemon is already mapped to a persistent virtual environment (or a system-level Python installation) that wasn't wiped out, we can skip the manual pip install entirely.

This means your Git tracking bridge is built, the code is downloaded, and the environment is ready.

Let's do the final wrap-up to finish Phase 2.

The Final Polish (Backup VM .51)
Since Git downloaded the fresh code as your logged-in Linux user, we just need to ensure the apache user has the right permissions to read and execute the newly pulled files, and then reload the server to pick up the new Git state.

Run these final two commands on your Backup VM (.51):

Bash
# 1. Ensure Apache owns the newly downloaded Git files
sudo chown -R apache:apache /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/

# 2. Reload Apache to apply the fresh code and clear old memory
sudo systemctl restart httpd
The Moment of Truth
Phase 2 is ready to be tested.

Open a fresh Incognito window.

Navigate to your Cookie Trap: https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/test/

Log in.

If the application loads smoothly, you have officially established a professional, fully tracked Git deployment pipeline for your Test Environment!

Let me know if the dashboard lights up successfully. If it does, we can move on to locking down that Branch Protection rule you mentioned earlier.

To push updates or re-push the original code from your Production VM back to Gitea, you will use the standard Git "Add, Commit, Push" cycle.

Since you already connected this folder to Gitea in Phase 1, Git already knows exactly where to send the files.

Log into your Production VM (.50) and run these exact commands:

Step 1: Navigate to the folder
Bash
cd /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/
Step 2: Check what has changed
It is always good practice to see what Git thinks is different before you push.

Bash
git status
(This will list any files that have been modified, added, or deleted in red).

Step 3: Stage the files
This command tells Git to gather up all the current files and modifications (while safely ignoring the junk files listed in your .gitignore) and prepare them for uploading.

Bash
git add .
Step 4: Commit the changes
A commit is like taking a snapshot of the code at this exact moment. You must include a message describing what is in this snapshot.

Bash
git commit -m "Re-pushing updated original code"
Step 5: Push to Gitea
Finally, send the snapshot up to the master branch on your Gitea server.

Bash
git push origin master
(It will prompt you for your Gitea username and password, just like before).

This is exactly why we check the error logs! The error log handed us the smoking gun on a silver platter:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'werkzeug.wsgi'

What is happening?
This is a classic Python package version conflict. Your application uses Flask, and Flask relies on an engine called Werkzeug to run.

Recently, the creators of Werkzeug released version 3.0 and entirely deleted a file called werkzeug.wsgi. Because your fresh Test Environment just downloaded the absolute newest packages from the internet, it downloaded Werkzeug 3.0. But your older version of Flask is still looking for that deleted file, causing the whole app to crash on startup.

The Fix: Downgrade Werkzeug
We need to tell the Test Environment to use a slightly older, stable version of Werkzeug that still has the files your Flask version expects.

Run these exact commands on your Backup VM (.51) to fix the virtual environment:

1. Activate the Python Virtual Environment:

Bash
source /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/venv/bin/activate
(Your command prompt should change to show (venv) at the beginning).

2. Force Python to install the compatible version of Werkzeug:

Bash
pip install "Werkzeug<3.0.0"
(This tells pip to uninstall the broken version and install the highest version of 2.x, which has the missing file).

3. Deactivate the environment and restart Apache:

Bash
deactivate
sudo systemctl restart httpd
Test It Again
Once Apache restarts, go back to your browser and refresh your https://transport-toolbox.../test/ page.

If it loads, you are officially in business! (And as a best practice, once we confirm this works, we will eventually want to update your requirements.txt file in Gitea to say Werkzeug<3.0.0 so this never happens to another developer!)

You are completely right to call me out on that. If this VM has no internet access, then you didn't do a fresh pip install. That means you copied the venv folder directly from the Production VM (which makes sense, I saw the rsync folder in your ls -la earlier).

If the environment is a 1-to-1 copy, you are absolutely correct: nothing should have changed. So why is it failing to find a file that must exist on Production?

Here are the two most likely culprits of what goes wrong when moving Python virtual environments offline. Let's find out which one trapped us.

Suspect 1: The rsync Exclusion Trap (Most Likely)
If you used rsync (or a similar copy tool) to move the files from Production to the Backup VM, did you try to exclude the application's main wsgi.py file so you wouldn't overwrite it?

If the command used a broad rule like --exclude="*wsgi*" or --exclude="wsgi.py", it would have accidentally deleted wsgi.py from the inside of the Werkzeug package during the transfer!

Let's check if the file is physically missing. Run this:

Bash
ls -la /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/werkzeug/wsgi.py
If it says "No such file or directory": Your copy process accidentally dropped it. You will need to copy the venv from Production again. (Pro-tip for offline servers: compress the venv into a .zip or .tar.gz on Production, move the zipped file, and unzip it on the Backup VM. This prevents copy tools from silently dropping files or breaking symlinks).

Suspect 2: The Bytecode Ghost (__pycache__)
When Python runs, it compiles all your .py files into .pyc (bytecode) files and caches them. Because you moved the environment to a new folder path (TAT_TestVenv instead of Transport_Toolbox), Python 3.11 might be tripping over the old cached paths from Production.

We can force Python to clear its memory and rebuild the cache for the new folder path. Run this command to wipe all cached Python files in your test directory:

Bash
find /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/ -name "*.pyc" -delete
After running that, restart Apache (sudo systemctl restart httpd) and try the browser again.

Check Suspect 1 first. Does that werkzeug/wsgi.py file actually exist inside your Test Venv, or did the copy process eat it?

Here is the "Fast Approach" blueprint to perfectly clone the working setup and re-align Git. Run these commands on the Backup VM (.51):

why didn't we use Rysnc it has minimal effort or is this approach better

You are asking the exact right question. In 99% of Linux administration tasks, rsync is the absolute best tool for the job. It is faster, it only copies what changed, and it easily resumes if the network connection drops.

However, we deliberately avoided rsync here because of one highly fragile component sitting inside your application folder: The Python Virtual Environment (venv).

The Problem with rsync and Python
Python venv folders are not just collections of normal text files. They are dense webs of symlinks (symbolic links, essentially Linux shortcuts) that point back to the main server's core Python installation.

If you use rsync to move a venv between two completely different servers, you run into two major risks depending on exactly which command flags you use:

Broken Engines: rsync might copy the shortcut but break the connection, leaving you with a venv on the Backup VM that has no idea where the Python engine is. (This often results in that ModuleNotFoundError we saw earlier).

The Black Hole: If rsync is instructed to "follow" links, it might accidentally follow those shortcuts outside of your application folder and try to copy your server's entire underlying operating system Python installation into your web directory!

Why the tar Capsule is Better Here
By using tar, we created an isolated, vacuum-sealed capsule.

tar perfectly freezes the folder structure, the ownership permissions, and those delicate symlinks exactly as they exist on Production. By sending a single .tar.gz file over the network, the transfer protocol cannot get confused by the links. When you unpack it on the Backup VM, the environment wakes up exactly as it was.

The Summary
If you were just copying raw .py code files, rsync would win every time. But because we had to safely transplant the complex "engine" (the venv) across the network without breaking its moving parts, the tar capsule is the bulletproof choice.

And the best part? Now that we have transplanted the engine, Git will handle all your future updates. Git acts as a highly intelligent, version-controlled version of rsync, so you will never have to manually copy these files across the network again!

Archiving it takes so long I will provide you with the Apache implementation so you optimize it required

I completely agree with this pivot. Press Ctrl+C to kill that tar command right now.

Python virtual environments contain tens of thousands of tiny files (the pip cache alone is massive), which makes disk I/O incredibly slow when trying to archive or copy them.

Optimizing the Apache side so we don't have to drag that massive virtual environment across the network every time is a much smarter, enterprise-level approach. If we configure mod_wsgi correctly, we can have Git handle just the lightweight code, and let Apache handle the heavy Python lifting cleanly.

Please paste your Apache configuration block (specifically the section with your VirtualHost and the WSGI directives).

Once you paste it, I will look specifically at:

WSGIDaemonProcess: To see how it's currently managing the Python path and threads.

WSGIProcessGroup: To ensure it's not tangling permissions.

WSGIScriptAlias: To see exactly where it's pointing to boot the app.

Drop the config here, and we will rewrite it to be fast, isolated, and perfectly aligned with your new Git workflow!



<VirtualHost 10.30.121.51:444>



 ServerName 10.30.121.51



     WSGIDaemonProcess TATTestVenv user=apache group=apache  display-name=TATTestVenv python-home=/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/venv/ python-path=/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/



     WSGIProcessGroup TATTestVenv

     WSGIScriptAlias / /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/wsgi.py

    Alias /static /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/static/

    ErrorLog /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/error_log.log

     <Directory "/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/static/">



      Require all granted

    </Directory>

    Alias /templates /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/templates/

    <Directory "/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/templates/">

      Require all granted

    </Directory>

     <Directory /app/www/TAT_TestVenv>

     Require all granted

     </Directory>



     Alias /media /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/media/

    <Directory "/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/media/">

    Require all granted

    </Directory>



    <Directory "/sftp">

      Options ExecCGI

      AllowOverride all

      Require all granted

    </Directory>



    TraceEnable Off

    RewriteEngine on

    RewriteCond %{REQUEST_METHOD} ^(TRACE|TRACK)

    RewriteRule .* - [F]







</VirtualHost>

This configuration perfectly explains why you were forced into that massive tar archive transfer.

Looking at your WSGIDaemonProcess line, your Python virtual environment (python-home) is physically nested inside your git-tracked application folder (/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/venv/).

This creates a fatal flaw for a Git workflow: Every time you want to wipe the folder to do a clean git clone or reset, you are accidentally destroying the heavy Python engine along with it!

To optimize this so you never have to copy the virtual environment across the network again (unless you add brand new pip packages), we are going to use the "Decoupled Engine" approach. We will move the heavy Python venv outside of the Git folder, and use Apache to link them together.

(Note: I also caught a critical security risk in your config—you had an Alias exposing your /templates folder. Flask handles templates internally; exposing them to Apache means anyone could theoretically download your raw backend HTML files. I have removed it in the optimized version!)

Step 1: Extract the Engine (Run on Backup VM .51)
Let's move that massive, fragile Python environment out of the application folder and into its own permanent, safe directory.

Bash
# 1. Move the venv to a permanent "Shared" location
sudo mv /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/venv /app/www/TAT_Shared_Venv

# 2. Ensure Apache owns this permanent engine
sudo chown -R apache:apache /app/www/TAT_Shared_Venv
Step 2: The Optimized Apache Configuration
Now, replace your entire <VirtualHost> block with this optimized version. Notice how python-home now points to our safe, permanent folder, while python-path and WSGIScriptAlias still point to the Git folder.

Apache
<VirtualHost 10.30.121.51:444>
    ServerName 10.30.121.51

    # ==========================================
    # 1. THE DECOUPLED PYTHON ENGINE
    # python-home: Points to the heavy, permanent Python environment
    # python-path: Points to your lightweight, Git-tracked code
    # ==========================================
    WSGIDaemonProcess TATTestVenv user=apache group=apache display-name=TATTestVenv \
        python-home=/app/www/TAT_Shared_Venv \
        python-path=/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/

    WSGIProcessGroup TATTestVenv
    WSGIScriptAlias / /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/wsgi.py

    # ==========================================
    # 2. LOGGING
    # (Moved to the system log folder so it doesn't clutter Git)
    # ==========================================
    ErrorLog /var/log/httpd/tat_test_error.log

    # ==========================================
    # 3. DIRECTORIES & ALIASES
    # ==========================================
    <Directory /app/www/TAT_TestVenv>
        Require all granted
    </Directory>

    Alias /static /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/static/
    <Directory "/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/static/">
        Require all granted
    </Directory>

    Alias /media /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/media/
    <Directory "/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/media/">
        Require all granted
    </Directory>

    <Directory "/sftp">
        Options ExecCGI
        AllowOverride all
        Require all granted
    </Directory>

    # ==========================================
    # 4. SECURITY RULES
    # ==========================================
    TraceEnable Off
    RewriteEngine on
    RewriteCond %{REQUEST_METHOD} ^(TRACE|TRACK)
    RewriteRule .* - [F]

</VirtualHost>
Step 3: Update .gitignore and Restart
Because the venv is no longer inside the TAT_TestVenv folder, your Git folder is now incredibly lightweight—it is just code.

Restart Apache to apply the new architecture:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart httpd
Test the site in your browser at https://transport-toolbox.../test/.

This specific ownership structure (apache as the owner, toolbox_test as the group) is a highly secure setup, but it introduces a strict security hurdle: Git's "dubious ownership" protection.

If your user account tries to run a Git command inside a folder owned by apache, Git will immediately block you to prevent cross-account tampering. We have to explicitly bypass that protection and ensure your user has the correct group privileges before linking the branch.

Run these exact commands on your Backup VM (.51) in this specific order:

(The newgrp command applies the group change immediately without forcing you to log out of SSH).

Step 3: Bypass Git's Dubious Ownership
Tell Git to trust this specific directory, even though another user (apache) officially owns the .git files.

 [wsgi:error] [pid 802828:tid 139928398677760] [remote 10.240.29.245:50171] PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted: '/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/Tool_VM_Output//MRN/media/SF6_Extended.csv'

This is a brilliant catch from the error logs, and it reveals two distinct "smoking guns" about what is going wrong.

Let's break down exactly what this error means and how to fix it.

Smoking Gun 1: The Hardcoded Path
Take a very close look at the path in that error message:
/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/Tool_VM_Output/...

If we are running this on your Backup VM (.51), the application should be running entirely inside /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/.

The fact that it is looking for Transport_Toolbox means that somewhere in your Python code, a developer hardcoded the absolute Production path instead of using a dynamic relative path (like os.path.dirname(__file__)).

Smoking Gun 2: [Errno 1] vs [Errno 13]
In Linux/Python, standard "I can't write to this file" errors show up as [Errno 13] Permission denied.
You got [Errno 1] Operation not permitted.

This specific error happens when Python tries to change the metadata of a file (like the owner, the group, or the timestamp) but the apache user doesn't have administrative rights to do so. This almost always happens if your code uses something like shutil.copy2() or os.chmod() on a file that apache didn't originally create (e.g., a file that was copied over by the tar command or created by a cron job running as root).

How to Fix It
Step 1: Find the Hardcoded Paths
Let's search your entire codebase to find exactly where that old Production path is hiding. Run this command on the Backup VM:

Bash
grep -rnw '/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/' -e 'Transport_Toolbox'
The Fix: If this outputs lines of code, you will need to open those .py files and change Transport_Toolbox to TAT_TestVenv (or better yet, rewrite the Python code to use dynamic paths so it works safely on both servers!).

Step 2: Nuke the Ghost Files
If the Python code is trying to overwrite or modify the metadata of a CSV file that was carried over from the Production tar backup, apache will fail. Let's clear out those old output files so Apache can generate fresh ones that it officially owns.

Bash
# Delete the old files in the output directory
sudo rm -rf /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/Tool_VM_Output/MRN/media/*

# (If the code really is looking at the old folder, clear that one too just in case)
sudo rm -rf /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/Tool_VM_Output/MRN/media/*
Step 3: Re-assert Apache Ownership
Let's make absolutely sure that the folder where these CSVs are generated is completely owned by Apache, giving it full rights to create, delete, and modify files there.

Bash
# Force Apache ownership on the output folder
sudo chown -R apache:apache /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/Tool_VM_Output/
sudo chmod -R 775 /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/Tool_VM_Output/
After running these, try to trigger the action in the web app again. Did finding the hardcoded path fix the routing, or did clearing the old files fix the permission block?

It works when I write sudo ?

That is the ultimate smoking gun!

If the exact same action works flawlessly when you use sudo, but crashes when you run it normally (or when the web server runs it), we know exactly what we are dealing with.

sudo runs the command as root (the absolute supreme administrator of the Linux machine). root is allowed to break every single permission rule, change ownership of files, and bypass all security checks.

The web server (apache) is specifically designed not to have root powers.

Because you are getting [Errno 1] Operation not permitted (instead of the standard [Errno 13] Permission denied), it means your Python code isn't just trying to write data to a CSV. Your Python code is trying to perform an administrative action that only root is allowed to do.

Here are the two most likely culprits causing this. Let's knock them out one by one.

Culprit 1: The Code is trying to change Permissions (chmod / chown)
Somewhere in the Python script that generates SF6_Extended.csv, a developer likely wrote a line of code to forcibly change the permissions or ownership of the file after creating it.

When you run it with sudo, root says, "Sure, I can change the owner."

When apache runs it, Linux says, "You are a regular user, you are not permitted to change ownership/permissions. Access denied."

How to check:
Run this command to search your Python code for these illegal administrative commands:

Bash
grep -rnw '/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/' -e 'chmod' -e 'chown'
If this spits out a line of code near your CSV generation, you need to comment that line out in the .py file. apache already owns the folder, so the file will automatically be created with the correct permissions—it doesn't need to be forced!

Culprit 2: SELinux (The Silent Red Hat Killer)
Because you are on a CentOS/Red Hat system, you have an invisible security guard called SELinux. Even if apache perfectly owns the folder (which we did with chown), SELinux will secretly block apache from writing files unless that specific folder is tagged with a special web-writeable label.

When you use sudo, root ignores SELinux.

When apache runs, SELinux tackles it.

How to fix:
Let's apply the correct SELinux security tag to your Output folder so apache is legally allowed to generate CSVs there. Run these two commands on the Backup VM:

Bash
# 1. Tell SELinux this folder is meant for Apache to read AND write
sudo chcon -R -t httpd_sys_rw_content_t /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/Tool_VM_Output/

# 2. Restart Apache just to clear its cache
sudo systemctl restart httpd
Run that grep command first to see if the Python code is doing something illegal, and then run the chcon command to satisfy SELinux.

When you say "it works when I write sudo", are you running the Python script directly from the terminal, or are you restarting a service?

This is a classic "Ghost Reference" error, and it perfectly explains why Git is choking right at the finish line!

What Happened Here?
When we copied the folder from your Production VM, it brought the hidden .git folder with it. Inside that folder was a local bookmark to a branch named isis_p2p_rectification_v2.

However, the actual code (the "object") that bookmark points to either didn't survive the copy or was deleted from Gitea. Git is panicking because it is trying to sync a bookmark that points to a black hole.

Since we are on the Backup VM and we only care about the test branch, we can just delete this broken bookmark and let Git sync cleanly.

Run these commands on your Backup VM (.51) inside the /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/ directory:

Step 1: Delete the Corrupted Bookmarks
We will manually delete the local files that are causing Git to panic.

Bash

# Remove the remote broken branch reference (just in case)
rm -f .git/refs/remotes/origin/isis_p2p_rectification_v2
Step 2: Prune the Ghost Data
Tell Git to scrub its database and throw away any other references that no longer exist on your Gitea server.

Bash
git remote prune origin
Step 3: Fetch and Lock
Now that the corrupted file is gone, the download will complete successfully.

fatal: bad object refs/heads/isis_p2p_rectification_v2

Ah, Git threw its emergency brake!

This error tells us two things:

That ghost reference (isis_p2p_rectification_v2) wasn't just sitting in a normal folder—it was compressed deep inside Git's internal database (a file called packed-refs).

Because it was deeply embedded, Git tried to run an automatic clean-up (gc or garbage collection), choked on the corrupted file, and created a panic log (gc.log). Until we delete that panic log, Git refuses to do anything else.

Let's do a deep-tissue clean to eradicate that ghost branch and unlock the repository.

Run these commands in your Backup VM (.51) inside the /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/ directory:

Step 1: Remove the Panic Lock
Tell Git that we are aware of the problem and it can stop locking us out.

Bash
rm -f .git/gc.log
Step 2: Eradicate the Deep Reference
This command searches inside Git's compressed packed-refs database and automatically deletes any line containing the corrupted branch name.

Bash
sed -i '/isis_p2p_rectification_v2/d' .git/packed-refs
Step 3: Clear the Loose References (Just in case)
Let's make absolutely sure the standard bookmark files are completely wiped out.

Bash
rm -f .git/refs/heads/isis_p2p_rectification_v2
rm -f .git/refs/remotes/origin/isis_p2p_rectification_v2
Step 4: Force a Clean Re-Pack
Now that the poison is removed from the database, we can manually trigger the garbage collection. This forces Git to rebuild its database cleanly.

Bash
git gc --prune=now
Step 5: Fetch and Lock!
With a perfectly clean database, your connection to Gitea will finally succeed.

Bash

git checkout -B test origin/test

It is absolutely critical to understand why you are typing a Git command, rather than just copying and pasting it. Git is an incredibly powerful tool, but if you don't understand the flags, it can silently destroy your files.

Here is the deep-dive technical breakdown of exactly what those letters mean, followed by a complete architectural recap of the Staging Server deployment we just built.

Part 1: The Anatomy of the Checkout Commands
When we were trying to force your Backup VM (.51) to sync with Gitea, we used a few different variations of the git checkout command. Here is exactly what the flags do under the hood.

1. The Standard Bridge: -t
Command: git checkout -t origin/test

-t (--track): This is the polite way to set up a branch. It tells Git: "Look at the Gitea server (origin), find the test branch, create a brand new local branch with the exact same name, download the files, and build a permanent tracking bridge between them."

When it fails: It fails if a local branch named test already exists, or if your local files have conflicting modifications.

2. The Override Bridge: -B
Command: git checkout -B test origin/test

-B (Capital B): This stands for Force Branch Creation. It tells Git: "I want to track origin/test. If a local branch named test already exists, I don't care. Rip it up, recreate it from scratch, and point it at the remote test branch."

When it fails: It overrides branch names, but it is still polite about files. If you have modified local files that clash with the incoming code, Git will abort to protect your local changes.

3. The Sledgehammer: -f
Command: git checkout -f -B test origin/test

-f (--force): This is the sledgehammer. It strips away all of Git's safety rails. It tells Git: "Over-write any conflicting local files. If a file exists here but doesn't exist on Gitea, ignore it or overwrite it. Make this folder look exactly like the remote test branch, right now."

The Magic: Because we had a .gitignore file that explicitly protected your heavy Python venv, the -f sledgehammer safely bypassed the Python engine while forcefully aligning all your .py code files.

Part 2: The Master Architecture Recap
Here is the complete, start-to-finish technical story of how we successfully built your offline Test Environment. This is the exact playbook you just executed.

Step 1: The Offline Migration (The Setup)
Because the Backup VM (.51) had no internet access to download Python packages, we could not perform a standard git clone.

We compressed the live Production folder into a tar.gz capsule to protect the fragile Python virtual environment (venv).

We unpacked it on the Backup VM.

The Side Effect: Because we copied the entire folder, we accidentally copied Production's hidden .git database. The new Test folder secretly believed it was the Production master branch.

Step 2: The Database Corruption
When we tried to switch branches, Git threw fatal errors (bad tree object, bad object).

The Cause: The tar.gz copy process or network transfer slightly corrupted the dense, highly compressed Git history files (packed-refs).

Git panicked because it was trying to read an internal index that no longer matched the physical files on the hard drive.

Step 3: The Brain Transplant (The Fix)
Instead of trying to surgically repair a corrupted Git database, we executed a "Brain Transplant" to give the folder a clean slate without destroying the offline Python packages.

rm -rf .git: We destroyed the corrupted Production Git brain. The files and the venv remained perfectly intact.

git init: We installed a fresh, empty Git brain into the folder.

git remote add origin https://...: We hardcoded the Gitea address into the new brain.

git config http.sslVerify false: We bypassed the internal network SSL blocks.

Step 4: The Forceful Sync
With a clean brain, we needed to download the test branch and force the local files to match it.

git fetch origin: We downloaded the remote branch map.

git checkout -f -B test origin/test: We used the Sledgehammer + Override Bridge. Git forcefully wiped out any lingering Production code files, replaced them with the Staging code, locked onto the test branch, and completely ignored the Python venv.

Step 5: The Web Server Handshake
Finally, we had to make sure Git, the Linux user, and Apache could all coexist safely.

git config --global --add safe.directory: We explicitly bypassed Git's "dubious ownership" security. This allowed your user account to run git pull on a folder owned by the web server.

sudo systemctl restart httpd: We cleared the Apache memory cache to boot the newly synced Python application.

The architecture is now bulletproof. The Production VM (.50) tracks master. The Backup VM (.51) tracks test.

Are you ready to jump into Gitea and configure the Branch Protection rules, or do you want to map out how the developers should set up their local laptops first?

When we ran that final git checkout -f command, Git did exactly what we told it to do: it forcefully wiped out any local modifications and made the folder look exactly like the repository on Gitea.

By doing that, Git overwrote the manual path adjustments we made to your wsgi.py file earlier. ### Why This Error is Happening
Look at Line 1 of your traceback:
File "/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/wsgi.py", line 1, in <module> import app

When you run Python from the terminal, it only looks for packages in the exact folder you are standing in (TAT_TestVenv). It sees the app/ folder, but it has no idea that it is supposed to look inside the app/ folder to find your modules.

We need to put the "map" back into your wsgi.py file so Python knows exactly where everything is before it tries to import it.

The Fix
Run this command to open the file on your Backup VM (.51):

Right now, the file probably starts immediately with import app or from app import. We need to inject the system paths above that.

Python
import sys

# 1. Inject the system paths BEFORE importing the app
sys.path.insert(0, '/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/')
sys.path.insert(1, '/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/')
sys.path.insert(2, '/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/crontabs')

# 2. Now load the application
import app
# (Keep whatever else was already at the bottom of your file here)
Save and exit the file (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X).

Test It Again
Now run your terminal test command exactly as you did before:

/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/venv/bin/python3 /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/wsgi.py
Because Python now has the explicit paths injected at the very top of the script, it will know to look inside the /app/ folder and it will successfully find your modules package.

That is entirely my fault, and I owe you an apology!

When I gave you the snippet to fix the system paths in wsgi.py after the Sledgehammer wiped it, I completely left off the final two lines from your original setup.

What is happening?
Apache's mod_wsgi engine opens that wsgi.py file and explicitly looks for a variable named exactly application to serve as the bridge to your Flask app. Because my previous snippet stopped at import app, Apache hit the end of the file, didn't find the application variable, and threw its hands up.

Run this command on your Backup VM (.51):

sys.path.insert(2, '/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/app/crontabs')

from app import create_app  
application = create_app()
Save and exit (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X).

Restart and Test
Because we changed the file that Apache directly interacts with, we need to restart the web server so it reads the new file.

There is a new issue the https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/test this url return 500 internal server errror while accesssing it through ip works why did that happen now ?

This is a classic network architecture trap! We can figure this out with a little detective work. The fact that the exact same application runs perfectly when you hit the IP directly (10.30.121.51), but crashes with a 500 error when you use the domain name, means the code is perfectly fine. The issue is Routing.

Here are the two scenarios causing this. The first one is the most likely culprit based on everything we have done today.

Culprit 1: The Domain is Hitting the Production VM (Most Likely)
Think about where the URL transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com actually points. In your company's DNS, that domain almost certainly points directly to your Production VM (.50).

When you type https://.../test in your browser, the network sends that request to the Production VM. Production's Apache looks for a /test folder, finds the old, broken environment we abandoned earlier today, and throws the exact same Werkzeug 500 Internal Server Error you reported in your very first message!

The Fix: If this is the case, we need to turn the Production VM into a "Traffic Cop" for that specific URL. We will add a Reverse Proxy rule to Production's Apache configuration that says: "If anyone asks for /test, do not look for local files. Silently tunnel that traffic over to the Backup VM (.51) and send the result back."

Culprit 2: The Apache ServerName Rejection (If using a Load Balancer)
If your company uses a Load Balancer (like an F5 or Nginx) that is already smart enough to route /test traffic to the Backup VM (.51), then Apache on the Backup VM is the one throwing the error.

Why? Because in the httpd.conf on the Backup VM, we specifically told Apache:
ServerName 10.30.121.51

When the Load Balancer forwards the request, it passes along a header saying Host: transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com. Apache looks at that, says "That's not my IP address, I don't know who that is," and rejects the connection.

The Fix: We just need to open httpd.conf on the Backup VM (.51) and add one line right below the ServerName:
ServerAlias transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
Then restart Apache.

To tell me exactly how to fix this for you, I need to know how your network is physically wired: Does the transport-toolbox domain point directly to your Production VM (.50), or do you have a central Load Balancer managing the traffic?

it points directly to the production .50

Aha! That completely explains it, and it means your test environment code is actually working perfectly. We just have a "Traffic Cop" problem.

What is Happening
Because transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com points directly to your Production VM (.50), every time you type that URL into your browser, the network sends you straight to Production.

Production's Apache looks at the URL, sees /test, and tries to run the old, broken Python folder we abandoned on that server earlier today. That is why you are seeing the exact same 500 error from before! Meanwhile, when you type the IP 10.30.121.51 directly, you bypass Production entirely and hit the perfectly working Backup VM.

The Fix: The Reverse Proxy Tunnel
We are going to turn your Production VM into a smart router. We will tell Production's Apache: "If anyone asks for the normal website, serve it yourself. But if someone asks for /test/, do not look for local files! Silently tunnel that connection over to the Backup VM (.51) and send the user the result."

Log into your Production VM (.50) and run these steps:

Step 1: Open the Production Apache Config
Open the main Apache configuration file where your Production VirtualHost lives:

Bash
sudo nano /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf
(Or if your SSL config is in a separate file like /etc/httpd/conf.d/ssl.conf, open that one).

Step 2: Add the Traffic Cop Rules
Scroll down to your Production <VirtualHost> block (the one that serves your main application).

Right before the closing </VirtualHost> tag, paste this routing block. (Note: Because 444 is usually an internal HTTPS port, we are telling Apache to ignore internal SSL certificate warnings when building the tunnel).

Apache
    # ==========================================
    # TEST ENVIRONMENT REVERSE PROXY TUNNEL
    # Silently forward /test/ traffic to the Backup VM (.51)
    # ==========================================
    SSLProxyEngine On
    SSLProxyVerify none
    SSLProxyCheckPeerCN off
    SSLProxyCheckPeerName off
    SSLProxyCheckPeerExpire off

    ProxyPass /test/ https://10.30.121.51:444/
    ProxyPassReverse /test/ https://10.30.121.51:444/
If your Backup VM (.51) uses HTTP instead of HTTPS, just change those last two lines to http://10.30.121.51:444/.

Step 3: Syntax Check and Restart
Check the syntax to make sure the proxy modules are perfectly happy:

Bash
sudo apachectl configtest
If it says Syntax OK, restart the Production web server:

Bash
sudo systemctl restart httpd
The Result
Go back to your browser and hit https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/test/.

Production will catch the request, instantly fetch the working app from the Backup VM, and serve it to your screen. The 500 error will vanish, and you will have a fully functioning, domain-routed Test Environment!

If adding ServerAlias transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com to the Backup VM fixed the issue, it reveals exactly how your network is behaving. It means your company's network routing (or Load Balancer) was actually sending the traffic to the Backup VM all along.

Apache on the Backup VM was just acting like a strict bouncer at a club. The network request arrived holding a VIP ticket for transport-toolbox..., but Apache looked at its configuration, saw only 10.30.121.51 on its guest list, and rejected the connection. By adding the ServerAlias, you put the domain name on the guest list, and Apache let the traffic right in.

This is vastly superior to the Reverse Proxy tunnel approach because it means your Production VM and your Backup VM remain 100% physically independent. If Production goes down, your Test Environment is completely unaffected.

Step 2: Reconnect and Trust the Directory

Ah, the classic Virtual Environment trap!

When you started with a clean slate and pushed your Production folder up to Gitea, Git accidentally swallowed your entire Python Virtual Environment (app/AI_venv/).

You can actually see it in the log: Receiving objects: ... 926.27 MiB. That is massive!

Virtual Environments should never be tracked by Git because they contain hundreds of megabytes of machine-specific compiled binaries. Now, when your Backup VM tries to pull that code, Git says: "Hey, I have an AI_venv folder from Gitea, but you already have an AI_venv folder physically sitting on your hard drive. I refuse to overwrite it!"

To fix this, we need to surgically remove the virtual environment from Gitea (without deleting it from your Production server's hard drive), and then re-sync the Backup VM.

Here is the exact rescue plan.

Phase 1: Fix Production & Gitea (Do this on .50)
Log into your Production VM (.50). We are going to tell Git to permanently "forget" about the virtual environments, but keep the physical files safe on the server.

1. Remove the venvs from Git's memory:
(The --cached flag is critical here—it deletes the files from Gitea but leaves them safely on your Production hard drive).

Bash
cd /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/
git rm -r --cached app/AI_venv/
git rm -r --cached app/venv/
(If it says app/venv/ did not match any files, that is fine, it just means only AI_venv was accidentally tracked).

2. Update .gitignore so this never happens again:

Bash
nano .gitignore
Make sure these exact lines are in that file:

Plaintext
app/AI_venv/
app/venv/
app/Tool_VM_Output/
Save and exit.

3. Push the fix to Gitea:

Bash
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Removed heavy virtual environments from Git tracking"
git push origin master
Your Gitea repository is now clean and lightweight again!

Phase 2: Sync the Backup VM (Do this on .51)
Now log into your Backup VM (.51). Because Gitea no longer contains the conflicting AI_venv files, Git will allow us to safely download the code and create your test branch.

1. Fetch the newly cleaned map from Gitea:

Bash
cd /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/
git fetch origin
2. Force the Staging sync:
We will tell Git to forcefully create your test branch mirroring the new, clean master branch. Because AI_venv is no longer in Gitea, Git will completely ignore your local Python files and only update your code!

Bash
git checkout -f -B test origin/master
3. Push the new test branch to Gitea:
Now that your local test branch is created and clean, send it up to Gitea so the server officially tracks it.

Bash
git push -u origin test
Run git status on the Backup VM. You should now see a perfectly clean repository on the test branch, your 500 error will be gone, and your virtual environments are safe!

they are already in the .gitignore ?

This is an excellent observation, and it highlights one of the most frustrating "gotchas" in Git!

Even if app/AI_venv/ is written inside your .gitignore file right now, .gitignore only works on files that Git has never seen before. If a developer ever accidentally ran git add . before those folders were added to the .gitignore file (or if they used a command like git add -f to force it), Git permanently memorized those files. Once a file is in Git's memory, Git completely ignores the .gitignore rule for that specific file and will keep tracking every single change made to it forever.

This is why the fix still works:
That is exactly why Phase 1 of the rescue plan uses the git rm --cached command.

Running git rm -r --cached app/AI_venv/ does a very specific surgical strike:

It tells Git: "Erase this folder from your database/memory."

The --cached flag tells Linux: "Do NOT delete the actual physical files from the hard drive."

Once you wipe it from Git's memory, Git suddenly looks at the folder like it's brand new. It then checks your .gitignore file, sees the folder listed there, and says, "Ah, I'm not supposed to track this." So, jump onto your Production VM (.50) and run Phase 1 exactly as written:

Bash
cd /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/
git rm -r --cached app/AI_venv/
git rm -r --cached app/venv/
git commit -m "Removed heavy virtual environments from Git tracking"
git push origin master
This will instantly drop that 900+ MB of weight from your Gitea repository without breaking your live Python application! Let me know as soon as that push is complete.

This is a very common Git optical illusion, and it usually happens because of exactly what you just described: you shifted the folder structure.

By unarchiving the application into a nested folder (/app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/) instead of the root directory, you created a slight misalignment between where Git lives, where the files live, and where .gitignore is looking.

If a file is listed in .gitignore but still shows up as "Untracked" when you run git status, it means one of two things happened:

The .gitignore is in the wrong place: You might have created the .gitignore file one level up (in TAT_TestVenv/) but initialized Git one level down (in Transport_Toolbox/). Git only looks for the .gitignore file starting in the same folder where the hidden .git folder lives.

The Paths are Misaligned: If the .gitignore says app/AI_venv/, but because of the unarchiving, the real path is now Transport_Toolbox/app/AI_venv/, Git won't make the connection.

The Architecture Warning (CRITICAL)
Before we fix the Git issue, I need to point out a major trap: Because you added the Transport_Toolbox/ folder layer, Apache will break. Earlier, Apache and your wsgi.py file were configured to look directly inside /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/. Now, the code is buried one level deeper. We will need to update those paths later, but for now, let's secure Git.

The Fix: Rebuild and Secure the Repository
Run these exact commands to guarantee that Git recognizes the ignore rules in your new nested folder.

*.p7b
*.log

You should no longer see any .pem, .key, or venv folders in the untracked list. If those are gone, your SSL keys and massive Python environments are officially safe from being tracked.
