<script>

// THEME

function toggleTheme() {

    const html = document.documentElement;

    const next = html.dataset.theme === "dark" ? "light" : "dark";

    html.dataset.theme = next;

    localStorage.setItem("theme", next);

}

document.documentElement.dataset.theme = localStorage.getItem("theme") || "dark";



// SIDEBAR

const links = document.querySelectorAll(".nav-link");

const frame = document.getElementById("dashboard-frame");

links.forEach(link => {

  link.addEventListener("click", () => {

    links.forEach(l => l.classList.remove("active"));

    link.classList.add("active");

    frame.src = link.dataset.url;

  });

});





// USER MENU



function toggleUserMenu() {

  const menu = document.getElementById("userMenu");

  menu.classList.toggle("show");

  function toggleUserMenu() {

  document.getElementById("notifMenu")?.classList.remove("show"); // close notif

  const menu = document.getElementById("userMenu");

  menu.classList.toggle("show");

}



}





document.addEventListener("click", function (e) {

  const avatarDropdown = document.querySelector(".user-dropdown:not(#notifDropdown)");

  const menu = document.getElementById("userMenu");



  if (avatarDropdown && !avatarDropdown.contains(e.target)) {

    menu.classList.remove("show");

  }

});







function filterContent() {

  const input = document.getElementById('globalSearch');

  const filter = input.value.toLowerCase();

  const frame = document.getElementById('dashboard-frame');

 

  // 1. Filter Parent Page (Sidebar/Topbar)

  // We filter sidebar links specifically

  const sidebarLinks = document.querySelectorAll('.nav-link span');

  sidebarLinks.forEach(span => {

    const parent = span.closest('.nav-link');

    if (span.innerText.toLowerCase().includes(filter)) {

      parent.style.display = "";

    } else {

      parent.style.display = "none";

    }

  });



  // 2. Filter Iframe Content

  try {

    const innerDoc = frame.contentDocument || frame.contentWindow.document;

   

    // Define what elements you want to search through (cards, table rows, paragraphs)

    // Adjust these selectors based on what's inside your sub-pages

    const searchableElements = innerDoc.querySelectorAll('tr, .card, p, h1, h2, h3, li');



    searchableElements.forEach(el => {

      const text = el.textContent || el.innerText;

      if (text.toLowerCase().includes(filter)) {

        el.style.display = ""; // Show

      } else {

        el.style.display = "none"; // Hide

      }

    });

  } catch (e) {

    console.warn("Could not access iframe content. Check if it's on a different domain.", e);

  }

}



// Reset search when switching tabs

const navLinks = document.querySelectorAll(".nav-link");

navLinks.forEach(link => {

  link.addEventListener("click", () => {

    document.getElementById('globalSearch').value = "";

    // Re-run filter to show all elements in the new page

    setTimeout(filterContent, 500);

  });

});

</script>

   <script>

function toggleNotifMenu(evt) {

  if (evt) evt.stopPropagation();

  const menu = document.getElementById("notifMenu");

  menu.classList.toggle("show");

  if (menu.classList.contains("show")) {

    loadNotifications();

  }

  document.getElementById("userMenu")?.classList.remove("show"); // close user menu



}





// close when clicking outside

document.addEventListener("click", function (e) {

  const dropdown = document.getElementById("notifDropdown");

  const menu = document.getElementById("notifMenu");

  if (dropdown && !dropdown.contains(e.target)) {

    menu.classList.remove("show");

  }

});



async function loadUnreadCount() {

  try {

    const res = await fetch("/notifications/unread_count", { credentials: "same-origin" });

    const data = await res.json();

    const badge = document.getElementById("notifCount");

    if (data.ok && data.unread > 0) {

      badge.textContent = data.unread;

      badge.style.display = "inline-block";

    } else {

      badge.style.display = "none";

    }

  } catch (e) {

    console.warn("Unread count failed", e);

  }

}



async function loadNotifications() {

  try {

    const res = await fetch("/notifications/feed?limit=20", { credentials: "same-origin" });

    const data = await res.json();

    const list = document.getElementById("notifList");

    list.innerHTML = "";



    if (!data.ok || !data.items || data.items.length === 0) {

      list.innerHTML = '<div style="opacity:.7;">No notifications</div>';

      return;

    }



    data.items.forEach(item => {

      const row = document.createElement("div");

      row.style.padding = "8px 0";

      row.style.borderBottom = "1px solid rgba(0,0,0,0.08)";

      row.style.cursor = "pointer";

      row.style.fontWeight = item.is_read ? "normal" : "bold";

      row.style.backgroundColor = item.is_read ? "transparent" : "var(--bg-main)";



      row.innerHTML = `

        <div>${escapeHtml(item.title || "")}</div>

        <div style="font-size:0.85rem; opacity:.8;">${escapeHtml(item.body || "")}</div>

      `;



      row.onclick = async () => {

        await markNotificationRead(item.id);



        // Redirect user to the page that corresponds to the notification

        // Use iframe navigation (keeps your shell UI)

        if (item.url) {

          const frame = document.getElementById("dashboard-frame");

          frame.src = item.url ;   // <-- this is the redirect

        }



        document.getElementById("notifMenu").classList.remove("show");

      };



      list.appendChild(row);

    });



  } catch (e) {

    console.error("Feed failed", e);

  }

}



async function markNotificationRead(id) {

  try {

    await fetch("/notifications/mark_read", {

      method: "POST",

      headers: {"Content-Type":"application/json"},

      credentials: "same-origin",

      body: JSON.stringify({notification_id: id})

    });

    loadUnreadCount();

  } catch (e) {

    console.warn("Mark read failed", e);

  }

}



// tiny escape to avoid HTML injection in dropdown

function escapeHtml(s) {

  return String(s)

    .replaceAll("&","&amp;")

    .replaceAll("<","&lt;")

    .replaceAll(">","&gt;")

    .replaceAll('"',"&quot;")

    .replaceAll("'","&#039;");

}



// initial + polling

loadUnreadCount();

setInterval(loadUnreadCount, 60000);

</script>



</body>

</html>

Here is the fully assembled, ready-to-work Main_Web.html.

I made two critical adjustments to your code to ensure it interacts perfectly with the ssl.conf routing we verified:

The Logic Check: I updated the {% if %} statements at the top banner and in the user menu to include request.cookies.get('AppEnv') == 'test'. Because your Apache server uses a proxy, the hostname might still show as the production URL even when you are inside the test VM. Checking for the cookie guarantees the UI always knows exactly which environment you are trapped in.

Dropdown UI Scaling: I slightly scaled down the images in your dropdown menu from 4.5rem to 2.5rem and adjusted the font sizes. Dropdown menus have a limited width, and xx-large fonts with huge images would physically break the menu box and push elements off the screen. This keeps your custom images but ensures the menu remains clean and professional.

Copy and paste this directly into your templates/Main_Web.html:

function toggleTheme() {

}

// SIDEBAR

function toggleUserMenu() {

}


document.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
  const avatarDropdown = document.querySelector(".user-dropdown:not(#notifDropdown)");
  const menu = document.getElementById("userMenu");

  if (avatarDropdown && !avatarDropdown.contains(e.target)) {
    menu.classList.remove("show");
  }
});



function filterContent() {
  const input = document.getElementById('globalSearch');
  const filter = input.value.toLowerCase();
  const frame = document.getElementById('dashboard-frame');
  
  // 1. Filter Parent Page (Sidebar/Topbar)
  // We filter sidebar links specifically
  const sidebarLinks = document.querySelectorAll('.nav-link span');
  sidebarLinks.forEach(span => {
    const parent = span.closest('.nav-link');
    if (span.innerText.toLowerCase().includes(filter)) {
      parent.style.display = "";
    } else {
      parent.style.display = "none";
    }
  });

  // 2. Filter Iframe Content
  try {
    const innerDoc = frame.contentDocument || frame.contentWindow.document;
    
    // Define what elements you want to search through (cards, table rows, paragraphs)
    // Adjust these selectors based on what's inside your sub-pages
    const searchableElements = innerDoc.querySelectorAll('tr, .card, p, h1, h2, h3, li');

    searchableElements.forEach(el => {
      const text = el.textContent || el.innerText;
      if (text.toLowerCase().includes(filter)) {
        el.style.display = ""; // Show
      } else {
        el.style.display = "none"; // Hide
      }
    });
  } catch (e) {
    console.warn("Could not access iframe content. Check if it's on a different domain.", e);
  }
}

// Reset search when switching tabs
const navLinks = document.querySelectorAll(".nav-link");
navLinks.forEach(link => {
  link.addEventListener("click", () => {
    document.getElementById('globalSearch').value = "";
    // Re-run filter to show all elements in the new page
    setTimeout(filterContent, 500); 
  });
});
</script>

   <script>
function toggleNotifMenu(evt) {
  if (evt) evt.stopPropagation();
  const menu = document.getElementById("notifMenu");
  menu.classList.toggle("show");
  if (menu.classList.contains("show")) {
    loadNotifications();
  }
  document.getElementById("userMenu")?.classList.remove("show"); // close user menu

}


// close when clicking outside
document.addEventListener("click", function (e) {
  const dropdown = document.getElementById("notifDropdown");
  const menu = document.getElementById("notifMenu");
  if (dropdown && !dropdown.contains(e.target)) {
    menu.classList.remove("show");
  }
});

async function loadUnreadCount() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch("/notifications/unread_count", { credentials: "same-origin" });
    const data = await res.json();
    const badge = document.getElementById("notifCount");
    if (data.ok && data.unread > 0) {
      badge.textContent = data.unread;
      badge.style.display = "inline-block";
    } else {
      badge.style.display = "none";
    }
  } catch (e) {
    console.warn("Unread count failed", e);
  }
}

async function loadNotifications() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch("/notifications/feed?limit=20", { credentials: "same-origin" });
    const data = await res.json();
    const list = document.getElementById("notifList");
    list.innerHTML = "";

    if (!data.ok || !data.items || data.items.length === 0) {
      list.innerHTML = '<div style="opacity:.7;">No notifications</div>';
      return;
    }

    data.items.forEach(item => {
      const row = document.createElement("div");
      row.style.padding = "8px 0";
      row.style.borderBottom = "1px solid rgba(0,0,0,0.08)";
      row.style.cursor = "pointer";
      row.style.fontWeight = item.is_read ? "normal" : "bold";
      row.style.backgroundColor = item.is_read ? "transparent" : "var(--bg-main)";

      row.innerHTML = `
        <div>${escapeHtml(item.title || "")}</div>
        <div style="font-size:0.85rem; opacity:.8;">${escapeHtml(item.body || "")}</div>
      `;

      row.onclick = async () => {
        await markNotificationRead(item.id);

        // Redirect user to the page that corresponds to the notification
        // Use iframe navigation (keeps your shell UI)
        if (item.url) {
          const frame = document.getElementById("dashboard-frame");
          frame.src = item.url ;   // <-- this is the redirect
        }

        document.getElementById("notifMenu").classList.remove("show");
      };

      list.appendChild(row);
    });

  } catch (e) {
    console.error("Feed failed", e);
  }
}

async function markNotificationRead(id) {
  try {
    await fetch("/notifications/mark_read", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {"Content-Type":"application/json"},
      credentials: "same-origin",
      body: JSON.stringify({notification_id: id})
    });
    loadUnreadCount();
  } catch (e) {
    console.warn("Mark read failed", e);
  }
}

// tiny escape to avoid HTML injection in dropdown
function escapeHtml(s) {
  return String(s)
    .replaceAll("&","&amp;")
    .replaceAll("<","&lt;")
    .replaceAll(">","&gt;")
    .replaceAll('"',"&quot;")
    .replaceAll("'","&#039;");
}

// initial + polling
loadUnreadCount();
setInterval(loadUnreadCount, 60000);
</script>

</body>

how can I make a certain branch the default origin and again what is the difference between remote origin and upstream I want the difference before and after applying the settings ?

Let’s break down exactly what happens under the hood. The terminology in Git can be confusing because "origin," "upstream," and "default" are often used interchangeably, even though they mean very different things to the Linux server.

Here is the exact difference between them, the "Before and After" of applying the settings, and how to lock in your defaults.

1. Remote Origin vs. Upstream
To understand the difference, think of the Gitea server as an apartment building, and the branches as individual apartments.

Remote origin (The Building): origin is just a shortcut word for your server's URL (git@transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com:TAT/Transport_Toolbox.git). It tells your local Git where the building is located. It does not specify a branch.

upstream (The Apartment Number): The upstream is the specific branch on that server that your local branch is permanently wired to (e.g., origin/test). It tells your local Git exactly which door to knock on.

The "Before" State (Untracked / No Upstream)
Before you configure an upstream, your local branch is completely disconnected from the server's branch.

What Git knows: It knows the server exists (origin), but it has no idea where your local code is supposed to go.

The Command: You are forced to be hyper-specific every single time. You must tell Git both the building and the apartment:
git pull origin test
git push origin test

The Danger: If you just type git pull, Git throws a fatal error because it is blind. It says, "There is no tracking information for the current branch."

The "After" State (Tracked / Upstream Set)
Once you set the upstream, you build a permanent, hardcoded bridge between your local branch and the remote branch.

What Git knows: Your local test branch is officially married to origin/test.

The Command: You no longer need to specify locations. You just type:
git pull
git push

The Benefit: Git looks at the bridge, sees it points to origin/test, and does the work automatically. Human error is eliminated. You cannot accidentally push to the wrong branch because the route is hardcoded.

2. How to Make a Branch the "Default"
When you say "default," there are two different places this applies: the Local Server and the Gitea UI.

A. Making it the Default Locally (Setting the Upstream)
If you want to wire a local branch to an upstream so you never have to type origin branch-name again, you run one of these commands from the terminal:

If you are pushing a branch for the very first time:
Add the -u (upstream) flag. This pushes the code and builds the permanent bridge at the same time.
git push -u origin test

If the branch already exists on both sides but they aren't connected:
Tell your local branch to track the remote one.
git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/test test

B. Making it the Default on the Gitea Server (The "Origin" Default)
When someone clones a repository without specifying a branch (e.g., git clone <URL>), Git automatically downloads whatever the server considers the "Default Branch." Usually, this is master or main.

If you want to change this so that test is the absolute default for the entire project:

Open your repository in the Gitea Web UI.

Go to Settings -> Branches.

Under "Default Branch," select test from the dropdown and click Update.

Now, if a new SPOC runs a standard git clone, they will be automatically placed on the test branch, keeping them safely away from production code.

Are you looking to lock down the local tracking on one of the specific VMs right now, or did you want to change the global default branch in the Gitea UI?

what if set the upstream to test branch and I was on a feature branch and typed git pull will it update the test branch



And Also elaborate on the Case of changing the default without cloning is setting the upstream with -u or git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/test test makes it default ?

These are excellent questions because they hit exactly on the mechanics of how Git handles data flow. Let's break down exactly what happens in both of these scenarios.

Scenario 1: The Cross-Branch Pull
The Setup: Your local branch is feature-branch, but you configured its upstream to track origin/test. You type git pull.

What actually happens:

Git Fetches: Git reaches out to Gitea and downloads the latest changes from the remote test branch.

Git Merges: Git takes those downloaded changes and merges them directly into the branch you are currently sitting in (feature-branch).

Will it update your local test branch?
No. Your local test branch remains completely untouched.

git pull only ever modifies the branch you are actively "checked out" on. In this scenario, Git essentially says: "You told me to always look at origin/test for updates to this branch. I found updates, so I'm bringing them into feature-branch."

This is a very common way developers keep their personal feature branches up-to-date with the main staging area. However, it highlights exactly why we locked down your .51 VM at the OS level: by forcing the server to only know about the test branch, we made it physically impossible for someone to accidentally check out a feature branch and pull the wrong code into the live web directory.

Scenario 2: The "Default" Confusion
Git is notorious for reusing words in confusing ways. Let's clarify exactly what git branch --set-upstream-to does versus the "Default Branch."

There are two completely different types of "defaults" in Git:

1. The Branch-Level Default (The Upstream)
When you run git push -u origin test or git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/test test, you are setting a local default.

What it does: It tells your specific local test branch, "Your default partner on the server is origin/test."

What it does NOT do: It does not change the global settings of the repository. It does not affect master or any other branch. It is a private contract between one local branch and one remote branch.

2. The Repository-Level Default (The Global HEAD)
This is what Gitea handles in its web interface (Settings -> Branches -> Default Branch).

What it does: It defines the primary branch for the entire project. When a new engineer joins the team and runs a raw git clone command without specifying a branch, Git asks the server, "What is the main branch here?" The server responds with the Global Default (usually master or main), and that is what gets downloaded. It is also the branch that displays automatically when you open the repository in your browser.

To answer your question directly: Using -u or --set-upstream-to does not change the global default of the repository. It only changes the local push/pull behavior for the branch you are currently working on.

If you want to change the global default so that new clones always land on test, you must do that in the Gitea UI. If you just want your local VM to seamlessly pull updates without typing out the remote name every time, the upstream commands are exactly what you need.

how to make sure through settings in gitea that only SPOCS and owners team can merge branches

This is the perfect final layer of security to add. While the CI/CD workflows and Git Hooks we built act as automated traffic cops, Gitea's native Branch Protection is what physically revokes the permission to click the "Merge" button for unauthorized users.

By configuring this, you ensure that even if a Pull Request perfectly passes all pipeline checks, a standard developer cannot merge it into your critical branches (master or test).

Here is exactly how to lock down the merge rights in Gitea:

Step 1: Access Branch Protection
Open your repository in the Gitea web interface.

Navigate to Settings -> Branches.

Look for the Branch Protection section.

If your target branch (e.g., master or test) is already listed, click Edit. If it is not, type the branch name into the "Protected branch name pattern" box and click Add Rule.

Step 2: Configure the Merge Whitelist
Once you are inside the protection settings for that specific branch, scroll down until you see the section governing Pull Requests.

Locate the option titled Enable merge whitelisting and check the box.

Two new fields will appear:

Whitelist users: (You can leave this blank if you are managing via teams).

Whitelist teams: Click this dropdown and select your Owners team and your SPOCS team.

Scroll to the bottom and click Save.

How this works in practice:
Once saved, the rules apply instantly.

If a user who is not in the SPOCS or Owners team opens a Pull Request and tries to merge it, the green "Merge Pull Request" button will be completely disabled (grayed out) for them.

They will see a message indicating that they do not have the required permissions to merge into this branch.

Only the users inside the teams you explicitly whitelisted will have an active, clickable merge button.

If you are applying this strictly to your master branch to keep production pristine, you would likely only whitelist the "Owners" (or your Admin team). If applying it to the test branch, whitelisting both Owners and SPOCs makes sense so your developers can push code to the staging server autonomously.

Okay perfect now there is a other milestone or project we need to do currently when there was an Admin they used to update a release note for each merge with the version I want to automate that within gitea refering to the branch names how can I migrate the release history we already have and continue on it

This is an excellent next milestone. Automating documentation is one of the highest-value things you can do in infrastructure engineering, especially since you already did the hard work of enforcing a strict branch naming convention (newtool/, bugfix/, update/). We can map those exact prefixes to automatically categorize the release notes.

Here is the blueprint for how we handle the historical data and build the automation engine moving forward.

Phase 1: The Migration (The Manual Cutover)
Before we turn on the automation, we need to deal with the existing history. For migrations like this, it is always safest to do a controlled, manual cutover rather than trying to script a parser to guess the formatting of old admin notes.

Create the Foundation File: In the root of your repository, create a clean Markdown file named RELEASE_NOTES.md. (Because this is Markdown, it will integrate perfectly if you decide to serve these notes through a custom internal documentation parser later).

Port the History: Manually copy the old release notes into this file, one by one. Format them consistently.

The Standardized Format: Use a structure that is easy for a machine to read and write. For example:

Markdown
## [v1.2.0] - 2026-04-10
### 🚀 New Tool
- Added the Leave Balance dashboard.

## [v1.1.5] - 2026-03-25
### 🐛 Bug Fix
- Resolved routing issue in proxy configuration.
Push to Master: Commit this foundational file into your master branch so the automation has a physical file to target.

Phase 2: The Automation Engine
We are going to use a Gitea Actions workflow. Instead of triggering on a standard push, this workflow will listen specifically for Pull Requests being closed and merged.

When a PR merges into master, the runner will wake up, look at the name of the branch that just merged, categorize it, append the note to RELEASE_NOTES.md, and silently commit the file back to the repository.

Here is the exact YAML script to drop into .gitea/workflows/auto-release-notes.yaml:

YAML
name: Automated Release Notes
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [closed]
    branches: [master]

jobs:
  update-notes:
    # ONLY run if the PR was actually merged (not just closed/rejected)
    if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true
    runs-on: rhel
    steps:
      - name: Phase 1 Checkout Code
        run: |
          # Clone the repo and checkout master
          git -c http.sslVerify=false clone https://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/${{ github.repository }}.git workspace
          cd workspace
          git checkout master

      - name: Phase 2 Generate and Commit Note
        run: |
          cd workspace
          
          # Extract data from the Gitea webhook event
          BRANCH_NAME="${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}"
          PR_TITLE="${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
          AUTHOR="${{ github.event.pull_request.user.login }}"
          DATE=$(date +'%Y-%m-%d')
          
          # Map your Git Hooks to visual categories
          if [[ "$BRANCH_NAME" == newtool/* ]]; then
            CATEGORY="🚀 New Tool"
          elif [[ "$BRANCH_NAME" == bugfix/* ]]; then
            CATEGORY="🐛 Bug Fix"
          elif [[ "$BRANCH_NAME" == update/* ]]; then
            CATEGORY="🔄 Update"
          else
            CATEGORY="🔧 Maintenance"
          fi
          
          # Format the new entry
          NEW_ENTRY="## [$DATE] - Auto-Merge\n### $CATEGORY\n- **Feature:** $PR_TITLE\n- **Branch:** \`$BRANCH_NAME\`\n- **Merged by:** $AUTHOR\n\n"
          
          # Prepend the new entry to the top of the file (below a main header if you have one)
          # This creates a temporary file, adds the new note, then appends the old history
          echo -e "$NEW_ENTRY" > temp_notes.md
          cat RELEASE_NOTES.md >> temp_notes.md
          mv temp_notes.md RELEASE_NOTES.md
          
          # Configure Git to act as the Automation Bot
          git config user.name "TAT Automation Bot"
          git config user.email "automation@tat.internal"
          
          # Commit and push directly back to master
          git add RELEASE_NOTES.md
          git commit -m "docs: auto-update release notes for $BRANCH_NAME"
          git -c http.sslVerify=false push origin master
The Architecture Catch (Branch Protection)
There is one critical infrastructure detail here: We just talked about locking down the master branch so only Owners and SPOCs can merge code.

Because this bot is pushing a commit directly to master, Gitea's Branch Protection rules might block it, thinking it is an unauthorized user. You will need to ensure that the user associated with the github.token (usually a built-in Gitea Actions service account) is either whitelisted to bypass branch protection, or you whitelist the specific file (RELEASE_NOTES.md) in your branch protection settings so the bot can write to it freely.

Are you handling standard version numbers (like v2.1, v2.2) right now, or do you want the bot to just use the calendar date as the version identifier for now?

Okay first of all I want the releases to added when we only merge to master but we merge the test branch to master branch every week so there are multiple updates that happens maybe there 6 different branch are merged and they are updates and newtools and bugfixes

This is a brilliant catch, and it highlights exactly why you are building the architecture the way you are.

If we used the standard script I provided earlier, and an Admin merged test into master on a Friday, the bot would look at the branch name, see "test," and just write: Maintenance - Merged test. You would lose all the visibility of the 6 tools, updates, and bug fixes your team built that week!

Because you strictly enforced your branch naming rules (newtool/, bugfix/, update/) at the OS level earlier, we can use a "Batch Parser." When test merges into master, the script will look backwards in time, scan the merge history, hunt down those specific prefixes, and automatically generate a beautiful, categorized weekly summary.

Here is the exact YAML to implement this.

The Batch-Release Workflow
Create or update your .gitea/workflows/auto-release-notes.yaml with this code:

YAML
name: Automated Release Notes
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [closed]
    branches: [master]

jobs:
  update-notes:
    if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true
    runs-on: rhel
    steps:
      - name: Checkout Code
        run: |
          # Full clone to ensure we have the Git history
          git -c http.sslVerify=false clone https://gitea-actions:${{ github.token }}@transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/gitea/${{ github.repository }}.git workspace
          cd workspace
          git checkout master

      - name: Generate Weekly Batch Note
        run: |
          cd workspace
          
          BRANCH_NAME="${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}"
          DATE=$(date +'%Y-%m-%d')
          
          # Use "CalVer" (Calendar Versioning) for weekly batch releases (e.g., v2026.15)
          VERSION="v$(date +'%Y.%W')" 
          
          # Initialize the Release Block
          RELEASE_BLOCK="## [$VERSION] - $DATE\n"
          
          # ==========================================
          # SCENARIO A: The Weekly Sync (Test -> Master)
          # ==========================================
          if [[ "$BRANCH_NAME" == "test" ]]; then
              echo "Processing Batch Merge from Staging..."
              
              # Git Time Machine: Look at all commits added since the last master update
              # HEAD^1 is old master. HEAD^2 is the test branch we just merged.
              MERGE_LOGS=$(git log HEAD^1..HEAD^2 --merges --oneline)
              
              # Hunt for our strict Git Hook prefixes using Regex
              NEW_TOOLS=$(echo "$MERGE_LOGS" | grep -oE 'newtool/[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+' | sed 's/newtool\//- /' | sort -u || true)
              UPDATES=$(echo "$MERGE_LOGS" | grep -oE 'update/[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+' | sed 's/update\//- /' | sort -u || true)
              BUG_FIXES=$(echo "$MERGE_LOGS" | grep -oE 'bugfix/[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+' | sed 's/bugfix\//- /' | sort -u || true)
              
              # Build the specific categories if they exist
              if [ ! -z "$NEW_TOOLS" ]; then RELEASE_BLOCK+="### 🚀 New Tools\n$NEW_TOOLS\n\n"; fi
              if [ ! -z "$UPDATES" ]; then RELEASE_BLOCK+="### 🔄 Updates\n$UPDATES\n\n"; fi
              if [ ! -z "$BUG_FIXES" ]; then RELEASE_BLOCK+="### 🐛 Bug Fixes\n$BUG_FIXES\n\n"; fi
          
          # ==========================================
          # SCENARIO B: Admin Emergency Hotfix (Direct to Master)
          # ==========================================
          else
              echo "Processing Single Hotfix Merge..."
              FEATURE_TITLE=$(echo "$BRANCH_NAME" | awk -F'/' '{print $2}')
              
              if [[ "$BRANCH_NAME" == bugfix/* ]]; then
                  RELEASE_BLOCK+="### 🚨 Emergency Hotfix\n- $FEATURE_TITLE\n\n"
              else
                  RELEASE_BLOCK+="### 🔧 Maintenance\n- Admin forced merge of $BRANCH_NAME\n\n"
              fi
          fi
          
          # Print to logs for debugging
          echo -e "$RELEASE_BLOCK"
          
          # Prepend to the top of the Markdown file
          echo -e "$RELEASE_BLOCK" > temp_notes.md
          
          # If the file exists, append the history. If not, this is the first release.
          if [ -f "RELEASE_NOTES.md" ]; then
              cat RELEASE_NOTES.md >> temp_notes.md
          fi
          mv temp_notes.md RELEASE_NOTES.md
          
          # Commit the changes as the Bot
          git config user.name "TAT Automation Bot"
          git config user.email "automation@tat.internal"
          git add RELEASE_NOTES.md
          git commit -m "docs: auto-update release notes for $VERSION"
          git -c http.sslVerify=false push origin master
How This Works Under the Hood
The Time Machine (HEAD^1..HEAD^2): When you click merge on Friday, Git creates a merge commit. HEAD^1 is what production looked like on Thursday. HEAD^2 is what the test branch looks like right now. By running a log between those two, the bot isolates only the new code introduced this week.

The Prefix Hunt: Because we built that pre-receive Git Hook earlier that blocks bad branch names, we can trust the log 100%. The grep -oE command scans the log, finds your prefixes, strips away the prefix (changing newtool/leave-balance into - leave-balance), and sorts them alphabetically under the correct headers.

The Hotfix Bypass: Admins occasionally have to push a bugfix/ directly to master to fix a critical crash. The script has an else statement to handle single-branch merges gracefully without running the batch processor.

This completely eliminates the manual admin task of tracking what was built during the week. The bot handles it instantly upon merge.

In the script above, I used a Calendar Versioning system (v2026.15 for the 15th week of 2026) to handle the weekly batch labeling. Do you prefer this automated calendar approach, or would you rather have the script extract a hardcoded version number (like v3.1.2) from a configuration file in your repository?

welll there is an issue so lets leave this feature for now, there is someone who is trying it to pull code but this error keeps getting in the way sometimes he can and sometimes the issue appears the thing is on linux level everything is set correctly

[AliM22@Transport-backup Transport_Toolbox]$ git pull



remote: Enumerating objects: 52, done.



remote: Counting objects: 100% (52/52), done.



remote: Compressing objects: 100% (36/36), done.



error: insufficient permission for adding an object to repository database .git/objects



fatal: failed to write object



fatal: unpack-objects failed

This is the classic "Tug of War" permission error, and it is incredibly common in CI/CD environments.

The reason it only happens sometimes is because AliM22 and your Baremetal Runner are fighting over ownership of the hidden .git folder.

When your automated runner pulls code (or when an Admin runs a command using sudo), the Linux operating system creates new files inside the .git/objects folder and assigns ownership of those files to the root user. Later, when AliM22 logs in via SSH as a standard user and types git pull, Git tries to unpack the new code but hits a brick wall because Linux blocks standard users from modifying root's files.

To permanently fix this, we need to tell Git that this repository is a shared workspace, and we need to set a special Linux permission called the SGID bit so that all future files inherit the correct group permissions, regardless of who runs the pull command.

Have an Admin (or AliM22 using sudo) run these exact commands inside the Transport_Toolbox directory on that server:

Step 1: Tell Git to Share
First, configure Git itself to handle group permissions automatically:

Bash
git config core.sharedRepository group
Step 2: Reset the Current Permissions
Next, forcibly grant the group read, write, and execute permissions recursively across the entire .git folder so AliM22 is no longer locked out of the existing files:

Bash
sudo chmod -R g+rwX .git
Step 3: The Permanent Fix (Set the SGID Bit)
Finally, run this find command. It looks for every directory inside the .git folder and applies the +s (Set Group ID) bit. This is the magic bullet: it guarantees that any new file created in this folder (whether by AliM22, you, or the automated runner) will automatically inherit the directory's group ownership rather than defaulting to root.

Bash
sudo find .git -type d -exec chmod g+s {} +

15 (Behind): The default branch has 15 new commits that your branch does not have. This means since the time you created this branch, other updates or pull requests have been merged into the default branch by your team (like AliM22 or V24RNafea).

The Gray Bar: This is just a visual representation of the ratio. The line in the middle separates the "Ahead" proportion from the "Behind" proportion.

The "Gotcha" with the Automation
If this is exactly how you want your engineers to operate, it is a fantastic architecture. However, we need to address one small ripple this causes with the Automated Release Notes script we discussed earlier.

If you shift to this new workflow—where a developer rebases their specific newtool/leave-balance branch onto master and opens a PR directly to master—the Weekly Batch script won't work as originally designed, because the test branch itself is no longer the vehicle delivering the code to production.

Instead of one massive "Weekly Sync" merge from test, your master branch will receive multiple individual PRs throughout the week (one for each feature).

How do you want to handle the Documentation?
Since the workflow is shifting to direct-to-master PRs for finished features, how would you like the Release Notes bot to behave?

Option A: The Instant Logger (Recommended for this workflow)
Every time a feature branch (e.g., newtool/...) is merged directly into master, the bot immediately wakes up, categorizes that single PR, and adds a new bullet point to the RELEASE_NOTES.md file right then and there.

Option B: The Weekly Cron Job

You hit the nail on the head regarding "hitch-hiker commits." When you merge a massive shared staging branch, you inevitably drag along half-finished experiments and broken code that someone forgot to clean up. Shifting to direct, rebased feature PRs is exactly how high-performing platform engineering teams keep their production environments bulletproof.

Since you are on the fence about how to handle the automated documentation for this new workflow, let’s look at how both options actually feel in day-to-day operations. When building internal automation tools that SPOCs and other engineers rely on, the right choice usually comes down to how your team prefers to communicate.

Here is the breakdown of how they compare in a real-world scenario:

Option A: The Real-Time Ledger (Instant Update)
In this model, the bot acts like a live ticker tape. The second AliM22 merges a bugfix/ PR, or you merge the newtool/leave-balance, the bot instantly appends it to RELEASE_NOTES.md.

The Big Pro: Ultimate Traceability. If a user reports that a dashboard broke on Wednesday at 2:00 PM, you can look at the release notes and instantly see that a PR was merged at 1:45 PM. You have a perfect, real-time audit trail.

The Drawback: Noise. If your team merges 10 tiny bug fixes in two days, your release notes will get very long, very fast. It reads more like a system log than a clean update announcement.

Option B: The Executive Summary (Weekly Cron Job)
In this model, the bot stays completely silent Monday through Thursday. On Friday at 5:00 PM, it wakes up, scans all the PRs merged into master over the last 7 days, categorizes them neatly (New Tools, Updates, Bug Fixes), and creates one clean entry for the week.

The Big Pro: Professional Polish. It generates a beautifully formatted, single version release (like v2026.16) that is incredibly easy to read. It's perfect if you send weekly summary emails to management or stakeholders about what the automation team accomplished.

The Drawback: The Blind Spot. If a tool is deployed on Tuesday, there is no official documentation of it in the repository until Friday. If an incident happens mid-week, the release notes won't help you troubleshoot.

The Recommendation
Given that you are managing critical internal infrastructure, Option A (The Real-Time Ledger) is usually the safest bet. When maintaining scripts and routing logic, having an immediate, visible record of exactly what was just injected into production is invaluable for quick rollbacks. You can always use the Antigravity IDE or another tool to parse that raw markdown file later if you need to generate a clean weekly report for management.

There is a new issue arised the restarting of the httpd service takes too long around a minute after all the modification we did how to solve this issue

A one-minute delay on a web server restart is a classic infrastructure bottleneck, and it usually means your pipeline is bleeding time unnecessarily.

Because of the specific architecture you are running—specifically the Python/Flask application and the poll-based notification system—I know exactly what is causing this 60-second hang.

It is called the Graceful Shutdown Trap.

Why it takes exactly a minute
When your automated runner types systemctl restart httpd, Apache doesn't just instantly die. It tries to be polite. It stops accepting new connections and waits for all existing connections to finish downloading.

Because your users' browsers are constantly polling the server in the background for new notifications, Apache sees those as "active" connections. It politely waits for them to close. The default Linux timeout for this polite waiting period is often exactly 60 seconds. Once the timer hits 60, Linux finally loses patience and kills the process forcefully.

Here are the three ways to solve this, ranked from the easiest to the most robust.

Solution 1: The "Reload" Bypass (Best for CI/CD)
You actually do not need to restart Apache to apply new code or routing rules. Restarting tears down the entire master process. Reloading just asks the master process to instantly read the new configuration and spin up new workers, without dropping existing connections.

Change your Baremetal Runner's pipeline script to use this instead:

Bash
sudo systemctl reload httpd
Result: The deployment should drop from 60 seconds to less than 1 second.

Solution 2: The Flask WSGI Trick (Zero-Downtime)
Since you are running a Python/Flask application, Apache is likely using mod_wsgi to serve it. mod_wsgi has a built-in feature specifically designed to prevent you from having to restart Apache at all when deploying new code.

If you simply update the "modified time" of your .wsgi file, the daemon will instantly recycle your Python application on the very next HTTP request.

Add this single line to your CI/CD runner script (adjusting the path to wherever your .wsgi file lives):

Bash
touch /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/app.wsgi
Result: You don't even need to touch the httpd service. The Python app refreshes instantly.

Solution 3: Force the Timeout (The Brutal Fix)
If you absolutely must perform a full hard restart of Apache and want to strip away its polite waiting period, you can change the global timeout setting.

Open your main Apache configuration file (usually /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf):

Bash
sudo nano /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf
Add this directive anywhere in the main server config:

Apache
GracefulShutdownTimeout 3
Result: When you run a restart, Apache will only wait 3 seconds for those notification pollers to hang up before aggressively shutting down and coming right back online.

Recommendation: Try Solution 1 (reload instead of restart) in your Gitea Action script first. It is the cleanest approach and ensures your SPOCs don't get an error page if they happen to click a link at the exact second the runner finishes deploying code.

so reload don't kill the old workers that is already serving users, and what is a worker ?

You hit the nail on the head. That is exactly the magic of a "reload" (which Apache calls a Graceful Restart).

To understand exactly why this bypasses your 60-second hang without breaking the application, we have to look at how Apache manages its workforce under the hood.

1. What is a "Worker"?
Think of the main Apache service (httpd) as a restaurant manager. This manager is called the Master Process.

The Master Process does not actually serve web pages to your users. Its only job is to read your ssl.conf files, bind to port 443, and hire "waiters."

Those waiters are the Workers.
A worker is a child process (or a thread) spawned by the Master. When a SPOC clicks on the TAT Dashboard, that incoming HTTP request is handed to exactly one Worker. That Worker executes the transaction: it talks to your Python/Flask application, grabs the database data, sends the HTML back to the user's browser, and then stands by for the next request.

2. The "Restart" vs. "Reload" Mechanics
In your poll-based notification system, users' browsers are constantly keeping Workers busy in the background, holding open connections to ask, "Are there any new unread messages?"

Here is how the two commands handle those busy Workers:

The Brutal Way: systemctl restart httpd

The Master Process immediately shuts down.

It violently kills every single Worker, regardless of what they are doing.

Any user who was mid-click or whose background notification was mid-poll gets a "Connection Reset" or "Bad Gateway" error.

The system waits 60 seconds trying to clean up the mess before the Master is allowed to start back up.

The Elegant Way: systemctl reload httpd

The Master Process stays alive. It instantly re-reads your configuration and the new code pulled by the Baremetal Runner.

The Master looks at all the Workers and issues a "Graceful" signal.

If a Worker is idle, it is immediately retired and replaced with a new Worker running the updated code.

If a Worker is currently busy holding open a notification poll, the Master says: "Finish your current transaction, send the data to the user, and then immediately clock out."

At the exact same time, the Master is spinning up brand new Workers to handle any new incoming clicks.

The Result
The 60-second delay completely vanishes for your CI/CD pipeline because the reload command finishes instantly. The Master process just issues the new orders and returns control to your runner. Meanwhile, in the background, the old workers slowly fade out as they finish their tasks, and the new workers seamlessly take over, resulting in zero downtime for the users.

Would you like to check your Apache MPM (Multi-Processing Module) settings to see exactly how many concurrent workers your .50 VM is actually configured to allow at maximum capacity?

so every user using the DNS name is a thread or a worked under the master apache process ?

You are incredibly close, but we need to tweak the mental model just a little bit. You are mixing up the "Phonebook" with the "Restaurant."

Here is the exact relationship between the user, the DNS name, and the Apache workers.

1. The DNS Name (The Phonebook)
The DNS name (transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com) has absolutely nothing to do with Apache or the workers.
It is simply the phonebook. When a user types that name into their browser, the browser asks the network, "What is the IP address for this name?" The network replies, "10.30.121.50." Once the browser gets that IP address, the DNS's job is completely finished.

2. The User vs. The Worker (The Connection)
A user is not a worker. Instead, every active HTTP request a user makes is handed to a worker.

Let's go back to the restaurant analogy:

The User is the Customer.

The Master Process is the Restaurant Manager.

The Worker (or Thread) is the Waiter.

The HTTP Request is the Customer asking for something.

When AliM22 opens his browser and goes to your TAT Dashboard, he is not assigned one permanent worker. Instead, his browser fires off a burst of rapid requests:

"Give me the Main_Web.html." (Manager assigns Waiter #1. Waiter #1 delivers the HTML and goes back to the breakroom).

"Give me the TAT_Logo.png." (Manager assigns Waiter #2. Waiter #2 delivers the image and goes back to the breakroom).

"Are there any new notifications in the database?" (Manager assigns Waiter #3. Waiter #3 asks Flask, gets a "0", delivers it, and goes back to the breakroom).

Why your specific app changes the rules
In a standard, static website, a user grabs the page, the workers deliver it, and then the server goes completely silent. The workers are totally free.

But you built a dynamic, poll-based Javascript application. In your Main_Web.html, you have this exact line of code:
setInterval(loadUnreadCount, 60000);

Because of that code, every single user who has the TAT dashboard open in a browser tab is automatically pinging the server every 60 seconds.
So, if you have 50 SPOCs with the tab open in the background, your Apache Master Process is constantly dispatching 50 workers every single minute to ask your Python script, "Any new notifications?" ### The "Thread vs. Worker" Technicality
You asked if it was a thread or a worker. In Apache, this depends on which MPM (Multi-Processing Module) is running:

Prefork MPM: Every "Worker" is an entirely separate, heavy Linux process. (Older, uses lots of RAM).

Worker / Event MPM: The Master spawns a few lightweight processes, and inside those processes are dozens of Threads. Each thread acts as the "waiter." (Modern, extremely fast, and handles thousands of concurrent requests easily).

So, to summarize your mental model: The user isn't the thread. The user's browser is constantly shouting requests, and your Apache Master assigns an idle thread to answer each shout. Does that clarify how the traffic actually flows from the user's browser down into your Python backend?

Now I have still have issue's with the hitch hicker commit ?

This is the absolute #1 pitfall when teams transition to the "Sandbox Philosophy."

If hitch-hiker commits are still sneaking into your master Pull Requests, it means the workflow is leaking. There are exactly two ways a hitch-hiker can infect a feature branch, and one Gitea setting you can use to automatically squash them.

Let’s diagnose exactly how they are getting in, how to rescue a branch that is currently infected, and how to stop it permanently.

How the Hitch-Hikers are Getting In (The Two Traps)
Trap 1: The Dirty Origin (Branching from Test)
When a developer is ready to build a new tool, they type git checkout -b newtool/my-tool.

The Error: If they are sitting on the test branch when they type that command, their new branch instantly inherits every single dirty experiment currently sitting in the test sandbox.

The Result: When they try to PR newtool/my-tool to master, Gitea sees all those sandbox experiments as "new code" and tries to merge them into production.

The Golden Rule: Always run git checkout master and git pull BEFORE creating a new branch.

Trap 2: The Reverse Infection (Merging Test into Feature)
A developer builds a clean feature. They push it to test to see if it works. It breaks. To fix it, the developer panics and types git merge test while inside their feature branch so they can debug locally.

The Error: They just pulled the entire dirty sandbox into their pristine feature branch.

The Result: The feature branch is permanently contaminated.

The Golden Rule: Code only flows ONE way. Feature branches go into test. Test NEVER goes into a feature branch.

The Emergency Rescue: How to Clean an Infected Branch Right Now
If you have a PR open right now that has 2 good commits and 15 hitch-hiker commits, you cannot just rebase it normally. You have to surgically extract your good code using Cherry-Picking.

Tell the developer who owns the infected branch to run these exact commands:

Go back to a clean slate (Master):
git checkout master
git pull

Create a brand new, clean rescue branch:
git checkout -b newtool/feature-rescue

Look at the Git history to find the IDs of the GOOD commits:
git log --oneline infected-branch-name
(Find the 7-character hashes of the commits that actually belong to the feature, like 38e3a66)

Surgically copy ONLY the good commits to the clean branch:
git cherry-pick <commit-hash-1> <commit-hash-2>

Push the clean rescue branch and open a new PR:
git push -u origin newtool/feature-rescue

You can then safely delete the infected branch. The hitch-hikers are gone.

The Permanent Fix: Enforce "Squash Merging" in Gitea
If the "hitch-hikers" you are talking about aren't code from other developers, but rather a messy history of a single developer's "wip", "fixed typo", "trying again" commits, you can force Gitea to clean this up automatically.

When a developer finishes a feature, you don't want 15 tiny commits hitting your master history. You want one clean commit that says: 🚀 New Tool: Finalized CM Feature.

How to lock this down in Gitea:

Go to your Repository Settings -> Branches.

Look at your Branch Protection rules for master.

Scroll down to the Merge Options section.

UNCHECK "Create a merge commit" (This is what allows hitch-hikers to survive).

CHECK "Enable Squash Merging" (and optionally make it the default).

What this does:
When you click the green "Merge" button on a PR, Gitea will take all 15 messy commits from that branch, crush them down into one single, clean commit, and apply that to master. The PR author gets to keep their messy local history while they work, but the production server only ever sees one perfect update block.

Are your hitch-hikers coming from other people's sandbox code (Trap 1/2), or is it just the messy "work-in-progress" history of the developers (The Squash Fix)?

/Okay explain the issue again and my default branch is test is that causing the issue

Yes, absolutely. Having test set as your default branch in Gitea is the exact root cause of the hitch-hiker problem! That is a massive "Aha!" moment for your architecture.

Let’s break down exactly why this happens using the "Sandbox" vs. "Clean Room" analogy, and why changing that one setting will fix your workflow instantly.

The Anatomy of the Hitch-Hiker (Why Default = Test breaks things)
Think of your branches as physical rooms:

master is the Clean Room. It only contains perfect, working code.

test is the Sandbox. It contains good code, but also half-finished experiments, broken scripts, and leftover debugging prints from every developer on the team.

When a developer types git checkout -b newtool/my-feature, Git acts like a shovel. It scoops up everything in the room the developer is currently standing in, and puts it into their new bucket (their branch).

Here is exactly how the hitch-hikers are getting in:

The Clone: Because test is your default branch in Gitea, when a developer runs git clone, Git automatically drops them straight into the Sandbox (test).

The Scoop: The developer wants to build a new tool. Without thinking, they type git checkout -b newtool/my-feature. Because they are standing in the Sandbox, Git scoops up all the messy, half-finished experiments sitting in test and puts them into the new branch.

The Infection: The developer writes their specific code. Their branch now contains: [Their Good Code] + [Everyone else's messy Sandbox code].

The PR: The developer finishes the tool and opens a Pull Request to master. Gitea compares the branch to master and says, "Wow, look at all this new code!" It tries to merge the new tool AND all the sandbox experiments (the hitch-hikers) into your production environment.

The Fix: Swap the Default Back to Master
To stop hitch-hikers permanently, developers must always scoop their new buckets from the Clean Room, never the Sandbox.

By changing the default branch in Gitea back to master, you force the correct GitOps flow:

The Clean Start: A developer clones the repo and automatically lands on master (The Clean Room).

The Clean Scoop: They branch off (git checkout -b newtool/my-feature). Their branch is completely pristine. It contains zero sandbox experiments.

The Test Phase: They push the branch and open a PR to test. The sandbox gets their new code to play with.

The Production Phase: Once it works perfectly in the sandbox, they open a PR from their pristine branch directly to master. Because the branch was originally scooped from master, it contains only their new tool. Zero hitch-hikers.

How to change it right now:
Open Gitea and go to your Transport_Toolbox repository.

Click Settings (top right corner of the repo).

In the left menu, click Branches.

At the top under Default Branch, change the dropdown from test to master.

Click Update.

Once you do this, tell your developers that before they start any new feature, they must run git checkout master and git pull. Your hitch-hiker problem will disappear completely.

Is there more protection I can apply or a workflow to ensure that this doesn't happen

Changing the default branch handles 90% of the problem, but as an automation engineer, you know that relying on humans to "just remember" to check out master is a recipe for that remaining 10% of failure.

If a developer accidentally branches off test, writes their code, and opens a Pull Request to master, the production server is in danger.

To make your repository completely bulletproof against this, you need to implement a Defense in Depth strategy. Here are the three layers of protection you can deploy right now, ranging from workflow rules to hard-coded automation.

Layer 1: The UI Tripwire & The "Two-Key" Lock (Gitea Settings)
Even if a developer makes a mistake locally, Gitea gives you the tools to stop it before it reaches the .50 production VM.

1. The "Files Changed" Tripwire (Training)
When a developer opens a Pull Request, Gitea displays a "Files Changed" tab. If AliM22 built a single Python script for a new feature, but his PR to master says Files Changed: 47, he has the hitch-hiker infection. You must train your reviewers to look at that number before looking at the code. If the number is suspiciously high, reject the PR immediately.

2. The "Two-Key" Lock (Branch Protection)
You must physically prevent the developer who wrote the code from clicking the "Merge" button to production themselves.

Go to your master Branch Protection settings in Gitea.

Check Enable pull request approval.

Set Required approvals to 1.

Check Restrict who can approve pull requests and select your Owners/Admins team.

Result: A SPOC can merge their experiments into test all day long, but they physically cannot merge into master without you or another Admin verifying that the "Files Changed" tab looks clean.

Layer 2: The Foolproof Git Alias (Developer Workflow)
Instead of telling your team, "Always remember to switch to master, pull the latest code, and then create your branch," you can give them a custom Git command that does it all automatically.

Have every developer run this exact command once in their local terminal:

Bash
git config --global alias.new-feature '!git checkout master && git pull origin master && git checkout -b'
How it changes their workflow:
Tomorrow, when a developer wants to build a new dashboard, they don't use standard checkout commands. Even if they are deep inside the dirty test sandbox, they simply type:

git new-feature newtool/leave-balance

Git will automatically jump to master, download the pristine production code, and cut the new branch perfectly. It completely removes human memory from the equation.

Layer 3: The "Poison Pill" Pipeline (Advanced Automation)
If you want to absolutely guarantee a mathematical block against hitch-hikers, we can inject a "Poison Pill" into your sandbox.

Here is how the architecture works:

You create an empty, hidden file on the test branch called .sandbox_poison_pill. You commit it only to the test branch. It never goes to master.

Because it lives in test, any developer who accidentally branches off test will silently scoop up that poison pill file into their new feature branch.

You add a tiny step to your existing Gitea Actions CI/CD pipeline that runs whenever a PR is opened against master:

YAML
      - name: Hitch-Hiker Check
        run: |
          if [ -f ".sandbox_poison_pill" ]; then
            echo "🚨 FATAL: This branch was cut from the Test Sandbox!"
            echo "It contains hitch-hiker code. Please recreate from Master."
            exit 1
          fi
The Result: If a dirty branch tries to enter master, the pipeline physically detects the poison pill, turns the PR red, and blocks the merge button. It is a 100% automated quarantine.

Which of these layers sounds like the best immediate fit for your team? We can set up the required approvals in Gitea right now, or deploy the Git Alias to your developers so they stop making the mistake locally.

I want it to be controlled in a more organized manner

If you want to move away from "trusting the developers" and implement a strict, highly organized system where mistakes are physically impossible, you need to implement a Zero-Trust GitOps Architecture.

In this setup, the repository manages the humans, not the other way around.

Here is the exact blueprint to lock down your repository so that code flows in a perfectly organized, controlled pipeline.

Phase 1: The "Iron Gate" (Gitea UI Settings)
We are going to use Gitea’s Branch Protection to take away the developers' ability to make mistakes.

Go to Settings -> Branches and apply these exact rules:

1. Lock the Clean Room (master)

Enable Branch Protection: Check the box.

Disable Push: Check the box. (No one, not even you, can push directly to master from the terminal).

Enable Pull Request Approval: Set to 1.

Restrict who can merge: Select your Owners or Admins team.

Merge Options: Check Enable Squash Merging. Uncheck Create a merge commit. (This forces all messy commits to be crushed into one clean line of history).

2. Lock the Sandbox (test)

Enable Branch Protection: Check the box.

Disable Push: Check the box. (Developers must open a PR to put their code in the sandbox. This creates a paper trail so you know exactly whose code broke the test environment).

Merge Options: Leave standard merging on so they can test multiple commits easily.

Phase 2: The Automated Bouncer (Gitea Actions)
Even with the UI locked down, a developer might still try to open a PR directly from the test branch to master. We are going to build a tiny, aggressive pipeline that acts as a bouncer.

If anyone tries to merge test into master, this pipeline will instantly fail, turn the PR red, and block the merge button.

Create a file named .gitea/workflows/enforce-workflow.yaml on your master branch:

YAML
name: Enforce Organized Workflow
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [master]

jobs:
  block-sandbox-merges:
    runs-on: rhel
    steps:
      - name: Verify Branch Origin
        run: |
          SOURCE_BRANCH="${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}"
          
          # 1. Block the Test branch from ever entering Master
          if [[ "$SOURCE_BRANCH" == "test" ]]; then
            echo "🚨 FATAL ERROR: Architecture Violation!"
            echo "You cannot merge the 'test' sandbox into 'master'."
            echo "You must PR your specific feature branch directly to master."
            exit 1
          fi
          
          # 2. Enforce Naming Conventions (Only allow your 3 approved prefixes)
          if [[ "$SOURCE_BRANCH" != newtool/* ]] && [[ "$SOURCE_BRANCH" != update/* ]] && [[ "$SOURCE_BRANCH" != bugfix/* ]]; then
            echo "🚨 FATAL ERROR: Invalid Branch Name!"
            echo "Branch must start with newtool/, update/, or bugfix/."
            exit 1
          fi
          
          echo "✅ Branch architecture approved. Proceed to code review."
Phase 3: The Official Organized Lifecycle
With these locks in place, your developers are forced onto a single, highly organized track. You can write this down as your official Standard Operating Procedure (SOP):

Start: Developer clones the repo (they land on master because you changed the default).

Create: They create a branch: git checkout -b newtool/cm-dashboard.

Sandbox Test: They push the branch and open a PR to test. The team merges it. They check .51 in their browser to verify it works.

Production Release: Once verified, the developer opens a second PR, this time from newtool/cm-dashboard to master.

The Gatekeeper: The Gitea Action verifies the branch isn't named test. It passes.

Approval: You (the Admin) look at the PR, see only the files for cm-dashboard, approve it, and click "Squash Merge."

Deployment: The .50 Baremetal Runner pulls the single, clean commit.

This matrix gives you absolute control. It eliminates hitch-hikers, enforces your naming conventions, and ensures your master branch remains a pristine, auditable history of the automation tools your team builds.

what if someone got confused and pulled the tests branch

This is one of the most common mistakes a developer will make when adapting to a new GitOps workflow. It happens to the best engineers!

If a developer is sitting on their clean feature branch (newtool/leave-balance) and accidentally types git pull origin test, they have just triggered The Reverse Infection.

Git does exactly what they asked: it downloads the entire messy test sandbox and forcefully merges it into their pristine feature branch.

Here is exactly what happens next, why your architecture keeps you safe, and how to tell the developer to fix it.

The Good News: Your Architecture Catches It
Because you set up the "Iron Gate" (Branch Protection) we discussed, this mistake cannot reach your .50 production VM.

Even if the confused developer pushes their infected branch and opens a PR to master, the system stops them:

They physically cannot merge it themselves (because they need 1 Admin approval).

When you (the Admin) look at the PR, the "Files Changed" tab will scream a warning at you. Instead of seeing the 2 files for the Leave Balance tool, you will see 85 files changed, including random experiments from AliM22 and V24RNafea.

You immediately reject the PR and tell them to clean their branch.

The Remedy: How to "Undo" the Mistake
How you fix this depends entirely on whether the developer realizes their mistake before they push to Gitea, or after.

Scenario A: They realize it instantly (The "Undo" Button)
If they run git pull origin test, see a massive wall of text downloading, and panic before typing git push, they can use Git's built-in time machine.

Tell them to run this exact command in their terminal:

Bash
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD
What this does: ORIG_HEAD is Git's emergency backup. Whenever a dangerous command like pull or merge changes the branch massively, Git saves the exact state of the branch right before the command was run. This command acts like Ctrl+Z, completely wiping away the sandbox code and returning their branch to the pristine state it was in 5 seconds prior.

Scenario B: They already pushed it to Gitea (The Surgical Rescue)
If they didn't notice the mistake, pushed the infected branch to Gitea, and opened a PR, ORIG_HEAD won't save them. Their branch is fully contaminated.

You must reject their PR and have them surgically extract their good code into a brand new branch using the Cherry-Pick method:

Delete the local infected branch and start over:
git checkout master
git pull
git checkout -b newtool/leave-balance-fixed

Find the ID of their specific good commit:
Have them look at their Git history or the closed PR to find the 7-character hash of their actual work (e.g., 38e3a66).

Copy only that good commit into the new branch:
git cherry-pick 38e3a66

Push the clean branch and open a new PR:
git push -u origin newtool/leave-balance-fixed

The Golden Rule for the Team
To prevent this, the rule of thumb you should communicate to your team is simple: "Code only flows upstream." Feature branches flow into test. test flows into master (or features flow directly to master). But you never, ever pull test down into a feature branch.

Okay first of all block users from ever doing git pull origin test

Second I want to know will solve merge conflicts on test branch when merging the PR's

I love where your head is at with trying to lock down the commands, but we have to face a hard truth about how Git is fundamentally designed.

1. Can we block git pull origin test?
The short answer is No, you cannot physically block someone from typing that command. Here is the technical reality: Git is a distributed system. git pull is a read operation. It asks the server, "Can I download a copy of this code?" As long as a developer has permission to view the repository, the Gitea server has no mechanism to stop them from downloading (pulling) a branch to their local laptop. The server can only block writes (pushes).

However, you don't need to block it. Because we set up the "Iron Gate" (Branch Protection and PR Approvals), you have neutralized the danger. If a developer gets confused, pulls test, infects their branch, and tries to push it... the architecture catches it. The PR will show 85 changed files, and you (the Admin) will reject it at the door. Let them make the local mistake; your server is perfectly safe.

2. Who Solves Merge Conflicts on the test Branch?
When a developer opens a Pull Request to test, and Gitea says "Merge Conflict," the responsibility to fix it falls 100% on the developer who opened the PR. The Admin should never fix a developer's merge conflict.

The Sandbox Dilemma: How to fix a conflict without getting infected
This is where the "Sandbox Philosophy" gets tricky.

Let's say AliM22 is building a feature in test that modifies Main_Web.html. You are building a new tool that also modifies Main_Web.html. You open your PR to test, and boom: Merge Conflict.

The Wrong Way (The Hitch-Hiker Trap):
The standard Git advice is to tell the developer to merge the target branch into their local code to fix the conflict.
If you type git merge test locally to fix the conflict, your feature branch instantly swallows AliM22's experimental code. You fix the conflict, the PR goes green, but your branch is now permanently infected with hitch-hikers.

The Right Way (The Clean Room Method):
If two developers are colliding in the test sandbox, it means their code is overlapping. You must fix the conflict using the Clean Room (master), not the Sandbox.

Tell the developer to follow this exact procedure:

Coordinate: Talk to AliM22. Find out whose feature is going to production first. Let's say AliM22's feature is finished.

Push to Production: AliM22 opens his PR to master and you approve it. His code is now officially part of the Clean Room.

The Clean Update: You go back to your local terminal and pull the safe code:
git checkout master
git pull

Rebase your feature: You update your feature branch with the new clean code:
git checkout newtool/my-tool
git rebase master

Fix the conflict safely: Git will pause and tell you there is a conflict. You fix the HTML file locally, finish the rebase, and force push your branch (git push -f).

Your PR to test will automatically update, the conflict will disappear, and your branch remains 100% free of hitch-hikers.

The Golden Rule of Conflicts
If there is a conflict in test, it means the team is stepping on each other's toes. The solution is almost always to get one of those features officially merged into master, and have the other developer rebase their work on top of the newly updated master branch.

This is a fantastic scenario. You are mapping out the exact day-to-day realities of a multi-developer team.

If this happens, you will hit a Merge Conflict in the Gitea UI on Developer B's Pull Request.

Here is exactly what happens step-by-step, why Git throws the error, and the trap Developer B must avoid.

The Sequence of Events
The Clean Start: Both developers scoop their branches from the Clean Room (master). At this exact moment, both branches are identical.

Developer A Moves First: They edit line 10 of Main_Web.html. They push and merge into test.

State of test: Line 10 now has Developer A's new code.

Developer B Moves Second: They are working on their local laptop. They also edit line 10 of Main_Web.html. Because they branched from master, they have no idea Developer A's code even exists.

The Collision: Developer B pushes their branch and opens a PR to test.

What Gitea Does
Gitea acts as the traffic cop. It looks at test (which has Developer A's code on line 10) and looks at Developer B's PR (which has different code on line 10).

Gitea stops the PR and says: "Merge Conflict. I don't know which version of line 10 to keep."

The Danger: The Gitea UI Trap
When this happens, Gitea will show a button that says something like "Resolve Conflicts".

Developer B must not click that button. If Developer B clicks "Resolve Conflicts" in the Gitea UI, Gitea will quietly merge the test sandbox into Developer B's feature branch to fix the file. Developer B's pristine feature branch is now instantly infected with hitch-hikers.

How to Safely Unblock Developer B
Because both developers touched the exact same file in the exact same place, they have a traffic jam. You cannot put two cars in the same parking spot in the Sandbox.

Here is how they safely resolve it using the workflow we established:

Step 1: The Team Huddle
Developer B talks to Developer A. "Hey, we both modified line 10 in Main_Web.html. Whose feature is finished and ready for Production?"

Step 2: Clear the Traffic Jam (Push to Master)
Let's say Developer A's feature is totally finished.
Developer A opens a PR from their feature branch directly to master. You approve it. master now officially includes Developer A's code.

Step 3: The Safe Update
Developer B goes to their local terminal and syncs up with the new, official reality:

Bash
git checkout master
git pull 
git checkout update/developer-b-feature
git rebase master
Step 4: Fix the Conflict Locally
During that rebase command, Git will pause and say, "Conflict on Main_Web.html." Developer B opens the file in their IDE, safely manually merges their code with Developer A's new code, and finishes the rebase.

Step 5: Force Push to Gitea
Developer B pushes their newly updated branch back to the server:

Bash
git push -f origin update/developer-b-feature
The Result: Developer B's Pull Request to test will automatically refresh. The conflict will disappear, the PR will turn green, and absolutely zero hitch-hikers were introduced. The pipeline remains perfectly clean.

You have a very sharp eye. In CI/CD, triggering a deployment at the wrong time is disastrous, so it is great that you are questioning this.

Here is the technical reality of how Gitea handles that trigger, and how we can make it explicitly bulletproof to match your exact intent.

Why the current trigger actually works
In Gitea (and GitHub), when you click the green "Merge" button on a Pull Request, the system executes that action by pushing the merged code to the target branch.

So, because you set up Branch Protection earlier that disabled direct pushes to master, no one can accidentally trigger the deployment from their terminal. The only way that push: branches: [master] event can physically happen is if an Admin successfully clicks "Merge" on a PR.

The "Explicit" Way (Recommended for Peace of Mind)
Even though the push trigger is safe, it feels a bit vague. If you want the pipeline to explicitly listen for the words "Pull Request Merged" so that anyone reading the file knows exactly what it does, we can change the trigger.

Here is the updated YAML that ignores all pushes and strictly listens for a successfully closed and merged Pull Request.

Replace the top of your deploy-master.yaml file with this:

YAML
name: Deploy to Main VM
on:
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - master
    types: [closed] # Triggers when a PR is closed (either merged or rejected)

jobs:
  deploy-production:
    # This 'if' statement is the magic lock. It ensures it only runs if the PR was actually merged, not just closed/rejected.
    if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true 
    runs-on: rhel
    steps:
      - name: SSH to .50, Pull, and Reload WSGI
        run: |
          ssh git@10.30.121.50 "cd /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/ && git pull origin master && touch WSGI.py"
Why this is the safest option:
It ignores Open PRs: It won't trigger while developers are just creating the PR.

It ignores Rejected PRs: If you close a PR without merging it, the if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true line acts as a bouncer and instantly cancels the deployment.

It only deploys success: It strictly waits for the successful merge into the master branch before waking up the runner on .51 to SSH into .50.

can they both be in the same workflow

Yes, absolutely. In fact, combining them into a single deploy.yaml file is the cleanest way to manage your CI/CD. It turns that one file into a "Router" that intelligently decides where the code needs to go based on which branch received the merge.

To do this, we combine the triggers at the top and use github.base_ref (which tells Gitea what branch the PR was targeting) to act as a traffic cop for the jobs.

Here is your unified, single-file deployment pipeline. You can delete the others and just commit this as .gitea/workflows/deploy.yaml:

YAML
name: Unified Deployment Pipeline
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [closed]
    branches:
      - master
      - test

jobs:
  # ---------------------------------------------------------
  # JOB 1: THE SANDBOX ROUTE (.51)
  # ---------------------------------------------------------
  deploy-sandbox:
    name: Deploy to Test Sandbox (.51)
    # The Magic Lock: Only run if it was MERGED and the target branch was TEST
    if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true && github.base_ref == 'test'
    runs-on: rhel
    steps:
      - name: Pull Test Code and Reload locally
        run: |
          cd /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/
          git pull origin test
          touch WSGI.py

  # ---------------------------------------------------------
  # JOB 2: THE PRODUCTION ROUTE (.50)
  # ---------------------------------------------------------
  deploy-production:
    name: Deploy to Production (.50)
    # The Magic Lock: Only run if it was MERGED and the target branch was MASTER
    if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true && github.base_ref == 'master'
    runs-on: rhel
    steps:
      - name: SSH to .50, Pull, and Reload WSGI
        run: |
          ssh git@10.30.121.50 "cd /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/ && git pull origin master && touch WSGI.py"
How this "Router" works in practice:
Someone opens a PR to test and you merge it.

Gitea wakes up this single workflow and checks the if statements.

The deploy-production job looks at the target branch, sees it is test (not master), and instantly Skips itself.

The deploy-sandbox job sees a perfect match, runs the local update, and finishes.

You now have a single, highly organized control panel for your entire infrastructure.

The Diagnosis
Look at the text right under the title in your screenshot:

You edited the Deploy.yaml file directly and committed it to the branch. This registered as a Push event.

However, look at our Magic Lock in the YAML:

When the runner woke up, it said: "Wait, V25KNabih just pushed this directly. This is not a merged Pull Request. Skip the deployment!" It protected the server from a direct edit, which is exactly why it says Skipped.

The Fix: Switching to "Push" Triggers
Since we decided to scrap all that "extra hassle" and strict PR rules earlier, we don't need this pipeline to be so restrictive. You want it to deploy whenever any new code hits those branches, whether you used a Pull Request or just pushed directly.

Let's change the trigger from pull_request to push, and change the lock to just check which branch received the code.

Replace your entire YAML with this. Notice I kept your rhel-baremetal label that you added:

YAML
name: Unified Deployment Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - master
      - test

jobs:

  # JOB 1: THE SANDBOX ROUTE (.51)
  # ---------------------------------------------------------
  deploy-sandbox:
    name: Deploy to Test Environment

    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/test'
