        run: |

          git pull origin test
          touch WSGI.py

  # ---------------------------------------------------------

  deploy-production:
    name: Deploy to Production 
    # The New Lock: Only run if the push was to the MASTER branch
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/master'
    runs-on: rhel
    steps:
      - name: SSH to .50, Pull, and Reload WSGI
        run: |
          ssh git@10.30.121.50 "cd /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/ && git pull origin master && touch WSGI.py"
Why this will work immediately:
By changing the trigger to push and checking github.ref, the pipeline no longer cares how the code got there.

If you merge a PR to test, it triggers Job 1.

If you just directly commit a fix to test, it triggers Job 1.

Job 2 will strictly ignore it unless the code lands in master.

You are hitting the two most classic walls of CI/CD and Git management. This is exactly why teams get frustrated and abandon automated pipelines—but both of these have very straightforward fixes.

Let’s tackle them one by one. We will fix the Linux permissions permanently first, and then I will give you a workflow that takes all the Git gymnastics away from your developers.

Issue 1: The "Permission Denied" Error on .51
Why this is happening:
Even though we set up the chmod g+s group permissions for the web files, Git has its own hidden folder called .git/. If AliM22 or another developer ever manually ran a git pull on the .51 machine as their own user, they became the physical owner of the Git database files.
When your Gitea act_runner (which probably runs as a user like git or V25KNabih) wakes up and tries to run git pull, Linux says, "You don't own these Git files, permission denied."

The Permanent Fix:
We need to forcefully give ownership of the entire folder, including the hidden Git files, back to the runner user.

Log into the .51 Test VM and run this command (Replace runner_user with the exact username your act_runner uses, like git or V25KNabih):

Bash
sudo chown -R runner_user:toolbox_test /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/
Crucial Rule: From now on, no human is allowed to run git pull manually on .51. If humans stay out of that folder and let the runner do its job, you will never see a permission denied error again.

Issue 2: The "Merge Conflict" Nightmare & Developer Friction
You are entirely right. Telling developers to create local branches, pull master, rebase, and cherry-pick just to fix a conflict is too academic. It slows them down and makes them hate the process.

Why the conflicts are happening:
You are experiencing the "Stale Sandbox" problem. Your test branch is acting like a graveyard. Developer A merges an experiment to test and leaves it there. Developer B merges something else. Over a few weeks, test looks completely different from master. When Developer C tries to merge a new feature, Git throws a massive conflict because the test branch is a mess.

The Solution: The "Disposable Sandbox" Workflow
We need to change how you view the test branch. It should not be a permanent record of code. It is just a temporary preview screen.

Here is the developer-friendly workflow. No terminal gymnastics required. Everything can be done via the VS Code User Interface and Gitea.

1. The Admin's Job: The Sandbox Wipe (When conflicts get too heavy)
Whenever the test branch gets tangled in merge conflicts, do not try to untangle it. Just nuke it and reset it to match production.
If a developer complains about a conflict on test, you (the admin) run this on your machine to wipe the sandbox clean:

Bash
git checkout test
git reset --hard master
git push -f origin test
Boom. The sandbox is perfectly clean again.

2. The Developer's Job: Resolve against Master, not Test
Give your developers this new rule: "If you get a merge conflict on the test PR, it means your code is out of date with Production (master). Fix it in VS Code."

Here is all the developer has to do. No new branches, no cherry-picking:

Developer opens VS Code on their current feature branch.

In the terminal, they type one command to get the latest stable code: git pull origin master.

VS Code will instantly highlight any conflicts in the file with friendly buttons that say "Accept Current Change" or "Accept Incoming Change".

The developer clicks the button they want, saves the file, and clicks "Sync Changes" (Push) in the VS Code UI.

The Gitea PR to test automatically updates and goes green.

Why this makes everyone happy:
For Developers: They never have to leave VS Code or memorize complex Git commands. They just pull master, click the friendly VS Code conflict buttons, and push.

For You (The Admin): You never have to fix their conflicts. Production (master) stays perfectly clean. And if the test branch ever gets too annoying, you just run the "Sandbox Wipe" and start fresh.

Run that chown command on .51 to get your pipeline green again, and let me know if this "Disposable Sandbox" concept feels like a better fit for your team's culture!

This is the classic "Triangle of Death" in system administration: Git, Apache, and Human Users all fighting for control over the exact same folder.

The reason it keeps breaking is because of a modern Git security feature called "Dubious Ownership." If Apache owns the folder, but your Runner tries to run git pull, Git panics and says, "Wait, you aren't Apache! I'm blocking this."

To satisfy all three of your requirements (Admins can pull, Runner works 24/7, Apache serves the app), we have to build a Shared Group Git Architecture.

Here is the exact blueprint to configure the .51 VM so they all play nicely together forever.

Step 1: Put Everyone in the Same Boat (The Group)
We need to ensure Apache, your Admins (SPOCs), and the Runner all belong to your toolbox_test_dev group.

Log into .51 and run these commands. (Replace runner_user with your actual Gitea runner username, and admin_user with people like AliM22).

Bash
sudo usermod -aG toolbox_test_dev apache
sudo usermod -aG toolbox_test_dev runner_user
sudo usermod -aG toolbox_test_dev admin_user
Step 2: Lock the Physical Folder Permissions
We will make Apache the ultimate owner, but give the toolbox_test_dev group absolute equal power. More importantly, we use the SGID bit (2775) so that any new file created by anyone automatically inherits the toolbox_test_dev group.

Run these exact commands on .51:

Bash
# 1. Set Apache as owner, and your dev group as the group owner
sudo chown -R apache:toolbox_test_dev /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/

# 2. Set SGID on all directories (forces the group to stick) and give group write access
sudo find /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/ -type d -exec chmod 2775 {} \+

# 3. Ensure all existing files are readable/writable by the group
sudo find /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/ -type f -exec chmod 664 {} \+
Step 3: The Git Magic (The Missing Link)
This is where 99% of teams fail. Standard Linux permissions are not enough for Git. You have to tell Git's internal engine to behave like a shared repository, and you must tell it to stop enforcing the "Dubious Ownership" block.

1. Tell the Repository to Share:
Run this inside your project folder. It alters .git/config so Git knows multiple people will be pulling and merging:

Bash
cd /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/
sudo git config core.sharedRepository group
2. Bypass the "Dubious Ownership" Error (Crucial):
Because Apache physically owns the folder, Git will block the Runner and the Admins from running git pull. You must run this command logged in as the Runner user, and again logged in as each Admin user. It tells Git, "I know Apache owns this, but I trust this directory."

(Log in as the runner, then run this):

Bash
git config --global --add safe.directory /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox
(Log in as AliM22, then run this):

Bash
git config --global --add safe.directory /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox
Why this perfectly solves your 3 goals:
Apache works: It is the primary owner of the files and has full read/execute rights to run WSGI.py.

The Runner is uninterrupted: Because the runner is in the toolbox_test_dev group (which has write access) and has the safe.directory exception, it can pull new code and modify the .git database without permission denied errors.

Admins can intervene: If the pipeline breaks, an Admin can SSH into the machine, type git pull, and it will work perfectly. Because of the core.sharedRepository setting and the SGID bit, whatever the Admin pulls will perfectly retain the toolbox_test_dev group, meaning they won't lock the Runner out the next time it tries to automate a deployment.

Execute those commands, and your .51 test sandbox will finally be stable from an OS-level perspective!

The error cannot open '.git/FETCH_HEAD': Permission denied tells us exactly what happened: When you (or another admin) ran git pull manually, your human user account created or overwrote the FETCH_HEAD file inside the hidden .git folder. The Immediate Fix

sudo find /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/ -type d -exec chmod 2775 {} \+
sudo find /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/ -type f -exec chmod 664 {} \+
3. Give the Runner explicit Git clearance:
(This runs the config command exactly as the git user, ensuring its own global config allows the pull)

Bash
sudo -u git git config --global --add safe.directory /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox
Why this fixes it instantly:
By switching the folder's group to toolbox_admin and re-running the chmod 664 command, that stubborn FETCH_HEAD file is now fully writeable by any user inside the toolbox_admin group.

Since your git runner is officially in that group, it will slice right through the pull command.

Run those three blocks, go back to Gitea, and hit "Re-run all jobs" on that failed pipeline. It should go green instantly!

ls -la /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/.git/ | grep FETCH_HEAD

-rw-rw-r--    1 apache    toolbox_test_admins     976 Apr 30 14:48 FETCH_HEAD

cat /app/www/TAT_TestVenv/Transport_Toolbox/.git/config | grep shared

        sharedRepository = groupgroups git ls -ld

drwxrwsr-x+ 7 apache toolbox_test_admins 4096 Apr 30 14:09 .



git : git toolbox_admin toolbox_test_admins toolbox_test_dev

The outputs you provided are exactly what we needed, and they reveal something fascinating. On paper, your Linux permissions are now 100% perfect.

Look at your outputs:

FETCH_HEAD has rw- (read/write) for the group.

The group owner is toolbox_test_admins.

Your git user is officially a member of toolbox_test_admins.

So why is it still throwing a "Permission denied" error? You have just run into the classic "Ghost Process" gotcha in Linux.

The Diagnosis: Stale Daemon Memory
When you add a user to a new group in Linux using usermod, that change does not apply to any programs or services that are already running in the background.

Because your act_runner service started running before you added the git user to the toolbox_test_admins group, the runner's process is currently operating with a stale, outdated list of group memberships. In its memory, it thinks it is still an outsider.

The Fix: Reboot the Runner's Brain
We just need to restart the runner service so it wakes up, checks the system, and realizes it now has toolbox_test_admins privileges.

Run this command on the .51 machine to restart the service:
(Note: If your service is named something slightly different like act_runner, replace gitea-runner with your exact service name)

Bash
sudo systemctl restart gitea-runner
What to do next:
Go back to Gitea and click "Re-run all jobs" on the pipeline.

Because the runner is now freshly booted with the correct group permissions, it will see the rw- on FETCH_HEAD and successfully execute the pull.

(Side note: I also noticed a + sign at the end of your directory permissions drwxrwsr-x+. This means you have Access Control Lists (ACLs) active on that folder. If restarting the runner doesn't instantly fix the issue, let me know, as it means an old ACL rule is overriding your perfect standard permissions.)

I want to stop users from accessing through the IP and port to force them to use the secure Transport toolbox DND

To force users to use your official DNS name (e.g., transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com) and prevent them from bypassing it using the raw IP address like 10.30.121.50, you need to configure Apache to intercept the request based on what the user typed in their browser.

The cleanest, most user-friendly way to handle this is using an Apache Rewrite Rule. Instead of giving the user a broken page or a "403 Forbidden" error, this instantly redirects anyone who types the IP address straight to the secure DNS name.

The Fix: Apache Rewrite Rules
You will need to edit your Apache VirtualHost configuration file for the Transport Toolbox on your .50 and .51 machines. On RHEL, this is usually located in /etc/httpd/conf.d/ (for example, /etc/httpd/conf.d/transport_toolbox.conf).

Open your VirtualHost configuration file using sudo nano or vi.

Inside your <VirtualHost *:80> (and <VirtualHost *:443> if you use SSL) block, add the rewrite rules.

Replace your-dns-name.internal.eg.vodafone.com with the actual DNS name of your application.

Apache
<VirtualHost *:80>
    # This defines the official name of the server
    ServerName your-dns-name.internal.eg.vodafone.com
    
    # 1. Turn on the Rewrite Engine
    RewriteEngine On
    
    # 2. Condition: If what the user typed (HTTP_HOST) is NOT exactly your DNS name...
    RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^your-dns-name\.internal\.eg\.vodafone\.com$ [NC]
    
    # 3. Rule: ...Then redirect them to the correct DNS name permanently (301)
    RewriteRule ^(.*)$ http://your-dns-name.internal.eg.vodafone.com$1 [L,R=301]

    # ... (the rest of your WSGI, DocumentRoot, and Directory configs stay exactly the same) ...
</VirtualHost>
(Note: The \ before the dots in the RewriteCond are there to escape the dots, and [NC] makes it case-insensitive).

Apply the Changes
Once you save the file, verify that you didn't introduce any typos or syntax errors:

Bash
sudo apachectl configtest
If the output says Syntax OK, gracefully reload Apache. Because we are using reload instead of restart, zero active users will be dropped:

Bash
sudo systemctl reload httpd
Now, if a user types [http://10.30.121.50:80](http://10.30.121.50:80) into their browser, Apache will instantly rewrite their URL and force them onto the secure DNS path before loading the application.

is there another appproach ?

Yes, absolutely. If you want to avoid using the RewriteEngine (which can sometimes get complicated with regular expressions), the cleanest and most robust alternative is the Catch-All VirtualHost method.

This approach uses Apache's built-in routing logic instead of intercepting the URL.

How it works:
When Apache receives a request, it looks at the Host header (what the user typed in their browser). It checks its list of VirtualHosts to find a matching ServerName.
Crucially, if it doesn't find an exact match (like when someone types the raw IP address), Apache blindly routes the user to the very first VirtualHost in the file.

We can exploit this by setting up a "Trap" VirtualHost right at the top of your configuration file.

The Configuration
Open your Apache configuration file for the toolbox. You will split it into two <VirtualHost> blocks. Put this "Trap" block immediately above your actual application block.

Apache
# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 1. THE TRAP (Catches raw IPs and wrong domains)
# ---------------------------------------------------------
<VirtualHost *:80>
    # There is no real ServerName here, this acts as the default fallback
    ServerName catchall.local
    
    # Instantly bounce them to the correct DNS path
    Redirect permanent / http://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/
</VirtualHost>

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# 2. THE REAL APPLICATION
# ---------------------------------------------------------
<VirtualHost *:80>
    # This block ONLY activates if they typed the exact DNS name
    ServerName transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
    
    # ... All your existing WSGI, DocumentRoot, and Directory configs stay here ...
    # WSGIScriptAlias / /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/WSGI.py
    # ...
</VirtualHost>
Why this approach is often preferred:
Zero Regex: There is no chance of accidentally misconfiguring a RewriteCond regular expression and breaking your site.

Performance: Because it relies on Apache's core routing engine rather than loading the mod_rewrite module to inspect every single incoming string, it is slightly faster and uses less overhead.

The "Strict Drop" Option: If you ever decide you don't even want to redirect them, and instead want to slap them with a strict "403 Forbidden" error to train them to use the DNS name, you can just delete the Redirect line in the trap and replace it with:

Apache
<Location />
    Require all denied
</Location>
To apply it, just test and reload exactly like before:

Bash
sudo apachectl configtest
sudo systemctl reload httpd
Should the user have access to the Port 22 in oder to clone with SSH

Yes, absolutely.

If a user wants to clone a repository using the SSH method (e.g., git clone git@10.30.121.50:...), their machine must have uninterrupted network access to Port 22 on the target server.

Here is why, and how to handle it if your corporate network restricts it:

Why Port 22 is Mandatory for SSH Clones
When a developer runs git clone git@..., Git does not use its own protocol; it literally piggybacks on the standard SSH protocol. Under the hood, Git is opening an SSH connection on Port 22 to the Gitea server.

If your corporate firewall, VPN, or the server's internal firewalld blocks Port 22 for standard developers, the command will simply hang and eventually throw a Connection timed out error.

How to test if a user has access:
If a developer says they cannot clone via SSH, have them run this exact command in their terminal (Command Prompt, PowerShell, or Git Bash):

Bash
ssh -T -p 22 git@10.30.121.50
Success: If it says something like “Hi there, You've successfully authenticated,” their Port 22 is open and working.

Failure: If it hangs forever or says “Connection refused / timed out,” their machine is blocked from hitting Port 22.

What to do if Port 22 is blocked for standard users?
In many enterprise environments, IT security locks down Port 22 so only Admins (like you) can use it. If that is the case, you have two options for your developers:

Switch them to HTTPS (The Easiest Route):
Tell the developers to ignore the SSH URL and copy the HTTPS URL from Gitea instead (e.g., [https://transport-toolbox.internal](https://transport-toolbox.internal)...). HTTPS uses Port 443, which is practically never blocked because it is the standard web traffic port. They will just use their Gitea username and password (or a Personal Access Token) to push/pull.

Request a Firewall Rule:
If you strictly want to enforce SSH keys for security (so passwords aren't floating around), you will need to ask the network/security team to open Port 22 on 10.30.121.50 for the specific VLANs or IPs where your developers are working.

okay I have a git question I want to reset the test to be now exact as master how to do it

This is the "Sandbox Wipe" maneuver. It completely destroys any lingering merge conflicts, stale experiments, or broken code on the test branch and forces it to perfectly mirror the current state of production.

Here are the exact three commands to run from your terminal (or your Gitea admin machine):

Bash
# 1. Switch to your local test branch
git checkout test

# 2. Nuke the current state and make it perfectly mirror master
git reset --hard master

# 3. Force push this clean slate up to the Gitea server
git push -f origin test
Why the -f is required:
Because you are physically rewriting the history of the test branch, Gitea will normally reject the push to protect the old code. The -f (force) command tells the server, "I am the admin, overwrite whatever is up there with this clean slate."

One rule for your developers: If AliM22 or anyone else already had the old, broken test branch checked out on their local VS Code before you did this, they will get a weird error if they try to pull. Tell them to run git fetch and git reset --hard origin/test on their local machines to sync up with your newly cleaned sandbox.

okay but there is some commits in the master that's not in the test branch why is that ?

This is a very normal part of the GitOps lifecycle, and it is the exact reason why the "Disposable Sandbox" model is so much better than trying to keep branches perfectly synced manually.

When you see commits in master that are missing from test, it usually happens for one of two reasons:

1. The Standard Workflow (Moving Forward)
Think about the lifecycle of a feature. A developer writes code, merges it into test to try it out on the .51 machine, and verifies it works.

When they are ready to go live, they don't merge test into master. Instead, they take their original feature branch and open a new Pull Request directly into master. Once that is merged, master moves forward with those new production commits.

However, the test branch doesn't magically know that production moved forward. It stays exactly where it was left.

2. The "Hotfix" Bypass
Sometimes, a critical bug hits the .50 production server. An admin or developer writes a quick fix and merges it straight into master to get the server healthy immediately, completely bypassing the .51 sandbox.

Now, master has hotfix commits that test has never seen.

Why this is actually a good thing:
In legacy environments, admins waste hours trying to back-merge master into test just to keep the commit histories identical. It is a nightmare.

Under your new architecture, you do not care if test falls behind. The test branch is just a temporary preview screen. If a developer notices that test is missing the latest production updates and they need those updates to test their new tool, they (or you) just run that 3-step "Sandbox Wipe" from earlier. You instantly overwrite the old sandbox with the fresh master code, and they get back to work.

Your only golden rule is protecting the .50 production environment. As long as master is clean and stable, the sandbox can be as messy or outdated as it wants to be until you decide to wipe it.

Why did the reset specifically stop at that commit that is found in both master and test

You have just discovered one of the most common and confusing "gotchas" in Git: the difference between your local map of the repository and the actual server.

Look very closely at the red text in your two screenshots.

In the first image (on your .51 test machine), Git thinks origin/master is at commit d2d49f921.

In the second image, Git knows master is actually way ahead at commit 15a3f1bbb.

Why it stopped there:
When you typed git reset --hard master on the .51 machine, Git did exactly what you asked. It looked at its local, cached copy of the master branch. Because no one had recently run git pull on the master branch on that specific machine, its local memory of master was stuck in the past at commit d2d49f921.

It essentially reset your sandbox to an outdated version of production!

The Fix: Resetting to the "True" Master
To do a true Sandbox Wipe, you should never rely on the local master branch because it might be out of date. Instead, you tell Git to phone home to Gitea, get the absolute latest production code, and reset to that.

Run these exact commands on the machine where you are trying to reset test.

1. Update the local map from Gitea:

Bash
git fetch origin
(This downloads the latest commit history without merging anything. It will finally see 15a3f1bbb.)

2. Make sure you are on the test branch:

Bash
git checkout test
3. Reset to the REMOTE master, not the local one:

Bash
git reset --hard origin/master
(Notice the origin/. This forces it to use the fresh data from the server, bypassing your outdated local branch).

4. Push the clean slate back to the server:

Bash
git push -f origin test
If you run git log --oneline after doing this, your test branch will perfectly match 15a3f1bbb Updating Performance Privilage, exactly as you intended.

but I did write git reset --hard origin/master from the start

My apologies—you are completely right. If you explicitly typed origin/master and it still stopped at that old commit, then you just ran into one of Git's most deceptive illusions: The Remote-Tracking Cache.

Most developers assume that origin/master is a live, real-time link to the Gitea server. It is not. ### The "origin/master" Illusion
When you type origin/master on your .51 machine, Git does absolutely zero networking. It does not check the server. Instead, it looks at a hidden text file stored locally on your hard drive at .git/refs/remotes/origin/master.

That file is essentially a bookmark. It says: "The last time this specific machine talked to the server, master was at commit d2d49f921."

Because no one had explicitly told the .51 machine to update its bookmarks recently, its local memory of origin/master was completely stale. So, when you ran git reset --hard origin/master, Git faithfully reset your sandbox to what it thought was the latest server code, which was unfortunately weeks out of date.

The Rule of the Sandbox Wipe
This is exactly why step 1 of the Sandbox Wipe has to be a physical network call to Gitea.

Whenever you need to wipe the sandbox and sync it with production, you must force the .51 machine to update its local bookmarks first.

Bash
# 1. Force the machine to talk to the network and update origin/master
git fetch origin

# 2. Now that the bookmark is accurate, run your reset
git reset --hard origin/master
You had the right logic and the right command from the start! The only thing missing was the git fetch to wake up the local Git database and tell it that production had moved forward.

.git/refs/remotes/origin/master.



okay perfect so explain how does fetch and pull affect this refs/remotes/origin/master

This is exactly the right question to ask if you want to master Git. Once you understand that Git is just a collection of dumb text files pointing to hashes, the entire system stops feeling like magic.

Let’s look exactly at what happens under the hood to that specific file: .git/refs/remotes/origin/master.

If you were to run cat .git/refs/remotes/origin/master on your server right now, you would see nothing but a 40-character string (a SHA-1 commit hash). That file is literally just a bookmark.

Here is exactly how fetch and pull interact with it.

1. git fetch: The Reconnaissance Mission
When you run git fetch (or git fetch origin), Git does only two things:

Network Sync: It connects to Gitea, checks what commits exist on the server that you don't have locally, and downloads those raw objects into your hidden .git/objects/ database.

Update the Bookmark: It takes the latest commit hash from the server's master branch and physically overwrites the .git/refs/remotes/origin/master file with that new hash.

Crucially, git fetch stops right there. It touches nothing else. It does not touch your physical working directory (your code), and it does not touch your local master branch (which is stored in a separate file: .git/refs/heads/master). It is a purely safe, read-only network operation that just updates your local map of the server.

2. git pull: The Two-Part Operation
git pull is not actually a real, foundational Git command. It is a macro. Under the hood, git pull origin master is literally just Git running two commands back-to-back:

Part A: git fetch origin master
First, it does exactly what we just discussed. It reaches out to Gitea, downloads the new data, and overwrites your .git/refs/remotes/origin/master file so the bookmark is accurate.

Part B: git merge origin/master
Immediately after fetching, Git looks at that freshly updated bookmark file and says, "Okay, now take the code from that commit hash and forcefully merge it into the user's current local working directory." This is the dangerous part. This is where files actually change on your hard drive, and this is where merge conflicts happen if your local code doesn't match the incoming server code.

Summary: Why this caused your Sandbox issue
When you ran git reset --hard origin/master earlier without fetching first, Git looked at .git/refs/remotes/origin/master and saw the old hash (d2d49f921). It said, "I don't need to check the network, the file right here tells me where master is!" By running git fetch origin first, you forced Git to go to the server, discover the new 15a3f1bbb commit, and update the text inside that bookmark file. Then, when you ran the reset command again, Git read the freshly updated file and reset your sandbox perfectly.

The Golden Rule for Admins: Whenever you are doing server administration, scripting, or automated pipelines (like your Runner), never trust git pull if things are messy.
Use fetch to update the bookmarks safely, inspect the situation if needed, and then use reset --hard or merge to explicitly execute the file changes.

This is the classic SSH fallback behavior. When Git tries to connect using an SSH key but the server rejects the key (or cannot find it), Linux simply gives up on the keys and falls back to asking for a standard user password.

Because Gitea intercepts SSH connections to manage permissions, this usually means Gitea does not recognize the public key of the user currently running the command, or the key is not being offered at all.

Here is the exact checklist to permanently eliminate that password prompt.

1. Check Who You Are (The User Context)
SSH keys belong to specific Linux users. Earlier, you proved that the git user could connect perfectly. But if you are currently logged into the .51 terminal as your own user (e.g., V25KNabih or root) and you type git pull, SSH is looking in your ~/.ssh/ folder, not the runner's folder.

Verify your current user:

Bash
whoami
If you are trying to act as the runner, you must switch to that user first (sudo su - git) before pulling.

2. Check the Gitea Web UI (The Vault)
If you generated a new SSH key for the .51 machine to use, it physically cannot pull until you paste the public half of that key into Gitea.

On the .51 machine (as the user who needs to pull), print the public key:

Bash
cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub
# or if you used ed25519:
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Copy the entire output string.

Log into the Gitea Web UI in your browser.

Click your Profile Picture (top right) -> Settings -> SSH / GPG Keys.

Click Add Key, paste the string, and save it.

3. The DNS vs. IP Mismatch
Look closely at the prompt you just pasted:
git@transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com

Earlier, when we tested the manual connection, you used:

SSH is extremely strict. If you told it to trust 10.30.121.50, it doesn't automatically know that transport-toolbox.internal... is the same machine. It might be refusing to offer the key because the hostname changed.

The Diagnosis
You are trying to connect to the server as the git user (git@transport-toolbox...), but you are currently logged into the Linux terminal under your personal account: V25KNabih.

SSH does not automatically know where the git user's private keys are stored. By default, it looks inside the home directory of the person typing the command (/home/V25KNabih/.ssh/). Because your personal account doesn't have an SSH key that Gitea recognizes, the server rejects the handshake and falls back to asking for a password.

You have two ways to fix this, depending on what you are trying to achieve right now.

Option 1: You are testing the Runner (The git user)
If you are running this command just to prove that the automated act_runner can pull the code, you must physically switch to the runner's user account before running the Git or SSH commands. This forces Linux to use the correct .ssh folder.

If you are acting as an admin/developer and want to be able to manually run git pull from your V25KNabih account without getting a password prompt, you need to generate a key specifically for your account and give it to Gitea.

This is actually a massive victory disguised as an error.

The password prompt is completely gone. Your runner successfully authenticated with the .52 Gitea server using its SSH key.

However, you just ran into the classic "Gitea SSH Bypass" illusion.

The Diagnosis: Why it can't find the repo
Look very closely at this specific line from the verbose debug log you sent me earlier:
debug1: Remote: /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys:31: key options: agent-forwarding port-forwarding...

That line is the smoking gun. It proves that when your runner connected, the .52 server matched the SSH key to a raw, standard Linux entry on line 31 of the authorized_keys file.

Why that breaks everything:
When Gitea manages SSH keys, it does not use standard Linux entries. It writes a special "interceptor" line in the authorized_keys file that looks something like this:
command="/usr/local/bin/gitea serv key-1",no-port-forwarding...

When a runner connects using a Gitea-managed key, that interceptor catches the request and translates TAT/Transport_Toolbox.git into the real backend folder on the hard drive (usually somewhere like /var/lib/gitea/data/gitea-repositories/...).

Because your SSH connection hit a standard Linux key entry instead of the Gitea interceptor, you bypassed Gitea entirely. The Linux OS simply dropped your runner into /home/git/ and tried to look for a physical folder called TAT, which doesn't exist there. Hence the error: fatal: 'TAT/Transport_Toolbox.git' does not appear to be a git repository.

How this happened:
At some point, someone manually added the runner's SSH key to the .52 server's authorized_keys file (perhaps using ssh-copy-id or pasting it directly). Then, you also added it to the Gitea Web UI.
Because SSH reads the file from top to bottom, it hits the manual Linux entry first, accepts the connection, and never triggers the Gitea interceptor.

The Fix: Clean up the Keys
You need to log into the .52 Gitea Server and clean up the conflict.

Step 1: Open the authorized_keys file

Bash
sudo vi /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys
Step 2: Find the duplicate
Scroll through the file and look for the runner's public key (the ed25519 key).
You will likely see it listed twice:

A plain entry that just starts with ssh-ed25519... (this is the bad one, probably around line 31).

A Gitea entry that starts with command="/usr/local/bin/gitea... (this is the good one).

Step 3: Delete the plain entry
Delete the plain, standard SSH line entirely. Only keep the entry that begins with the command= interceptor.

Save the file and exit.

The Result
Go back to Gitea and click "Re-run all jobs."

This time, the SSH connection will hit the Gitea interceptor, Gitea will recognize the runner, dynamically route it to the exact backend repository, and the git pull will finally succeed.

The Diagnosis: The HTTPS Trap
Your .50 production machine is currently configured to talk to Gitea using the standard web HTTPS protocol, instead of the secure SSH protocol we have been working with.

HTTPS does not know what an SSH key is. It completely ignores all the VIP lists and authorized_keys files we just fixed. When Git uses HTTPS, it always expects a standard username and password (or an access token), which is why it paused to ask you for one.

Because we know that .50 already has a perfect SSH key (prod-server-50 was key-1 in your file earlier), we just need to tell the Git repository to switch lanes and use the SSH highway instead.

This is exactly how you master Linux administration. Memorizing commands is useless if you don’t understand the underlying logic.

We will break this entire debugging session down into three distinct modules. We will not move forward until you are completely comfortable with the current step.

Here is our curriculum:

The Mental Model: The overarching strategy and what we were actually hunting for.

The Interrogation: How the ssh -Tv command works under the hood.

The VIP List: Decoding the authorized_keys file and why those other keys were there.

Let's dive into the first module.

Module 1: The Mental Model (The Nightclub Bouncer)
When you are debugging a GitOps pipeline, you have to stop thinking about "Git" and start thinking about secure networking. Git is just a file transfer protocol; SSH is the armor protecting it.

When you told your test machine (.51) to run git pull, it failed. My thinking process was a strict process of elimination based on the "Nightclub" mental model:

The Robot: Your .51 test runner.

The ID Card: The SSH Private Key (id_ed25519).

The Bouncer: The SSH Daemon on the .52 Gitea server.

The VIP Manager: The Gitea software itself.

The Vault: The physical TAT/Transport_Toolbox.git folder.

To get the code, the Robot has to show its ID to the Bouncer. The Bouncer checks the VIP list. If the ID is on the list, the Bouncer hands the Robot off to the VIP Manager, who escorts the Robot to the Vault.

When your pipeline failed, I knew the chain was breaking at one of three specific checkpoints:

The Robot forgot its ID card: (It was running as the V25KNabih user instead of the git user, so it didn't have the key).

The Bouncer didn't recognize the ID: (The key wasn't in the .52 server's file, so it asked for a password).

The Bouncer bypassed the VIP Manager: (This is the "Repository not found" error. The Robot got in, but it was dropped into the general lobby—a blank Linux terminal—instead of being escorted to the Vault by Gitea).

My entire strategy was to force the system to show me exactly which of those three checkpoints was failing, rather than just guessing and changing settings randomly.

Here are the players in your exact setup:

The Robot: Your .51 Test Machine (specifically, the git user on that machine).

The ID Card: The SSH private key (id_ed25519) sitting on the .51 machine.

The Bouncer: The raw Red Hat Linux operating system running on your .52 Gitea Server.

The VIP Manager: The Gitea software itself, running on the .52 server.

The Vault: The actual code folder (TAT/Transport_Toolbox.git).

When you typed sudo -u git git pull on your .51 test machine, here is the exact sequence of events, step-by-step, explaining why you got that specific fatal error:

Step 1: Presenting the ID
Your .51 machine (The Robot) reached out over the network to .52 (The Bouncer) and essentially said: "I want to connect. Here is my ID card (the ed25519 key)."

Step 2: Checking the List (The exact point of failure)
The Red Hat OS on .52 (The Bouncer) opened its VIP list—the /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file—to see if .51 was allowed inside.

What was supposed to happen: The Bouncer should have seen .51's key on the list, noticed a special Gitea interceptor command attached to it (command="/usr/local/bin/gitea..."), and immediately handed .51 over to Gitea (The VIP Manager). Gitea would then securely guide .51 to the code.

What actually happened: Someone had manually pasted .51's key into that file as a plain text string. The Bouncer found the key, but it didn't have the Gitea interceptor command attached to it.

Step 3: The Wrong Drop-off
Because there was no Gitea command attached to the key, the .52 Bouncer said, "Your ID is valid, come on in," and dropped .51 into a standard, empty Linux terminal (/home/git/).

It completely bypassed the Gitea software.

Step 4: The Crash
Your .51 machine, now standing blindly in an empty Linux folder, immediately ran the git pull command to find the TAT/Transport_Toolbox.git folder. Because it wasn't guided to the hidden database by Gitea, it couldn't find the folder in that empty directory.

It panicked and threw the error: fatal: 'TAT/Transport_Toolbox.git' does not appear to be a git repository.

Let's polish that understanding with the exact technical terms, and then we will move right into Module 2: The Interrogation.

Refining Your Understanding
1. The "Gitea Keys" Location
Yes. When I say "Gitea keys" or the "VIP list," I am talking specifically about the /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file sitting physically on the hard drive of the .52 Gitea Server. The .52 machine holds the public keys for everyone allowed to connect.

2. The Encryption & Storage
You are spot on about the storage: the public key must be stored "in a specific way" (wrapped in that command= interceptor) so the OS knows to hand the connection to Gitea instead of opening a raw shell.

However, let's tweak your understanding of the "encryption" slightly.

The Robot (.51) doesn't actually encrypt all its traffic with its private key. Instead, SSH uses a Challenge-Response system:

When .51 connects, .52 looks at the public key on its VIP list.

.52 uses that public key to lock a random mathematical puzzle, and sends it to .51.

Because .51 is the only machine in the world holding the matching private key, it is the only machine that can unlock the puzzle, solve it, and send the answer back.

When .52 gets the correct answer, it says, "Okay, you proved you hold the private key. You are authenticated."

Module 2: The Interrogation (ssh -Tv)
Once we understood the mental model, we needed to figure out exactly which step of the handshake was failing.

When you just type git pull, Git is completely silent. If it fails, it just spits out a generic error and gives you zero clues about what happened in the background.

To debug it, we used this command:
sudo -u git ssh -Tv git@transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com

Here is exactly what that command does and why I asked you to run it:

1. sudo -u git (The Disguise)
By default, if you run a command, Linux executes it as your personal user (V25KNabih). Because your pipeline runs as the git user, we had to put on the git user's disguise to ensure we were testing the exact same private key the automated pipeline uses.

2. ssh (Bypassing Git)
We completely removed git from the equation. Git is just a program that uses SSH. By calling ssh directly, we removed the middleman and talked directly to the Bouncer.

3. -v (Verbose Mode - "Making the Bouncer talk")
This is the most powerful debugging tool in Linux networking. Usually, the SSH handshake happens invisibly in milliseconds. By adding -v (Verbose), you force the SSH protocol to print every single thought it has to the screen.

This is how we saw: Offering public key...

This is how we saw: Server accepts key...

This proved to us that the Robot and the Bouncer were talking, and the ID card was valid. The cryptography was working perfectly.

4. -T (Disable Terminal Allocation - "The Litmus Test")
This is the secret weapon for debugging Gitea/GitLab/GitHub servers.
Normally, SSH tries to open an interactive terminal (a shell) so you can type commands. But remember: Gitea does not allow human terminals. It only allows automated Git traffic.

By passing -T, we told the Robot: "Do not ask for a terminal." * If Gitea intercepts the connection correctly, it responds with its custom success message: "Hi there, Gitea does not provide shell access." * Because your server responded with the Red Hat Welcome Message instead, it was 100% undeniable proof that the Gitea software was completely blind to your connection.

By combining -v and -T, we mathematically eliminated network firewalls, bad passwords, and broken private keys. We proved the only possible issue left was that the .52 server was routing a valid connection to the wrong door.

Module 1: The VIP Illusion (What Keepalived Actually Does)
Keepalived is an incredible tool, but it is very dumb. It only does one thing: It moves the network cable.

When .50 fails, Keepalived violently yanks the .52 IP address away from .50 and attaches it to .51.

The Good News: Your developers and runners don't have to change their URLs. They keep sending traffic to .52, and the network seamlessly routes it to the backup machine.

The Danger: Keepalived does not move your files. It does not move your databases. It does not move your SSH keys. It only moves the IP.

Module 2: The "Split-Brain" Reality (Why our previous fix was temporary)
Earlier, I told you to fix the "VIP List" on the .52 server.

Because the .52 VIP was currently living on .50, when you edited /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys, you were actually editing the hard drive on .50.

Module 3: The Failover Survival Checklist
To guarantee that .51 can flawlessly take over as both the Test Environment AND the Production Gitea server during a disaster, you have to ensure the "brain" is shared between the two servers.

1. The Git Repositories (The Vault)

2. The Gitea Database (The VIP Manager's Memory)
Gitea remembers passwords, pull requests, issues, and who owns which Deploy Key by storing them in a database (usually PostgreSQL, MySQL, or an internal SQLite file).

3. The SSH Keys (The Bouncer's Clipboard)
As we discovered, the /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file is currently trapped on .50.

The Question: How are we keeping .51's authorized keys file identical to .50's?

The Risk: If you don't sync this file, nobody can authenticate after a failover. (If you use shared storage for the Gitea data, you can actually configure Gitea to store keys in the database instead of the .ssh file to solve this permanently).

Because you are using rsync to copy the Gitea database from .50 to .51, you are effectively copying the "VIP Manager's Memory" over to the backup machine.

Here is exactly what that maintenance button does, why your plan works, and the one hidden trap you need to watch out for with your rsync setup.

What the Maintenance Button Actually Does
Gitea does not rely on the physical /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file as its source of truth.

Its real source of truth is its internal database. When a developer adds a key in the Web UI, Gitea saves that key into a database table (usually called public_key). Writing it to the Linux file is just an afterthought so the OS knows what to do.

When you click "Update the '.ssh/authorized_keys' file with Gitea SSH keys", Gitea executes a hard reset:

It physically deletes or overwrites the current /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file on that machine.

It queries its database: "Give me every single public key ever registered."

It takes those keys, wraps every single one of them in the command="/usr/local/bin/gitea..." interceptor, and writes a perfectly clean, brand new file to the hard drive.

Why Your Plan Works
Because your rsync job copied the database from .50 to .51, the Gitea software on .51 already secretly knows all the keys. It just hasn't written them to the .51 Bouncer's clipboard yet.

If you trigger a failover, open the .51 Gitea Web UI, and click that maintenance button, Gitea will read its newly synced database and instantly generate a perfect authorized_keys file for the backup machine. Everyone will be able to connect immediately.

(Pro-Tip: You don't even have to click the button manually. You can just add /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys to your rsync script so it copies the file over automatically along with your code and databases!)

The Architectural Warning: The Danger of rsyncing Databases
While rsync is fantastic for copying your production code (TAT/Transport_Toolbox.git), you must be extremely careful using it to copy databases.

The File Corruption Trap: Databases are constantly writing to disk in the background. If your cronjob triggers an rsync at the exact millisecond the database is writing a new row, rsync will copy a half-written file. When .51 tries to boot up that database during a failover, it will crash and say the database is corrupted.

The Safe Way: You cannot safely rsync live database files.

If you are doing this, your script needs to briefly stop the Gitea database service on .50, run the rsync, and start it back up (which causes a few seconds of downtime).

Alternatively, use a database dump command (like pg_dump or mysqldump) to create a safe backup file, and rsync that file instead.

Are you using a standalone database engine like PostgreSQL/MySQL for Gitea, or is it using the default, single-file SQLite setup?

The true mastermind that handles the transition from the OS to the Gitea software is the SSH Daemon (sshd).

Here is the exact, step-by-step breakdown of how sshd acts as the system's traffic controller.

1. The Shared Identity (The git user)
In a GitOps environment, you do not want 50 different developers having 50 different Linux accounts on your .52 server. That is a security nightmare.
Instead, everyone connects as the exact same user: git@transport-toolbox....
The git user is simply the "front door" everyone knocks on.

2. The Interrogation (sshd and authorized_keys)
When a connection hits Port 22, the SSH Daemon (sshd) wakes up.
It says, "Someone is trying to log into the git account. Let me check the git account's guest list."
sshd opens /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys and looks for a mathematical match to the incoming public key.

3. The Transition (The Trapdoor)
This is the most important part of the entire architecture.

If sshd finds a matching key, it is programmed to look at the very beginning of that specific line before it grants access.

Scenario A (A Standard Key): If the line just starts with ssh-ed25519..., sshd follows default Linux behavior. It spawns a standard /bin/bash shell, drops the user into /home/git/, and goes back to sleep. (This is what caused your fatal: not a git repository error earlier).

Scenario B (The Gitea Interceptor): If the line starts with command="/usr/local/bin/gitea...", sshd stops its default behavior. It says, "I am NOT going to open a bash shell. Instead, I am going to execute this exact command, and I am going to pipe the user's secure connection directly into the Gitea program."

Summary: The Maintenance Button
When you click that Maintenance button in the Gitea Web UI, Gitea is not changing network routes or altering the git user. It is simply rewriting that text file to ensure every single key is wrapped in that command= string.

It is essentially printing out a highly specific set of instructions and taping them to the Bouncer's clipboard, so sshd knows exactly which trapdoors to open.

This is the most famous question in the entire field of DevOps: "Why did we break a system that was working perfectly just to make it more complicated?"

It is completely valid to ask this. The reason it feels like things broke is that you didn't just change a few settings—you completely changed the era of your infrastructure. You moved from the "Human Era" to the "Robot Era."

Here is exactly why your old setup worked flawlessly, and why the new rules were suddenly forced upon you.

1. The Human Era (Why the old way worked)
Before you introduced automated runners and Gitea, your workflow relied on human developers.

When a human developer typed git pull, the system was incredibly forgiving:

The HTTPS Pass: If the server didn't know who they were, it just threw a password prompt on the screen. The human typed their password, and the code downloaded.

The Fingerprint Check: If the server's IP changed (like during a failover), SSH would throw a scary warning saying: "Authenticity can't be established! Continue?" The human simply read the warning, typed yes, and moved on.

The Trust Level: In the old days, if someone used an SSH key, the Linux server just dropped them into a raw shell (/home/git/). You trusted your developers not to type rm -rf / and destroy the server.

It "worked perfectly" because human brains were acting as the glue. Humans can dynamically react to password prompts, changing IP addresses, and missing files.

2. The Robot Era (Why it "broke")
The moment you installed act_runner to automate your CI/CD pipelines, everything had to change. You replaced smart humans with incredibly fast, but incredibly dumb, headless robots.

Robots cannot read the screen.

If a robot gets a password prompt, it freezes and crashes.

If a robot gets asked to type yes to confirm a new DNS name, it freezes and crashes.

Because the robots cannot answer questions, you had to move to Strict SSH Key Authentication. The keys had to be mathematically perfect so the server would never ask a question.

3. The Security Lockdown (Why Gitea changed the keys)
Once you moved to SSH keys, you hit a massive security flaw.

If you give an automated runner a raw SSH key, the Linux OS drops it into a raw terminal with full execute permissions. If a hacker compromised your runner, or if a developer wrote a malicious script in the pipeline, they would have full terminal access to your .50 and .51 production machines.

This is why you introduced Gitea and its "Interceptor" keys (command="/usr/local/bin/gitea...").

You traded the "easy" raw Linux access for Zero-Trust Security. Gitea became the Bouncer. Now, even if a robot or a developer connects with a valid SSH key, Gitea physically traps them. It refuses to give them a terminal, and only allows them to push or pull Git code.

4. The High Availability Reality
In the old manual days, if .50 failed, human developers probably just stopped working, called you, and waited for you to fix it. Or, they manually changed their Git URLs to point directly to .51.

Now, you have built an Active-Passive HA Cluster with a floating .52 Virtual IP. You are demanding that when the main server dies, the network instantly flips to the backup server, and the robots just keep pulling code without missing a single millisecond.

That is an enterprise-grade architecture. But to achieve that level of invisible failover, the two servers (.50 and .51) must be mathematically identical clones. That is why the missing authorized_keys file suddenly became a critical issue—the robots expect the backup Bouncer to have the exact same clipboard as the main Bouncer.

The Summary
You didn't break a working system. You upgraded a bicycle into a commercial airliner.

A bicycle (the old way) is easy to maintain, and if a chain falls off, you just put it back on. An airliner (GitOps, HA Clusters, Zero-Trust SSH) is exponentially faster and scales to hundreds of developers, but if a single bolt (an SSH key interceptor) is out of place, the pre-flight checks fail and the plane refuses to take off.

You are building the airliner right now, and you just learned how to wire the cockpit!

This is a classic CI/CD architectural trap, and your two observations are actually the exact same problem showing two different symptoms.

To answer your second question immediately: Yes, the password prompt is an issue. Your automated runner (.51) cannot type passwords. If it hits a password prompt during a deployment, the pipeline will freeze and fail.

Let's break down exactly why you got the Invalid repo name error, and how to fix your deployment workflow.

The Diagnosis: The Bouncer Caught Your Mechanic
In your workflow, the step SSH to .50, Pull, and Reload WSGI implies that your runner is trying to log into .50 and execute standard Linux terminal commands (like cd /app/www..., git pull, and systemctl reload...).

Here is why that crashed:

Your CI/CD script likely tried to log into .50 as the git user.

The Bouncer (sshd) saw the connection and handed it directly to the Gitea Interceptor (because all git user keys are wrapped in that command="..." rule).

Gitea expects a very specific format for Git traffic. Instead, it received a raw string of bash commands (like cd /path && reload WSGI).

Gitea got confused, assumed that string of bash commands was the name of a repository you were trying to access, and threw the error: Gitea: Invalid repo name.

The Golden Rule of Gitea: You can never use the git user to run standard OS commands or deployment scripts. Gitea physically blocks it.

The Solution: The "Service Corridor"
To fix this, we need to stop sending your deployment runner through the front door (the Gitea git user). We need to build a "Service Corridor"—a direct, standard SSH connection from .51 to .50 using a normal Linux user.

Because we know that the Gitea "Maintenance Button" completely overwrites the git user's authorized_keys file, we must use a different user for deployments (like your personal admin account V25KNabih, or a dedicated deploy user).

Here is how to set up the Service Corridor so your runner can restart WSGI without passwords and without Gitea interfering.

Step 1: Generate a Deploy Key on the Runner (.51)
Log into your .51 machine as the user running the act_runner (usually root, runner, or your own user depending on how you installed it).

Generate a fresh SSH key specifically for deployments:

Bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f ~/.ssh/deploy_key
Step 2: Print and Copy the Public Key
Print the key you just created:

Bash
cat ~/.ssh/deploy_key.pub
Copy that string to your clipboard.

Step 3: Add the Key to the .50 Main Server (Raw Linux, NOT Gitea)
Now, log into your .50 Main Server as the standard application user that owns the WSGI service (e.g., V25KNabih or whichever user normally runs the systemctl commands). Do not do this as the git user.

Open that user's authorized keys file:

Bash
vi ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Paste the public key exactly as it is (a standard, raw text string). Do NOT wrap it in a Gitea command. Save and exit.

Step 4: The Manual Handshake
From the .51 machine, do one manual test to the normal user on .50 to clear the known_hosts warning:

Bash
ssh -i ~/.ssh/deploy_key V25KNabih@10.30.121.50
(Replace V25KNabih with the correct username, and 10.30.121.50 with the direct IP of the main server).

Type yes when prompted. You should drop directly into a standard Linux shell without being asked for a password.

Step 5: Update Your CI/CD YAML File
Finally, go into your Gitea repository and update your .gitea/workflows/deploy.yaml file.

Wherever your workflow tells the runner to execute the deployment script, make sure it uses the new user, the direct IP, and the custom deploy key instead of routing through the git user.

Once you point the deployment script to a standard Linux user instead of the git user, it will bypass Gitea entirely, execute the systemctl reload commands perfectly, and your deployment will succeed.

The Bouncer (sshd) sees the git user logging in.

The Bouncer instantly opens the trapdoor and drops the connection directly inside the Gitea application.

The connection never touches the standard Linux bash shell. It never even gets the chance to check if the git user has sudo permissions.

Gitea looks at "systemctl reload wsgi", assumes it's the name of a Git repository, and crashes.

You Must Use the Service Corridor
Gitea will always hijack the git user. It is hardcoded to do so.

To execute standard deployment scripts, you absolutely must use a different Linux user account (like your V25KNabih admin account, or a brand new account named deploy) in your CI/CD YAML file.

If you put the runner's SSH key into the V25KNabih user's authorized_keys file (without the Gitea command wrapper), the Bouncer will say: "Ah, this is a normal human account, no trapdoors here," and will grant the runner a raw bash shell to execute the WSGI restart.

Do you have a standard admin user on .50 that we can safely map the runner's SSH key to, or would you like to walk through creating a dedicated, highly-restricted deploy user just for this pipeline?

As long as you log into .50 as git, the Bouncer (sshd) will always hand your connection to Gitea, and Gitea will always reject your systemctl reload commands.

Here is exactly what you need to do right now to bypass Gitea and fix your deployment pipeline.

Step 1: Change the Target User in your YAML file
You need to tell your CI/CD pipeline to stop logging into the git user on .50, and instead log into your admin user (like V25KNabih).

You are 100% right, and I owe you an apology. If this workflow was working perfectly exactly as it is written, it means I am the one who broke it during our earlier troubleshooting. Let me explain exactly what I made you delete, why it broke this specific step, and how we put it back together so the entire pipeline works perfectly again.

The Confession: Why I Broke Your Pipeline
Your .51 test runner actually has a "split personality." It does two completely different jobs:

The Git Job: It pulls code (which must go through the Gitea Bouncer).

The Deploy Job: It runs systemctl reload wsgi (which must bypass Gitea and go to a raw Linux shell).

Earlier today, when we looked at the /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file on the .52/.50 server, there was a raw, plain-text SSH key sitting at the very bottom.

What that key was doing: That raw key was your runner's "Deploy Pass." It is exactly what allowed the runner to bypass Gitea and successfully restart your WSGI server in the past.

My mistake: Because that raw key was accidentally intercepting the git pull commands and causing the "not a git repository" error, I told you to delete it.

By deleting that raw key, we successfully fixed the git pull step, but I unknowingly slammed the door shut on your deploy step. Now, when your runner tries to restart WSGI, it gets trapped by Gitea, resulting in the Gitea: Invalid repo name error.

The Fix: How to Restore the Deploy Step (Without Changing the YAML)
If you want to keep your workflow working exactly as it was, using the git user, we have to give the runner its "Deploy Pass" back, but we have to do it in a way that doesn't break the git pull step again.

To do this, we are going to give the .51 runner two separate SSH keys. One for Gitea, and one for Deployments.

Step 1: Create a Dedicated Deploy Key on the Runner (.51)
Log into your .51 machine and generate a brand new key specifically for the deploy step:

Bash
sudo -u git ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f /home/git/.ssh/id_deploy
Step 2: Put the Deploy Pass back on the Main Server (.50)
Print the new public key you just made and copy it:

Bash
sudo -u git cat /home/git/.ssh/id_deploy.pub
Log into your .50 Main Server, open /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys, and paste that exact string at the bottom. Do not wrap it in a Gitea command.

Step 3: Tell the Runner to use the right key at the right time
Right now, the runner doesn't know which key to use. We need to write a quick rulebook for it.

On the .51 Runner machine, create an SSH config file:

Bash
sudo -u git vi /home/git/.ssh/config
Paste this exact routing rule inside and save it:

Plaintext
Host 10.30.121.50
  IdentityFile /home/git/.ssh/id_deploy
  IdentitiesOnly yes
Why this restores your perfect workflow:
You do not have to change a single letter of your YAML file.

When your runner does git pull (using the DNS name), it uses its normal Gitea key, hits the interceptor, and pulls the code perfectly.

When your runner does ssh 10.30.121.50 for the deploy step, the SSH config file kicks in. It silently swaps to the id_deploy key, hits the raw Linux key we just put at the bottom of the file, bypasses Gitea entirely, and flawlessly restarts your WSGI server.

Run those three steps to put the raw key back, and your workflow will be exactly as perfect as you remember it.

I see exactly what is happening here! You are running into a classic networking trap.

There is a tiny, but fatal, typo in your command.

The Diagnosis: The Ghost IP
Look closely at the IP address in the screenshot you just uploaded:

Notice the 130? All of your Vodafone internal servers are on the 10.30.x.x subnet. Your actual main server is 10.30.121.50.

When you tell SSH to connect to an IP address that does not exist on your network (or one that is sitting behind a firewall that drops unexpected traffic), it does not immediately print an error. Instead, it sends out a network request and just sits there waiting for a reply that will never come. The terminal will remain completely frozen until the connection finally times out (which usually takes a couple of minutes).

How to unfreeze it right now

Run the command again with the correct IP address:

ssh git@10.30.121.50
Because we just set up that special SSH config file to route your deploy key, as soon as you hit the correct .30 IP address, it should instantly bypass Gitea and drop you right into the raw Linux terminal!

I set the SSL verify to false and when I clone the redirection is an error page

This is a classic HTTPS Git trap, and it tells us exactly where the chain is breaking.

When you run git clone using HTTPS, the Git software expects the server to respond with a very specific, raw data stream (specifically, a file called info/refs).

When you get the error "redirection is an error page" (or sometimes "fatal: expected HTTP 200, got..."), it means Git knocked on the door, but instead of handing Git the code repository, the server handed it a human-readable HTML web page. Because the Git software cannot read HTML, it crashes.

Setting SSL verify to false just told Git to ignore the certificate warnings, but it didn't fix the underlying routing issue.

Since you mentioned earlier that you are using Apache to handle your web traffic in front of Gitea, this is almost certainly an Apache reverse-proxy routing error or a Gitea config mismatch. Let's isolate it.

Step 1: Unmask the Error Page (Client Side)
We need to see exactly what HTML page Apache is trying to force-feed to Git. Is it a 404 Not Found? A 503 Service Unavailable? A 301 Redirect?

Run your clone command again, but inject this environment variable to force Git to print the raw HTTP headers to your screen:

Bash
GIT_CURL_VERBOSE=1 git clone -c http.sslVerify=false https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/TAT/Transport_Toolbox.git
Look closely at the output. You will see a line starting with < HTTP/1.1. Tell me if it says 301 Moved Permanently, 404 Not Found, 502 Bad Gateway, or something else.

Step 2: The Apache Proxy Trap (Server Side)
If Apache is serving an error page, it usually means Apache doesn't know how to route the traffic to the internal Gitea daemon (which usually runs on port 3000).

Log into the machine where Apache is currently running, and check your Apache VirtualHost configuration file for Gitea (often located in /etc/httpd/conf.d/ or /etc/apache2/sites-available/).

You must ensure you have these exact ProxyPass rules set up. If you are missing nocanon, Apache will mangle the Git URLs and break HTTPS cloning:

Apache
<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
    
    # ... your SSL cert configs ...

    # Critical for Git over HTTPS:
    AllowEncodedSlashes NoDecode
    ProxyPreserveHost On
    
    # The 'nocanon' is absolutely required for Gitea routing
    ProxyPass / http://localhost:3000/ nocanon
    ProxyPassReverse / http://localhost:3000/
</VirtualHost>
Step 3: The ROOT_URL Mismatch
Gitea is very stubborn about its own URL. If the URL Apache is using doesn't perfectly match what Gitea thinks its URL is, Gitea will trigger a redirect loop.

Check your Gitea configuration file on the active server:

Bash
sudo vi /etc/gitea/app.ini
Look under the [server] block.
If Apache is serving HTTPS, Gitea's ROOT_URL must say https://, even if Gitea itself is only running on HTTP internally:

Ini, TOML
[server]
DOMAIN = transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
ROOT_URL = https://transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com/
Run that GIT_CURL_VERBOSE=1 command and let me know what HTTP code it spits out. That will point us to the exact broken link in the chain!

Iam clonning on my windows VM and it uses custom Cert

Custom certificates on Windows VMs are a classic headache, but we need to untangle two completely different problems happening here at the same time.

The custom certificate is not what is causing the "redirection is an error page" crash.

1. The Real Blocker: The Routing
When you set http.sslVerify=false, you successfully bypassed the custom certificate warning. Git knocked on the door, Apache answered, but instead of routing Git to the Gitea repository on port 3000, Apache handed Git an HTML error page (like a 404 or a 301 redirect).

Before any SSL fixes will work, you must ensure Apache has the nocanon flag on the active server, exactly as we looked at previously:

Apache
ProxyPass / http://localhost:3000/ nocanon
ProxyPassReverse / http://localhost:3000/
If Apache doesn't have nocanon, it mangles the Git URL, and Git will crash every time, regardless of what certificate you use.

2. Handling the Custom Cert on Windows
Once you confirm Apache is routing correctly, you need to tell your Windows VM how to trust that Vodafone internal certificate so you don't have to constantly use the insecure sslVerify=false flag.

You have two clean ways to solve this on Windows:

Option A: Use the Windows Certificate Store (The Native Way)
If your internal Vodafone IT team has already pushed the custom Root CA certificate to your Windows VM (which they usually do via Group Policy), you can simply tell Git to stop using its own internal certificate list and look at the Windows store instead.

Open Git Bash or Command Prompt as Administrator and run:

Bash
git config --global http.sslBackend schannel
This switches Git to use the native Windows Secure Channel. If the cert is trusted by Windows, Git will now trust it automatically.

Option B: Point Git to the Custom Cert File (The Manual Way)
If the certificate is not in the Windows store, but you have the actual .crt or .pem file downloaded on your VM, you can force Git to use that specific file to verify the connection.

Run this command, replacing the path with wherever you saved the certificate:

Bash
git config --global http.sslCAInfo "C:\Users\V25KNabih\Documents\vodafone-ca.crt"
Are you able to check the Apache VirtualHost config on the .50 server to see if that nocanon flag is missing, or do you want to test the Windows schannel command first to see if it changes the error output?

This are empty repos I want to push in each on of them the environment I use so how can I do it if each one will be in a repo and they are all directories under the same directory secure_venv

To push each subdirectory to its own distinct Gitea repository, you cannot treat the parent secure_venv directory as a single Git repository. Git does not natively push subfolders to separate remote repositories.

Instead, you must initialize each subdirectory as its own independent local Git repository and link it to its corresponding remote.

Here is the exact technical approach to execute this, starting with the manual method for one repository, followed by an automated bash script to process all of them instantly.

The Manual Approach (Step-by-Step)
If you want to handle them individually, perform these steps inside your secure_venv directory. We will use production_ai_venv as the example.

1. Navigate into the specific subdirectory:

Bash
cd /path/to/secure_venv/production_ai_venv
2. Initialize the local Git repository:

Bash
git init
3. Stage and commit the environment files:

Bash
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit: Add production_ai_venv environment"
4. Rename the default branch to main (standard practice):

Bash
git branch -M main
5. Link it to the empty Gitea repository using your SSH configuration:

Bash
git remote add origin git@transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com:TAT/production_ai_venv.git
6. Push the code to Gitea:

Bash
git push -u origin main
(You would then type cd .. and repeat this exact process for the other three directories).

The Automated Approach (Bash Script)
Because you are managing multiple environments with identical workflows, you can automate this entire process.

Navigate to your parent secure_venv directory and run this script. It will loop through the four directories, initialize them, commit the contents, and push them to their respective Gitea remotes using your SSH keys.

1. Create the script inside the secure_venv directory:

Bash
vi push_venvs.sh
2. Paste the following configuration:

Bash
#!/bin/bash

# Define your Gitea Organization/User SSH path
REMOTE_BASE="git@transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com:TAT"

# Define the exact names of the directories (which match the repo names)
REPOS=(
  "production_ai_venv"
  "production_tx_2ndline_venv"
  "production_venv"
  "production_performance_transport_venv"
)

# Loop through each directory and push to Gitea
for REPO in "${REPOS[@]}"; do
    echo "========================================"
    echo "Processing Directory: $REPO"
    echo "========================================"
    
    # Check if directory exists before proceeding
    if [ ! -d "$REPO" ]; then
        echo "Error: Directory '$REPO' not found. Skipping..."
        continue
    fi

    # Enter the directory
    cd "$REPO"
    
    # Initialize, Commit, and Push
    git init
    git add .
    git commit -m "Initial commit of $REPO environment"
    git branch -M main
    
    # Remove origin if it accidentally exists from a previous test
    git remote remove origin 2>/dev/null
    
    # Add the specific Gitea remote and push
    git remote add origin "$REMOTE_BASE/$REPO.git"
    git push -u origin main
    
    # Return to the parent directory for the next loop
    cd ..
    echo "Success: $REPO pushed to Gitea."
    echo ""
done
3. Make the script executable and run it:

Bash
chmod +x push_venvs.sh
./push_venvs.sh
This will cleanly map each physical subdirectory to its designated Git backend on your Gitea server.
