This is a classic High Availability permission clash. Your rsync command is actually perfectly formatted, but it is running headfirst into a Linux ownership wall.

The Diagnosis: The Ownership Clash
Your Gitea data directory (/app/www/gitea/) and all the files inside it are owned by the git user.

When you run your command, you are logging into the .51 Backup Machine as the rsync user. The rsync user is looking at the git user's files and trying to delete them (because of the --delete flag) and alter their timestamps and Access Control Lists (because of the -a and -A flags).

The Linux OS on .51 steps in and says: "You are 'rsync'. You do not own these 'git' files. Permission Denied."

The Hidden Trap
In a normal Linux environment, the easy fix would be to just change your command to log in as the git user (ssh -l git).

You cannot do that here. If you remember the "Bouncer" trap we solved earlier, if you try to rsync over SSH as the git user, the .51 SSH daemon will instantly hand your connection to Gitea. Gitea will look at the rsync data stream, get completely confused, and crash with that exact same Gitea: Invalid repo name error.

The Fix: Elevate the Remote Receiver
We need to keep using the rsync user for the SSH connection so we bypass Gitea. But once the rsync user gets inside the .51 machine, we need it to briefly put on a root disguise so it has the authority to overwrite the git files.

We do this using a brilliant built-in rsync flag called --rsync-path.

Here is the exact blueprint to fix this permanently.

Step 1: Allow passwordless sudo for rsync on the Backup Machine
We need to tell the .51 machine that the rsync user is allowed to run the rsync command as root, without being prompted for a password (otherwise your automated backup script will freeze).

Log into your .51 Backup Machine.

Open the sudoers file safely:

Bash
sudo visudo
Scroll to the very bottom of the file and paste this exact line:

Plaintext
rsync ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/rsync
Save and exit the file.

Step 2: Update your rsync command on the Main Machine
Now, go back to your .50 Main Machine.

You are going to run the exact same command you tried earlier, but we are injecting --rsync-path="sudo rsync". This tells the destination machine to execute the receiving end of the file transfer as the root user.

Run this:

Bash
sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete --rsync-path="sudo rsync" -e 'ssh -l rsync' /app/www/gitea/ 10.30.121.51:/app/www/gitea/
The Result
The command will connect as rsync (bypassing Gitea's trapdoor), instantly elevate to root on the backup server, and flawlessly synchronize, delete, and apply the exact git ACLs and timestamps without a single "Operation not permitted" error.

I have a toolbox_admin group that Rsync is a member in it

That is an excellent detail to bring up. Using dedicated administrative groups like toolbox_admin is exactly how enterprise Linux environments should be structured.

It makes perfect logical sense to think: "If the rsync user is in the admin group, it should have permission to overwrite the files, so I shouldn't need sudo."

However, in the context of an Active-Passive High Availability (HA) Cluster, relying on group permissions will actually break your backup server.

Here is exactly why the toolbox_admin group is not enough to solve the rsync error, and why you still need that --rsync-path="sudo rsync" trick.

The Problem: Editing vs. Owning
There is a massive difference in Linux between having permission to edit a file and having permission to give a file away.

Let's assume you give the toolbox_admin group full read/write access to /app/www/gitea/.
If your rsync user copies a file over, that file will successfully write to the disk. But because the rsync user wrote it, the file will be owned by rsync.

In your command, you are using the -a (Archive) flag: rsync -arupAg.
The Archive flag tells rsync: "Make a mathematically perfect clone. Keep the exact timestamps, keep the exact ACLs, and most importantly, keep the exact file owner."

The "Chown" Wall
Because the files on the .50 main server are owned by the git user, your rsync command arrives at the .51 backup server and tries to do this:

Write the new file to the disk.

Run a hidden chown git:git command to hand ownership of the file to the git user (so the backup matches the main).

This is where Linux blocks you. For security reasons, Linux dictates that a standard user cannot give files away to another user. Even if you are in the toolbox_admin group, you are not allowed to change a file's owner to git.

Only one user in the entire Linux operating system has the authority to run chown and assign files to other users: root.

The HA Cluster Requirement
If you drop the -o (preserve owner) flag to avoid the error, the files will copy over successfully, but they will be owned by rsync:toolbox_admin on the backup server.

If your .50 server catches fire, and the VIP switches to .51, Gitea will boot up, look at /app/www/gitea/, and realize it is running as the git user, but all the files are owned by rsync. Gitea will crash because it cannot read its own database or repository files.

The Verdict
Your toolbox_admin group is great for human administrators running day-to-day commands.

But for a true HA failover, the two servers must be perfect cryptographic clones of each other, right down to the specific user ownership of every single text file. To achieve that perfect clone over SSH, the receiving end of the rsync pipe must temporarily hold root privileges.

I highly recommend proceeding with the visudo and --rsync-path="sudo rsync" solution we mapped out previously. It is the industry standard for safely bypassing this exact Linux ownership restriction in automated failover pipelines.

okay but there are toolbox_admin are in both

Having the toolbox_admin group perfectly mirrored on both the main and backup servers is fantastic architectural design. That proves you are building a true High Availability cluster where the OS configurations match perfectly.

However, having matching groups across both servers still does not bypass the specific error you are hitting.

This comes down to a hardcoded security rule inside the Linux kernel itself, and how the Gitea application behaves. Here is why mirroring the group doesn't solve the file ownership problem.

1. The Linux Kernel Rule (CAP_CHOWN)
Linux security is extremely rigid about who is allowed to change the owner of a file.

What you can do: Because rsync is in the toolbox_admin group, it is legally allowed to assign files to that group. (e.g., chgrp toolbox_admin file.txt).

What you cannot do: A normal user is never allowed to give a file away to another user. It does not matter if they share a group, share a folder, or share a department. The rsync user cannot run chown git file.txt.

Only one account holds the kernel capability to give files to other users: root.

Because your rsync -a command tells the system to perfectly preserve the original file owner (which is git), the rsync user on .51 tries to hand the file to git and the Linux kernel immediately slaps it down with: Operation not permitted.

2. The Gitea "Group Permissions" Trap
You might be thinking: "What if I just tell rsync to stop trying to preserve the owner? What if I let the files be owned by rsync, but make sure the toolbox_admin group has full Read/Write permissions so git can still access them?"

You can do this by removing the -a (Archive) flag and using specific flags instead, but it will break Gitea.

Gitea and Git are highly sensitive to file ownership, not just group access:

The SSH Bouncer: If the /home/git/.ssh/ directory and the authorized_keys file are not strictly owned by the git user, the SSH daemon will assume the system has been hacked. It will completely disable key authentication, and all your runners will be locked out.

Git Security: Recent versions of Git have a built-in security feature called safe.directory. If a user (like git) tries to read a repository that is owned by a completely different user (like rsync), Git will immediately throw a fatal error and refuse to touch the code, even if the group permissions technically allow it.

The Verdict: There is No Group Bypass
To have a fully functional Gitea backup, the files on .51 must be strictly owned by the git user, not just accessible via the toolbox_admin group.

Because rsync cannot give files to git without being root, you have exactly two choices to make this pipeline work:

Choice A (The Standard Way): Use the --rsync-path="sudo rsync" trick we discussed previously so rsync can briefly act as root and set the correct git ownership.

Choice B (The Messy Way): Run the rsync without preserving owners, let everything land as owned by rsync, and then write a secondary automated script on the .51 server that runs as root every 5 minutes to recursively chown -R git:git the entire Gitea folder.

Choice A is significantly cleaner and less prone to race conditions during a sudden failover!

Now suppose that we are building this HA Cluster how to correctly set everything up

Stepping back to look at the macro architecture is exactly the right move. When building enterprise-grade High Availability, piecemeal troubleshooting usually just creates fragile edge cases. If you are engineering a Keepalived failover cluster for a production team, the backup machine cannot just be a copy—it must be a perfect, seamless imposter.

When Keepalived violently swings that .52 Virtual IP from .50 over to .51, neither the human developers nor the automated runners should even realize a server just died.

To achieve zero-downtime GitOps failover, you must perfectly synchronize three distinct layers: The System Identity, The Application Data, and The Database.

Here is the complete, no-fluff architectural blueprint for correctly configuring this HA cluster.

Phase 1: The System Identity Clone (The Missing Link)
This is the exact layer you are asking about, and it is where 90% of HA failovers break.

If .51 takes over the .52 IP, but it presents different cryptographic keys to the network, every single automated pipeline and developer will get a massive, fatal WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED (Man-in-the-Middle) error, and SSH will permanently lock them out.

You must clone two things at the OS level:

1. The SSH Host Keys (The Server's Passport)
You must physically copy the SSH Host Keys from .50 to .51 so the backup server proves it is the same machine.

Action: Copy all files matching /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key and /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key.pub from .50 and overwrite the ones on .51.

Restart: Run systemctl restart sshd on .51 after copying.

2. The git User's Keys (The Bouncer's Clipboard)
As we established, Gitea controls the git user's authorized_keys file. You must sync this directory so the backup server knows who is allowed in.

Action: Add a line to your synchronization script that copies /home/git/.ssh/ from .50 to .51.

Permission Enforcement: Ensure this directory is strictly owned by git:git on the backup server.

Phase 2: The Application State (The Vault)
This is your /app/www/gitea/ directory. It holds the physical Git repositories, user avatars, and custom configurations (app.ini).

Action: You must use the elevated rsync approach we discussed to ensure the file ownership remains flawlessly attributed to the git user.

The Command: ```bash
sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete --rsync-path="sudo rsync" -e 'ssh -l rsync' /app/www/gitea/ 10.30.121.51:/app/www/gitea/


Phase 3: The Brain (The Database)
Gitea's memory—who owns what Deploy Key, pull request history, and repository mapping—lives entirely in its database. You cannot safely use rsync on a live, writing database file. If .50 crashes mid-write while rsync is reading, your .51 backup will boot up with a corrupted database.

Action: Your failover strategy must include a safe database replication or dumping mechanism. If Gitea crashes on .50, the Gitea service on .51 must connect to a database that holds the exact same rows up to the second.

Phase 4: The Keepalived Trigger
Keepalived is just a network router; it doesn't actually start or stop your web services.

When Keepalived on .51 detects that .50 is dead, it must execute a notify_master script.

Action: Configure Keepalived on .51 to run a bash script the moment it assumes the MASTER state. This script should simply execute:

Bash
systemctl start gitea
systemctl reload httpd
(Note: Gitea should remain stopped on .51 during normal operations to prevent split-brain database writes. It only wakes up when Keepalived pulls the trigger).

If you lock down those four phases, your failover will be invisible and mathematically perfect. To finalize this architecture, how is the Gitea database currently configured—is it a local SQLite file sitting inside that /app/www/gitea directory, or are you running a dedicated MySQL/PostgreSQL instance that we need to configure replication for?

it is stored in a local MySQL database

This is the final, critical piece of the puzzle. The fact that you are using a local MySQL database changes the entire failover strategy.

Because MySQL is constantly locking tables and writing to disk, you can never, ever use rsync to copy the /var/lib/mysql directory. If Keepalived triggers an rsync while MySQL is processing a transaction, the .51 database will boot up completely corrupted.

To achieve true zero-downtime failover, you must implement MySQL Master-Master (Active-Active) Replication.

In this setup, both databases are running 24/7. When .50 gets a new pull request, it instantly streams that data to .51 in the background. If .50 dies, .51 already has the exact data. When .50 wakes back up, .51 streams the missed data back to .50.

Here is the exact architectural blueprint to build the Master-Master replication specifically for your .50 and .51 nodes.

Phase 1: The Collision Prevention (The my.cnf Config)
If a momentary network glitch causes a "split-brain" where both servers think they are active, they might both try to create a new user and assign it Database ID 105. When they sync, the database will crash from a Primary Key collision.

We solve this using mathematical offsets: .50 will only create Odd IDs, and .51 will only create Even IDs.

1. On your .50 Main Server:
Open /etc/my.cnf (or /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf) and add this exactly under the [mysqld] block:

Ini, TOML
[mysqld]
bind-address = 0.0.0.0
server-id = 1
log_bin = /var/log/mysql/mysql-bin.log
binlog_do_db = gitea
auto_increment_increment = 2
auto_increment_offset = 1
Restart MySQL: sudo systemctl restart mysqld

2. On your .51 Backup Server:
Open the same config file and add this:

Ini, TOML
[mysqld]
bind-address = 0.0.0.0
server-id = 2
log_bin = /var/log/mysql/mysql-bin.log
binlog_do_db = gitea
auto_increment_increment = 2
auto_increment_offset = 2
Restart MySQL: sudo systemctl restart mysqld

Phase 2: The Diplomatic Immunity (Replication Users)
The databases need secure permission to talk to each other over the network.

Run this exact SQL command on BOTH .50 and .51 (log into MySQL as root):

SQL
CREATE USER 'replicator'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'YourStrongPassword123!';
GRANT REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'replicator'@'%';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;
Phase 3: The Brain Transplant (Initial Sync)
Right now, .50 has all your Gitea data, and .51 is empty. We need to freeze .50, dump its brain, and inject it into .51 so they start from the exact same mathematical position.

1. On the .50 Main Server:
Log into MySQL and lock the tables to prevent changes during the backup:

SQL
FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK;
SHOW MASTER STATUS;
(Write down the File name and Position number it outputs. You need them in Step 4).

Keep that SQL window open (closing it unlocks the tables!). Open a second terminal to .50 and create the dump:

Bash
mysqldump -u root -p gitea > /tmp/gitea_backup.sql
Go back to your first SQL window and unlock the tables so your developers can keep working:

SQL
UNLOCK TABLES;
2. Move the Brain to .51:
Copy the dump file to the backup server:

Bash
scp /tmp/gitea_backup.sql V25KNabih@10.30.121.51:/tmp/
3. On the .51 Backup Server:
Import the brain into the empty database:

Bash
mysql -u root -p gitea < /tmp/gitea_backup.sql
Phase 4: Crossing the Streams
Now we tell them to start listening to each other.

1. Tell .51 to listen to .50:
Log into MySQL on .51 and run this (using the File and Position you wrote down earlier):

SQL
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO 
  SOURCE_HOST='10.30.121.50',
  SOURCE_USER='replicator',
  SOURCE_PASSWORD='YourStrongPassword123!',
  SOURCE_LOG_FILE='mysql-bin.000001', 
  SOURCE_LOG_POS=456; 

START REPLICA;
SHOW REPLICA STATUS \G;
(Look for Replica_IO_Running: Yes and Replica_SQL_Running: Yes. Note: if you are on an older MySQL/MariaDB, the syntax is CHANGE MASTER TO MASTER_HOST... and START SLAVE)

2. Tell .50 to listen to .51:
First, find out exactly where .51 is at by running SHOW MASTER STATUS; on .51. Write down its File and Position.
Then, log into MySQL on .50 and run the reverse:

SQL
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO 
  SOURCE_HOST='10.30.121.51',
  SOURCE_USER='replicator',
  SOURCE_PASSWORD='YourStrongPassword123!',
  SOURCE_LOG_FILE='mysql-bin.000001', 
  SOURCE_LOG_POS=123; 

START REPLICA;
The Architecture Summary
You now have a flawless, military-grade failover pipeline:

MySQL runs 24/7 on both machines, silently syncing data across the .50 and .51 IPs in real-time.

Keepalived watches .50. If it dies, the .52 VIP teleports to .51.

Your Keepalived Script on .51 instantly starts the Gitea service.

Gitea wakes up, looks at /app/www/gitea/ (which your elevated rsync kept perfectly updated with git ownership), and looks at localhost:3306 (which MySQL replication kept perfectly synced).

Because the Host Keys, the SSH Bouncer clipboard, the physical files, and the database are mathematically identical, the developers and the automated runners will continue pushing and pulling code without ever knowing a server died.

If a disaster happens, you simply unzip all_database.sql.gz on .51 and import it. Your "Warm Standby" database strategy is completely sound.

2. rsync_app.sh (The File Synchronization)
This is where we need to apply the fixes. I have updated your script to do two critical things:

Fix the Gitea Permission Error: I injected the --rsync-path="sudo rsync" command into the Gitea line. (I also removed the * at the end of /app/www/gitea/, which is a best practice to ensure rsync copies hidden files like .git at the root folder level).

Add the Bouncer's Clipboard: I added a brand new line to sync /home/git/.ssh/. This ensures the .51 server knows exactly which SSH keys are allowed to access Gitea.

Here is your final, complete rsync_app.sh script:

Bash
#!/bin/bash

VAR=`nmcli | grep 10.30.121.52/29`

if [[ "$VAR" =~ "inet4 10.30.121.52/29" ]]
then
  # 1. Sync the Main App, EXCLUDING the read-only bind mounts
  sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete \
    --exclude='venv' \
    --exclude='AI_venv' \
    -e 'ssh -l rsync' /app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/* 10.30.121.51:/app/www/Transport_Toolbox/app/
  
  # 2. Sync the SFTP directory, EXCLUDING its read-only bind mount
  sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete \
    --exclude='transport/venv' \
    -e 'ssh -l rsync' /sftp/* 10.30.121.51:/sftp/
  
  # 3. Sync Global Access (Exclude RO mount)
  sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete \
    --exclude='Tx_2ndline_venv' \
    -e 'ssh -l rsync' /app/www/Global_Access/* 10.30.121.51:/app/www/Global_Access/
  
  # 4. Sync Gitea Data (UPDATED: Added sudo rsync path and fixed trailing slash)
  sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete --rsync-path="sudo rsync" -e 'ssh -l rsync' /app/www/gitea/ 10.30.121.51:/app/www/gitea/

  # 5. NEW: Sync Gitea SSH Access Keys (The Bouncer's Clipboard)
  sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete --rsync-path="sudo rsync" -e 'ssh -l rsync' /home/git/.ssh/ 10.30.121.51:/home/git/.ssh/

  # 6. Sync the actual physical Secure Vault directly
  sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete -e 'ssh -l rsync' /app/www/secure_env/* 10.30.121.51:/app/www/secure_env/
fi

echo "$(date +%F) Rsync_Process"

It is completely normal to look at an rsync command and feel like you are reading alphabet soup. rsync is one of the oldest and most powerful tools in Linux, but its syntax is notoriously dense.

Let's dissect your exact command piece by piece so you know exactly what is happening under the hood.

Here is the master command we are breaking down:
sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete --rsync-path="sudo rsync" -e 'ssh -l rsync' /app/www/gitea/ 10.30.121.51:/app/www/gitea/

1. The Disguise (sudo -u rsync)
By default, if you run a command as V25KNabih, the system executes it using your personal permissions. This prefix forces the local .50 machine to temporarily switch your identity to the rsync user before executing the rest of the line.

2. The Alphabet Soup (-arupAg)
These are the core behavioral flags. Fun fact: because you are using -a, half of these flags are technically redundant, but they are perfectly harmless to keep!

-a (Archive Mode): This is the "God Mode" flag. It tells rsync to be a perfect mirror. It automatically turns on recursion (looks inside all folders), and strictly preserves file Owners, Groups, Timestamps, Symlinks, and Permissions.

-r (Recursive): Looks inside subdirectories. (Redundant because -a does this automatically).

-u (Update): This tells rsync to skip any files on the .51 backup that are mathematically newer than the files on .50. It saves bandwidth and prevents overwriting emergency changes made on the backup server.

-p (Preserve Permissions): Keeps the exact Read/Write/Execute bits. (Redundant because -a does this).

-A (Preserve ACLs): This is a crucial one. Standard Linux permissions (Owner/Group/World) are sometimes not enough. Access Control Lists (ACLs) allow complex rules like "Let User X read, but User Y write." The -a flag does not copy ACLs, so you must explicitly include -A.

-g (Preserve Group): Keeps the group ownership the same. (Redundant because -a does this).

3. The Mirror Enforcer (--delete)
Without this flag, rsync only adds or updates files. If a developer deleted a repository on the .50 main server, that deleted repository would sit on the .51 backup server forever, slowly filling up your hard drive. --delete tells rsync: "If a file is missing on the source, destroy it on the destination."

4. The Remote Elevator (--rsync-path="sudo rsync")
This is the magic trick we added to bypass the Linux kernel's file ownership rules. Normally, rsync logs into the remote machine and just runs the rsync receiver program. This flag intercepts that process and says: "When you get to the .51 machine, run sudo rsync instead." This instantly elevates the receiver to root, giving it the authority to assign the git user as the owner of the copied files.

5. The Transport Vehicle (-e 'ssh -l rsync')
The -e flag stands for "execute." It tells rsync exactly how to travel across the network.
In this case, it says: "Do not use a standard TCP connection. Wrap all the data inside an encrypted SSH tunnel, and log into the remote .51 server specifically as the user rsync (-l rsync)."

6. The Source and Destination
/app/www/gitea/: The folder you are copying from. Note the trailing slash / at the end! In rsync, a trailing slash means "copy the contents of this folder". If you forgot the slash, it would create a folder inside a folder (e.g., /app/www/gitea/gitea/).

10.30.121.51:/app/www/gitea/: The target IP and the exact directory to drop the files into.

Now that the architecture is fully engineered and the scripts are locked in, how frequently are you planning to schedule this script via cron to run in the background?

The Inquiry is on what does the database handle and what does the the directory /app/www/gitea handles ?

To understand exactly how to secure your GitOps infrastructure, you have to separate Gitea into two distinct halves: the Physical Vault (the directory) and the Ledger (the database).

They do entirely different jobs, and one is completely useless without the other.

Here is the exact technical breakdown of what lives where.

1. The Directory (/app/www/gitea/)
This is the Physical Vault. It stores the actual, heavy byte-data of your infrastructure. It does not know who owns the data; it only stores the raw files.

If you open this directory, you will find:

The Raw Git Repositories (data/gitea-repositories/): This is the most critical folder. It contains the actual .git directories for every project (your code, branches, commits, and tags).

Large File Storage (LFS): If your developers push large binary files, compiled assets, or machine learning models via Git LFS, they are physically saved here, not in the database.

User Uploads & Attachments: Any images, PDFs, or logs attached to an Issue or Pull Request in the Web UI are saved to the physical disk here.

Avatars: The profile pictures for your users.

The Configuration File (custom/conf/app.ini): The master settings file that tells Gitea what port to run on, what domain name to use, and exactly how to connect to the MySQL database.

2. The Database (MySQL)
This is the Ledger (The Brain). It stores the metadata, relationships, and state of the system. It does not hold any actual code; it holds the rules for accessing the code.

If you query the MySQL database, you will find:

Users and Authentication: Usernames, email addresses, password hashes, and Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) secrets.

The VIP List (SSH Keys): The actual strings of every public SSH key uploaded by your developers and automated runners. (This is the table Gitea queries when you click the "Update authorized_keys" maintenance button).

Repository Metadata: It tracks that the repository production_ai_venv exists, and maps it to the specific physical folder path in the Directory.

Access Control: The strict mapping of which users belong to which Teams, and which Teams have Read/Write/Admin access to which repositories.

Social and Workflow Data: The text of every Issue, Pull Request comment, code review approval, and webhook configuration.

How They Work Together (The git pull Workflow)
When your .51 runner attempts to pull code from the .50 main server, here is how the two halves interact in milliseconds:

The Database Check: The SSH Bouncer intercepts the runner and asks Gitea, "Is this SSH key allowed?" Gitea queries the MySQL Database. The database confirms the key belongs to an active runner and has Read permissions for production_ai_venv.

The Directory Fetch: Now that permission is granted, Gitea reaches into the Physical Directory (/app/www/gitea/data/gitea-repositories/TAT/production_ai_venv.git), grabs the actual raw code files, and streams them back to the runner.

Why This Matters for Your Backups
If you only back up the Directory, you will have all your code, but if a server dies, Gitea will boot up with zero users, zero passwords, and zero SSH keys. Nobody will be able to log in to see the code.

If you only back up the Database, Gitea will boot up, recognize all your users, and show all your repositories in the Web UI. But the moment a developer clicks on a repository, Gitea will throw a 500 Internal Server Error because the physical code folders it is looking for do not exist on the hard drive.

By perfectly syncing /app/www/gitea/ via rsync and syncing the MySQL database via mysqldump, you ensure the Ledger and the Vault remain perfectly aligned.

Okay another thing the App_Rsync.sh there are things that ends with /* and with / only what is the difference isn't /* supposed to copy all ?

This is one of the most dangerous and misunderstood traps in the entire Linux ecosystem. rsync handles paths very differently than standard commands like cp or mv.

You are asking the exact right question. The difference between / and /* in rsync is the difference between a complete backup and a broken server.

Here is exactly how rsync and the Linux shell interpret these symbols, and why I specifically changed your script to remove the *.

The Three rsync Path Rules
Let’s use your Gitea directory (/app/www/gitea) as the example.

Scenario 1: No Slash at the end (/app/www/gitea)
What it means: "Copy this literal folder and put it inside the destination."

The Result: If you sync to 10.30.121.51:/app/www/gitea/, it will create a nested folder: /app/www/gitea/gitea/. (This ruins your paths).

Scenario 2: Trailing Slash (/app/www/gitea/) — The Correct Way
What it means: "Do not copy the folder itself. Instead, look inside this folder, grab every single thing, and dump it into the destination."

The Result: It perfectly mirrors the contents, including all standard files, folders, and critically, all hidden files (like .git, .ssh, or .env).

Scenario 3: The Asterisk (/app/www/gitea/*) — The Trap
What it means: When you use *, rsync doesn't actually see the asterisk. Your Linux bash shell intercepts the command before rsync runs, expands the * into a list of all visible files, and feeds that list to rsync.

The Trap: By default in Linux, the * wildcard ignores hidden files.

The Result: If you use /app/www/gitea/*, rsync will copy custom/, data/, and log/. But it will completely ignore critical hidden files sitting at the root level, leaving your backup incomplete.

Why I Changed Your Script
In your original rsync_app.sh, you had:
rsync ... /app/www/gitea/* 10.30.121.51:/app/www/gitea/

If Gitea ever drops a hidden configuration file (like a .env or a .gitea directory) at the root of that folder, your /* command would completely ignore it. When your .50 server dies, .51 would boot up missing those hidden files and crash.

By changing it strictly to a trailing slash:
rsync ... /app/www/gitea/ 10.30.121.51:/app/www/gitea/

We bypass the bash shell's wildcard rules entirely. We give rsync total control, and rsync guarantees that absolutely 100% of the contents (hidden or visible) are cloned to the backup machine.

For enterprise backups, always trust the trailing slash /, and never trust the asterisk /*.

Okay there is an error with the script

rsync: send_files failed to open "/app/www/gitea/data/indexers/issues.bleve/store/000000000bd6.zap": Permission denied (13)

rsync error: some files/attrs were not transferred (see previous errors) (code 23) at main.c(1189) [sender=3.1.3]

This is the exact reason why High Availability pipelines are notoriously tricky. You successfully fixed the Receiver (.51), but now the Sender (.50) is failing.

If you look at the very end of your error message, you will see [sender=3.1.3]. This tells us exactly where the chain broke.

The Diagnosis: The Sender is Blind
Because your command starts with sudo -u rsync rsync, you are forcing the .50 main machine to run the local rsync scanner as the rsync user.

However, the file it crashed on (data/indexers/issues.bleve/store/...) is a highly secure, locked-down text indexing database owned exclusively by the git user. The local rsync user does not have the Linux permission to read that file, so it throws Permission denied (13) and aborts the transfer.

The Elegant Fix: Split the Privileges
We need the local rsync scanner to run as root so it can read every single file on the hard drive. But, we still need the network connection (SSH) to run as rsync so we bypass Gitea's Bouncer on the remote side.

We can achieve this by dropping the sudo -u rsync from the beginning of the line, and moving it inside the -e (SSH) flag instead.

Change your Gitea line in rsync_app.sh to this exact command:

Bash
sudo rsync -arupAg --delete --rsync-path="sudo rsync" -e 'sudo -u rsync ssh -l rsync' /app/www/gitea/ 10.30.121.51:/app/www/gitea/
Why this is mathematically airtight:
sudo rsync: The local scanner runs as root. It easily reads the locked bleve indexes without permission errors.

-e 'sudo -u rsync ssh -l rsync': When it is time to transmit the data over the network, root temporarily drops its privileges and fires up the SSH tunnel as the rsync user. This ensures it uses the correct SSH keys and bypasses the Gitea interceptor on .51.

--rsync-path="sudo rsync": Once the data lands on .51, it elevates back to root to properly assign the git ownership to the restored files.

Update that single line, and your Gitea vault will sync flawlessly from end to end!

what is the sshl -l rsync ?

Ah, there's a tiny typo there—it is actually ssh, not sshl!

The snippet ssh -l rsync is the command used to open the secure tunnel between your two servers. Let's break down exactly what those two pieces mean and why they are critical for your backup pipeline:

ssh (Secure Shell): This is the standard Linux program used to securely log into another machine over the network.

-l rsync (Login Name): The -l flag stands for "login". It explicitly tells the SSH program: "When you knock on the door of the destination server, tell them your name is rsync."

Why this was mandatory for your script:
Remember how we had to change the local scanner to run as root so it could read those locked Gitea index files? (The sudo rsync part).

If we didn't include -l rsync, the SSH command would default to the user that is currently running the command. Since root is running the command, SSH would secretly translate your connection attempt to: ssh root@10.30.121.51.

That would cause two massive problems for your High Availability setup:

Most enterprise Linux servers (especially in environments like Vodafone) are configured to block direct root logins over SSH for security reasons. The connection would be instantly rejected.

We specifically set up the SSH keys and the visudo bypass on the .51 machine for the rsync user, not the root user.

By injecting -l rsync, you are telling the local root user on .50: "Scan the local hard drive with your God-mode permissions so you don't get 'Permission Denied', but when you transmit the data over the network, put on the rsync nametag so the .51 server recognizes you and lets you in."

It is functionally the exact same thing as writing rsync@10.30.121.51.

sudo -u rsync rsync -arupAg --delete --rsync-path="sudo rsync" -e 'ssh -l rsync' /home/git/.ssh/ 10.30.121.51:/home/git/.ssh/

Authorized uses only. All activity may be monitored and reported.

rsync: change_dir "/home/git/.ssh" failed: Permission denied (13)

rsync error: some files/attrs were not transferred (see previous errors) (code 23) at main.c(1189) [sender=3.1.3]

This is the exact same "Sender is Blind" trap we just solved for the /app/www/gitea/ directory!

If you look closely at your command, you are still using the old syntax (sudo -u rsync rsync) for this specific line.

Because /home/git/.ssh/ is the Bouncer's clipboard, Linux locks that folder down incredibly tight (usually with 700 permissions, meaning absolutely no one except the git user can even look inside it). When the local rsync user tries to cd into that directory to scan it, the OS immediately rejects it with Permission denied (13).

The Fix
You just need to apply the exact same Split Privileges fix to this line that we applied to the Gitea data line.

We need the local scanner to run as root, but the network tunnel to run as rsync.

Change your command to this:

Bash
sudo rsync -arupAg --delete --rsync-path="sudo rsync" -e 'sudo -u rsync ssh -l rsync' /home/git/.ssh/ 10.30.121.51:/home/git/.ssh/
Script Check
Make sure both of those lines in your rsync_app.sh script match this exact structure.

sudo rsync ... at the very beginning.

-e 'sudo -u rsync ssh -l rsync' in the middle.

Once you update that line, root will bypass the local folder lock, rsync will securely cross the network, and the SSH keys will clone perfectly.

So -e executes on my local machine or does it execute on the backup machine ?

The -e flag executes entirely on your local machine (the .50 Main Server).

Here is exactly the execution order of how rsync handles the network connection under the hood.

When you run your command, the local rsync program starts up and needs to figure out how to transport the data to the backup server. The -e (execute) flag is simply the local rsync program asking the local Linux OS: "What command should I run right here, right now, to build the network bridge?"

The Local Trigger (-e): Your local .50 machine physically executes sudo -u rsync ssh -l rsync. This establishes the outgoing SSH tunnel from .50 and knocks on the door of .51.

The Remote Trigger (--rsync-path): This is the exact opposite of -e. The --rsync-path flag is what gets sent through that SSH tunnel. It tells the remote .51 machine: "Now that the tunnel is open, execute sudo rsync on your end to receive my files."

The Golden Rule of Rsync Networking
-e defines the Transport Vehicle built and executed on the local machine.

--rsync-path defines the Receiver Program executed on the remote machine.

Because that vehicle is built locally, your local .50 machine needs the correct permissions to run that ssh command. That is exactly why we had to inject sudo -u rsync into the -e string earlier—so the local root scanner wouldn't try to build a root SSH tunnel and get rejected by the remote Bouncer.

Let's cut right to the chase and permanently rebuild the "Dual Key" architecture.

As we discovered during our previous troubleshooting, your runner on the Backup VM (.51) has a split personality: it needs to do a git pull (which must be caught by Gitea) and an ssh deployment (which must bypass Gitea entirely).

To fix this without changing a single line of your perfectly working deployment YAML, we need to give the runner a dedicated "Deploy Pass" and tell it exactly when to use it.

Here is the exact, step-by-step blueprint to rebuild this from scratch.

Phase 1: Create the Deploy Key (On the .51 Backup VM)
We must generate a brand new SSH key on the runner machine strictly for deployments, completely separate from its normal Git operations.

Log into your .51 Backup VM.

Generate the dedicated deployment key as the git user (press Enter to accept the defaults, leaving the passphrase empty):

Bash
sudo -u git ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f /home/git/.ssh/id_deploy
Print the public key to your screen and copy the entire string to your clipboard:

Bash
sudo -u git cat /home/git/.ssh/id_deploy.pub
Phase 2: Plant the Deploy Pass (On the .50 Main VM)
We now need to give this specific key raw, unfiltered access to the .50 machine so it bypasses the Gitea "Bouncer".

Log into your .50 Main VM.

Open the git user's authorized keys file:

Bash
sudo -u git vi /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys
Scroll to the very bottom of the file.

Paste the public key exactly as you copied it. * Critical Check: Do not wrap this specific key in the command="/usr/local/bin/gitea..." string that you see on the other lines. It must be a raw SSH key string starting with ssh-ed25519.

Save and exit the file.

Phase 3: Set the Traffic Rules (On the .51 Backup VM)
Right now, the runner has the key, but it doesn't know when to use it. We must force it to use the new id_deploy key whenever it runs your YAML's deployment command.

Go back to your .51 Backup VM.

Create or edit the SSH configuration file for the git user:

Bash
sudo -u git vi /home/git/.ssh/config
Paste this exact routing block inside the file:

Plaintext
Host 10.30.121.50
  IdentityFile /home/git/.ssh/id_deploy
  IdentitiesOnly yes
Save and exit the file.

Fix the file permissions so SSH doesn't complain:

Bash

Phase 4: The Final Handshake Test
Before running your pipeline, do one manual test from the .51 Backup VM to ensure the tunnel is working and to clear the network warning.

Run this command:

Bash
sudo -u git ssh 10.30.121.50
If it asks "Are you sure you want to continue connecting?", type yes.

If everything is configured correctly, it will instantly bypass the Gitea: Invalid repo name error and drop you directly into a standard Linux terminal on .50.

Type exit to close the connection.

Once you complete that test, trigger your CI/CD deployment in Gitea. The runner will use its default key to pull the code flawlessly, and then silently swap to the id_deploy key to reload WSGI without hitting the Gitea trapdoor.

what about the deploy keys that we set up in Gitea GUI

That is a brilliant question. The term "Deploy Key" is actually one of the most confusing naming conventions in CI/CD because it means two completely different things depending on whether you are talking to the Gitea application or the Linux operating system.

Here is the exact difference between the "Deploy Keys" you set up in the Gitea Web UI and the raw "Deploy Pass" we just manually planted on the .50 server.

1. Gitea GUI Deploy Keys (The "Code Readers")
When you go into the Gitea Web UI, navigate to a repository's settings, and add a "Deploy Key," you are strictly granting Git-level access.

What Gitea does: Gitea takes that public key and writes it into the authorized_keys file. However, it automatically wraps that key in the Bouncer script: command="/usr/local/bin/gitea --config=/etc/gitea/app.ini serv...".

What it can do: It allows a remote machine to run git pull or git clone to securely download the code without needing a human password.

What it CANNOT do: Because it is trapped by the Bouncer, it can never execute an operating system command. It cannot run cd /app/www... and it absolutely cannot run systemctl reload wsgi.

2. Our OS-Level Deploy Pass (The "Server Admins")
The id_deploy key we manually planted at the very bottom of the /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file on the .50 server is an OS-level key.

What we did: By manually pasting it without the Gitea command="..." wrapper, we hid it from Gitea entirely.

What it can do: When the runner uses this specific key, the Linux SSH daemon sees that there is no trapdoor attached to it. It grants the runner a raw, unfiltered Linux bash shell.

What it CANNOT do: You generally wouldn't use this key to run git clone because it circumvents Gitea's internal tracking, branch protections, and repository permission mapping.

Why Your Pipeline Needs Both
To execute a true automated deployment, your .51 runner actually acts as two different employees, requiring two different badges:

The Code Fetcher: First, the runner acts like a developer. It uses its standard Gitea-managed key (or a GUI Deploy Key) to securely git pull the latest code changes. Gitea intercepts this, verifies permissions, and hands over the files.

The Systems Administrator: Second, the runner acts like a SysAdmin. It switches to the id_deploy key, SSHs back into the .50 server, bypasses Gitea completely, and executes the systemctl reload wsgi command in the raw Linux terminal to restart the application.

If you strictly relied on the Gitea GUI Deploy Keys, your pipeline would successfully pull the code, but the moment it tried to restart the web server, it would crash with that Gitea: Invalid repo name error. By keeping the Git keys in the GUI and the OS keys raw, your Dual Key architecture perfectly bridges the gap between version control and server administration.

Okay I want to Reset the GUI deploy keys again since they can't be found

Resetting the Gitea GUI Deploy Keys is a quick process, but because we just built that "Dual Key" architecture, we have to be very careful not to accidentally break our raw OS Deploy Pass while we fix the Gitea side.

When you say the GUI deploy keys "can't be found," there are two different ways this usually happens. Here is exactly how to fix both scenarios safely.

Scenario A: The Keys are in the GUI, but the Runner is Locked Out
Sometimes Gitea's database knows the keys exist (they show up in the Repository Settings), but the physical /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file got wiped or corrupted.

Instead of deleting and re-adding everything manually, Gitea has a built-in reset button to rebuild the file perfectly.

1. Rebuild the Keys via Gitea:

Log into the Gitea Web UI as a Site Administrator.

Go to Site Administration (usually via the profile dropdown in the top right).

Go to the Dashboard tab.

Scroll down to Maintenance Operations.

Find "Update the '.ssh/authorized_keys' file with Gitea SSH keys" and click Run.

(Gitea will instantly rewrite the file, putting all its Bouncer-wrapped keys back exactly where they belong).

2. The Critical Aftermath (Protecting the OS Key):
When Gitea runs that Maintenance Operation, it acts like a bulldozer—it deletes the entire authorized_keys file and writes a fresh one. This means it just deleted the raw id_deploy key we planted at the bottom of the file earlier.

You must immediately log back into the .50 server and paste your id_deploy.pub key back at the bottom of /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys so your systemctl reload step doesn't break!

Scenario B: The Keys are Completely Missing from the GUI
If the Deploy Keys were accidentally deleted from the Web UI entirely, we just need to re-add the runner's standard identity back into Gitea.

1. Grab the Runner's Standard Key (On the .51 Backup VM):
We want the standard Gitea key, NOT the deployment key we made earlier. Run this command to print the default identity:

Bash
sudo -u git cat /home/git/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Copy that string.

2. Add it to the Repository (In the Gitea GUI):

Open your specific repository in the Gitea Web UI (e.g., Transport_Toolbox).

Go to Settings -> Deploy Keys.

Click Add Deploy Key.

Title: Name it something obvious (e.g., "Runner 51 Pull Key").

Content: Paste the standard key you just copied.

Leave "Enable Write Access" unchecked (runners should only pull code, not push it).

Click Add Deploy Key.

As soon as you click add, Gitea will automatically wrap that key in its Bouncer script and drop it into the authorized_keys file. Your .51 runner will instantly regain the ability to git pull the code, and because you didn't run the bulldozer reset, your manual id_deploy key sitting at the bottom of the file is perfectly safe!

Everything is working yet those two keys has no existence

This is a classic "Ghost in the Machine" scenario with Gitea, and it is a very common source of confusion.

If your pipelines are successfully pulling code, and the screenshot shows those keys were Last used on Jun 4, 2026 (which is today), those keys absolutely do exist and the system is perfectly healthy. You do not need to fix or reset anything.

The reason you cannot find them is because of how modern Gitea handles SSH authentication behind the scenes. Here is exactly what is happening.

The Illusion of the File
When you say they "have no existence," I assume you are opening /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys and manually looking for the names act-runner-51 or the SHA256 string.

You won't necessarily see them there for two reasons:

1. Gitea obfuscates the file:
When Gitea writes a key to the authorized_keys file, it doesn't always use the friendly name you gave it in the GUI. It wraps the raw cryptographic string in that massive command="/usr/local/bin/gitea..." interceptor script. If you are just skimming the file, the keys blend into a giant wall of base64 text.

2. The Database Bypass (AuthorizedKeysCommand):
In many enterprise setups, Gitea doesn't even use the authorized_keys file for its GUI keys anymore! Instead, the Linux SSH daemon is configured to look directly into the MySQL Database every time a connection comes in.

SSH says: "A runner is knocking. Do you know this key?"

Gitea queries the database, sees the act-runner-51 key, and says: "Yes, let them in."

The flat text file is completely bypassed for Git operations.

How to Prove They Exist
If you want to pull back the curtain and see exactly what the Linux SSH daemon sees when it looks for those keys, run this command on your .50 Main Server:

Bash
sudo -u git /usr/local/bin/gitea keys -e git -u git -t ssh-ed25519 -k "YOUR_RUNNER_PUBLIC_KEY_STRING"
(Note: Your Gitea binary path might be slightly different).

This command forces Gitea to dump the exact key mapping it has stored in its internal database.

The Bottom Line
As long as the "Last used" date in that GUI is updating and your CI/CD pipeline is turning green, do not touch those GUI keys. Gitea is managing them perfectly in the background.

Just ensure that your single, raw, OS-level id_deploy key (the one we created manually for the systemctl reload step) is safely sitting at the bottom of the physical /home/git/.ssh/authorized_keys file. Gitea handles the code pulling; your raw key handles the server deployment!

Okay remind how did we set it up before make sure to use the exact same steps

If you want to completely wipe the slate clean and rebuild those exact GUI Deploy Keys (act-runner-51 and act-runner-50) from absolute scratch to ensure the system is perfectly mapped, here is the exact, step-by-step protocol to recreate them.

This will re-establish the "Code Fetcher" identities for both of your runners so Gitea recognizes them natively.

Phase 1: Rebuild the Backup Runner (act-runner-51)
First, we need to grab the standard Git identity from your .51 backup machine.

1. Retrieve the Runner's Key
Log into your .51 Backup VM and print the standard git user's public key:

Bash
sudo -u git cat /home/git/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
(Note: If the system says "No such file or directory," it means the key was deleted. You can generate a fresh one by running: sudo -u git ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f /home/git/.ssh/id_ed25519 and then hitting Enter to accept the empty passphrases, then print it again).

Copy that entire ssh-ed25519 ... string to your clipboard.

2. Plant it in the Gitea GUI

Open your Gitea Web UI and navigate to the Transport_Toolbox repository.

Go to Settings -> Deploy Keys.

Click the blue Add Deploy Key button.

Title: act-runner-51

Content: Paste the public key you just copied.

Leave "Enable Write Access" UNCHECKED. (Runners should strictly pull code, never push).

Click Add Deploy Key.

Phase 2: Rebuild the Main Runner (act-runner-50)
Now we do the exact same process for your .50 main machine so its local runner has the same permissions.

1. Retrieve the Runner's Key
Log into your .50 Main VM and print its git user's standard public key:

Bash
sudo -u git cat /home/git/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
Copy this string to your clipboard.

2. Plant it in the Gitea GUI

Go back to the Deploy Keys page in the Gitea GUI.

Click Add Deploy Key.

Title: act-runner-50

Content: Paste the .50 public key.

Leave "Enable Write Access" UNCHECKED.

Click Add Deploy Key.

Phase 3: The Initial Handshake (Crucial)
Whenever you reset keys, you must clear the network's known_hosts warning, or the automated pipeline will freeze waiting for a human to type "yes".

Run this test from both the .51 VM and the .50 VM:

Bash
sudo -u git ssh -T git@transport-toolbox.internal.eg.vodafone.com
(If you use the direct IP in your clone URLs, use git@10.30.121.50 instead).

The terminal will ask: "Are you sure you want to continue connecting?"

Type yes and press Enter.

You should receive a message saying: "Hi there, You've successfully authenticated, but Gitea does not provide shell access."

That specific message is the ultimate green light. It means Gitea's database successfully recognized the GUI Deploy Keys, intercepted the connection perfectly, and your runners are officially cleared to pull code again!
